akrotiri-village-evacuation.summary: 1996 Khalid Sheikh Mohammed–planned operation, prepared in a Manila, Philippines apartment, to hijack as many as fourteen Boeing 747s and crash them into buildings along the U.S. West Coast; disrupted only by accident, when a cleaning lady let herself into the apartment while the planner was out, recognized the materials laid out as a terrorist plot, and called the police — who alerted Filipino intelligence and, in turn, the CIA. The plot's architect was known to U.S. intelligence for the next six years only by the alias "Mukhtar," his true identity as Khalid Sheikh Mohammed surfacing only when Abu Zubaydah named him to FBI agent Ali Soufan in 2002.

akrotiri-village-evacuation.title: CIA–FBI interagency rivalry and 9/11
akrotiri-village-evacuation.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the historical CIA–FBI rivalry, dating to J. Edgar Hoover's opposition to the 1947 National Security Act, and how it manifested before September 11 when Cofer Black's Counterterrorism Center withheld from the FBI that hijackers Nawaf al-Hazmi and Khalid al-Mihdhar had been granted U.S. visas.

akrotiri-village-evacuation.title: Founding of the CIA (1947)
akrotiri-village-evacuation.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the CIA's creation under the National Security Act of 1947 — built with British MI6 help after a chaotic 1945-47 interregnum, and opposed by J. Edgar Hoover until Truman falsely promised him the new agency would be part of the FBI.

akrotiri-village-evacuation.title: US Military Venture Capital
akrotiri-village-evacuation.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the U.S. military now purchases technology using a venture-capital investment model, a shift he cites as a warning sign about how national-security institutions acquire emerging tech.

al-qaeda-software.title: Kiriakou's transfer to the Directorate of Operations
al-qaeda-software.summary: John Kiriakou's roughly two-month internal campaign to transfer from the CIA's analytic Directorate of Intelligence to the operational Directorate of Operations, overcoming what he calls a "natural bias in operations against the eggheads on the analytic side," followed by an Athens posting secured because he was the only person in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic. Covers his full CIA career arc from 1988/1990 recruitment through analyst years on Iraq, the switch to operations, 9/11, the enhanced-interrogation refusal, executive assistant to the deputy director for operations, and his eventual resignation and post-CIA career.

al-qaeda-software.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
al-qaeda-software.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

al-qaeda-software.title: Mitchell and Jessen
al-qaeda-software.summary: The two American psychologists who pitched the CIA's enhanced interrogation program to Director George Tenet at a cocktail party in late October 2001; designers of the program and its theoretical underpinning, "learned helplessness."

al-qaeda-software.title: Zawahiri assassination
al-qaeda-software.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the drone strike that killed al-Qaeda's Ayman al-Zawahiri — using a bladed, warhead-less missile fired as he stepped onto a balcony to smoke, deliberately chosen to avoid killing the women and children inside.

al-qaeda-software.title: Alfreda Bikowsky
al-qaeda-software.summary: Senior CIA officer who headed Alec Station and, before that, served as its chief of operations, overseeing the CIA's torture program; per John Kiriakou, "bad news from the get-go," and part of a failed attempt with Rich Blee to turn a San Diego al-Qaeda cell into double agents.

al-qaeda-software.title: Zbigniew Brzezinski
al-qaeda-software.summary: Kiriakou links Brzezinski to the Analysis Corporation, and notes he once voted for the communist presidential candidate Gus Hall.

al-qaeda-training-manual-interrogation-t.title: Djibouti
al-qaeda-training-manual-interrogation-t.summary: John Kiriakou's observations on Djibouti — Camp Lemonnier, once split by a fence between an American and a French base, now divided between an American side and a Chinese side; and the country's tiny intelligence service, whose entire director's office, Kiriakou says, was smaller than his own rental townhouse living room.

al-qaeda-training-manual-interrogation-t.title: CIA and the UFO question
al-qaeda-training-manual-interrogation-t.summary: John Kiriakou's consistent answer that UFOs and alien technology are a Pentagon matter, not a CIA one — though he says nearly every former fighter-pilot friend of his has seen something inexplicable, sometimes emerging from the ocean.

al-qaeda-training-manual-interrogation-t.title: Guantanamo Bay
al-qaeda-training-manual-interrogation-t.summary: U.S. naval base in Cuba; site of CIA detention operations during the post-9/11 enhanced interrogation program; briefly served by John Kiriakou as interim Chief during the summer of 2002.

al-qaeda-training-manual-interrogation-t.title: Irish intelligence services
al-qaeda-training-manual-interrogation-t.summary: Ireland's intelligence and law-enforcement services, which John Kiriakou toured and met with during a speaking trip to Belfast, Cork, Dublin, and Waterford. Per Kiriakou, Irish intelligence and the Garda are especially strong at anti-money-laundering investigation and counterterrorism — the latter traced, he says, to the large number of Irish militants trained by Carlos the Jackal in Libya and Lebanon during the 1970s.

al-qaeda-training-manual-interrogation-t.title: Joby Warrick's Washington Post resignation
al-qaeda-training-manual-interrogation-t.summary: John Kiriakou's account of his friend Joby Warrick, a multiple Pulitzer Prize-winning investigative journalist, resigning from the Washington Post because investigative journalism at the paper was dead — amid an 80% staff reduction since Jeff Bezos bought the paper.

al-qaeda-training-manual-interrogation-t.title: Strait of Hormuz transit fees
al-qaeda-training-manual-interrogation-t.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Iran's proposal to charge ships up to $2 million to transit the Strait of Hormuz, payable in yuan rather than dollars, and of the U.S. Navy's subsequent announcement that it had taken control of the strait and closed it — reversing decades of U.S. policy that the strait must remain open.

alan-dershowitz.title: Piers Morgan
alan-dershowitz.summary: British broadcaster whose panel show became John Kiriakou's 2025 sparring ring — "the equivalent of a WWE Smackdown with Alan Dershowitz<Cite s="2026-06-27-deep-focus-report-john-kiriakou-on-iran-endless-wars-and-u-s-fo" t="9:18" />." Paired with Scott Horton against Dershowitz and former Mossad chief Moshe Yaalon, Kiriakou said on air that Israel spies on the United States and that Jeffrey Epstein was an Israeli access agent, drawing a chuckle from the general and the claim that spying stopped when Pollard was caught — "General, with all due respect, that's just simply not true." Morgan's producer had to instruct the polite ex-spy not to be afraid to interrupt.

alan-dershowitz.title: Kiriakou prison manipulation tactics
alan-dershowitz.summary: John Kiriakou's account of applying CIA tradecraft — including deliberate deception, forged paperwork, and manipulating other inmates into violence — to protect himself and control his environment during his federal prison sentence.

alan-dershowitz.title: Ross Ulbricht
alan-dershowitz.summary: Founder of the online marketplace Silk Road, sentenced to life plus 75 years before being pardoned by President Trump; John Kiriakou met Ulbricht's mother and sister two weeks before the pardon and calls the length of the original sentence a sickening miscarriage of justice.

alan-dershowitz.title: Abraham Bolden
alan-dershowitz.summary: The first African-American Secret Service agent assigned to a presidential detail; per John Kiriakou, he quite literally saved John F. Kennedy's life in Chicago in October 1963 and was subjected to overt racism by fellow agents, who told him to his face they would not protect Kennedy from assassination because of his civil-rights sympathies.

alan-dershowitz.title: David Ransom
alan-dershowitz.summary: U.S. Ambassador to Bahrain during the period of John Kiriakou's posting there; characterized by Kiriakou as one of the finest people he worked for in his CIA career

alan-dershowitz.title: Rhodes Jewish deportation and family rescue story
alan-dershowitz.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the 1944 Nazi roundup and deportation of roughly 2,000 Jewish residents of the island of Rhodes to Auschwitz, of whom only 14 survived — and of his own great-grandfather, a chauffeur, hiding his Jewish employer from the Nazis until the war's end.

albert-stubblebine.title: Lynn Buchanan
albert-stubblebine.summary: A Fort Meade-trained Army intelligence veteran of the CIA and NSA remote-viewing programs — a primary source, Kiriakou says, not a TV psychic.

albert-stubblebine.title: Russell Targ
albert-stubblebine.summary: Named in a post-produced narration segment appended to an interview featuring John Kiriakou, describing Targ as an original Stanford Research Institute scientist behind government remote-viewing protocols — not a claim made by Kiriakou himself, who elsewhere expresses skepticism that remote viewing ever worked.

albert-stubblebine.title: Project Stargate
albert-stubblebine.summary: The CIA's remote-viewing program, which Kiriakou says burned millions for decades and failed — and which he understands is being revisited.

albert-stubblebine.title: Bay Path University
albert-stubblebine.summary: Per John Kiriakou, he teaches in the graduate intelligence-studies program at Bay Path University in Massachusetts, covering introduction to intelligence, the history of terrorism, and intelligence and cybersecurity.

albert-stubblebine.title: Sweat Lodge
albert-stubblebine.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the federal prison where he was incarcerated had a Native American sweat lodge that was shut down after it was misused for sex rather than religious ceremony; he says he has never personally been in a sweat lodge.

albert-stubblebine.title: Mark Zuckerberg–Angela Merkel Meeting
albert-stubblebine.summary: Kiriakou on Zuckerberg flying to Berlin to help Chancellor Merkel define hate speech — and why he objects to that call being Zuckerberg's.

aldrich-ames.title: James Woolsey
aldrich-ames.summary: Director of Central Intelligence for twenty-three months at the start of the Clinton administration, forced out over his refusal to discipline anyone after the exposure of Aldrich Ames, and later chairman of Booz Allen Hamilton; John Kiriakou notes that his family attributed four years of illness before his death to Havana syndrome.

aldrich-ames.title: Jennings Randolph
aldrich-ames.summary: Longtime U.S. Senator from West Virginia who, in a phone call John Kiriakou made to thank him as a college student, gave him the advice he says shaped his life: always do the right thing, not the expedient one.

aldrich-ames.title: Saudi nuclear program
aldrich-ames.summary: Saudi Arabia's decades-long pursuit of uranium enrichment, nominally for nuclear power, which John Kiriakou notes was already old news when he arrived at the CIA in 1990 and which conventional wisdom has always read as a weapons programme.

aldrich-ames.title: Sandy Grimes
aldrich-ames.summary: CIA analyst who, per John Kiriakou, was the person who actually broke the Aldrich Ames case. After a 27-year-old security officer sat on an Ames file for eighteen months without action, Grimes independently noticed that Ames made $100,000–$150,000 bank deposits within days of every trip to Mexico City — the pattern that identified him as a spy. After Ames's arrest, she submitted a hot-wash paper recommending 27 reprimands across the chain of command that had promoted a known alcoholic into the most sensitive counterintelligence position in the CIA. Director John Deutch responded with strongly worded letters for seven. Grimes resigned in 1993.

aldrich-ames.title: Steven Lalas
aldrich-ames.summary: American with top-secret clearance recruited as a spy for Greece's National Intelligence Service (EYP) in a provocative mid-1990s operation run by the country's conservative government. Per John Kiriakou, who did not know Lawless personally, the case was so sensitive that his handler reported directly to the EYP director out of fear the CIA had planted a mole inside the service. Lawless was caught, served about seven years, and was given Greek citizenship on release.

aldrich-ames.title: How Can I Keep from Singing
aldrich-ames.summary: Biography of folk singer Pete Seeger and John Kiriakou's stated favorite book. Per Kiriakou, Seeger was the most important man in his life besides his father and grandfather; the two exchanged Christmas cards for years, and Seeger rallied publicly to Kiriakou's defense during his prosecution. Kiriakou identifies Seeger's 1958 defiance of HUAC — pleading the First Amendment rather than the Fifth and going to prison for it — as the model for how he wanted to live his own life.

alec-baldwin.title: Abu Omar rendition
alec-baldwin.summary: The CIA's kidnapping of a Milan cleric, Abu Omar, who was sent to Egypt to be tortured; the case is what ultimately sent John Kiriakou to prison, after he confirmed a former colleague's surname to a journalist writing a book about it.

alec-baldwin.title: CIA animal surveillance experiments
alec-baldwin.summary: Cold-War CIA efforts to turn animals into listening devices, which John Kiriakou describes as failures — including microphones and cameras mounted on pigeons trained to land on the Soviet embassy, which could reach the compound but never captured anything meaningful.

alec-baldwin.title: Citizens United
alec-baldwin.summary: The Supreme Court decision John Kiriakou blames for legalizing unlimited corporate political money — which he says lets AIPAC pour tens of millions into single congressional races to defeat candidates who cross Israel.

alec-baldwin.title: Havana Syndrome
alec-baldwin.summary: Cluster of neurological symptoms — including nausea, ringing in the ears, vertigo, and traumatic brain injury — reported by American diplomatic and intelligence personnel beginning in Havana, Cuba, and subsequently at posts around the world. Per John Kiriakou, his initial skepticism gave way when a friend developed Havana Syndrome with an MRI-confirmed traumatic brain injury after a meeting outside the Russian Foreign Ministry; Kiriakou attributes the syndrome to Russian or Chinese directed-energy weapons and acknowledges the United States used a similar weapon during the operation to capture Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro.

alec-baldwin.title: MK-Ultra
alec-baldwin.summary: The CIA's mid-twentieth-century umbrella program of mind-control, behavioral-modification, and biological-warfare experimentation, encompassing subprojects such as MK-Chickwit and MK-Seesaw; active 1952–1975; documented practices included LSD dosing of unwitting American citizens in CIA-rented brothels and the aerosolized release of pathogens into the San Francisco fog; 80% of the program's documentation was destroyed by the CIA in defiance of a 1975 preservation order from Senator Frank Church.

alec-baldwin.title: Jennings Randolph
alec-baldwin.summary: Longtime U.S. Senator from West Virginia who, in a phone call John Kiriakou made to thank him as a college student, gave him the advice he says shaped his life: always do the right thing, not the expedient one.

alex-karp.title: In-Q-Tel
alex-karp.summary: The CIA's openly acknowledged venture capital arm; provided Palantir Technologies its first $1.5 million in seed funding; in John Kiriakou's account the principal vehicle by which the agency finances private-sector development of technologies it intends to use.

alex-karp.title: Palantir Technologies
alex-karp.summary: U.S. data-analytics and intelligence-software company; received its first $1.5 million in seed funding from the CIA's In-Q-Tel venture-capital arm around 2002; characterized by John Kiriakou as functionally inseparable from the CIA in 2025, drawing the majority of its revenue from agency contracts and operating across DARPA, NSA, and the broader U.S. national-security apparatus.

alex-karp.title: Peter Thiel
alex-karp.summary: U.S. venture capitalist; co-founder of Palantir Technologies; subject of a biographical assessment commissioned from John Kiriakou by an unnamed interest group alongside Palantir CEO Alex Karp.

alex-karp.title: Arrais Corporation
alex-karp.summary: Private intelligence firm; companion entity to The Analysis Corporation; originally an LLC pass-through for retired Senior Intelligence Service personnel from the CIA's operations side; subsequently acquired by IBM for over $1 billion.

alex-karp.title: CIA National Resources Division
alex-karp.summary: The Central Intelligence Agency's domestic intelligence-collection arm, created in the 1980s by Director William J. Casey

alex-karp.title: Balochistan drone base
alex-karp.summary: Secret CIA drone surveillance base in southwestern Pakistan's Balochistan region; its location was inadvertently disclosed when investigative journalist Jason Leopold filed a Freedom of Information Act request for Pentagon aviation-fuel-delivery records and identified an outsized fuel flow to the otherwise-undocumented base.

alex-padilla.title: AIPAC
alex-padilla.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

alex-padilla.title: Donald Trump
alex-padilla.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

alex-padilla.title: Giuliani Pardon Solicitation
alex-padilla.summary: Per John Kiriakou, a meeting at the Trump International Hotel in Washington in which Rudy Giuliani's associate solicited $2 million in exchange for a presidential pardon — a story that subsequently appeared as a front-page New York Times article. Giuliani publicly denied ever meeting Kiriakou; Kiriakou sent the Times the photograph taken at the meeting that morning, and the paper published the story with the note that it had seen documentary proof.

alex-padilla.title: Iran 12-Day War
alex-padilla.summary: 2025 Israeli air campaign against Iran during which Israel killed at least fourteen Iranian nuclear scientists by destroying the apartment buildings they lived in; preceded for each scientist by Farsi-language telephone calls from Iranian-Jewish Mossad and Shin Bet officers offering defection in lieu of certain death; characterized by John Kiriakou as a categorical departure from CIA targeting doctrine in its acceptable-civilian-casualty calculus.

alex-padilla.title: Iran Nuclear Assessment
alex-padilla.summary: Per John Kiriakou's assessment, the US–Israeli military campaign against Iran was a war of choice driven by Israeli political pressure rather than genuine intelligence indicating an Iranian nuclear weapons threat. The CIA produced two National Intelligence Estimates concluding Iran had no nuclear weapons program; Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei issued a fatwa in the 1980s forbidding such a program. The U.S. went to war anyway, in Kiriakou's view, after President Trump replaced the Joint Chiefs of Staff with officers willing to accept Israeli intelligence and proceed.

alex-padilla.title: Israel-United States relations
alex-padilla.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the U.S.-Israel relationship, including his own first visit to Israel as a tourist in 2022 and his characterization of Israel's willingness to destroy an entire city block to kill a single target, confident that the United States will not object.

alex-station.title: Ali Mohamed
alex-station.summary: Egyptian-American former U.S. Army sergeant who trained at Fort Bragg while secretly working for Egyptian intelligence, later trained some of the 9/11 hijackers and other al-Qaeda operatives, and was arrested in connection with the 1998 U.S. embassy bombings before disappearing under the George W. Bush administration; John Kiriakou speculates he was actually a double agent working for al-Qaeda — or possibly Israeli intelligence — against his CIA handlers.

alex-station.title: Cofer Black
alex-station.summary: Former head of the CIA Counterterrorism Center during and immediately after the September 11 attacks; principal architect of the agency's paramilitary turn on September 12, 2001; later Vice President of Blackwater under Erik Prince.

alex-station.title: 9/11 attribution of responsibility
alex-station.summary: John Kiriakou's evolving view of who bears ultimate responsibility for the September 11 attacks — that al-Qaeda carried them out but was, in his current view, "allowed" to, amid a distracted Bush administration, an uninvestigated Saudi government, and an Israeli government he believes had a vested interest in the attacks proceeding.

alex-station.title: Mir Aimal Kansi CIA headquarters attack
alex-station.summary: The 1993 shooting outside CIA headquarters by Pakistani gunman Mir Aimal Kansi, who killed two and wounded seven CIA-bound commuters before fleeing to Pakistan; per John Kiriakou, the CIA located Kansi months later but had to hand the arrest to the FBI, and the resulting "how the FBI got their man" Time magazine cover so enraged senior CIA officers that it shaped the agency's insistence on going it alone against al-Qaeda after 9/11.

alex-station.title: Sandy Berger
alex-station.summary: National Security Adviser under President Bill Clinton; per John Kiriakou, the official who shut down CIA case officer Bob Baer's mid-1990s plan to assassinate Saddam Hussein from northern Iraq, by calling the CIA after an NSA intercept and threatening Baer with a conspiracy charge unless he was recalled.

alex-station.title: Operation Mega
alex-station.summary: A 1997 FBI investigation into a senior U.S. government official believed to be passing highly sensitive information to Israel, opened after the NSA intercepted an Israeli intelligence communication referring to a source code-named "Mega." Per John Kiriakou, unlike similar investigations into other countries, the case never resulted in an indictment or public disclosure, and the identity of the American official was never revealed.

alexa.title: Central Intelligence Agency
alexa.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

alexa.title: FISA
alexa.summary: The Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act, the U.S. legal framework governing surveillance warrants for foreign-intelligence purposes. Per John Kiriakou, FISA is dangerously easy to abuse — he cites Carter Page, whose life was ruined and who was driven into bankruptcy after the Steele dossier was used to support four FISA applications against him. Kiriakou groups FISA with the Patriot Act and Section 702 as the legal architecture stripping Americans of constitutional protections, opposed by only a handful of legislators.

alexa.title: John Kiriakou
alexa.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

alexa.title: Patriot Act
alexa.summary: U.S. law passed after the September 11 attacks that vastly expanded domestic surveillance authority. Per John Kiriakou, the Patriot Act ''opened up everything'' — and he disputes the common belief that 9/11 was required to pass it: ''You underestimate Congress. They didn''t need a catastrophe — they would just pass it because they can.'' He ties it to NSA bulk-collection programs that vacuum up every phone call, text, email, and piece of metadata from Americans, in violation of the NSA''s own charter.

alexa.title: Revolutionary Organization 17 November
alexa.summary: Greek far-left urban guerrilla group active 1975–2002; the deadliest terrorist organization in Greek history

alexa.title: NSA
alexa.summary: Kiriakou on the agency whose Utah facility boasts room to store every American's calls, texts and emails for the next 500 years.

alfreda-bikowsky.title: Mike Scheuer
alfreda-bikowsky.summary: Founder and chief of "Alec Station", the CIA unit dedicated to tracking Osama bin Laden in the years before September 11, 2001; per John Kiriakou — alongside his New York FBI counterpart John O'Neill — "100 percent correct" about bin Laden, and uniformly hated for it inside the agency.

alfreda-bikowsky.title: Al Qaeda Software
alfreda-bikowsky.summary: A claim raised on a Kiriakou-appearance podcast that "Al-Qaeda" is also the name of a terrorist-tracking software, alongside its use as the name of the terrorist organization.

alfreda-bikowsky.title: Ali Soufan
alfreda-bikowsky.summary: FBI special agent who handled Abu Zubaydah immediately after his March 2002 capture; through patient, respectful interrogation produced the only actionable intelligence ever obtained from the detainee, including the first identification of "Mukhtar" as Khalid Sheikh Mohammed.

alfreda-bikowsky.title: CIA–FBI interagency rivalry and 9/11
alfreda-bikowsky.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the historical CIA–FBI rivalry, dating to J. Edgar Hoover's opposition to the 1947 National Security Act, and how it manifested before September 11 when Cofer Black's Counterterrorism Center withheld from the FBI that hijackers Nawaf al-Hazmi and Khalid al-Mihdhar had been granted U.S. visas.

alfreda-bikowsky.title: Giuliani Pardon Solicitation
alfreda-bikowsky.summary: Per John Kiriakou, a meeting at the Trump International Hotel in Washington in which Rudy Giuliani's associate solicited $2 million in exchange for a presidential pardon — a story that subsequently appeared as a front-page New York Times article. Giuliani publicly denied ever meeting Kiriakou; Kiriakou sent the Times the photograph taken at the meeting that morning, and the paper published the story with the note that it had seen documentary proof.

alfreda-bikowsky.title: Hezbollah
alfreda-bikowsky.summary: Lebanese Shia militant organization and political party. Per John Kiriakou, Israel''s strategic goal regarding Hezbollah is not to defeat it outright but to keep Lebanon in a state of chaos that serves Israeli interests. He cites two Israeli operations: the simultaneous pager-detonation attack that decapitated Hezbollah''s leadership, which he called ''the most incredible operation I''ve ever seen,'' and the strike that killed former leader Hassan Nasrallah by leveling an entire complex and killing roughly 300 people — which he characterized as a war crime.

ali-abdullah-saleh.title: Houthis
ali-abdullah-saleh.summary: The Iran-aligned movement that controls the most important parts of Yemen, described by John Kiriakou as fierce fighters who beat the Saudi military over a decade of war and who in July 2026 declared a naval blockade of Saudi shipping.

ali-abdullah-saleh.title: Yemen
ali-abdullah-saleh.summary: Country on the southern Arabian Peninsula; setting of five John Kiriakou trips between 1990 and approximately 2010, spanning the country's brief unification, its civil war, and its present condition as a high-threat operating environment for U.S. and allied diplomatic personnel.

ali-abdullah-saleh.title: Bab al-Mandab
ali-abdullah-saleh.summary: The strait where the Horn of Africa nearly meets the south-western tip of the Arabian Peninsula, which John Kiriakou identifies as one of the few American national interests in Yemen and as a chokepoint whose closure would push the global economy into recession.

ali-abdullah-saleh.title: John Kiriakou
ali-abdullah-saleh.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

ali-abdullah-saleh.title: Dead Drop (podcast)
ali-abdullah-saleh.summary: John Kiriakou''s narrative podcast, launched in late 2025 — a season-long, memoir-style retelling of his life in intelligence, from recruitment ("The New Recruit") through Athens ("Golden Boy") to the post-9/11 hunt ("The Hunt Begins"), with mini-episodes like "A Spy''s Guide to Sofia." Written by Kiriakou with Alan Katz, produced by Costard & Touchstone Productions, with Kiriakou, Katz, and Nick Mechanic as executive producers. Its stated goal: "the deepest possible perspective on the world of spying and what makes any spy tick."

ali-abdullah-saleh.title: Saudi nuclear program
ali-abdullah-saleh.summary: Saudi Arabia's decades-long pursuit of uranium enrichment, nominally for nuclear power, which John Kiriakou notes was already old news when he arrived at the CIA in 1990 and which conventional wisdom has always read as a weapons programme.

ali-hassan-al-majid.title: Saddam Hussein
ali-hassan-al-majid.summary: President of Iraq from 1979 until the 2003 U.S. invasion; subject of John Kiriakou's CIA portfolio from January 1990 onward, in which capacity Kiriakou became, at age 25, "Saddam Hussein's intelligence community biographer" and the analyst who briefed President George H. W. Bush in the Oval Office on the morning of the 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

ali-hassan-al-majid.title: Ahmed Chalabi
ali-hassan-al-majid.summary: Iraqi exile and founder of the Iraqi National Congress; per John Kiriakou, a Shia-Kurdish con man who looted Petra Bank in Jordan of $36 million in the 1980s, was sentenced to death in absentia, was pardoned at CIA request, then pocketed $6 million in CIA seed funding for the INC and bought a Mayfair house in cash; later resurrected by Dick Cheney to feed the Pentagon fabricated WMD intelligence used to justify the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

ali-hassan-al-majid.title: Iraqi invasion of Kuwait
ali-hassan-al-majid.summary: John Kiriakou''s most detailed account of the intelligence process around the 1990 Iraqi invasion of Kuwait and its 1991 liberation. As a first-year CIA analyst on a ''training account'' covering Iraq, Kiriakou produced the June 30, 1990 warning paper for the White House; suggested calling the US Defense Attaché in Baghdad to drive to the border and report what he saw (the answer: ''Literally the entire Iraqi military is heading south''); briefed the August 2 Oval Office meeting with Bush; and later took a single phone call from General Colin Powell that led, eight hours later, to 47 cruise missiles striking the Iraqi Intelligence Service headquarters in Baghdad.

ali-hassan-al-majid.title: Uday Hussein
ali-hassan-al-majid.summary: Eldest son of Saddam Hussein; described by John Kiriakou as so dangerous a successor-in-waiting that Saddam's two sons-in-law — Hussein Kamel and Saddam Kamel — defected to Jordan in January 1993 specifically out of fear of him.

ali-hassan-al-majid.title: Petra Bank
ali-hassan-al-majid.summary: Jordan-based bank founded by Ahmed Chalabi and used by the Iraqi refugee community in Jordan; per John Kiriakou, looted of $36 million in a single night when Chalabi transferred every dollar to secret Swiss accounts and fled to Syria in the trunk of his secretary / girlfriend's car. Chalabi was tried and sentenced to death in absentia, then later pardoned at CIA request.

ali-hassan-al-majid.title: William Webster
ali-hassan-al-majid.summary: Director of Central Intelligence during the 1990 invasion of Kuwait; the only person to have served as both Director of the FBI and Director of the CIA; per John Kiriakou, "a lovely man … just a very kind, nice man" — and a "giant" to whom Kiriakou first briefed at 4 a.m. during the invasion task force, with fifteen minutes' warning.

ali-mohamed.title: Alex Station
ali-mohamed.summary: CIA unit that tracked Osama bin Laden beginning in 1995; per John Kiriakou, who served as chief of its counterintelligence branch, the unit kept extremely tight security around its files, limited FBI investigators' access to information about future 9/11 hijackers Khaled al-Mihdhar and Nawaf al-Hazmi, and — under a deliberate policy of non-cooperation with the FBI — failed to watchlist participants in the Malaysia summit where al-Qaeda planned the attacks.

ali-mohamed.title: 9/11 attribution of responsibility
ali-mohamed.summary: John Kiriakou's evolving view of who bears ultimate responsibility for the September 11 attacks — that al-Qaeda carried them out but was, in his current view, "allowed" to, amid a distracted Bush administration, an uninvestigated Saudi government, and an Israeli government he believes had a vested interest in the attacks proceeding.

ali-mohamed.title: Cofer Black
ali-mohamed.summary: Former head of the CIA Counterterrorism Center during and immediately after the September 11 attacks; principal architect of the agency's paramilitary turn on September 12, 2001; later Vice President of Blackwater under Erik Prince.

ali-mohamed.title: Charlie Kirk shooting
ali-mohamed.summary: Kiriakou questions the official account: a court filing says the ATF could not match the autopsy bullet to the rifle tied to the suspect.

ali-mohamed.title: CIA liaison relationships
ali-mohamed.summary: John Kiriakou's critique of CIA intelligence-liaison relationships with foreign governments — sharply expanded after 9/11 — arguing that officers do not consider the long-term risk that disclosing sensitive operations to foreign services hands those governments leverage, including potential blackmail material, over the United States, and that no one left in Congress has the will to provide real oversight of the practice.

ali-mohamed.title: Mir Aimal Kansi CIA headquarters attack
ali-mohamed.summary: The 1993 shooting outside CIA headquarters by Pakistani gunman Mir Aimal Kansi, who killed two and wounded seven CIA-bound commuters before fleeing to Pakistan; per John Kiriakou, the CIA located Kansi months later but had to hand the arrest to the FBI, and the resulting "how the FBI got their man" Time magazine cover so enraged senior CIA officers that it shaped the agency's insistence on going it alone against al-Qaeda after 9/11.

ali-soufan.title: Brian Ross
ali-soufan.summary: American investigative journalist and seven-time Emmy Award winner who was a prominent reporter at ABC News when, in December 2007, he conducted the on-camera interview with John Kiriakou that produced the first public confirmation by a U.S. official that the CIA waterboarded prisoners. Per Kiriakou, Ross called him out of the blue with the assertion that a source said Kiriakou had personally tortured Abu Zubaydah; Kiriakou's decision to give the interview anyway — driven by the conclusion that 'Brian Ross's source is at the White House and they're going to pin this on me' — became the pivot point of his entire post-CIA life.

ali-soufan.title: James Angleton
ali-soufan.summary: Long-serving Chief of the CIA Counterintelligence Center; the figure under whose tenure — per a first-day-on-the-job anecdote relayed by an unnamed Kiriakou CIA mentor — an entire wall of CCI files at agency headquarters consisted of dossiers on American citizens, in violation of the statutory prohibition on CIA domestic surveillance.

ali-soufan.title: Sharon Scranage
ali-soufan.summary: CIA secretary stationed in Ghana in the 1980s; the only other American besides John Kiriakou to have been charged under the Intelligence Identities Protection Act of 1982; revealed the names of CIA officers and sources in Ghana to a Ghanaian intelligence-service lover during pillow talk, leading to the execution of the named sources by Ghanaian authorities; sentenced to nine months in prison.

ali-soufan.title: Khobar Towers bombing
ali-soufan.summary: June 25, 1996 truck bombing of a U.S. military housing complex in Khobar, Saudi Arabia, that killed 19 U.S. Air Force personnel. John Kiriakou, then a CIA officer living across the water in Bahrain, felt the blast shatter his own windows and drove to the scene the next morning. He says the U.S. government worked hard to blame Iran and a small Saudi Hezbollah cell with no evidence, when the attack was in fact carried out by a radical Saudi group — a predecessor of al-Qaeda, which took credit for it.

ali-soufan.title: Martha Kesler
ali-soufan.summary: Long-serving CIA Syria analyst; author of the standard-issue analytical primer "Syria: Fragile Mosaic of Power"; John Brennan''s first supervisor and the figure who first fired him from the agency, before being herself fired by Brennan when their roles inverted under George Tenet''s patronage.

ali-soufan.title: Muammar Gaddafi
ali-soufan.summary: Libya's ruler and, in John Kiriakou's telling, the cautionary tale that teaches every proliferator never to disarm. In February 2003 the CIA's Steve Kappes secretly visited Gaddafi with an ultimatum — the U.S. was about to overthrow Saddam, and Libya would meet the same fate unless it surrendered its weapons of mass destruction. Gaddafi complied — and was later overthrown and lynched anyway, "at the insistence of the United States." A bad guy, Kiriakou stresses, but one Washington had a healthy working relationship with, who hated al-Qaeda as much as America did; flipping sides to destroy him was "a terrible policy error" that left anarchy.

allen-dulles.title: United Fruit and the Arbenz coup
allen-dulles.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the 1954 CIA overthrow of Guatemala's President Arbenz after he nationalized the banana crop — engineered by the Dulles brothers, who sat on the board of the United Fruit Company, and followed by half a century of dictatorship.

allen-dulles.title: James Jesus Angleton
allen-dulles.summary: The CIA counterintelligence chief old-timers were 'genuinely afraid' of — and the wall of illegal files on American citizens kept in his office.

allen-dulles.title: Operation Paperclip
allen-dulles.summary: The program by which the CIA's predecessor brought Nazi scientists to the United States after World War II; John Kiriakou notes the FBI opposed it, that the Nazis surrendered to the U.S. fearing the Soviets, and that V-2 rocket father Wernher von Braun is buried near his home in Virginia.

allen-dulles.title: Kim Philby
allen-dulles.summary: The British MI6 deputy director secretly working for the KGB — and, in John Kiriakou's telling, James Angleton's best man and his child's godfather; his decades of betrayal broke Angleton, and he escaped from Beirut through a bathroom window to Moscow.

allen-dulles.title: Monroe Doctrine
allen-dulles.summary: John Kiriakou's history of the Monroe Doctrine — ignored for decades after 1823, humiliated in the Falklands and Venezuela, and only made real by Teddy Roosevelt in 1905 — which he sees revived today in the seizure of Maduro as a message that the hemisphere is America's.

allen-dulles.title: Presidents and the CIA
allen-dulles.summary: John Kiriakou's observation that some presidents actively lead the CIA while others are led around by it — citing George H.W. Bush's ongoing "love affair" with the agency after his 11-month stint as director, and Richard Nixon's close relationship with the CIA, which Kiriakou says was one of the things that brought down his presidency.

amaryllis-fox-kennedy.title: The botched pitch
amaryllis-fox-kennedy.summary: The one operation John Kiriakou describes as a failure of his career: a two-year development of a terrorist working under journalist cover, brought to the point of a recruitment pitch and destroyed at the table when his station chief seized the meeting and threatened the target instead of pitching him. The target fled screaming for police, the host government''s deputy prime minister complained to the American ambassador, and the man later described the encounter to a third intelligence service as an approach by "two caricatures of CIA men."

amaryllis-fox-kennedy.title: Flock cameras
amaryllis-fox-kennedy.summary: Automated licence-plate reading cameras mounted on police vehicles and on poles disguised as utility poles. John Kiriakou describes them as blanket, constant surveillance and a direct assault on civil liberties, more dangerous than the public realises, and says they are the point at which Edward Snowden's predictions have already come true.

amaryllis-fox-kennedy.title: Kiriakou on travel
amaryllis-fox-kennedy.summary: John Kiriakou''s own ranking of the countries he has visited: Greece his favourite and, he insists, the best food anywhere; Oman the most beautiful landscape; Syria the most extraordinary civilisation; and Chile the cheapest, illustrated by a bottle of a vineyard''s locked-away reserve that cost $8.50 on his honeymoon.

amaryllis-fox-kennedy.title: Sharia law
amaryllis-fox-kennedy.summary: Islamic jurisprudence. Challenged by a viewer who equated it with executions of gay people, forced child marriage and the criminalisation of apostasy, John Kiriakou answers that those acts are largely the work of ISIS rather than of any government, and that Sharia is in substance a body of civil law covering inheritance, insurance, education, property ownership and commercial disputes.

amaryllis-fox-kennedy.title: Wealth concentration
amaryllis-fox-kennedy.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the present distribution of wealth is historically unprecedented and politically unsustainable — that trillionaires have never existed before, that five men hold as much as the bottom eighty per cent of the world, and that a defence budget approaching $1.5 trillion cannot be reconciled with the social spending it would have to displace.

amaryllis-fox-kennedy.title: Seyyed Hossein Nasr
amaryllis-fox-kennedy.summary: The scholar of Islamic philosophy under whom John Kiriakou studied Shiism as an undergraduate. Kiriakou calls him probably the most important Shia Muslim scholar in the world, notes that he is the father of Vali Nasr, and remarks that at ninety-eight he is still teaching.

american-psychological-association.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
american-psychological-association.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

american-psychological-association.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
american-psychological-association.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

american-psychological-association.title: Waterboarding
american-psychological-association.summary: Torture technique in which a prisoner is restrained on an inclined board with the head lower than the feet, a cloth placed over the face, and water poured continuously over it to simulate drowning. Per John Kiriakou, waterboarding was treated as a criminal act under U.S. and international law for decades before 2002 — including a post–World War II execution of Japanese soldiers who waterboarded American POWs, and a 1968 court-martial of a U.S. soldier photographed waterboarding a North Vietnamese prisoner — before the CIA reauthorized it after September 11. Abu Zubaydah was waterboarded 83 times; Khalid Sheikh Mohammed 187 times.

american-psychological-association.title: Cold cell
american-psychological-association.summary: A CIA interrogation technique in which a stripped detainee is chained to a ceiling eyebolt in a cell chilled to 50°F, then doused with a bucket of ice water at hourly intervals; never authorized; documented to have killed at least two prisoners.

american-psychological-association.title: Osama bin Laden
american-psychological-association.summary: Founder and leader of al-Qaeda and the central target of the manhunt that shaped John Kiriakou's counterterrorism career. Per Kiriakou, bin Laden came from a billionaire Saudi construction family, was never one of the CIA-funded Afghan mujahideen, overruled subordinates who wanted to attack Israel and insisted the 9/11 attacks hit the United States to crash its economy, escaped Tora Bora dressed as a woman, and spent his final years next to Pakistan's equivalent of West Point — where, Kiriakou says, you would have to be a "mental defective" not to know he was there. Kiriakou believes the United States never intended to capture him alive.

american-psychological-association.title: Cameo
american-psychological-association.summary: The personalised-video app John Kiriakou joined in February 2026 and turned into an unexpected second career — around 2,600 videos, roughly 900 of them in his first month alone. Half are birthday messages and most of the rest are requests for CIA stories, but about two hundred have been appeals for advice or a pep talk, and three of those people later told him he had talked them out of suicide.

amnesty-international.title: Human Rights Watch
amnesty-international.summary: The organization whose 2005 report that the CIA was torturing its prisoners — two years before John Kiriakou''s ABC interview — anchors his defense that he confirmed rather than revealed the program. In his account of his own arrest, Human Rights Watch also sits inside the fateful chain of custody: when the FBI traced a classified name found in its hands, the trail ran to journalist Matthew Cole, and Cole named Kiriakou — bringing two dozen FBI agents to his door.

amnesty-international.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
amnesty-international.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

amnesty-international.title: Kiriakou's transfer to the Directorate of Operations
amnesty-international.summary: John Kiriakou's roughly two-month internal campaign to transfer from the CIA's analytic Directorate of Intelligence to the operational Directorate of Operations, overcoming what he calls a "natural bias in operations against the eggheads on the analytic side," followed by an Athens posting secured because he was the only person in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic. Covers his full CIA career arc from 1988/1990 recruitment through analyst years on Iraq, the switch to operations, 9/11, the enhanced-interrogation refusal, executive assistant to the deputy director for operations, and his eventual resignation and post-CIA career.

amnesty-international.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
amnesty-international.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

amnesty-international.title: James Bond
amnesty-international.summary: The fictional spy who got John Kiriakou — and, he says, half the Directorate of Operations — into the business. Kiriakou wanted to be Bond as a kid (walkie-talkies at nine, logs on the neighbor kids), concedes "literally none of it is true to life" (he carried a gun only in Athens and Pakistan), but vouches for one scene: Bond always runs into the CIA officer at the party, "and that happens every day in real life." Even the CIA''s venture fund In-Q-Tel, he notes, put the Q in its name as a wink to Bond''s gadget master.

amnesty-international.title: Witness K case
amnesty-international.summary: Australian intelligence scandal in which a former ASIS officer known as Witness K exposed Australia's bugging of the East Timorese cabinet during oil and gas revenue negotiations; his lawyer, Bernard Collaery, describes the ASIO raids on both their homes and offices as paralleling the FBI's raid on John Kiriakou.

analysis-corporation.title: John Brennan
analysis-corporation.summary: Former Director of the CIA; characterized in KiriPedia's source corpus as the principal architect of the agency's enhanced interrogation program and as having plotted against an elected President

analysis-corporation.title: Arrais Corporation
analysis-corporation.summary: Private intelligence firm; companion entity to The Analysis Corporation; originally an LLC pass-through for retired Senior Intelligence Service personnel from the CIA's operations side; subsequently acquired by IBM for over $1 billion.

analysis-corporation.title: Zbigniew Brzezinski
analysis-corporation.summary: Kiriakou links Brzezinski to the Analysis Corporation, and notes he once voted for the communist presidential candidate Gus Hall.

analysis-corporation.title: Central Intelligence Agency
analysis-corporation.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

analysis-corporation.title: John Kiriakou
analysis-corporation.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

analysis-corporation.title: Private Intelligence
analysis-corporation.summary: Post-CIA commercial intelligence work performed by John Kiriakou — both operational (surveillance, bribery, dossier-building for private clients) and analytical (paid forecasts for hedge funds, mutual funds, and a global mining company). Per Kiriakou, his clients ranged from a Cypriot billionaire investigating his daughter's fiancé to the ninth-largest hedge fund in the world.

andres-serrano.title: Ai Weiwei
andres-serrano.summary: Chinese contemporary artist and pro-democracy activist; designer of the Beijing Olympic Stadium; per John Kiriakou, produced a Lego portrait of him as one of 178 political prisoners in the series, with Kiriakou's panel positioned next to Martin Luther King Jr.; the work is now in the permanent collection of the Smithsonian Institution.

andres-serrano.title: Robert Hanssen
andres-serrano.summary: FBI counterintelligence chief and Soviet/Russian mole; framed CIA counterintelligence chief Brian Kelley as the source of compromised assets — leading the FBI to surveil Kelly for a year and a half and threaten his family with the death penalty — before Hanssen himself was identified as the actual traitor.

andres-serrano.title: Scholar-in-Residence program
andres-serrano.summary: The current CIA recruitment program, in operation as of the late 2020s, under which the agency places retiring senior officers as 'CIA Scholar in Residence' professors at major American universities. Per John Kiriakou, the program serves as the agency's principal university-recruitment channel since the 1993 Equal Employment Opportunity Act forbade the older practice of having professors covertly recruit students into the CIA. Officers identified as scholars in residence are openly disclosed; the recruitment work continues, just no longer in secret.

andres-serrano.title: Central Intelligence Agency
andres-serrano.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

andres-serrano.title: Tora Bora
andres-serrano.summary: Mountainous cave complex in eastern Afghanistan that served as an al-Qaeda redoubt after the September 11 attacks. Per John Kiriakou — chief of counterterrorism operations in Pakistan at the time — the CIA killed al-Qaeda military-affairs chief Mohammed Atef there in October 2001, and Tora Bora was the backdrop to the hunt for the senior al-Qaeda leadership that culminated in the capture of Abu Zubaydah. Kiriakou also recounts an Egyptian al-Qaeda fighter he later recruited who survived a cruise-missile strike on a Tora Bora cave — one of only two who came out alive, his ears bleeding, describing the explosion as the most hideous sound he had ever heard.

andres-serrano.title: Access Agent
andres-serrano.summary: CIA (and foreign intelligence service) term for a recruited asset whose value lies not in the secrets they hold directly but in their regular social access to high-value targets — politicians, executives, heads of state — who cannot themselves be recruited. Per John Kiriakou, the access agent is funded generously to maintain an environment in which the targets feel comfortable and return repeatedly; kompromat — compromising photographs or recordings — may be collected as a secondary tool. Kiriakou identifies Jeffrey Epstein as a textbook access agent, in his assessment working for Israeli intelligence.

andrew-bustamante.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
andrew-bustamante.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

andrew-bustamante.title: John Kiriakou
andrew-bustamante.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

andrew-bustamante.title: Presidents and the CIA
andrew-bustamante.summary: John Kiriakou's observation that some presidents actively lead the CIA while others are led around by it — citing George H.W. Bush's ongoing "love affair" with the agency after his 11-month stint as director, and Richard Nixon's close relationship with the CIA, which Kiriakou says was one of the things that brought down his presidency.

andrew-bustamante.title: Roy Cohn
andrew-bustamante.summary: Closeted McCarthy-era prosecutor and fixer, later a mentor, advisor and attorney to Donald Trump from the 1970s onward; per John Kiriakou, one of the darkest, ugliest figures in modern American history, who — while closely allied with a similarly closeted J. Edgar Hoover — was central to ruining the lives of gay men, and who died of AIDS in the 1980s alone and unloved.

andrew-bustamante.title: UK secrecy laws
andrew-bustamante.summary: John Kiriakou's view that Britain is even harsher on whistleblowers and dissent than the United States, using the Official Secrets Act and Terrorism Act to stop people at airports and threaten arrest merely for supporting Palestinian rights.

andrew-bustamante.title: Wealth concentration
andrew-bustamante.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the present distribution of wealth is historically unprecedented and politically unsustainable — that trillionaires have never existed before, that five men hold as much as the bottom eighty per cent of the world, and that a defence budget approaching $1.5 trillion cannot be reconciled with the social spending it would have to displace.

andrew-feinstein.title: Meredith Whittaker
andrew-feinstein.summary: Per John Kiriakou, Meredith Whittaker is developing a new, and by his account successful, business model for the encrypted-messaging app Signal, an alternative he cites alongside ProtonMail's compromised attempt at the same thing.

andrew-feinstein.title: Ai Whistleblower Initiative
andrew-feinstein.summary: The AI Whistleblower Initiative, working on legal protections for the wave of whistleblowers now coming out of the artificial-intelligence industry.

andrew-feinstein.title: Belmarsh Prison
andrew-feinstein.summary: The London prison where Julian Assange was held — one more stage, Kiriakou notes, in a life spent almost entirely in some form of confinement.

andrew-feinstein.title: Ethan Mccord Collateral Murder
andrew-feinstein.summary: The US soldier who carried wounded children out of the street in the Collateral Murder video released by WikiLeaks.

andrew-feinstein.title: Plus 972
andrew-feinstein.summary: The Israeli platform that, per a 2026 Berlin panel, has published a striking number of IDF whistleblowers as AI enters modern warfare.

andrew-feinstein.title: Securedrop
andrew-feinstein.summary: The encrypted submission tool pioneered by WikiLeaks to let sources hand over documents without exposing themselves.

andrew-warren.title: Mary Margaret Graham
andrew-warren.summary: CIA Senior Intelligence Service officer and later Deputy Director of National Intelligence for Collection under John Negroponte — described by John Kiriakou as a career "reports officer" who had never personally recruited a source, and as his difficult chief of station in a later domestic assignment.

andrew-warren.title: Deloitte Consulting Career
andrew-warren.summary: John Kiriakou's post-CIA career at Deloitte Consulting (2004–2008), covering two corporate acquisitions he says he drove — India Tiger Analysis and, in effect, Bering Point — and ending in his effective firing weeks before his ABC News whistleblower interview aired.

andrew-warren.title: John Kiriakou
andrew-warren.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

andrew-warren.title: Central Intelligence Agency
andrew-warren.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

andy-warhol-encounter.title: Agnes von Kurowsky grave story
andy-warhol-encounter.summary: John Kiriakou's account of discovering the Washington, D.C. grave of Agnes von Kurowsky, the World War I Red Cross nurse whose four-month wartime romance with a young ambulance driver, Ernest Hemingway, made her the model for the lead female character in six of his books, including A Farewell to Arms.

andy-warhol-encounter.title: Bashar al-Assad
andy-warhol-encounter.summary: President of Syria; John Kiriakou recounts warning Senator John Kerry to stop publicly calling Assad 'my dear friend' after a speech enraged Washington's Lebanese community, with Kerry citing motorcycle rides they had taken together to the Golan Heights.

andy-warhol-encounter.title: Chinese spy balloon incident
andy-warhol-encounter.summary: 2023 controversy over a high-altitude balloon that crossed U.S. airspace, widely labeled in media coverage as a "Chinese spy balloon"; John Kiriakou notes no U.S. government official ever officially confirmed it was conducting espionage, and says he personally believes it was likely a weather balloon, since satellite surveillance already renders such balloons unnecessary for spying.

andy-warhol-encounter.title: Jack Murphy NATO Sabotage Story
andy-warhol-encounter.summary: John Kiriakou's account of a story reported by podcaster Jack Murphy — over a year in the making, drawing on CIA and Army intelligence sources — alleging the CIA worked through a NATO partner to conduct sabotage inside Russia, including munitions-warehouse fires and rail explosions; killed before publication after the CIA deputy director denied it on a call with the editor and blamed "rogue Ukrainians."

andy-warhol-encounter.title: Remains of the Day Treasury Clerk Story
andy-warhol-encounter.summary: John Kiriakou's account of finding the grave of an obscure Treasury Department clerk who, during the 1814 British burning of Washington, rescued the Declaration of Independence, Constitution, Bill of Rights, and Washington's military commission from the National Archives — and who, after later being deemed too difficult, was quietly transferred to the National Lighthouse Service, where out of boredom he invented the refractor light still used in American lighthouses today.

andy-warhol-encounter.title: U.S. foreign policy process
andy-warhol-encounter.summary: Three foreign-policy observations from John Kiriakou — the narrow legal basis for U.S. military presence abroad, which he says does not cover American special forces in Syria; the formal congressional travel-clearance process that undercuts Pentagon and White House claims of no advance knowledge of Nancy Pelosi's Taiwan trip; and the depth of U.S.-China economic interdependence that Kiriakou says makes antagonizing Beijing strategically unwise.

angry-birds.title: John Kiriakou's Briefing Room
angry-birds.summary: A twice-weekly news and commentary programme launched by John Kiriakou in July 2026, presented as analysis rather than partisan opinion, and distinct from his storytelling podcast Dead Drop.

angry-birds.title: 2026 Iran war
angry-birds.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

angry-birds.title: 2028 presidential field
angry-birds.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of the wide-open 2028 presidential race — the first in his life, he says, where he has no idea who either party will nominate. Predictive markets were listing 44 Democrats and 26 Republicans as possible candidates. His own preferred candidate is Tucker Carlson, whom he says he has repeatedly begged to run; his working assumption about anyone who does want the job is that they are "a narcissist and probably a sociopath on top of it."

angry-birds.title: Abraham Accords
angry-birds.summary: The Trump-brokered normalization deals between Israel and Gulf Arab states — in John Kiriakou's judgment "a terrible idea in the first place," a great victory for Israel and the Gulf Arabs that was "a punch in the throat to the Palestinians." He argues the Accords are how Trump meant to "solve the Middle East in a day" — by screwing the Palestinians — that Hamas read the abandonment correctly, that October 7 shattered the project, and that reviving the Accords (Saudis in, victory declared, Nobel collected) remains the organizing goal of Trump's regional policy.

angry-birds.title: Amaryllis Fox Kennedy
angry-birds.summary: Former CIA non-official-cover officer who worked under commercial cover as an international art consultant, later a Trump campaign manager and nominee for deputy CIA director. Per John Kiriakou, Senator Tom Cotton threatened to filibuster her appointment; the president responded by naming her deputy national security adviser instead — a job Kiriakou considers more powerful, since the CIA director reports to the national security adviser.

angry-birds.title: Kiriakou cameo practice
angry-birds.summary: John Kiriakou's post-2026 use of the Cameo personalised-video service — running at roughly 25 to 30 hours a week, some 900 messages in the month of March 2026 alone, nearly 2,000 messages in total by July 2026 — that he says has produced three cases in which the person receiving the video message afterwards told him he had talked them out of committing suicide, including a 15-year-old bulimic girl to whom Kiriakou gave his personal phone number.

antisemitism-and-anti-zionism.title: Germany and Israel
antisemitism-and-anti-zionism.summary: John Kiriakou's account of German support for Israeli policy as an overcorrection driven by shame over the Nazi past, and of the resulting cultural blacklisting of critics of Israel in Germany — a pattern he put to Roger Waters, who described being effectively unpublishable in the German press.

antisemitism-and-anti-zionism.title: Roger Waters
antisemitism-and-anti-zionism.summary: Founding member of the British rock band Pink Floyd; outspoken supporter of Palestinian human rights; anonymously paid off John Kiriakou's second mortgage during his federal prison sentence, sparing his wife and children the loss of the family home; only discovered to be the benefactor years later; subsequently a personal friend of Kiriakou and a recurring guest on his programme.

antisemitism-and-anti-zionism.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
antisemitism-and-anti-zionism.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

antisemitism-and-anti-zionism.title: Christian Zionism
antisemitism-and-anti-zionism.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that American evangelical Christianity functions as an arm of Zionism, and that its support for Israel is helping extinguish the oldest Christian communities on earth — a position he says he argued directly with the evangelical students he was invited to teach, and which he grounds in the projection that Nazareth, Christian for two thousand years, may soon have no Christians left.

antisemitism-and-anti-zionism.title: Famine in Gaza
antisemitism-and-anti-zionism.summary: The starvation of the civilian population of the Gaza Strip, which John Kiriakou describes as a United Nations-declared famine caused not by an absence of food but by an Israeli refusal to let food reach the people who need it; Kiriakou characterises it as a war crime, a crime against humanity and a form of genocide, attributing that characterisation to the United Nations and the International Court of Justice rather than to himself.

antisemitism-and-anti-zionism.title: Muslim Brotherhood terrorist designation
antisemitism-and-anti-zionism.summary: John Kiriakou''s objection to the designation of the Muslim Brotherhood, or elements of it, as a terrorist organisation: that the group is more than a century old, has never carried out an anti-American terrorist operation, and had never been so designated by any previous administration. He distinguishes fundamentalism and hostility from terrorism.

anwar-al-awlaki.title: Avril Haines
anwar-al-awlaki.summary: Per John Kiriakou, a National Security Council official and later CIA deputy director who personally approved lethal drone strikes, including the killings of American citizens Anwar al-Awlaki, his teenage son, and a nephew, none of whom were given due process.

anwar-al-awlaki.title: Falls Church mosque
anwar-al-awlaki.summary: Large mosque on Route 7 in Falls Church, Virginia; the site at which John Kiriakou, in 1993 as a CIA Arabic-language trainee, met then-imam Anwar al-Awlaki on a class field trip; the same mosque at which the September 11 hijackers prayed the night before the attacks.

anwar-al-awlaki.title: Haqqani White House meeting
anwar-al-awlaki.summary: A mid-to-late-1980s White House meeting between President Ronald Reagan and a Taliban delegation, per John Kiriakou — a former boss of his served as translator. One member of that delegation, a man named Haqqani, went on to found the Haqqani network, later responsible for the capture of Bowe Bergdahl and the kidnapping, rape, and torture of a Canadian couple.

anwar-al-awlaki.title: Kiriakou and Cenk Uygur
anwar-al-awlaki.summary: A grievance John Kiriakou carried for a decade — that Cenk Uygur had spent thirty minutes attacking him over his first letter from prison — resolved live on air in July 2026 when Uygur produced his archive, found no such segment, and both men concluded it had been mistaken identity.

anwar-al-awlaki.title: OnlyFans
anwar-al-awlaki.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the man who owned OnlyFans — whom he describes as Ukrainian-American rather than Israeli — was a major donor and strong supporter of Israel, part of a broader claim Kiriakou makes about Israeli involvement in the porn industry.

anwar-al-awlaki.title: Prince Muhammad bin Naif
anwar-al-awlaki.summary: Saudi prince and former head of Saudi intelligence; survivor of an al-Qaeda assassination attempt by a suicide bomber who concealed an explosive device internally in his own body, in approximately 2009.

april-glaspie.title: Saddam Hussein
april-glaspie.summary: President of Iraq from 1979 until the 2003 U.S. invasion; subject of John Kiriakou's CIA portfolio from January 1990 onward, in which capacity Kiriakou became, at age 25, "Saddam Hussein's intelligence community biographer" and the analyst who briefed President George H. W. Bush in the Oval Office on the morning of the 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

april-glaspie.title: Hussein Kamel
april-glaspie.summary: Saddam Hussein's son-in-law and Iraq's Minister of Industry and Military Industrialization; defected to Jordan in January 1993 with his brother Saddam Kamel out of fear of Uday Hussein; demanded U.S. weapons and air cover in exchange for cooperation but refused to disclose WMD locations; per John Kiriakou, the CIA burned him with a planted Arab-press leak that triggered Saddam to destroy his chemical-weapons stockpile.

april-glaspie.title: John Kiriakou
april-glaspie.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

april-glaspie.title: Kurds
april-glaspie.summary: The stateless people John Kiriakou calls generationally pro-American — he escorted visiting Kurdish delegations around Washington as a young analyst and bristled at officials who talked down to them. In his telling the Kurds were the only genuine opposition inside Saddam's Iraq, the only faction of the exile circus that ever amounted to anything (Jalal Talabani ended up president of Iraq), the victims of Saddam's chemical weapons and of a no-fly zone that forgot to ban helicopters — and the common enemy that actually united Turkey and ISIS.

april-glaspie.title: Norman Schwarzkopf
april-glaspie.summary: U.S. Army general and commander of CENTCOM during the 1991 Gulf War; per John Kiriakou, the architect of the "visionary" flanking maneuver that bypassed Iraq's fortified Kuwait–Saudi border, struck from the north, and produced the Highway of Death.

april-glaspie.title: Mort Halperin
april-glaspie.summary: Former Assistant Secretary of State, Assistant Secretary of Defense, and senior director of the National Security Council; author of the law John Kiriakou was convicted of violating (the Intelligence Identities Protection Act); wrote to President Obama stating that this is not why he wrote the law and that Kiriakou should be pardoned.

aq-khan.title: ISI
aq-khan.summary: Pakistan''s Inter-Services Intelligence agency, the CIA''s principal counterterrorism partner during John Kiriakou''s 2002 posting. Per Kiriakou, there were effectively ''two parallel ISIs'': one made up of Sandhurst-trained, FBI-schooled professionals he calls heroes who risked their lives on counterterrorism, and another — ''people with long beards who gave you a dirty look'' — who had created Kashmiri terrorist groups like Jaish-e-Mohammed and were attacking Shia mosques and Americans. Because of this, the CIA never told the ISI the identity of high-value targets, referring to Abu Zubaydah only as ''Mr. Fish.''

aq-khan.title: Pervez Musharraf
aq-khan.summary: Pakistani general and military dictator who ruled during John Kiriakou's 2002 posting as CIA chief of counterterrorism operations in Pakistan. Per Kiriakou, the United States 'essentially just purchased Musharraf,' paying tens of millions in cash to the ISI and meeting him several times a week — and in return 'he would let us do whatever we wanted.' Kiriakou says Musharraf, fearing the nuclear arsenal could fall into terrorist hands, unofficially turned control of Pakistan's nuclear weapons over to the Pentagon. Musharraf later pardoned proliferator A.Q. Khan.

aq-khan.title: Composition of the Saudi military
aq-khan.summary: John Kiriakou's long-standing claim that there are almost no Saudi nationals in the Saudi armed forces below the most senior ranks, and that the rank and file are Pakistanis hired from among Pakistan's poor. He treats it as a standing joke in the Gulf and as a limit on what Saudi Arabia can contribute to any war with Iran.

aq-khan.title: Tora Bora
aq-khan.summary: Mountainous cave complex in eastern Afghanistan that served as an al-Qaeda redoubt after the September 11 attacks. Per John Kiriakou — chief of counterterrorism operations in Pakistan at the time — the CIA killed al-Qaeda military-affairs chief Mohammed Atef there in October 2001, and Tora Bora was the backdrop to the hunt for the senior al-Qaeda leadership that culminated in the capture of Abu Zubaydah. Kiriakou also recounts an Egyptian al-Qaeda fighter he later recruited who survived a cruise-missile strike on a Tora Bora cave — one of only two who came out alive, his ears bleeding, describing the explosion as the most hideous sound he had ever heard.

aq-khan.title: Pakistan Station (2002)
aq-khan.summary: John Kiriakou's January 2002 arrival in Islamabad to become CIA chief of counterterrorism operations — a journey via London and Kuwait with lost luggage, a warning that steered him away from the soon-to-be-bombed Marriott, a skeleton counterterrorism branch of seven CIA retirees, and the raids that followed.

arianna-huffington.title: Bureau of Prisons
arianna-huffington.summary: The federal agency that ran John Kiriakou's incarceration — and one of his most persistent post-prison targets. The BOP overrode his judge's camp recommendation by deeming him "a threat to the public safety," threatened him with "diesel therapy" until 1,600 logged phone calls and letters from a dozen House members and two senators backed it off, and, per Kiriakou, functions as "an employment agency for unemployable semi-literate rural white men" and "a dumping ground for failed medical professionals" — an agency for which a prisoner's death is cheaper than his treatment.

arianna-huffington.title: Oliver Stone
arianna-huffington.summary: American film director with whom John Kiriakou struck up a friendship after his release from prison. Stone optioned the rights to one chapter of Kiriakou's first book, co-developed an unmade History Channel series with him, blurbed his book on Abu Zubaydah, and was among the public figures who campaigned against the Bureau of Prisons' attempt to shut down Kiriakou's prison blog. The two disagree sharply over whether the CIA killed John F. Kennedy.

arianna-huffington.title: FCI Loretto
arianna-huffington.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

arianna-huffington.title: Jake Tapper
arianna-huffington.summary: CNN anchor who drove to FCI Loretto to interview the imprisoned John Kiriakou — and who asked President Obama at a press conference why he had insisted on prosecuting a man who exposed a crime, a question Obama answered by walking away from the podium. Kiriakou wielded Tapper's name as a shield inside ("let's see what Jake Tapper has to say about it — why don't we give him a call?"), and the two stayed in touch after his release. "Jake was different."

arianna-huffington.title: Letter from Loretto
arianna-huffington.summary: Prison newsletter written by John Kiriakou from FCI Loretto, modeled on Martin Luther King's "Letter from Birmingham Jail," which exposed two crimes committed against him by guards and went viral after being relayed to the Huffington Post, drawing national press to the prison.

arianna-huffington.title: Martin Luther King Jr.
arianna-huffington.summary: The civil rights leader whose Letter from Birmingham Jail John Kiriakou explicitly honored in naming his own Letters from Loretto, and whose example — with Mandela and Gandhi — anchored Kiriakou''s decision to forgive his prosecutors: "I only lost two years of my life, not 35." Kiriakou''s parents marched for civil rights with King; he quotes King''s line about preaching nonviolence while his government is the world''s major purveyor of violence, and lists King''s assassination among the acts attributed to the unelected security state.

arkady-shevchenko.title: Gore Vidal
arkady-shevchenko.summary: American novelist and essayist; per John Kiriakou, a Sidwell Friends/St. Albans/Phillips Exeter alumnus who enlisted after Pearl Harbor rather than attend college, wrote the controversial 1948 novel The City and the Pillar, won a National Book Award in 1993, and was buried near his one lasting partner, Howard Austen, and his boyhood best friend, James Trimble, who was killed at Iwo Jima.

arkady-shevchenko.title: Joseph B. Chambers
arkady-shevchenko.summary: Civil War Medal of Honor recipient buried at Oak Park Cemetery in New Castle, Pennsylvania, whose grave John Kiriakou discovered as a child while looking for salamanders — sparking a lifelong interest in history.

arkady-shevchenko.title: Remains of the Day (book)
arkady-shevchenko.summary: John Kiriakou's book, announced for publication by Simon and Schuster in March 2026, billed as a definitive guide to the historic cemeteries of Washington DC and the first in a planned series; the second installment will cover the Mafia graves of New York City.

arlington-cemetery-spies.title: Francis Gary Powers
arlington-cemetery-spies.summary: U-2 pilot whose 1960 shoot-down over the Soviet Union and subsequent capture the CIA initially denied any knowledge of, denying not only that he was CIA but that he was U.S. government at all, until trading him in a bridge-of-spies prisoner exchange. Buried at Arlington National Cemetery. Per John Kiriakou, after his U-2 career Powers ended up piloting a Los Angeles traffic helicopter, and was killed when it crashed.

arlington-cemetery-spies.title: Vernon Walters
arlington-cemetery-spies.summary: U.S. Army general who served as Deputy Director of the CIA, Ambassador to Germany, Ambassador to the United Nations, and as Nixon''s occasional secret envoy to foreign leaders. Per John Kiriakou — who met him at an early-career analysts'' dinner — Walters said the only time he was ever afraid for his safety was during a secret Nixon-ordered peace mission to Fidel Castro in Cuba, when it occurred to him that Castro could poison him and no one but Nixon would know he was there: ''I wouldn''t trust Nixon to call my wife.'' Then he looked at Castro and thought: ''I can take this scrawny son of a bitch.''

arlington-cemetery-spies.title: William Donovan
