arlington-cemetery-spies.summary: General William "Wild Bill" Donovan — Medal of Honor recipient, decorated World War I veteran, Wall Street figure, and founder of the wartime Office of Strategic Services (OSS). Per John Kiriakou, Donovan became the natural first leader of American centralized intelligence after President Truman cleared the path by lying to FBI Director J. Edgar Hoover — telling him the new CIA would be a division of the FBI to get him to drop his opposition.

arlington-cemetery-spies.title: William and Elizabeth Friedman
arlington-cemetery-spies.summary: American cryptologists who, per John Kiriakou, broke the Nazi Enigma encryption largely by exploiting a single known fact: every German communication ended with ''Heil Hitler'' — sometimes spelled out, sometimes abbreviated ''HH.'' Working outward from the letters H, E, I, L, T, R, they cracked the code one letter at a time. Their work led directly to the founding of the National Security Agency. Both are buried at Arlington National Cemetery.

arlington-cemetery-spies.title: Bill Buckley
arlington-cemetery-spies.summary: CIA station chief in Beirut kidnapped by Palestinian Islamic Jihad in March 1984; tortured at length over fifteen months; killed in captivity; the case from which the agency derived a generation of operational-security lessons including the abandonment of single-point tracking devices in CIA officers' personal kit.

arlington-cemetery-spies.title: Falls Church mosque
arlington-cemetery-spies.summary: Large mosque on Route 7 in Falls Church, Virginia; the site at which John Kiriakou, in 1993 as a CIA Arabic-language trainee, met then-imam Anwar al-Awlaki on a class field trip; the same mosque at which the September 11 hijackers prayed the night before the attacks.

arnon-milchan.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
arnon-milchan.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

arnon-milchan.title: Israeli Nuclear Program
arnon-milchan.summary: Israel's widely assumed but officially unacknowledged nuclear arsenal; per John Kiriakou, the conventional wisdom within the CIA is that Israel possesses between 120 and 220 nuclear weapons, and the U.S. government's refusal to formally acknowledge this is driven by a specific legal obligation under the Glenn-Symington Act, which would require cutting off all foreign aid to any nuclear-armed country not party to the Non-Proliferation Treaty.

arnon-milchan.title: John Kerry
arnon-milchan.summary: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts; chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee during John Kiriakou's 2009 service as the committee's senior investigator; subsequently U.S. Secretary of State; characterized by Kiriakou as a coward who buckled under CIA pressure on the Dasht-i-Leili reopening and as personally fixated on his perceived theft of the Secretary of State position by Hillary Clinton; the famously thrown medals were duplicates purchased at the post exchange.

arnon-milchan.title: BDS movement
arnon-milchan.summary: The Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement against Israel; John Kiriakou notes that some 40 U.S. states now have anti-BDS laws that can require a speaker at a publicly funded university to sign a pledge of support for Israel — which he refuses to do.

arnon-milchan.title: Donald Trump
arnon-milchan.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

arnon-milchan.title: Hamas
arnon-milchan.summary: The Palestinian movement behind the October 7, 2023 attack; John Kiriakou argues that a case could be made for calling it a freedom-fighting organization dedicated to the liberation of its people rather than simply a terrorist group, notes it is labeled a terrorist organization by only a small minority of UN member states, and has ruled Gaza since Israel's 2005 withdrawal.

arrais-corporation.title: In-Q-Tel
arrais-corporation.summary: The CIA's openly acknowledged venture capital arm; provided Palantir Technologies its first $1.5 million in seed funding; in John Kiriakou's account the principal vehicle by which the agency finances private-sector development of technologies it intends to use.

arrais-corporation.title: Palantir Technologies
arrais-corporation.summary: U.S. data-analytics and intelligence-software company; received its first $1.5 million in seed funding from the CIA's In-Q-Tel venture-capital arm around 2002; characterized by John Kiriakou as functionally inseparable from the CIA in 2025, drawing the majority of its revenue from agency contracts and operating across DARPA, NSA, and the broader U.S. national-security apparatus.

arrais-corporation.title: The Analysis Corporation
arrais-corporation.summary: Arlington, Virginia–based [private intelligence firm](/wiki/private-intelligence); one of two companion entities (alongside Arrais Corporation) created as LLC pass-throughs for retired Senior Intelligence Service personnel; John Brennan was appointed its CEO in 2005.

arrais-corporation.title: John Brennan
arrais-corporation.summary: Former Director of the CIA; characterized in KiriPedia's source corpus as the principal architect of the agency's enhanced interrogation program and as having plotted against an elected President

arrais-corporation.title: Central Intelligence Agency
arrais-corporation.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

arrais-corporation.title: Private Intelligence
arrais-corporation.summary: Post-CIA commercial intelligence work performed by John Kiriakou — both operational (surveillance, bribery, dossier-building for private clients) and analytical (paid forecasts for hedge funds, mutual funds, and a global mining company). Per Kiriakou, his clients ranged from a Cypriot billionaire investigating his daughter's fiancé to the ninth-largest hedge fund in the world.

aryan-brotherhood.title: The Italians at Loretto
aryan-brotherhood.summary: The mafia contingent at FCI Loretto — men with last names like Gambino, Bonanno, Lucchese, Genovese, DeCavalcante — who adopted John Kiriakou in his second year, largely because he hated the FBI as much as they did. The cast included the boss of the Gambino family (in on a dozen-plus murder counts, the man who replaced John Gotti), Pete the Bonanno captain across the hall who asked why he sat "with those Nazi retards," and a crooked guard on the payroll delivering pork loin and fresh mozzarella. When the FBI later came to Kiriakou's door asking him to inform on Pete, his answer was "get off my property."

aryan-brotherhood.title: Bureau of Prisons
aryan-brotherhood.summary: The federal agency that ran John Kiriakou's incarceration — and one of his most persistent post-prison targets. The BOP overrode his judge's camp recommendation by deeming him "a threat to the public safety," threatened him with "diesel therapy" until 1,600 logged phone calls and letters from a dozen House members and two senators backed it off, and, per Kiriakou, functions as "an employment agency for unemployable semi-literate rural white men" and "a dumping ground for failed medical professionals" — an agency for which a prisoner's death is cheaper than his treatment.

aryan-brotherhood.title: Prison racial segregation
aryan-brotherhood.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the rigid racial and ethnic division of American prisons — a cafeteria split like the 1950s South — and his argument that segregating and hardening inmates for years, then releasing them with no skills, makes society less safe.

aryan-brotherhood.title: PTSD
aryan-brotherhood.summary: Post-traumatic stress disorder runs through John Kiriakou''s life and worldview — he had it coming out of Greece after an assassination attempt, brought it home from Pakistan alongside his shock at colleagues'' willingness to kill, and was blindsided by a delayed post-prison version that helped end his marriage. For six months after release he dreamed the same dream nightly: that he was out by mistake and had to get back inside before midnight count. He still takes a repurposed blood-pressure drug that stops the dreams, and he extends the diagnosis outward — to secret-site interrogators who came back crying, to drone pilots, and to prisoners released angry and untreated.

aryan-brotherhood.title: Espionage Act
aryan-brotherhood.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

aryan-brotherhood.title: Mort Halperin
aryan-brotherhood.summary: Former Assistant Secretary of State, Assistant Secretary of Defense, and senior director of the National Security Council; author of the law John Kiriakou was convicted of violating (the Intelligence Identities Protection Act); wrote to President Obama stating that this is not why he wrote the law and that Kiriakou should be pardoned.

asel-al-ghabandi.title: Iraqi invasion of Kuwait
asel-al-ghabandi.summary: John Kiriakou''s most detailed account of the intelligence process around the 1990 Iraqi invasion of Kuwait and its 1991 liberation. As a first-year CIA analyst on a ''training account'' covering Iraq, Kiriakou produced the June 30, 1990 warning paper for the White House; suggested calling the US Defense Attaché in Baghdad to drive to the border and report what he saw (the answer: ''Literally the entire Iraqi military is heading south''); briefed the August 2 Oval Office meeting with Bush; and later took a single phone call from General Colin Powell that led, eight hours later, to 47 cruise missiles striking the Iraqi Intelligence Service headquarters in Baghdad.

asel-al-ghabandi.title: 1993 Bush Kuwait assassination plot
asel-al-ghabandi.summary: Iraqi intelligence plot, foiled by Kuwaiti authorities, to assassinate former President George H. W. Bush during his post-liberation "victory lap" visit to Kuwait; the U.S. response, per John Kiriakou's first-person account of his telephone call with Chairman of the Joint Chiefs Colin Powell, was 47 cruise missiles fired into the Iraqi Intelligence Service headquarters in Baghdad eight hours later.

asel-al-ghabandi.title: Ahmed Chalabi
asel-al-ghabandi.summary: Iraqi exile and founder of the Iraqi National Congress; per John Kiriakou, a Shia-Kurdish con man who looted Petra Bank in Jordan of $36 million in the 1980s, was sentenced to death in absentia, was pardoned at CIA request, then pocketed $6 million in CIA seed funding for the INC and bought a Mayfair house in cash; later resurrected by Dick Cheney to feed the Pentagon fabricated WMD intelligence used to justify the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

asel-al-ghabandi.title: Ali Hassan al-Majid
asel-al-ghabandi.summary: Saddam Hussein cousin known as "Chemical Ali" and "the Butcher of Kurdistan"; per John Kiriakou, also briefly served as the Iraqi-installed governor of occupied Kuwait — "the Butcher of Kuwait" — and was engaged in the wholesale slaughter of Kurds in the north, Shia in the south, and Kuwaitis under occupation.

asel-al-ghabandi.title: Gerald Bull
asel-al-ghabandi.summary: British inventor of the "big gun" — a barrel so large it had to be leaned against a mountain — first offered to Israel and rejected, then sold to Iraq under Saddam Hussein; assassinated by Mossad in Brussels once Iraqi engineers solved the cracking problem with a barrel-smoothing sleeve nicknamed "the condom," after which the Israelis also bombed the gun itself.

asel-al-ghabandi.title: Kuwait oil fires
asel-al-ghabandi.summary: The February 1991 sabotage by retreating Iraqi forces of an estimated 600–800 Kuwaiti oil wells; per John Kiriakou's first-person account, the fires blackened the desert and blotted out the sun as far away as Riyadh, vaporized two French journalists who drove onto a sheet of melted-sand glass, and were extinguished only by an international team led by American specialist Red Adair using a Rolls-Royce jet engine to blow the flames out.

assange-plea-deal.title: Barry Pollock
assange-plea-deal.summary: Washington defense attorney who represented Julian Assange; John Kiriakou credits Pollock with negotiating the deal that let Assange be processed in Saipan — the U.S. district closest to Australia — rather than be brought to Virginia.

assange-plea-deal.title: Espionage Act
assange-plea-deal.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

assange-plea-deal.title: Israeli torture of Palestinian prisoners
assange-plea-deal.summary: John Kiriakou's account of systematic abuse in Israeli detention after October 7 — thousands held, whistleblower reports of forced amputations, and a prison-wide rule that Palestinian inmates must crawl rather than walk, on pain of being beaten with rebar.

assange-plea-deal.title: Leonie Brinkema
assange-plea-deal.summary: U.S. federal judge in the Eastern District of Virginia — informally the 'Espionage Court' — a Reagan appointee John Kiriakou calls "a hanging judge." Per Kiriakou, Brinkema systematically reserved all major national security cases for herself rather than allowing them to be distributed randomly among judges, and ruled in Kiriakou's case that his reason for blowing the whistle was legally irrelevant and that classified documents could not be used in his defense — effectively making it impossible to mount one.

assange-plea-deal.title: Abu Zubaydah
assange-plea-deal.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

assange-plea-deal.title: Chelsea Manning
assange-plea-deal.summary: Former U.S. Army intelligence analyst who provided WikiLeaks its 2010 trove of military and diplomatic documents. Per John Kiriakou, Manning meets the legal definition of whistleblower for exposing war crimes, was a torture victim of prolonged solitary confinement with forced nudity, and was sentenced to 35 years in prison before Barack Obama commuted — not pardoned — her sentence. Kiriakou says Manning later refused a grand jury's offer of immunity and chose renewed jail time rather than testify against Julian Assange.

asset-acquisition-cycle.title: Brett McGurk
asset-acquisition-cycle.summary: Senior U.S. diplomat; John Kiriakou cites reporting that McGurk was caught in a sexual encounter atop a U.S. embassy while overseeing the campaign against ISIS, offering it as an example of the adultery culture he considers a security risk.

asset-acquisition-cycle.title: French intelligence (DGSE)
asset-acquisition-cycle.summary: The French foreign intelligence service; characterized as exceptionally talented, exceptionally aggressive, and routinely lethal in the conduct of its operations

asset-acquisition-cycle.title: The "Soylent Green is people" cable easter egg
asset-acquisition-cycle.summary: A long-running CIA case-officer in-joke in which the line "Soylent Green is people" is hidden inside classified operational cables as a sequence of incongruously lowercase letters

asset-acquisition-cycle.title: Gay Diplomat Operation
asset-acquisition-cycle.summary: Per John Kiriakou, a CIA recruitment operation he ran against a foreign diplomat who was closeted and gay. After months of cultivation under cover as a gay man, Kiriakou attempted to kiss the diplomat at his apartment and was deflated by the response: ''I am gay. I''m just not into hairy guys.'' The romantic gambit failed — but the recruitment ultimately succeeded anyway, because the diplomat had been passed over for a promotion and was angry enough at his own government to cooperate. Kiriakou cites the operation as evidence that financial motivation and personal grievance, not coercion, are the reliable drivers of recruitment.

asset-acquisition-cycle.title: Kompromat
asset-acquisition-cycle.summary: Russian-derived term for compromising material — recordings, photographs, or documentation of an individual''s criminal, sexual, or embarrassing behavior — used to coerce cooperation or silence. Per John Kiriakou, the CIA''s formal policy conclusion is that kompromat doesn''t work as a recruitment tool: faced with the binary choice between confessing to a spouse and committing treason, most targets confess. The agency therefore prefers voluntary, ideologically or financially motivated recruitment.

asset-acquisition-cycle.title: Mad minute
asset-acquisition-cycle.summary: CIA case-officer procedure for the opening seconds of every meeting with a recruited source — confirm the source is safe, confirm a clean surveillance-detection route, and set the next meeting — so that if the door is kicked in, the operational essentials have already been taken care of.

athens-bank-fraud-report.title: Overcriminalization
athens-bank-fraud-report.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the United States criminalizes too much — locking up 25% of the world's prisoners with 5% of its population, and adding roughly 50 new felonies a year — illustrated by a NOAA employee prosecuted for whistling at a whale.

athens-bank-fraud-report.title: Japanese diplomat FBI sting
athens-bank-fraud-report.summary: John Kiriakou's account of an FBI entrapment operation in which an agent posing as a Japanese diplomat cold-pitched him for classified information over five lunches, hoping he would commit actual espionage they could charge — a scheme he discovered only in his own case discovery.

athens-bank-fraud-report.title: Abu Zubaydah
athens-bank-fraud-report.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

athens-bank-fraud-report.title: Bill Clinton
athens-bank-fraud-report.summary: 42nd U.S. president whom John Kiriakou describes as wholly disinterested in intelligence — briefed by the CIA only twice in eight years, with Vice President Al Gore taking the daily briefing instead and relaying anything important.

athens-bank-fraud-report.title: Bob Trout
athens-bank-fraud-report.summary: The attorney who came to John Kiriakou''s house to urge him to take the plea deal: ''If you were my own brother, I would beg you to take this deal.''

athens-bank-fraud-report.title: Dick Cheney
athens-bank-fraud-report.summary: U.S. Vice President under George W. Bush. Per John Kiriakou — recounting CIA Director George Tenet's memoir — Cheney intercepted the presidential finding authorizing the CIA's enhanced interrogation program in the Oval Office anteroom and took it from Tenet before Bush could sign it. Tenet later concluded the president probably never actually signed the finding and probably told the truth when he said he had no idea the program was taking place. Kiriakou characterizes Cheney as the one who actually ran foreign policy, intelligence policy, and defense policy during the Bush years.

avril-haines.title: Senate Torture Report
avril-haines.summary: The December 2014 executive summary of the U.S. Senate Select Committee on Intelligence's study of the CIA's post-9/11 detention and interrogation program; the first public disclosure of techniques including rectal feeding with hummus, sexual assault with broomsticks, and prolonged sleep deprivation.

avril-haines.title: Abolish the CIA
avril-haines.summary: John Kiriakou's position that the CIA should be abolished because its functions are already duplicated by the other 17 U.S. intelligence agencies — analysis by the State Department, human spying by the Pentagon, technology by DARPA, NSA and the private sector.

avril-haines.title: Anwar al-Awlaki
avril-haines.summary: American-born al-Qaeda propagandist; in 1993 the imam of the Falls Church, Virginia mosque visited by John Kiriakou's CIA Arabic-language class on a field trip; in 2001 the cleric at whose mosque the 9/11 hijackers prayed the night before the attacks; killed by U.S. drone strike in Yemen in approximately 2011.

avril-haines.title: Bill Burns
avril-haines.summary: Career U.S. diplomat named CIA director in 2021. John Kiriakou wrote a positive op-ed on his appointment, calling him "finally, an adult in the room," but says Burns ended up serving as the Biden administration's de facto Secretary of State and was drawn into the CIA's culture of drone warfare, rendition, and domestic spying.

avril-haines.title: Code Pink
avril-haines.summary: The women-led peace group co-founded by Medea Benjamin. John Kiriakou first saw them as a Senate staffer — a room full of pink t-shirts at a hearing he'd organized for Senator Kerry, where he was caught smiling at their chants and told to keep his opinions to himself. When he was arrested, Code Pink "was right there next to me," threw his going-away party before prison, ran the sustained call campaign that helped stop his diesel-therapy transfer, stood with him through the 2019 Venezuelan embassy siege — and after prison he volunteered as coordinator of Code Pink Congress.

avril-haines.title: Dianne Feinstein
avril-haines.summary: Longtime Democratic U.S. senator from California and Senate Intelligence Committee chair; per John Kiriakou, one of the greatest disappointments on Capitol Hill — fully bought into the intelligence community even after CIA director John Brennan called her a liar over the committee's finding that the CIA had monitored Senate investigators, a finding that proved true.

bab-al-mandab.title: Houthis
bab-al-mandab.summary: The Iran-aligned movement that controls the most important parts of Yemen, described by John Kiriakou as fierce fighters who beat the Saudi military over a decade of war and who in July 2026 declared a naval blockade of Saudi shipping.

bab-al-mandab.title: John Kerry
bab-al-mandab.summary: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts; chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee during John Kiriakou's 2009 service as the committee's senior investigator; subsequently U.S. Secretary of State; characterized by Kiriakou as a coward who buckled under CIA pressure on the Dasht-i-Leili reopening and as personally fixated on his perceived theft of the Secretary of State position by Hillary Clinton; the famously thrown medals were duplicates purchased at the post exchange.

bab-al-mandab.title: Yemen
bab-al-mandab.summary: Country on the southern Arabian Peninsula; setting of five John Kiriakou trips between 1990 and approximately 2010, spanning the country's brief unification, its civil war, and its present condition as a high-threat operating environment for U.S. and allied diplomatic personnel.

bab-al-mandab.title: Ali Abdullah Saleh
bab-al-mandab.summary: President of Yemen for decades, close to both Saudi Arabia and the United States until Yemen's 1990 Security Council vote on Kuwait, after which his country collapsed into civil war; he fled to Saudi Arabia and was killed by a bomb planted in the palace where he had taken refuge.

bab-al-mandab.title: Saudi nuclear program
bab-al-mandab.summary: Saudi Arabia's decades-long pursuit of uranium enrichment, nominally for nuclear power, which John Kiriakou notes was already old news when he arrived at the CIA in 1990 and which conventional wisdom has always read as a weapons programme.

bab-al-mandab.title: Somaliland
bab-al-mandab.summary: Self-declared breakaway state in the Horn of Africa that Israel became the only country in the world to recognize as independent, gaining a military base positioned roughly 30 seconds' flight time from Yemen; John Kiriakou, who visited Somaliland while posted with the Senate Foreign Relations Committee in Djibouti, describes it as a functioning city of about 100,000 unconnected to Mogadishu, al-Shabaab, or piracy.

bahrain-1994-1996-posting.title: Galls.com sponsor story
bahrain-1994-1996-posting.summary: John Kiriakou's account of outfitting the CIA's post-9/11 Islamabad station for terrorist-safe-house raids by ordering roughly $50,000 of tactical gear from the law-enforcement retailer galls.com on his CIA credit card, shipped to Pakistan via State Department diplomatic pouch in under a week — a story he now retells as an ad-read for the retailer, which sponsors one of his podcast appearances.

bahrain-1994-1996-posting.title: 2026 congressional landscape
bahrain-1994-1996-posting.summary: John Kiriakou's read on two developments affecting the 2026 midterm landscape — the Supreme Court's disallowance of Virginia's redistricting, which he says makes a Democratic House win less certain given widespread Republican-favoring gerrymandering, and Marjorie Taylor Greene's resignation despite winning her last race with 77.5% of the vote, because she knew she could not survive another Republican primary.

bahrain-1994-1996-posting.title: Witness K case
bahrain-1994-1996-posting.summary: Australian intelligence scandal in which a former ASIS officer known as Witness K exposed Australia's bugging of the East Timorese cabinet during oil and gas revenue negotiations; his lawyer, Bernard Collaery, describes the ASIO raids on both their homes and offices as paralleling the FBI's raid on John Kiriakou.

bahrain-1994-1996-posting.title: Scholar-in-Residence program
bahrain-1994-1996-posting.summary: The current CIA recruitment program, in operation as of the late 2020s, under which the agency places retiring senior officers as 'CIA Scholar in Residence' professors at major American universities. Per John Kiriakou, the program serves as the agency's principal university-recruitment channel since the 1993 Equal Employment Opportunity Act forbade the older practice of having professors covertly recruit students into the CIA. Officers identified as scholars in residence are openly disclosed; the recruitment work continues, just no longer in secret.

bahrain-1994-1996-posting.title: Admiral William Crowe
bahrain-1994-1996-posting.summary: Former Chairman of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff; visited Bahrain during John Kiriakou's posting there, with Kiriakou assigned as his control officer; present during Kiriakou's "I have my eye on you" handshake confrontation with the Bahraini Prime Minister, Prince Khalifa bin Salman Al Khalifa.

bahrain-1994-1996-posting.title: Mary Margaret Graham
bahrain-1994-1996-posting.summary: CIA Senior Intelligence Service officer and later Deputy Director of National Intelligence for Collection under John Negroponte — described by John Kiriakou as a career "reports officer" who had never personally recruited a source, and as his difficult chief of station in a later domestic assignment.

bahrain-fishing-officer-demarche.title: Below World's End
bahrain-fishing-officer-demarche.summary: Film in which John Kiriakou made his acting debut, filmed entirely in Mexico during October 2025; Kiriakou's performance earned him a Screen Actors Guild membership card, and Sean Penn told him after a private screening that he had unknowingly been acting throughout his entire CIA career.

bahrain-fishing-officer-demarche.title: Big Assawoman Bay NASA launch
bahrain-fishing-officer-demarche.summary: John Kiriakou's account of being taken, as a junior CIA analyst, to watch a NASA rocket launch near the village of Big Assawoman on Virginia's Eastern Shore, where he was startled to find foreign space-agency officials present unsupervised.

bahrain-fishing-officer-demarche.title: Chinese illegal fishing
bahrain-fishing-officer-demarche.summary: John Kiriakou calls Chinese overfishing one of the world's biggest under-discussed problems, citing the near-extinction of Chilean sea bass and heavy overfishing of Alaskan and Atlantic cod, and recounting personally seeing Chinese fishing vessels in Antarctica on his honeymoon.

bahrain-fishing-officer-demarche.title: Joe Weisberg
bahrain-fishing-officer-demarche.summary: Former CIA Counterterrorism Center officer and colleague of John Kiriakou who resigned abruptly, saying he did not have it in him to convince people to commit treason, then moved to Hollywood and created the television series The Americans.

bahrain-fishing-officer-demarche.title: Mike Baker
bahrain-fishing-officer-demarche.summary: Former CIA case officer; John Kiriakou's predecessor as the CIA's lead officer working the Revolutionary Organization 17 November problem in Athens; characterized by Kiriakou as "the real deal" and as having laid the groundwork for the operations Kiriakou subsequently inherited.

bahrain-fishing-officer-demarche.title: Myanmar's civil war, per Kiriakou
bahrain-fishing-officer-demarche.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Myanmar as the only country in the world continuously at war without a single day of peace since World War II, its Buddhist-majority persecution of Muslims, Christians, and Hindus, his view that Aung San Suu Kyi should have her Nobel Peace Prize stripped, and his argument that the world ignores the country's atrocities because it has gems rather than oil.

bahrain-intifada-1994.title: Bahrain Posting (1994–1996)
bahrain-intifada-1994.summary: John Kiriakou's 1994–1996 assignment to Bahrain under U.S. State Department cover as second secretary for economic affairs — arriving with his wife Joanne and infant son Chris on August 1, 1994, into a tiny Gulf monarchy whose sectarian tensions erupted, two months later, into the first Intifada.

bahrain-intifada-1994.title: Bahrain Prime Minister "Mr. 10 Percent"
bahrain-intifada-1994.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Bahrain's long-serving prime minister, the Amir's uncle, universally nicknamed "Mr. 10 Percent" for allegedly requiring a 10 percent cash cut on business deals — a cold, calculating figure Kiriakou calls "the definition of corruption," pointedly excluded from the national motto, yet credited with turning Bahrain into the Gulf's banking hub.

bahrain-intifada-1994.title: Isa bin Salman Al Khalifa
bahrain-intifada-1994.summary: Amir of Bahrain from 1961 until his death in 1999; per John Kiriakou, who was posted to Bahrain 1994–1996, a short, "roly poly," sweet-natured ruler who kept an open beach palace for Westerners, disliked Jordan's King Hussein, and was heartbroken by the Columbine shooting even as he privately could not grasp why he should extend more support to his own Shia majority.

bahrain-intifada-1994.title: Office of Leadership Analysis
bahrain-intifada-1994.summary: CIA analytic office — internally called LDA, for Leadership Development Analysis — founded by CIA psychiatrist Jerome Post, where John Kiriakou was hired at the start of his CIA career and spent his first seven and a half years as Saddam Hussein's classified psychological profiler. His first assignment, given on his first day, was covering Iraq and Kuwait, a portfolio his boss described as so quiet the office sometimes went days without a single incoming cable.

bahrain-intifada-1994.title: Pakistan Station (2002)
bahrain-intifada-1994.summary: John Kiriakou's January 2002 arrival in Islamabad to become CIA chief of counterterrorism operations — a journey via London and Kuwait with lost luggage, a warning that steered him away from the soon-to-be-bombed Marriott, a skeleton counterterrorism branch of seven CIA retirees, and the raids that followed.

bahrain-intifada-1994.title: Abu Zubaydah
bahrain-intifada-1994.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

bahrain-prime-minister-mr-10-percent.title: Bahrain Posting (1994–1996)
bahrain-prime-minister-mr-10-percent.summary: John Kiriakou's 1994–1996 assignment to Bahrain under U.S. State Department cover as second secretary for economic affairs — arriving with his wife Joanne and infant son Chris on August 1, 1994, into a tiny Gulf monarchy whose sectarian tensions erupted, two months later, into the first Intifada.

bahrain-prime-minister-mr-10-percent.title: Bahrain Intifada (1994)
bahrain-prime-minister-mr-10-percent.summary: The first Bahraini Intifada, a Shia uprising against the Sunni Al Khalifa monarchy that began roughly two months into John Kiriakou's 1994 Bahrain posting with a bombing at the Ministry of Labor, led by Abdul Amir Al-Jamri, and met by the government first with police, then armored personnel carriers and tanks, and executions.

bahrain-prime-minister-mr-10-percent.title: Isa bin Salman Al Khalifa
bahrain-prime-minister-mr-10-percent.summary: Amir of Bahrain from 1961 until his death in 1999; per John Kiriakou, who was posted to Bahrain 1994–1996, a short, "roly poly," sweet-natured ruler who kept an open beach palace for Westerners, disliked Jordan's King Hussein, and was heartbroken by the Columbine shooting even as he privately could not grasp why he should extend more support to his own Shia majority.

bahrain-prime-minister-mr-10-percent.title: Admiral William Crowe
bahrain-prime-minister-mr-10-percent.summary: Former Chairman of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff; visited Bahrain during John Kiriakou's posting there, with Kiriakou assigned as his control officer; present during Kiriakou's "I have my eye on you" handshake confrontation with the Bahraini Prime Minister, Prince Khalifa bin Salman Al Khalifa.

bahrain-prime-minister-mr-10-percent.title: John Kiriakou
bahrain-prime-minister-mr-10-percent.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

bahrain-prime-minister-mr-10-percent.title: Office of Leadership Analysis
bahrain-prime-minister-mr-10-percent.summary: CIA analytic office — internally called LDA, for Leadership Development Analysis — founded by CIA psychiatrist Jerome Post, where John Kiriakou was hired at the start of his CIA career and spent his first seven and a half years as Saddam Hussein's classified psychological profiler. His first assignment, given on his first day, was covering Iraq and Kuwait, a portfolio his boss described as so quiet the office sometimes went days without a single incoming cable.

barack-obama.title: Brett McGurk
barack-obama.summary: Senior U.S. diplomat; John Kiriakou cites reporting that McGurk was caught in a sexual encounter atop a U.S. embassy while overseeing the campaign against ISIS, offering it as an example of the adultery culture he considers a security risk.

barack-obama.title: Christopher Hitchens
barack-obama.summary: British-American journalist and author who, at John Kiriakou's telling, famously argued in the mid-2000s that CIA waterboarding was 'nothing … not a big deal,' agreed in 2008 to undergo a filmed waterboarding demonstration, tapped out after roughly seventeen seconds, and thereafter suffered panic attacks for the rest of his life whenever he could not breathe for a moment.

barack-obama.title: Peter Strzok
barack-obama.summary: Senior FBI counterintelligence officer who, per John Kiriakou, oversaw the FBI operation that included a fake Japanese-diplomat sting designed to induce Kiriakou to commit espionage, and who personally placed Kiriakou in handcuffs when he was arrested on January 12, 2012. Kiriakou did not learn Strzok's identity until 2017, when a Washington Post reporter called to ask for comment on Strzok's firing.

barack-obama.title: Presidents and the CIA
barack-obama.summary: John Kiriakou's observation that some presidents actively lead the CIA while others are led around by it — citing George H.W. Bush's ongoing "love affair" with the agency after his 11-month stint as director, and Richard Nixon's close relationship with the CIA, which Kiriakou says was one of the things that brought down his presidency.

barack-obama.title: Steve Kappes
barack-obama.summary: Former Deputy Director of the Central Intelligence Agency; encountered by John Kiriakou in the lobby of the Sanaa Marriott during Kiriakou's final Yemen trip as a Senate Foreign Relations Committee investigator.

barack-obama.title: Military Ethics
barack-obama.summary: The hypothetical Kiriakou puts to college audiences — and the line no CIA training class ever teaches an officer where to draw.

barry-pollock.title: Assange plea deal
barry-pollock.summary: The 2024 agreement under which Julian Assange pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit espionage, was processed in Saipan, and returned to Australia; John Kiriakou details its odd terms — a Chelsea Manning purge affidavit and a 25-year green-card ban — and the debate over whether it sets a precedent.

Per Kiriakou, Brinkema systematically reserved all major national security cases for herself rather than allowing them to be distributed randomly among judges, and ruled in Kiriakou's case that his reason for blowing the whistle was legally irrelevant and that classified documents could not be used in his defense — effectively making it impossible to mount one.

barry-pollock.title: Abu Zubaydah
barry-pollock.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

barry-pollock.title: Edward Snowden
barry-pollock.summary: Former NSA contractor who in 2013 disclosed the scope of U.S. [mass surveillance](/wiki/mass-surveillance), including the Section 702 collection program. Per John Kiriakou — who counts Snowden among the small group of national-security whistleblowers prosecuted under the Espionage Act — Snowden was ''stuck between two awful slippery slopes'': breaking his oath and chain of command on one side, and on the other catching something ''cut and dry against the Constitution'' that no one would act on. Kiriakou notes Snowden could not use his chain of command (as Kiriakou could not, his own chain being Jose Rodriguez), and that Judge Leonie Brinkema had reserved the Snowden case for herself before he fled the country.

barry-pollock.title: George Tenet
barry-pollock.summary: Director of Central Intelligence from 1997 to 2004, spanning the September 11 attacks and the early enhanced-interrogation program; identified by John Kiriakou as John Brennan's institutional patron at the agency; the figure who ordered the Five Eyes intelligence services to "open the files" to each other in the early 2000s.

bashar-al-assad.title: Hezbollah
bashar-al-assad.summary: Lebanese Shia militant organization and political party. Per John Kiriakou, Israel''s strategic goal regarding Hezbollah is not to defeat it outright but to keep Lebanon in a state of chaos that serves Israeli interests. He cites two Israeli operations: the simultaneous pager-detonation attack that decapitated Hezbollah''s leadership, which he called ''the most incredible operation I''ve ever seen,'' and the strike that killed former leader Hassan Nasrallah by leveling an entire complex and killing roughly 300 people — which he characterized as a war crime.

bashar-al-assad.title: ISIS
bashar-al-assad.summary: The Islamic State, in John Kiriakou''s account, is an American policy failure made flesh — created because a faction decided al-Qaeda was not radical or violent enough, founded by Baghdadi while he sat in a U.S. military prison in Iraq, armed with hardware captured from the U.S.-supplied Iraqi army, and — per an email he cites from Hillary Clinton to John Podesta — funded by the governments of Saudi Arabia and Qatar. Kiriakou repeatedly punctured the anti-ISIS coalition''s logic: ISIS operated in seven countries while the U.S. bombed two, and Turkey had no real quarrel with ISIS at all — their common enemy was the Kurds.

bashar-al-assad.title: Remains of the Day Treasury Clerk Story
bashar-al-assad.summary: John Kiriakou's account of finding the grave of an obscure Treasury Department clerk who, during the 1814 British burning of Washington, rescued the Declaration of Independence, Constitution, Bill of Rights, and Washington's military commission from the National Archives — and who, after later being deemed too difficult, was quietly transferred to the National Lighthouse Service, where out of boredom he invented the refractor light still used in American lighthouses today.

bashar-al-assad.title: Souda Bay Vulnerability and Nasser on American Decisions
bashar-al-assad.summary: Two observations John Kiriakou has made on U.S. Mediterranean strategy and decision-making — a U.S. military contact's warning that Souda Bay in Crete, the nearest major port able to host a U.S. aircraft carrier like the USS Gerald Ford, is a possible vulnerability; and Kiriakou's favorite quote from Gamal Abdel Nasser, that Americans never make clear-cut stupid decisions, only complicated ones.

bashar-al-assad.title: U.S. foreign policy process
bashar-al-assad.summary: Three foreign-policy observations from John Kiriakou — the narrow legal basis for U.S. military presence abroad, which he says does not cover American special forces in Syria; the formal congressional travel-clearance process that undercuts Pentagon and White House claims of no advance knowledge of Nancy Pelosi's Taiwan trip; and the depth of U.S.-China economic interdependence that Kiriakou says makes antagonizing Beijing strategically unwise.

bashar-al-assad.title: Liberty University
bashar-al-assad.summary: Evangelical university in Lynchburg, Virginia — the largest in the world — where John Kiriakou taught for several years as an adjunct professor of intelligence studies in the Jesse Helms School of Government. He says he warned the school he disagreed with it on 95% of the issues and was hired anyway, on the dean's reasoning that "torture's not Christian"; he enjoyed the post while clashing constantly with the institution over the treatment of Middle Eastern Christians.

bay-path-university.title: Albert Stubblebine
bay-path-university.summary: Per John Kiriakou, General Albert "Bert" Stubblebine was among the Army Intelligence figures behind the original Project Stargate remote-viewing program; Kiriakou interviewed the program's top people and says Stubblebine, like remote viewer Lyn Buchanan, had to sign non-disclosure agreements with the NSA and CIA.

bay-path-university.title: Espionage Act
bay-path-university.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

bay-path-university.title: Ilhan Omar
bay-path-university.summary: U.S. Representative whom John Kiriakou credits with sponsoring a rewrite of the Espionage Act in two consecutive Congresses — legislation he says is dead on arrival with a Republican House because of who she is.

bay-path-university.title: Lynn Buchanan
bay-path-university.summary: A Fort Meade-trained Army intelligence veteran of the CIA and NSA remote-viewing programs — a primary source, Kiriakou says, not a TV psychic.

bay-path-university.title: Mark Zuckerberg–Angela Merkel Meeting
bay-path-university.summary: Kiriakou on Zuckerberg flying to Berlin to help Chancellor Merkel define hate speech — and why he objects to that call being Zuckerberg's.

bay-path-university.title: Sweat Lodge
bay-path-university.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the federal prison where he was incarcerated had a Native American sweat lodge that was shut down after it was misused for sex rather than religious ceremony; he says he has never personally been in a sweat lodge.

bds-movement.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
bds-movement.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

bds-movement.title: UK secrecy laws
bds-movement.summary: John Kiriakou's view that Britain is even harsher on whistleblowers and dissent than the United States, using the Official Secrets Act and Terrorism Act to stop people at airports and threaten arrest merely for supporting Palestinian rights.

bds-movement.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
bds-movement.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

bds-movement.title: Jeffrey Epstein
bds-movement.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

bds-movement.title: CIA and NSA exotic programs
bds-movement.summary: Two obscure U.S. intelligence programs John Kiriakou has discussed — a late-1980s FBI/Defense Department investigation into a senior NSA officer who came out as a member of the Church of Satan and was accused of ritual sacrifice (which found no evidence), and a 1990s CIA battlefield laser weapon designed to blind rather than kill enemy soldiers, shelved after lawyers determined it violated international law.

bds-movement.title: Jamaal Bowman
bds-movement.summary: Former U.S. Representative from New York; cited by John Kiriakou alongside Cori Bush as the second documented case of AIPAC successfully primarying an incumbent House member for criticizing Israeli conduct in the Gaza war.

beirut.title: Spies of Arlington National Cemetery
beirut.summary: On the Walk With History podcast, John Kiriakou — author of Remains of the Day: A Definitive Guide to Washington D.C.''s Historic Cemeteries — toured Arlington National Cemetery and told personal and historical stories about the intelligence figures buried there, including OSS founder William Donovan, deputy CIA director Vernon Walters, codebreakers William and Elizabeth Friedman, slain station chiefs Richard Welch and William Buckley, U-2 pilot Francis Gary Powers, and Mike Spann, the first CIA officer killed after 9/11.

beirut.title: Curveball
beirut.summary: Cryptonym for the German-handled Iraqi defector whose fabricated WMD intelligence the German BND laundered to the CIA in the run-up to the 2003 Iraq War; per John Kiriakou, in fact a dishwasher at a Shish Kebab restaurant who scraped fake reports from newspaper articles and told the Germans he was an Iraqi scientist with access to weapons of mass destruction; the Germans refused to let the CIA meet or polygraph him, and his fabricated intelligence — biological, chemical, nuclear, and long-range delivery — became one of the central pillars of the Bush administration's WMD case.

beirut.title: Greek Intelligence Service
beirut.summary: Greece's intelligence service, with which John Kiriakou worked closely during his Athens posting; its head of surveillance called off surveillance on him after watching him make a large offering at Saint Nectarios's tomb on the island of Aegina.

beirut.title: Publications Review Board
beirut.summary: The CIA office that must clear anything a former officer publishes. John Kiriakou says everything he writes goes to it — books, articles, "even a letter to the editor of Home and Garden magazine" — and describes how the turnaround tracked his standing at the agency: his first book took 22 months to clear while the leadership hated him; his most recent six cleared in days.

beirut.title: Steven Lalas
beirut.summary: American with top-secret clearance recruited as a spy for Greece's National Intelligence Service (EYP) in a provocative mid-1990s operation run by the country's conservative government. Per John Kiriakou, who did not know Lawless personally, the case was so sensitive that his handler reported directly to the EYP director out of fear the CIA had planted a mole inside the service. Lawless was caught, served about seven years, and was given Greek citizenship on release.

beirut.title: Bab al-Mandab
beirut.summary: The strait where the Horn of Africa nearly meets the south-western tip of the Arabian Peninsula, which John Kiriakou identifies as one of the few American national interests in Yemen and as a chokepoint whose closure would push the global economy into recession.

belmarsh-prison.title: Wikileaks as a System
belmarsh-prison.summary: Per John Kiriakou, WikiLeaks functions less as a single leader than as a durable system — one that protected whistleblowers, helped popularize the term "whistleblower" itself, was credited with contributing to the Arab Spring, weathered pressure to become a defanged NGO, and outlasted the political fallout of its 2010 cable releases (including, in Kiriakou's account, an unintended assist to Donald Trump's election).

belmarsh-prison.title: Ai Whistleblower Initiative
belmarsh-prison.summary: The AI Whistleblower Initiative, working on legal protections for the wave of whistleblowers now coming out of the artificial-intelligence industry.

belmarsh-prison.title: Andrew Feinstein
belmarsh-prison.summary: Referenced on the same WikiLeaks-conference panel as John Kiriakou; the description of Feinstein's talk on the multiple factors that ended apartheid was given by another panelist putting a question to Kiriakou, not by Kiriakou himself.

belmarsh-prison.title: Chaos Computer Club Wikileaks
belmarsh-prison.summary: The Berlin hacker collective that shaped WikiLeaks' early years — and where a journalist first met Daniel Domscheit-Berg under a pseudonym.

belmarsh-prison.title: Chelsea Manning
belmarsh-prison.summary: Former U.S. Army intelligence analyst who provided WikiLeaks its 2010 trove of military and diplomatic documents. Per John Kiriakou, Manning meets the legal definition of whistleblower for exposing war crimes, was a torture victim of prolonged solitary confinement with forced nudity, and was sentenced to 35 years in prison before Barack Obama commuted — not pardoned — her sentence. Kiriakou says Manning later refused a grand jury's offer of immunity and chose renewed jail time rather than testify against Julian Assange.

belmarsh-prison.title: Plus 972
belmarsh-prison.summary: The Israeli platform that, per a 2026 Berlin panel, has published a striking number of IDF whistleblowers as AI enters modern warfare.

below-worlds-end.title: John Kiriakou
below-worlds-end.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

below-worlds-end.title: The Farm
below-worlds-end.summary: The CIA's clandestine training facility in Virginia; site of approximately 80% of all CIA operational training

below-worlds-end.title: Asset acquisition cycle
below-worlds-end.summary: The four-step process — spot, assess, develop, recruit — taught as the first lesson of CIA case officer training

below-worlds-end.title: Bahrain fishing officer demarche
below-worlds-end.summary: Kiriakou's account of serving, while stationed in Bahrain, as the embassy's econ officer and by extension its fishing, banking, aviation, and environment officer — including delivering a formal U.S. demarche to Bahrain's deputy foreign minister over a U.S.-Canada dispute about whether clams legally count as fish.

below-worlds-end.title: Big Assawoman Bay NASA launch
below-worlds-end.summary: John Kiriakou's account of being taken, as a junior CIA analyst, to watch a NASA rocket launch near the village of Big Assawoman on Virginia's Eastern Shore, where he was startled to find foreign space-agency officials present unsupervised.

below-worlds-end.title: Chinese illegal fishing
below-worlds-end.summary: John Kiriakou calls Chinese overfishing one of the world's biggest under-discussed problems, citing the near-extinction of Chilean sea bass and heavy overfishing of Alaskan and Atlantic cod, and recounting personally seeing Chinese fishing vessels in Antarctica on his honeymoon.

benazir-bhutto.title: John Kiriakou
benazir-bhutto.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

benazir-bhutto.title: Abu Zubaydah
benazir-bhutto.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

benazir-bhutto.title: Central Intelligence Agency
benazir-bhutto.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

benazir-bhutto.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
benazir-bhutto.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

benazir-bhutto.title: Jose Rodriguez
benazir-bhutto.summary: Senior CIA officer of the post-9/11 era; identified by John Kiriakou as among those responsible for crimes committed in the name of national security; described as believing himself to be a good guy.

benazir-bhutto.title: Ahmed Chalabi
benazir-bhutto.summary: Iraqi exile and founder of the Iraqi National Congress; per John Kiriakou, a Shia-Kurdish con man who looted Petra Bank in Jordan of $36 million in the 1980s, was sentenced to death in absentia, was pardoned at CIA request, then pocketed $6 million in CIA seed funding for the INC and bought a Mayfair house in cash; later resurrected by Dick Cheney to feed the Pentagon fabricated WMD intelligence used to justify the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

benjamin-netanyahu.title: Kiriakou and Cenk Uygur
benjamin-netanyahu.summary: A grievance John Kiriakou carried for a decade — that Cenk Uygur had spent thirty minutes attacking him over his first letter from prison — resolved live on air in July 2026 when Uygur produced his archive, found no such segment, and both men concluded it had been mistaken identity.

benjamin-netanyahu.title: The Kite Runner rescue mission
benjamin-netanyahu.summary: 2007 covert operation in which John Kiriakou, newly departed from the CIA and working as a corporate-intelligence consultant, was hired by Paramount Studios to secretly evacuate the Afghan child actors of the film "The Kite Runner" and their extended families after real death threats over the film's content.

benjamin-netanyahu.title: Maria Butina
benjamin-netanyahu.summary: Russian gun-rights activist convicted in the United States of failing to register as a foreign agent; John Kiriakou cites her case as an example of the "process crime" of FARA violations, contrasting the severity of her 18-month solitary-confinement sentence with federal guidelines calling for 0-6 months.

benjamin-netanyahu.title: OnlyFans
benjamin-netanyahu.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the man who owned OnlyFans — whom he describes as Ukrainian-American rather than Israeli — was a major donor and strong supporter of Israel, part of a broader claim Kiriakou makes about Israeli involvement in the porn industry.

benjamin-netanyahu.title: Souda Bay Vulnerability and Nasser on American Decisions
benjamin-netanyahu.summary: Two observations John Kiriakou has made on U.S. Mediterranean strategy and decision-making — a U.S. military contact's warning that Souda Bay in Crete, the nearest major port able to host a U.S. aircraft carrier like the USS Gerald Ford, is a possible vulnerability; and Kiriakou's favorite quote from Gamal Abdel Nasser, that Americans never make clear-cut stupid decisions, only complicated ones.

benjamin-netanyahu.title: The false volunteer
benjamin-netanyahu.summary: A walk-in at an American embassy who claimed access to a high-priority target, was placed under surveillance and found to be a restaurant dishwasher, and whom John Kiriakou deliberately intimidated into never approaching an American embassy again.

bernie-kerik.title: Rudy Giuliani
bernie-kerik.summary: Former U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York and Mayor of New York City; in 2018 attempted to extort $2 million from John Kiriakou in exchange for arranging a presidential pardon from President Trump; the attempt was reported to the New York Times by Kiriakou himself and corroborated by Giuliani's then-aide Noelle Dunphy after Giuliani sexually harassed her.

bernie-kerik.title: Bruce Fein
bernie-kerik.summary: John Kiriakou's longtime attorney; former Deputy Attorney General under President Reagan and former General Counsel of the Federal Communications Commission; Harvard Law and Berkeley graduate; present at the 2018 Trump International Hotel meeting at which Rudy Giuliani's aide solicited $2 million from Kiriakou in exchange for a presidential pardon.

bernie-kerik.title: Noelle Dunphy
bernie-kerik.summary: Former aide to Rudy Giuliani; independently corroborated to the New York Times John Kiriakou's account of Giuliani's 2018 $2 million pardon-extortion attempt, after Giuliani's subsequent sexual harassment of her caused her to come forward.

bernie-kerik.title: Robert MacLean
bernie-kerik.summary: TSA whistleblower; the person to whom John Kiriakou first described Rudy Giuliani's 2018 $2 million pardon-extortion attempt the same evening it occurred, and who in turn tipped the FBI (which declined interest) and then the New York Times.

bernie-kerik.title: Sebastian Gorka
bernie-kerik.summary: Former Trump administration deputy assistant; subject of John Kiriakou's second attempted pardon transaction in 2018, in which Gorka asked Kiriakou for $5,000 at a book launch at the Trump International Hotel in exchange for tweeting at the president on his behalf. Kiriakou refused.

bernie-kerik.title: April Glaspie
bernie-kerik.summary: U.S. Ambassador to Iraq in the run-up to the 1990 invasion of Kuwait; per John Kiriakou, delivered to Saddam Hussein — on a State Department cable from Secretary James Baker — the line that the United States had "no position on inter-Arab disputes," which Saddam read as a green light to invade.

bezalel-smotrich.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
bezalel-smotrich.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

bezalel-smotrich.title: Itamar Ben-Gvir
bezalel-smotrich.summary: Israel's far-right Minister of National Security; John Kiriakou cites him as a convicted hate-crime felon placed in charge of security in Gaza and the West Bank over his victims, blames his insistence that any attack would come from the West Bank for diverting forces before October 7, and cites the death-penalty law passed under his portfolio for Palestinian detainees as the first reinstatement of capital punishment in Israel since it was abolished in 1956, excepting only the execution of Adolf Eichmann.

bezalel-smotrich.title: The 1991 Saudi plan for Gaza
bezalel-smotrich.summary: A proposal John Kiriakou says he watched Ambassador Chas Freeman float to the Saudis during his first overseas tour in 1991 — that Saudi Arabia fund a port, an airport, a desalination plant and an electrical grid in Gaza. The Saudis agreed; Israel refused outright. Kiriakou raises it because the identical arrangement resurfaced in the Israeli press more than three decades later.

bezalel-smotrich.title: John Kiriakou
bezalel-smotrich.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

bezalel-smotrich.title: Iran's 2024 drone retaliation
bezalel-smotrich.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Iran's telegraphed 2024 drone strike on Israel — hundreds of slow drones, launched with advance warning to the U.S. and Jordan, nearly all shot down, which he reads as a controlled show of force and an intelligence victory that exposed the Iron Dome.

bezalel-smotrich.title: Piers Morgan
bezalel-smotrich.summary: British broadcaster whose panel show became John Kiriakou's 2025 sparring ring — "the equivalent of a WWE Smackdown with Alan Dershowitz<Cite s="2026-06-27-deep-focus-report-john-kiriakou-on-iran-endless-wars-and-u-s-fo" t="9:18" />." Paired with Scott Horton against Dershowitz and former Mossad chief Moshe Yaalon, Kiriakou said on air that Israel spies on the United States and that Jeffrey Epstein was an Israeli access agent, drawing a chuckle from the general and the claim that spying stopped when Pollard was caught — "General, with all due respect, that's just simply not true." Morgan's producer had to instruct the polite ex-spy not to be afraid to interrupt.

big-assawoman-bay-nasa-launch.title: Bahrain fishing officer demarche
big-assawoman-bay-nasa-launch.summary: Kiriakou's account of serving, while stationed in Bahrain, as the embassy's econ officer and by extension its fishing, banking, aviation, and environment officer — including delivering a formal U.S. demarche to Bahrain's deputy foreign minister over a U.S.-Canada dispute about whether clams legally count as fish.

big-assawoman-bay-nasa-launch.title: Below World's End
big-assawoman-bay-nasa-launch.summary: Film in which John Kiriakou made his acting debut, filmed entirely in Mexico during October 2025; Kiriakou's performance earned him a Screen Actors Guild membership card, and Sean Penn told him after a private screening that he had unknowingly been acting throughout his entire CIA career.

big-assawoman-bay-nasa-launch.title: Chinese illegal fishing
big-assawoman-bay-nasa-launch.summary: John Kiriakou calls Chinese overfishing one of the world's biggest under-discussed problems, citing the near-extinction of Chilean sea bass and heavy overfishing of Alaskan and Atlantic cod, and recounting personally seeing Chinese fishing vessels in Antarctica on his honeymoon.

big-assawoman-bay-nasa-launch.title: Iran Nuclear Assessment
big-assawoman-bay-nasa-launch.summary: Per John Kiriakou's assessment, the US–Israeli military campaign against Iran was a war of choice driven by Israeli political pressure rather than genuine intelligence indicating an Iranian nuclear weapons threat. The CIA produced two National Intelligence Estimates concluding Iran had no nuclear weapons program; Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei issued a fatwa in the 1980s forbidding such a program. The U.S. went to war anyway, in Kiriakou's view, after President Trump replaced the Joint Chiefs of Staff with officers willing to accept Israeli intelligence and proceed.

big-assawoman-bay-nasa-launch.title: Joe Weisberg
big-assawoman-bay-nasa-launch.summary: Former CIA Counterterrorism Center officer and colleague of John Kiriakou who resigned abruptly, saying he did not have it in him to convince people to commit treason, then moved to Hollywood and created the television series The Americans.

big-assawoman-bay-nasa-launch.title: Mike Baker
big-assawoman-bay-nasa-launch.summary: Former CIA case officer; John Kiriakou's predecessor as the CIA's lead officer working the Revolutionary Organization 17 November problem in Athens; characterized by Kiriakou as "the real deal" and as having laid the groundwork for the operations Kiriakou subsequently inherited.

bilderberg-weapon-sales.title: Kissinger and the petrodollar
bilderberg-weapon-sales.summary: John Kiriakou's endorsement of the theory that Henry Kissinger deliberately structured the 1970s petrodollar to tie the U.S. to Middle Eastern oil — creating a standing rationale for policing the region, even as America exports its own fracked oil.

bilderberg-weapon-sales.title: CIA and FBI ties to organized crime
bilderberg-weapon-sales.summary: John Kiriakou's survey of documented U.S. intelligence partnerships with organized crime — the FBI securing wartime ports with the Genovese family, the CIA's Castro plots with the Trafficantes, its work with the Escobar cartel against Colombian communists, and a mob hitman deployed against the Klan.

bilderberg-weapon-sales.title: CIA and the UFO question
bilderberg-weapon-sales.summary: John Kiriakou's consistent answer that UFOs and alien technology are a Pentagon matter, not a CIA one — though he says nearly every former fighter-pilot friend of his has seen something inexplicable, sometimes emerging from the ocean.

bilderberg-weapon-sales.title: Permanent wartime economy
bilderberg-weapon-sales.summary: John Kiriakou's thesis that since 9/11 the United States has run a permanent wartime economy so large that cutting the defense budget would trigger a depression — likening the dependency to crack addiction and warning it makes war almost inevitable.

bilderberg-weapon-sales.title: CIA political action group
bilderberg-weapon-sales.summary: The CIA's most secretive clandestine propaganda arm — successor to the Cold War 'active measures group' — which John Kiriakou says places and funds propagandists worldwide; no officer of it has been publicly identified since 1982, and he encountered its work funding the DNC's and RNC's international arms in post-war Kuwait.

bilderberg-weapon-sales.title: Cold War
bilderberg-weapon-sales.summary: The U.S.–Soviet confrontation that built the CIA John Kiriakou joined. Kiriakou argues the Cold War was real "but also at a certain level desired" — America has always needed an ism to oppose — and that its habits never died: "The Russians thought the Cold War was over, but no one told the US." From its memoirs he draws a standing tradecraft lesson (the CIA''s best recruits were always walk-ins), and in the new Russia and China confrontations he sees a Cold War 2.0 rebuilt on the old exaggerations.

bill-barr.title: Lee Zeldon
bill-barr.summary: Per Megyn Kelly's opening monologue, the EPA administrator reportedly considered by Trump as a possible replacement for Attorney General Pam Bondi.

bill-barr.title: Gail Slater
bill-barr.summary: Per Sean Davis, speaking on the same Megyn Kelly panel as Kiriakou, the head of the DOJ antitrust unit under Pam Bondi who was stripped of authority and then fired.

bill-barr.title: OnlyFans
bill-barr.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the man who owned OnlyFans — whom he describes as Ukrainian-American rather than Israeli — was a major donor and strong supporter of Israel, part of a broader claim Kiriakou makes about Israeli involvement in the porn industry.

bill-barr.title: Cory Booker
bill-barr.summary: Per John Kiriakou, he was "especially furious" with Democratic senator Cory Booker for running through the halls of Congress to get to a photo op standing behind Benjamin Netanyahu, which Kiriakou cites as an example of Democratic silence in the face of AIPAC pressure.

bill-barr.title: LSD Mind Manipulation
bill-barr.summary: Kiriakou on the CIA dosing unwitting men with LSD in safe houses, using sex workers as bait, to find out whether the drug could unlock secrets.

bill-barr.title: Podcast Bros
bill-barr.summary: Per Sohrab Ahmari, speaking on the same Megyn Kelly panel as Kiriakou, podcast bros.

bill-binney.title: Russiagate
bill-binney.summary: John Kiriakou''s rebuttal of the claim that Russia swung the 2016 U.S. election: the Mueller report found no interference, the DNC emails were leaked in person rather than remotely hacked, and Russia''s roughly $50,000 in Facebook ads — half spent after the election — was trivial against billions in campaign spending.

bill-binney.title: Havana Syndrome
bill-binney.summary: Cluster of neurological symptoms — including nausea, ringing in the ears, vertigo, and traumatic brain injury — reported by American diplomatic and intelligence personnel beginning in Havana, Cuba, and subsequently at posts around the world. Per John Kiriakou, his initial skepticism gave way when a friend developed Havana Syndrome with an MRI-confirmed traumatic brain injury after a meeting outside the Russian Foreign Ministry; Kiriakou attributes the syndrome to Russian or Chinese directed-energy weapons and acknowledges the United States used a similar weapon during the operation to capture Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro.

bill-binney.title: Craig Murray
bill-binney.summary: Former British Ambassador to Uzbekistan whom John Kiriakou cites as a whistleblower of extreme torture: during a meeting at the Uzbek intelligence service, Murray heard screaming, walked in, and saw a man being boiled in oil — reporting it cost him his career.

bill-binney.title: James Woolsey
bill-binney.summary: Director of Central Intelligence for twenty-three months at the start of the Clinton administration, forced out over his refusal to discipline anyone after the exposure of Aldrich Ames, and later chairman of Booz Allen Hamilton; John Kiriakou notes that his family attributed four years of illness before his death to Havana syndrome.

bill-binney.title: John Kiriakou
bill-binney.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

bill-binney.title: Kiriakou's Russian media work
bill-binney.summary: John Kiriakou's account of hosting a daily Sputnik radio show for seven and a half years with full contractual freedom to criticize anyone, including Putin — which he did on the morning of the Ukraine invasion — offered as a rebuttal to claims that Russian outlets are mere propaganda.

bill-buckley.title: Mike Spann
bill-buckley.summary: CIA officer; first American killed in combat in Afghanistan after the September 11 attacks; killed during the November 2001 Qala-i-Jangi prison uprising; worked in the Counterterrorism Center bullpen alongside John Kiriakou.

bill-buckley.title: Spies of Arlington National Cemetery
bill-buckley.summary: On the Walk With History podcast, John Kiriakou — author of Remains of the Day: A Definitive Guide to Washington D.C.''s Historic Cemeteries — toured Arlington National Cemetery and told personal and historical stories about the intelligence figures buried there, including OSS founder William Donovan, deputy CIA director Vernon Walters, codebreakers William and Elizabeth Friedman, slain station chiefs Richard Welch and William Buckley, U-2 pilot Francis Gary Powers, and Mike Spann, the first CIA officer killed after 9/11.

bill-buckley.title: Dead Drop (podcast)
bill-buckley.summary: John Kiriakou''s narrative podcast, launched in late 2025 — a season-long, memoir-style retelling of his life in intelligence, from recruitment ("The New Recruit") through Athens ("Golden Boy") to the post-9/11 hunt ("The Hunt Begins"), with mini-episodes like "A Spy''s Guide to Sofia." Written by Kiriakou with Alan Katz, produced by Costard & Touchstone Productions, with Kiriakou, Katz, and Nick Mechanic as executive producers. Its stated goal: "the deepest possible perspective on the world of spying and what makes any spy tick."

bill-buckley.title: Francis Gary Powers
bill-buckley.summary: U-2 pilot whose 1960 shoot-down over the Soviet Union and subsequent capture the CIA initially denied any knowledge of, denying not only that he was CIA but that he was U.S. government at all, until trading him in a bridge-of-spies prisoner exchange. Buried at Arlington National Cemetery. Per John Kiriakou, after his U-2 career Powers ended up piloting a Los Angeles traffic helicopter, and was killed when it crashed.

bill-buckley.title: Hezbollah
bill-buckley.summary: Lebanese Shia militant organization and political party. Per John Kiriakou, Israel''s strategic goal regarding Hezbollah is not to defeat it outright but to keep Lebanon in a state of chaos that serves Israeli interests. He cites two Israeli operations: the simultaneous pager-detonation attack that decapitated Hezbollah''s leadership, which he called ''the most incredible operation I''ve ever seen,'' and the strike that killed former leader Hassan Nasrallah by leveling an entire complex and killing roughly 300 people — which he characterized as a war crime.

bill-buckley.title: Richard Welch
bill-buckley.summary: CIA Athens station chief assassinated December 23, 1975; the first victim of [Revolutionary Organization 17 November](/wiki/revolutionary-organization-17-november)

bill-burns.title: Donald Trump
bill-burns.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

bill-burns.title: Kiriakou's transfer to the Directorate of Operations
bill-burns.summary: John Kiriakou's roughly two-month internal campaign to transfer from the CIA's analytic Directorate of Intelligence to the operational Directorate of Operations, overcoming what he calls a "natural bias in operations against the eggheads on the analytic side," followed by an Athens posting secured because he was the only person in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic. Covers his full CIA career arc from 1988/1990 recruitment through analyst years on Iraq, the switch to operations, 9/11, the enhanced-interrogation refusal, executive assistant to the deputy director for operations, and his eventual resignation and post-CIA career.

bill-burns.title: Havana Syndrome
bill-burns.summary: Cluster of neurological symptoms — including nausea, ringing in the ears, vertigo, and traumatic brain injury — reported by American diplomatic and intelligence personnel beginning in Havana, Cuba, and subsequently at posts around the world. Per John Kiriakou, his initial skepticism gave way when a friend developed Havana Syndrome with an MRI-confirmed traumatic brain injury after a meeting outside the Russian Foreign Ministry; Kiriakou attributes the syndrome to Russian or Chinese directed-energy weapons and acknowledges the United States used a similar weapon during the operation to capture Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro.

bill-burns.title: John Ratcliffe
bill-burns.summary: CIA director under Trump's second term; per John Kiriakou, a "bombthrower" he mostly disagrees with politically but supports as a needed disruptor for the agency, though Kiriakou doubts Ratcliffe has the wherewithal to meaningfully reform the CIA — noting that if Bill Burns couldn't do it, Ratcliffe likely can't either.

bill-burns.title: Abolish the CIA
bill-burns.summary: John Kiriakou's position that the CIA should be abolished because its functions are already duplicated by the other 17 U.S. intelligence agencies — analysis by the State Department, human spying by the Pentagon, technology by DARPA, NSA and the private sector.

bill-burns.title: Allen Dulles
bill-burns.summary: Long-serving CIA director whom John Kiriakou calls a 'monster' — a United Fruit board member who helped overthrow Guatemala's Arbenz, whose bust greeted visitors at CIA headquarters, and who was, unlike James Angleton, aware of his own guilt.

bill-casey.title: Church Committee
bill-casey.summary: U.S. Senate investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 that examined domestic intelligence abuses by the CIA, FBI, and NSA; per John Kiriakou, the Church Committee — alongside the concurrent Pike Committee in the House — was the last genuine moment of legislative oversight over the intelligence community, born of a national consensus that government had gone dangerously off course. Its work led to the creation of the permanent Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, which Kiriakou says ceased to function as real oversight roughly seven years after its founding.

bill-casey.title: CIA National Resources Division
bill-casey.summary: The Central Intelligence Agency's domestic intelligence-collection arm, created in the 1980s by Director William J. Casey

bill-casey.title: Central Intelligence Agency
bill-casey.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

bill-casey.title: CIA Political Psychology Division
bill-casey.summary: The Central Intelligence Agency unit founded by Dr. Gerald Post in the 1970s to produce long-distance psychiatric evaluations of foreign leaders

bill-casey.title: USAID as a CIA cover vehicle
bill-casey.summary: John Kiriakou's account of USAID's use by the CIA as a channel for covert operations and money laundering rather than as an undercover posting for individual officers — including a declassified 1972 exchange in which Henry Kissinger confirmed the CIA had paid Laotian mercenaries through USAID payroll checks.

bill-casey.title: Mahmud (alias)
bill-casey.summary: Pseudonym for an Egyptian al-Qaeda fighter recruited by John Kiriakou in an unnamed country during the early 2000s

bill-clinton.title: Christopher Hitchens
bill-clinton.summary: British-American journalist and author who, at John Kiriakou's telling, famously argued in the mid-2000s that CIA waterboarding was 'nothing … not a big deal,' agreed in 2008 to undergo a filmed waterboarding demonstration, tapped out after roughly seventeen seconds, and thereafter suffered panic attacks for the rest of his life whenever he could not breathe for a moment.

bill-clinton.title: Thirty-year mandatory declassification
