bill-clinton.summary: The statutory requirement, described by John Kiriakou, that classified American documents be released after thirty years — a law he says virtually nobody knows about, and which he raises against the continued withholding of Kennedy assassination records more than sixty years on. He also describes the redaction practice that operates alongside it.

bill-clinton.title: FISA court
bill-clinton.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the secret Foreign Intelligence Surveillance court — created under Carter, sitting atop the Justice Department, issuing warrants that are never public — which he says was abused against Carter Page as part of what he believes was John Brennan's plan to deny Trump the presidency.

bill-clinton.title: Mack McLarty
bill-clinton.summary: U.S. political consultant and Bill Clinton's former White House Chief of Staff; founder of McLarty Associates (formerly Kissinger McLarty), at which John Kiriakou was given a private office and part-time secretary in 2008.

bill-clinton.title: Watching naval movements
bill-clinton.summary: One of the first lessons John Kiriakou says he learned at the CIA: to read American military intentions, watch naval movements — one carrier strike group means business, two means war. He used it to correctly predict the 2026 strike on Iran days in advance.

bill-clinton.title: Marjorie Taylor Greene
bill-clinton.summary: American congresswoman whom John Kiriakou, despite deep political disagreement, has repeatedly credited for breaking with her party on the Epstein files, on military aid to Israel, and on Gaza. He describes her as courageous for pressing Donald Trump to release the files unredacted, and says the pressure ultimately forced her out of Washington.

bill-pulte.title: Office of the Director of National Intelligence
bill-pulte.summary: The intelligence-community layer created in 2004, which John Kiriakou argues should never have existed. He traces its origin to George Tenet's failures over 9/11 and Iraq, notes it grew from sixteen employees to roughly twenty-four thousand, and points out that most agencies nominally under it are Defense Department bodies over which it controls nothing but the budget.

bill-pulte.title: Tulsi Gabbard
bill-pulte.summary: U.S. Director of National Intelligence; a longtime family friend of John Kiriakou's, who has known her since she was 12; Kiriakou calls her appointment "an inspired choice" despite disagreeing with her decision to join the Republican Party, and says she appears to have given up her opposition to Section 702 surveillance to secure Senate confirmation.

bill-pulte.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
bill-pulte.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

bill-pulte.title: Five Eyes
bill-pulte.summary: The intelligence-sharing partnership of the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand

bill-pulte.title: Kiriakou pardon request
bill-pulte.summary: John Kiriakou's public campaign for a presidential pardon from Donald Trump to restore the pension and firearm rights he lost after his 2013 felony conviction for disclosing the identity of a covert CIA officer; includes a five-second Mar-a-Lago encounter in which Trump referred him to Attorney General Pam Bondi, a Kalshi prediction-market contract that opened at roughly 19 to 20 percent odds on his being pardoned, and letters of support from Tucker Carlson, Judge Andrew Napolitano and Dr. Phil.

bill-pulte.title: Antisemitism and anti-Zionism
bill-pulte.summary: The conflation of criticism of the Israeli state with hatred of Jews, which John Kiriakou describes as a worldwide confusion and, according to a young Israeli he spoke to, an explicit lesson of the Israeli school system; a subject Kiriakou says he personally struggles with.

bill-richardson.title: John Kerry
bill-richardson.summary: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts; chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee during John Kiriakou's 2009 service as the committee's senior investigator; subsequently U.S. Secretary of State; characterized by Kiriakou as a coward who buckled under CIA pressure on the Dasht-i-Leili reopening and as personally fixated on his perceived theft of the Secretary of State position by Hillary Clinton; the famously thrown medals were duplicates purchased at the post exchange.

bill-richardson.title: John Kiriakou
bill-richardson.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

bill-richardson.title: Mack McLarty
bill-richardson.summary: U.S. political consultant and Bill Clinton's former White House Chief of Staff; founder of McLarty Associates (formerly Kissinger McLarty), at which John Kiriakou was given a private office and part-time secretary in 2008.

bill-richardson.title: Dasht-i-Leili massacre
bill-richardson.summary: Late-November 2001 mass suffocation of approximately 2,000 surrendered Taliban prisoners in unventilated shipping containers in the Afghan desert; the prisoners' surrender was negotiated by the CIA via the Northern Alliance, the transport order was issued by the CIA, and the operation was overseen by Northern Alliance warlord Abdul Rashid Dostum; John Kiriakou in 2009 as Senate Foreign Relations Committee investigator attempted to reopen the case under a 2008 Obama campaign promise; the CIA's classified response was, per Kiriakou, "go fuck yourself."

bill-richardson.title: Bill Clinton
bill-richardson.summary: 42nd U.S. president whom John Kiriakou describes as wholly disinterested in intelligence — briefed by the CIA only twice in eight years, with Vice President Al Gore taking the daily briefing instead and relaying anything important.

bill-richardson.title: Deloitte Consulting Career
bill-richardson.summary: John Kiriakou's post-CIA career at Deloitte Consulting (2004–2008), covering two corporate acquisitions he says he drove — India Tiger Analysis and, in effect, Bering Point — and ending in his effective firing weeks before his ABC News whistleblower interview aired.

billy-waugh.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
billy-waugh.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

billy-waugh.title: Carlos the Jackal
billy-waugh.summary: Venezuelan-born militant (Ilich Ramírez Sánchez) active in the 1970s and 1980s; per John Kiriakou, 'the Osama bin Laden of the 70s and 80s.' Kiriakou spent his Athens posting trying to identify the middleman linking Carlos to the Greek terrorist group 17 November, then six months working the lead with MI5 in London; Carlos was finally run down by CIA contractor Billy Waugh in a Khartoum vegetable market and captured in 1994.

billy-waugh.title: Counterterrorism Center
billy-waugh.summary: The CIA's Counterterrorism Center (CTC) — the unit where John Kiriakou spent the defining years of his operational career. He joined in the late 1990s as the only officer in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic, served as chief of counterintelligence in the bin Laden unit, watched the Center swell from a few hundred employees to nearly 2,000 by September 12, 2001, and it was to CTC that he walked back down in May 2002 to refuse the torture program — the moment, he says, the CIA began to turn on him.

billy-waugh.title: Kiriakou's transfer to the Directorate of Operations
billy-waugh.summary: John Kiriakou's roughly two-month internal campaign to transfer from the CIA's analytic Directorate of Intelligence to the operational Directorate of Operations, overcoming what he calls a "natural bias in operations against the eggheads on the analytic side," followed by an Athens posting secured because he was the only person in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic. Covers his full CIA career arc from 1988/1990 recruitment through analyst years on Iraq, the switch to operations, 9/11, the enhanced-interrogation refusal, executive assistant to the deputy director for operations, and his eventual resignation and post-CIA career.

billy-waugh.title: Abu Zubaydah
billy-waugh.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

billy-waugh.title: Cofer Black
billy-waugh.summary: Former head of the CIA Counterterrorism Center during and immediately after the September 11 attacks; principal architect of the agency's paramilitary turn on September 12, 2001; later Vice President of Blackwater under Erik Prince.

black-cube.title: MOSSAD
black-cube.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

black-cube.title: AIPAC
black-cube.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

black-cube.title: Mujahedin-e Khalq (MEK)
black-cube.summary: Iranian opposition group that John Kiriakou describes as 'a quasi-communist cult' and a former U.S.-designated terrorist organization. Founded by a husband-and-wife team in the 1960s and based in northeastern Iraq, the MEK launched cross-border terrorist attacks into Iran and, per Kiriakou, attempted to murder the American ambassador and the senior U.S. general in Iran — carrying out anti-American attacks for decades. After Saddam Hussein expelled them they relocated to Paris; current leader Maryam Rajavi is widely believed to have killed or had killed her vanished husband to take over. In 2009 the MEK hired high-powered Washington lobbyists (from Howard Dean to Rudy Giuliani) to get off the terrorism list, and Kiriakou says it is now funded by Israel and used as assassins-for-hire in Tehran.

black-cube.title: Khaled Mashal
black-cube.summary: Senior Hamas political leader; survived a 1997 Mossad poisoning attempt in Amman, Jordan; the operation's failure and the political fallout in Jordan are the canonical example, in John Kiriakou's account, of Israeli operational hostility carried out in friendly third-country territory without regard for the diplomatic consequences.

black-cube.title: Mahmoud al-Mabhouh
black-cube.summary: Senior Hamas figure assassinated by Mossad in a Dubai hotel room in January 2010; the operation has been studied by intelligence services worldwide for its tradecraft, in particular the unsolved question of how the assassination team locked the hotel-room door from the inside after killing him.

black-cube.title: Veterans' benefits for IDF service
black-cube.summary: A bill sponsored by a Republican congressman from Pennsylvania and one from Ohio that would extend US veterans' benefits to any American who joins the Israel Defense Forces. John Kiriakou calls it an outrage and, as an American, treason.

blackwater.title: Cofer Black
blackwater.summary: Former head of the CIA Counterterrorism Center during and immediately after the September 11 attacks; principal architect of the agency's paramilitary turn on September 12, 2001; later Vice President of Blackwater under Erik Prince.

blackwater.title: Executive Order 12333
blackwater.summary: The U.S. presidential directive — in its post-9/11 amended form — that grants the CIA the legal authority to kill any individual anywhere in the world deemed by the agency to pose a "clear and present danger" to the United States; the legal foundation underlying both CIA paramilitary operations and the agency's contractor relationships including with Blackwater.

blackwater.title: Erik Prince
blackwater.summary: Founder of Blackwater; CIA non-official-cover officer with a 201 file; identified publicly by Leon Panetta in front of the House Intelligence Committee; lives in Dubai outside U.S. jurisdiction; in popular culture invoked, alongside Elon Musk, as the composite figure for the billionaire in the Tyrell Vanto film featuring John Kiriakou.

blackwater.title: Title 10 vs Title 50
blackwater.summary: The U.S. legal-code distinction governing which kinds of armed action fall under military authority (Title 10) and which fall under intelligence authority (Title 50); the operative legal frame for the post-9/11 question of whether CIA contractors can lawfully kill in the agency's name, addressed in the 2025 Ninth Circuit ruling in the Abu Zubaydah contractor case.

blackwater.title: Global Response Staff
blackwater.summary: The CIA's protective-security program for case officers operating in high-threat environments; run for the agency by Blackwater; especially active in Baghdad's Green Zone during the Iraq War, where movement between fixed locations was treated as life-threatening.

blackwater.title: Special Activities Division
blackwater.summary: The CIA's paramilitary arm; described by John Kiriakou as having two organizationally distinct components — the pre-9/11 SAD, a covert-action division within the Directorate of Operations, and a post-9/11 special activities group within the Counterterrorism Center, staffed largely by personnel on secondment from Delta Force, SEAL Team 6, and other special-operations units.

bluffdale-nsa-facility.title: NSA Surveillance
bluffdale-nsa-facility.summary: ''It is part of NSA''s founding charter that it is not allowed to spy on Americans'' — Kiriakou on warrantless collection and the Bluffdale warehouse.

bluffdale-nsa-facility.title: Vault 7
bluffdale-nsa-facility.summary: The 2017 WikiLeaks disclosure of thousands of pages of CIA Directorate of Science and Technology documents — leaked by agency engineer Joshua Schulte — revealing CIA technical capabilities including remote takeover of internet-connected cars, conversion of smart-TV speakers into covert microphones, and the planting of Russian or Persian language fragments in foreign systems to mislead attribution.

bluffdale-nsa-facility.title: Central Intelligence Agency
bluffdale-nsa-facility.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

bluffdale-nsa-facility.title: Patriot Act
bluffdale-nsa-facility.summary: U.S. law passed after the September 11 attacks that vastly expanded domestic surveillance authority. Per John Kiriakou, the Patriot Act ''opened up everything'' — and he disputes the common belief that 9/11 was required to pass it: ''You underestimate Congress. They didn''t need a catastrophe — they would just pass it because they can.'' He ties it to NSA bulk-collection programs that vacuum up every phone call, text, email, and piece of metadata from Americans, in violation of the NSA''s own charter.

bluffdale-nsa-facility.title: Balochistan drone base
bluffdale-nsa-facility.summary: Secret CIA drone surveillance base in southwestern Pakistan's Balochistan region; its location was inadvertently disclosed when investigative journalist Jason Leopold filed a Freedom of Information Act request for Pentagon aviation-fuel-delivery records and identified an outsized fuel flow to the otherwise-undocumented base.

bluffdale-nsa-facility.title: FCI Loretto
bluffdale-nsa-facility.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

bob-baer.title: Sandy Berger
bob-baer.summary: National Security Adviser under President Bill Clinton; per John Kiriakou, the official who shut down CIA case officer Bob Baer's mid-1990s plan to assassinate Saddam Hussein from northern Iraq, by calling the CIA after an NSA intercept and threatening Baer with a conspiracy charge unless he was recalled.

bob-baer.title: The Reluctant Spy
bob-baer.summary: John Kiriakou''s 2009 memoir, The Reluctant Spy: My Secret Life in the CIA''s War on Terror, begun in secret months before he blew the whistle and reaching number five on the New York Times bestseller list.

bob-baer.title: Saddam Hussein
bob-baer.summary: President of Iraq from 1979 until the 2003 U.S. invasion; subject of John Kiriakou's CIA portfolio from January 1990 onward, in which capacity Kiriakou became, at age 25, "Saddam Hussein's intelligence community biographer" and the analyst who briefed President George H. W. Bush in the Oval Office on the morning of the 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

bob-baer.title: Bahrain Posting (1994–1996)
bob-baer.summary: John Kiriakou's 1994–1996 assignment to Bahrain under U.S. State Department cover as second secretary for economic affairs — arriving with his wife Joanne and infant son Chris on August 1, 1994, into a tiny Gulf monarchy whose sectarian tensions erupted, two months later, into the first Intifada.

bob-baer.title: George H.W. Bush
bob-baer.summary: The 41st president — and the one John Kiriakou briefed a number of times, finding him "far more worldly" than the others, as befits a former CIA director. Kiriakou credits him with throwing away his presidency by keeping his word and stopping short of Baghdad, faults the ceasefire's helicopter loophole that let Saddam slaughter the Shia, calls him the last president to give the Arabs a fair shake — cutting off loan guarantees until Israel stopped building settlements — and traces the second Iraq war's personal edge to Saddam's 1993 attempt to assassinate him.

bob-baer.title: Souda Bay Vulnerability and Nasser on American Decisions
bob-baer.summary: Two observations John Kiriakou has made on U.S. Mediterranean strategy and decision-making — a U.S. military contact's warning that Souda Bay in Crete, the nearest major port able to host a U.S. aircraft carrier like the USS Gerald Ford, is a possible vulnerability; and Kiriakou's favorite quote from Gamal Abdel Nasser, that Americans never make clear-cut stupid decisions, only complicated ones.

bob-cia-hr.title: John Kiriakou
bob-cia-hr.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

bob-cia-hr.title: Jerrold Post
bob-cia-hr.summary: American political psychiatrist and CIA officer who recruited John Kiriakou into the agency in 1988 through the CIA's covert campus recruiting program, working undercover as a George Washington University professor; founder of the CIA's Political Psychology Division (also called the Office of Leadership Analysis). Held a bachelor's, master's, and PhD in psychology and a PhD in political science, all from Yale, plus an MD from Harvard, and authored a dozen books on the psychology of world leaders and terrorists. Per Kiriakou, Post identified in him not just writing talent but "sociopathic tendencies" — and, when Kiriakou later blew the whistle, called to congratulate him, telling him that reaction proved he was not a true sociopath. Died of COVID-19, approximately 2022.

bob-cia-hr.title: CIA Political Psychology Division
bob-cia-hr.summary: The Central Intelligence Agency unit founded by Dr. Gerald Post in the 1970s to produce long-distance psychiatric evaluations of foreign leaders

bob-cia-hr.title: United Food and Commercial Workers
bob-cia-hr.summary: The huge K Street labor union where a young John Kiriakou — from a family with a long labor history — was working when Dr. Jerrold Post''s class assignment changed his life: shadow your boss for a week and write his psychological profile. Kiriakou''s boss was a mean old-school organizer whose back had been broken by scabs; halfway through the week Kiriakou called him a racist ("which he was"), and the resulting paper diagnosed the man as a sociopath and potentially dangerous. The paper is what put Kiriakou on the CIA''s radar.

bob-cia-hr.title: Asset acquisition cycle
bob-cia-hr.summary: The four-step process — spot, assess, develop, recruit — taught as the first lesson of CIA case officer training

bob-cia-hr.title: William J. Casey
bob-cia-hr.summary: Director of Central Intelligence under the Reagan administration; creator of the CIA's domestic intelligence-collection arm

bob-grenier.title: George Tenet
bob-grenier.summary: Director of Central Intelligence from 1997 to 2004, spanning the September 11 attacks and the early enhanced-interrogation program; identified by John Kiriakou as John Brennan's institutional patron at the agency; the figure who ordered the Five Eyes intelligence services to "open the files" to each other in the early 2000s.

bob-grenier.title: Pakistan Station (2002)
bob-grenier.summary: John Kiriakou's January 2002 arrival in Islamabad to become CIA chief of counterterrorism operations — a journey via London and Kuwait with lost luggage, a warning that steered him away from the soon-to-be-bombed Marriott, a skeleton counterterrorism branch of seven CIA retirees, and the raids that followed.

bob-grenier.title: Jim Pavitt
bob-grenier.summary: Long-serving CIA Deputy Director for Operations during the early post-9/11 period; characterized by John Kiriakou as "a legendary officer and a really great guy"; mocked John Brennan openly within the agency for Brennan's recurring stated ambition to head his own intelligence agency.

bob-grenier.title: Matt DeHart
bob-grenier.summary: American Army veteran and whistleblower prosecuted on charges including child pornography that the Justice Department later admitted, in court, did not exist; per John Kiriakou, DeHart fled to Canada at the first sign of military trouble, was returned to the U.S., and was held without bond as a flight risk.

bob-grenier.title: Girls' madrasa raid error
bob-grenier.summary: A mistaken CIA raid, conducted the night of the Abu Zubaydah operation, on the home of an elderly Pakistani man running an unlicensed girls' madrasa — the only phone in the neighborhood, which al-Qaeda fighters had been using and the CIA had been intercepting. John Kiriakou personally apologized to the man on the president's behalf and arranged compensation.

bob-trout.title: Mark McDougall
bob-trout.summary: U.S. criminal defense attorney; part of John Kiriakou's defense team in the 2012–2013 Espionage Act prosecution; the attorney whose framing of the case — "your problem is you think this is about justice and it's not about justice; it's about mitigating damage" — Kiriakou credits as the argument that persuaded him to take the final plea deal.

bob-trout.title: Doing Time Like a Spy
bob-trout.summary: Prison memoir by John Kiriakou, full title Doing Time Like a Spy: How the CIA Taught Me to Survive and Thrive in Prison; winner of two literary awards and reissued in a second edition by Simon and Schuster.

bob-trout.title: Prison racial segregation
bob-trout.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the rigid racial and ethnic division of American prisons — a cafeteria split like the 1950s South — and his argument that segregating and hardening inmates for years, then releasing them with no skills, makes society less safe.

bob-trout.title: Tora Bora
bob-trout.summary: Mountainous cave complex in eastern Afghanistan that served as an al-Qaeda redoubt after the September 11 attacks. Per John Kiriakou — chief of counterterrorism operations in Pakistan at the time — the CIA killed al-Qaeda military-affairs chief Mohammed Atef there in October 2001, and Tora Bora was the backdrop to the hunt for the senior al-Qaeda leadership that culminated in the capture of Abu Zubaydah. Kiriakou also recounts an Egyptian al-Qaeda fighter he later recruited who survived a cruise-missile strike on a Tora Bora cave — one of only two who came out alive, his ears bleeding, describing the explosion as the most hideous sound he had ever heard.

bob-trout.title: Plato Cacheris
bob-trout.summary: Legendary Washington, D.C. defense attorney who served as John Kiriakou''s lead counsel in his 2012–2013 Espionage Act prosecution. Per Kiriakou, when discovery revealed the FBI had run a fake-diplomat sting against him, Cacheris explained the government''s posture bluntly: ''Because they have a shit case and they know it''s shit, and that''s why we''re going to trial.'' He spent most of the case urging trial, then drove to Kiriakou''s house on decision day and said ''You stupid son of a bitch — take the deal.'' Cacheris also represented FBI spy Robert Hanssen.

bob-trout.title: FCI Loretto
bob-trout.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

bob-woodward-cia-access.title: Nord Stream pipeline sabotage
bob-woodward-cia-access.summary: The 2022 destruction of the Nord Stream gas pipelines, whose responsibility John Kiriakou treats as genuinely unresolved — citing Seymour Hersh's reporting that the CIA did it, a later Ukrainian special-forces claim of a sailboat-based operation carried out without Zelensky's knowledge, and a retired CIA colleague's private theory that Putin blew up his own pipeline to blame the Americans.

bob-woodward-cia-access.title: Ray McGovern
bob-woodward-cia-access.summary: Former senior CIA analyst turned antiwar dissident, and one of John Kiriakou's closest friends — "like a brother to me." Kiriakou began working at the CIA on the Monday after the Friday McGovern retired in January 1990, so the two never overlapped inside; they became comrades in the whistleblower world instead. McGovern coined the "MICIMATT" framing Kiriakou often borrows, went into Putin's office with Oliver Stone for a 40-minute meeting, and — per Kiriakou — believes 9/11 was a conspiracy, a view Kiriakou affectionately notes is far from his own.

bob-woodward-cia-access.title: Adnan Khashoggi
bob-woodward-cia-access.summary: Saudi arms dealer and Iran-Contra middleman whom John Kiriakou says was mentioned 'all the time' at the CIA — in pointed contrast to Jeffrey Epstein, whose name he never once heard there.

bob-woodward-cia-access.title: Andrew Bustamante
bob-woodward-cia-access.summary: Former CIA officer who sells CIA-style training online; John Kiriakou identifies him as the lone critic of his work hosting a show on a Russian network, and argues Bustamante's training business — open to anyone who pays — is the more problematic of the two.

bob-woodward-cia-access.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
bob-woodward-cia-access.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

bob-woodward-cia-access.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
bob-woodward-cia-access.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

bojinka-plot.title: Abu Zubaydah
bojinka-plot.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

bojinka-plot.title: John Kiriakou
bojinka-plot.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

bojinka-plot.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
bojinka-plot.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

bojinka-plot.title: Ali Soufan
bojinka-plot.summary: FBI special agent who handled Abu Zubaydah immediately after his March 2002 capture; through patient, respectful interrogation produced the only actionable intelligence ever obtained from the detainee, including the first identification of "Mukhtar" as Khalid Sheikh Mohammed.

bojinka-plot.title: Khalid Sheikh Mohammed
bojinka-plot.summary: Mastermind of the September 11, 2001 attacks; identified to the CIA by Abu Zubaydah, in the course of FBI interrogator Ali Soufan's rapport-based debriefing at the black site, as the man behind the kunya "Mukhtar" the agency had been hunting since at least 1996 for the Bojinka plot; per Kiriakou's relay of his self-account, radicalized by news video of an Israeli soldier with his boot on the neck of a Palestinian woman.

bojinka-plot.title: John Brennan
bojinka-plot.summary: Former Director of the CIA; characterized in KiriPedia's source corpus as the principal architect of the agency's enhanced interrogation program and as having plotted against an elected President

brett-mcgurk.title: CIA adultery culture
brett-mcgurk.summary: John Kiriakou's recurring characterization of the CIA officer corps as riddled with adultery and casual sex — which he frames not as gossip but as a systemic counterintelligence vulnerability that makes officers easy to recruit.

brett-mcgurk.title: Asset acquisition cycle
brett-mcgurk.summary: The four-step process — spot, assess, develop, recruit — taught as the first lesson of CIA case officer training

brett-mcgurk.title: Barack Obama
brett-mcgurk.summary: 44th U.S. president; in John Kiriakou's account, Obama publicly recounted refusing Benjamin Netanyahu's demand to bomb Iran and calling Israel's threat to use nuclear weapons a bluff — a bluff Kiriakou says Donald Trump later believed.

brett-mcgurk.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
brett-mcgurk.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

brett-mcgurk.title: Caspar Weinberger
brett-mcgurk.summary: U.S. Secretary of Defense under Ronald Reagan; John Kiriakou cites Weinberger's assessment that Jonathan Pollard's espionage caused "grave damage" — the highest category of harm — to U.S. national security.

brett-mcgurk.title: Church Committee
brett-mcgurk.summary: U.S. Senate investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 that examined domestic intelligence abuses by the CIA, FBI, and NSA; per John Kiriakou, the Church Committee — alongside the concurrent Pike Committee in the House — was the last genuine moment of legislative oversight over the intelligence community, born of a national consensus that government had gone dangerously off course. Its work led to the creation of the permanent Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, which Kiriakou says ceased to function as real oversight roughly seven years after its founding.

brian-kelley.title: Robert Hanssen
brian-kelley.summary: FBI counterintelligence chief and Soviet/Russian mole; framed CIA counterintelligence chief Brian Kelley as the source of compromised assets — leading the FBI to surveil Kelly for a year and a half and threaten his family with the death penalty — before Hanssen himself was identified as the actual traitor.

brian-kelley.title: Eric O'Neill
brian-kelley.summary: Former FBI analyst placed as Robert Hanssen's nominal assistant in the final months of the FBI's mole investigation; his role was to observe Hanssen and detect tradecraft slip-ups that would confirm Hanssen as the mole. After Hanssen's arrest, O'Neill resigned from the FBI, citing the stress of the operation. Subject of the 2007 film Breach.

brian-kelley.title: Harold James Nicholson
brian-kelley.summary: Former CIA Station Chief, Singapore; the third major modern CIA mole for the Russians after Aldrich Ames and Robert Hanssen. Per John Kiriakou, Nicholson was a senior officer at the CIA Counterterrorism Center during Kiriakou's tenure there. Sentenced to 31 years and seven months in 1997. While in prison, attempted to recruit his own son to act as a courier between him and the Russian intelligence service so his espionage payments could continue to compound for his eventual release — and was caught when his son walked up to the Russian embassy in Washington under FBI surveillance.

brian-kelley.title: Afghan heroin policy
brian-kelley.summary: The post-2001 U.S. policy in Afghanistan of protecting, and per John Kiriakou actively encouraging, the cultivation of heroin poppy. Under the Taliban in 2000 Afghanistan produced 0% of the world's heroin; by 2009 under American occupation it produced 93%. Per a DEA officer Kiriakou consulted with on the policy paper he was preparing for Senator Kerry, the strategic rationale was that nearly all of the heroin flowed to Iran and Russia, addiction in those countries was considered desirable as a long-run societal weakener, and the same logic now operates in reverse with Chinese fentanyl flowing into the United States.

brian-kelley.title: Ahmed Khatib
brian-kelley.summary: Iraqi-installed occupation governor of Kuwait announced on August 2, 1990, hours after the invasion; medical doctor trained at the American University of Beirut whose mother had been a Sudanese slave in the Kuwaiti royal household; college roommate of George Habash and co-founder of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine.

brian-kelley.title: Ai Weiwei
brian-kelley.summary: Chinese contemporary artist and pro-democracy activist; designer of the Beijing Olympic Stadium; per John Kiriakou, produced a Lego portrait of him as one of 178 political prisoners in the series, with Kiriakou's panel positioned next to Martin Luther King Jr.; the work is now in the permanent collection of the Smithsonian Institution.

brian-ross.title: John Kiriakou
brian-ross.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

brian-ross.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
brian-ross.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

brian-ross.title: Abu Zubaydah
brian-ross.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

brian-ross.title: John Brennan
brian-ross.summary: Former Director of the CIA; characterized in KiriPedia's source corpus as the principal architect of the agency's enhanced interrogation program and as having plotted against an elected President

brian-ross.title: Ali Soufan
brian-ross.summary: FBI special agent who handled Abu Zubaydah immediately after his March 2002 capture; through patient, respectful interrogation produced the only actionable intelligence ever obtained from the detainee, including the first identification of "Mukhtar" as Khalid Sheikh Mohammed.

brian-ross.title: MOSSAD
brian-ross.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

british-bases-in-cyprus.title: Akrotiri Village Evacuation
british-bases-in-cyprus.summary: Kiriakou says the drone that hit Britain's Akrotiri base in Cyprus was likely an Israeli operation, staged and then falsely blamed on Iran.

british-bases-in-cyprus.title: John Kiriakou
british-bases-in-cyprus.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

british-bases-in-cyprus.title: Abu Nidal Organization
british-bases-in-cyprus.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the CIA destroyed the Abu Nidal Organization from within by exploiting Abu Nidal''s pathological paranoia: rather than recruiting members (impossible given the group''s extreme anti-American orientation), the agency planted false signals that various members were already cooperating with US intelligence. Members began killing each other one by one. Kiriakou: ''Next thing you know, they''ve all killed each other and the only one left is Abu Nidal.'' He also disbelieves the official heart-attack cause of Abu Nidal''s death, attributing it to a Saddam Hussein ''control'' decision.

british-bases-in-cyprus.title: Aldrich Ames
british-bases-in-cyprus.summary: Senior CIA officer — a GS-15 who rose to chief of counterintelligence for the Soviet branch — who spied for the KGB. Per John Kiriakou, Ames's first act of betrayal was selling the identities of two CIA agents to the Russians for $50,000 to pay off a credit-card debt; both agents were immediately executed. He ultimately caused the deaths of twelve people, accumulated $2 million, bought a house in Arlington for that amount, drove a Jaguar to work on a $70,000 salary, and built an in-ground pool with a gazebo — all while being known throughout the office as a daily drunk. A 27-year-old officer sat on the initial security file for eighteen months. Analyst Sandy Grimes ultimately caught him.

british-bases-in-cyprus.title: Bojinka plot
british-bases-in-cyprus.summary: 1996 Khalid Sheikh Mohammed–planned operation, prepared in a Manila, Philippines apartment, to hijack as many as fourteen Boeing 747s and crash them into buildings along the U.S. West Coast; disrupted only by accident, when a cleaning lady let herself into the apartment while the planner was out, recognized the materials laid out as a terrorist plot, and called the police — who alerted Filipino intelligence and, in turn, the CIA. The plot's architect was known to U.S. intelligence for the next six years only by the alias "Mukhtar," his true identity as Khalid Sheikh Mohammed surfacing only when Abu Zubaydah named him to FBI agent Ali Soufan in 2002.

british-bases-in-cyprus.title: CIA–FBI interagency rivalry and 9/11
british-bases-in-cyprus.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the historical CIA–FBI rivalry, dating to J. Edgar Hoover's opposition to the 1947 National Security Act, and how it manifested before September 11 when Cofer Black's Counterterrorism Center withheld from the FBI that hijackers Nawaf al-Hazmi and Khalid al-Mihdhar had been granted U.S. visas.

bruce-fein.title: Rudy Giuliani
bruce-fein.summary: Former U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York and Mayor of New York City; in 2018 attempted to extort $2 million from John Kiriakou in exchange for arranging a presidential pardon from President Trump; the attempt was reported to the New York Times by Kiriakou himself and corroborated by Giuliani's then-aide Noelle Dunphy after Giuliani sexually harassed her.

bruce-fein.title: Robert MacLean
bruce-fein.summary: TSA whistleblower; the person to whom John Kiriakou first described Rudy Giuliani's 2018 $2 million pardon-extortion attempt the same evening it occurred, and who in turn tipped the FBI (which declined interest) and then the New York Times.

bruce-fein.title: Saddam Hussein
bruce-fein.summary: President of Iraq from 1979 until the 2003 U.S. invasion; subject of John Kiriakou's CIA portfolio from January 1990 onward, in which capacity Kiriakou became, at age 25, "Saddam Hussein's intelligence community biographer" and the analyst who briefed President George H. W. Bush in the Oval Office on the morning of the 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

bruce-fein.title: Sebastian Gorka
bruce-fein.summary: Former Trump administration deputy assistant; subject of John Kiriakou's second attempted pardon transaction in 2018, in which Gorka asked Kiriakou for $5,000 at a book launch at the Trump International Hotel in exchange for tweeting at the president on his behalf. Kiriakou refused.

bruce-fein.title: Central Intelligence Agency
bruce-fein.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

bruce-fein.title: Bernie Kerik
bruce-fein.summary: Former New York Police Department Commissioner; the person who, in 2018, introduced John Kiriakou to Rudy Giuliani for what became Giuliani's $2 million pardon-extortion attempt.

bureau-of-prisons-advisory-board.title: Kiriakou's prison designation
bureau-of-prisons-advisory-board.summary: The discrepancy between the minimum-security work camp John Kiriakou was sentenced to and the low-security prison the Bureau of Prisons actually placed him in, which he cites whenever the subject of preferential designations arises.

bureau-of-prisons-advisory-board.title: The false volunteer
bureau-of-prisons-advisory-board.summary: A walk-in at an American embassy who claimed access to a high-priority target, was placed under surveillance and found to be a restaurant dishwasher, and whom John Kiriakou deliberately intimidated into never approaching an American embassy again.

bureau-of-prisons-advisory-board.title: Spy films John Kiriakou considers accurate
bureau-of-prisons-advisory-board.summary: Kiriakou's assessment of which espionage films get it right — Argo, The Recruit and Bridge of Spies — and his flat rejection of the action genre's premises, including the hidden weapons stash.

bureau-of-prisons-advisory-board.title: The spy shop
bureau-of-prisons-advisory-board.summary: A London shop with a New York sister branch where, John Kiriakou says, the CIA bought a good deal of the equipment it needed, on the reasoning that a thousand-dollar purchase beat a million-dollar development programme.

bureau-of-prisons-advisory-board.title: Kiriakou's Cypriot ancestry
bureau-of-prisons-advisory-board.summary: The DNA result showing John Kiriakou to be 24 per cent Cypriot — his largest single ancestry — which corrected a family belief that the line came from Crete and coincided with an invitation to address a Cypriot diaspora conference.

bureau-of-prisons-advisory-board.title: Origin of the Kiriakou name
bureau-of-prisons-advisory-board.summary: The Kiriakou surname originates in a clerical error at a Rhodes courthouse, where John Kiriakou's great-great-grandfather, arrested for stealing a potato while starving, gave a patronymic that was written down as his family name and never corrected.

bureau-of-prisons.title: The Taliban spokesman setup
bureau-of-prisons.summary: Kiriakou's account of a prisoner transferred into FCI Loretto for five days who presented himself as the Taliban's American spokesman, while a guard photographed the encounter from the treeline — an attempt, in his telling, to manufacture a second case against him.

bureau-of-prisons.title: Witness K case
bureau-of-prisons.summary: Australian intelligence scandal in which a former ASIS officer known as Witness K exposed Australia's bugging of the East Timorese cabinet during oil and gas revenue negotiations; his lawyer, Bernard Collaery, describes the ASIO raids on both their homes and offices as paralleling the FBI's raid on John Kiriakou.

bureau-of-prisons.title: Jim Moran
bureau-of-prisons.summary: Democratic congressman from Virginia who wrote twice to the director of the Bureau of Prisons asking that his constituent John Kiriakou receive at least nine months of halfway-house time, and whom Kiriakou thanked in a postscript to a letter from Loretto.

bureau-of-prisons.title: Kiriakou's prison designation
bureau-of-prisons.summary: The discrepancy between the minimum-security work camp John Kiriakou was sentenced to and the low-security prison the Bureau of Prisons actually placed him in, which he cites whenever the subject of preferential designations arises.

bureau-of-prisons.title: Education at FCI Loretto
bureau-of-prisons.summary: The classes, drug programme and good-conduct rules at FCI Loretto, which Kiriakou described in a letter from Loretto as correcting nothing — and which taught him, he wrote, how to cook methamphetamine and defraud a mortgage company.

bureau-of-prisons.title: Jake Tapper
bureau-of-prisons.summary: CNN anchor who drove to FCI Loretto to interview the imprisoned John Kiriakou — and who asked President Obama at a press conference why he had insisted on prosecuting a man who exposed a crime, a question Obama answered by walking away from the podium. Kiriakou wielded Tapper's name as a shield inside ("let's see what Jake Tapper has to say about it — why don't we give him a call?"), and the two stayed in touch after his release. "Jake was different."

butler-rally-shooting.title: Washington political culture
butler-rally-shooting.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how Washington changed across the forty-four years he has lived in it — from a city where members of opposing parties shared houses, churches and Friday-night poker games to one he calls hideous, angry and backstabbing, in which the polarisation is itself the reason nothing gets done and political violence keeps being waved past.

butler-rally-shooting.title: Charlie Kirk shooting
butler-rally-shooting.summary: Kiriakou questions the official account: a court filing says the ATF could not match the autopsy bullet to the rifle tied to the suspect.

butler-rally-shooting.title: Israel-United States relations
butler-rally-shooting.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the U.S.-Israel relationship, including his own first visit to Israel as a tourist in 2022 and his characterization of Israel's willingness to destroy an entire city block to kill a single target, confident that the United States will not object.

butler-rally-shooting.title: John Kiriakou
butler-rally-shooting.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

butler-rally-shooting.title: Kiriakou pardon request
butler-rally-shooting.summary: John Kiriakou's public campaign for a presidential pardon from Donald Trump to restore the pension and firearm rights he lost after his 2013 felony conviction for disclosing the identity of a covert CIA officer; includes a five-second Mar-a-Lago encounter in which Trump referred him to Attorney General Pam Bondi, a Kalshi prediction-market contract that opened at roughly 19 to 20 percent odds on his being pardoned, and letters of support from Tucker Carlson, Judge Andrew Napolitano and Dr. Phil.

butler-rally-shooting.title: Advanced Counterterrorism Operations
butler-rally-shooting.summary: The six-week specialist course at CIA headquarters that John Kiriakou attended roughly eighteen months before 9/11 as one of fourteen officers selected worldwide — weapons, explosives, counterterrorist and desert driving, bugs, cameras, satellites and drones — and which, by accident of timing, meant a cadre was trained and able to deploy the moment the attacks came.

cameo.title: FBI manufactured terrorism cases
cameo.summary: John Kiriakou's account of terrorism prosecutions in which the FBI supplies the plot, the target, the explosives and the transport, then arrests the person it recruited. His central case is the 2026 Miami trial of a mentally ill homeless man facing six counts each carrying life without parole, in which Kiriakou testified for the defence and told the court that the FBI was "clearly the criminal in this case." The defendant was acquitted on every count.

cameo.title: Kiriakou cameo practice
cameo.summary: John Kiriakou's post-2026 use of the Cameo personalised-video service — running at roughly 25 to 30 hours a week, some 900 messages in the month of March 2026 alone, nearly 2,000 messages in total by July 2026 — that he says has produced three cases in which the person receiving the video message afterwards told him he had talked them out of committing suicide, including a 15-year-old bulimic girl to whom Kiriakou gave his personal phone number.

cameo.title: AIPAC
cameo.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

cameo.title: American Psychological Association
cameo.summary: The world's largest body of psychologists, which John Kiriakou cites constantly for one devastating datum — its research shows people begin to lose their minds at around day seven without sleep, and begin to die at day nine. Mitchell and Jessen were nonetheless authorized to keep chained, naked prisoners awake past that threshold, which is why Kiriakou insists sleep deprivation — a technique the APA has deemed a form of torture — was always worse than waterboarding.

cameo.title: Amnesty International
cameo.summary: The human rights organization whose 2006 torture report forms part of John Kiriakou's core defense — the CIA's crimes were already public knowledge before he confirmed them on ABC — and the organization whose silence during his own prosecution he cannot forgive. He begged Amnesty for even a one-sentence statement about his case; the director of Amnesty International USA sent him a New Yorker subscription and a letter saying they wanted nothing to do with it. "After about a year I got tired of begging."

cameo.title: The Analysis Corporation
cameo.summary: Arlington, Virginia–based [private intelligence firm](/wiki/private-intelligence); one of two companion entities (alongside Arrais Corporation) created as LLC pass-throughs for retired Senior Intelligence Service personnel; John Brennan was appointed its CEO in 2005.

camp-david-final-talks.title: Bill Clinton
camp-david-final-talks.summary: 42nd U.S. president whom John Kiriakou describes as wholly disinterested in intelligence — briefed by the CIA only twice in eight years, with Vice President Al Gore taking the daily briefing instead and relaying anything important.

camp-david-final-talks.title: MOSSAD
camp-david-final-talks.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

camp-david-final-talks.title: Prince Andrew
camp-david-final-talks.summary: British royal named repeatedly by John Kiriakou as one of the un-recruitable principals whose access made Jeffrey Epstein valuable to a foreign intelligence service. Kiriakou has asked why Andrew was never charged over conduct with minors, and has said that his 2026 arrest — over the alleged provision of classified Ministry of Defence documents to Epstein — is evidence that Epstein was collecting for a foreign power rather than for himself.

camp-david-final-talks.title: Central Intelligence Agency
camp-david-final-talks.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

camp-david-final-talks.title: Hezbollah
camp-david-final-talks.summary: Lebanese Shia militant organization and political party. Per John Kiriakou, Israel''s strategic goal regarding Hezbollah is not to defeat it outright but to keep Lebanon in a state of chaos that serves Israeli interests. He cites two Israeli operations: the simultaneous pager-detonation attack that decapitated Hezbollah''s leadership, which he called ''the most incredible operation I''ve ever seen,'' and the strike that killed former leader Hassan Nasrallah by leveling an entire complex and killing roughly 300 people — which he characterized as a war crime.

camp-david-final-talks.title: Mack McLarty
camp-david-final-talks.summary: U.S. political consultant and Bill Clinton's former White House Chief of Staff; founder of McLarty Associates (formerly Kissinger McLarty), at which John Kiriakou was given a private office and part-time secretary in 2008.

carlos-the-jackal.title: Revolutionary Organization 17 November
carlos-the-jackal.summary: Greek far-left urban guerrilla group active 1975–2002; the deadliest terrorist organization in Greek history

carlos-the-jackal.title: Abu Zubaydah
carlos-the-jackal.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

carlos-the-jackal.title: Billy Waugh
carlos-the-jackal.summary: Long-serving CIA paramilitary contractor; U.S. Army Special Forces ("Green Beret") veteran of World War II, Korea, and Vietnam; holder of approximately seventeen Purple Hearts (license plate "17 HITS"); resident of Niceville, Florida; died in his nineties.

carlos-the-jackal.title: USAID as a CIA cover vehicle
carlos-the-jackal.summary: John Kiriakou's account of USAID's use by the CIA as a channel for covert operations and money laundering rather than as an undercover posting for individual officers — including a declassified 1972 exchange in which Henry Kissinger confirmed the CIA had paid Laotian mercenaries through USAID payroll checks.

carlos-the-jackal.title: CIA political action group
carlos-the-jackal.summary: The CIA's most secretive clandestine propaganda arm — successor to the Cold War 'active measures group' — which John Kiriakou says places and funds propagandists worldwide; no officer of it has been publicly identified since 1982, and he encountered its work funding the DNC's and RNC's international arms in post-war Kuwait.

carlos-the-jackal.title: Mike Mastrovito
carlos-the-jackal.summary: Twenty-five-year Secret Service veteran; founder and first director of the Secret Service Intelligence Division; later, after a forced retirement, a CIA contractor specializing in Greek terrorism; close colleague of John Kiriakou in Athens. Started his career at the end of the Eisenhower administration, was in Dallas with President Kennedy, and was effectively removed from the Secret Service after Sara Jane Moore's 1975 attempt on President Ford — having interviewed Moore two weeks earlier on a threatening letter she had sent.

caspar-weinberger.title: Jonathan Pollard
caspar-weinberger.summary: U.S. Navy civilian intelligence analyst convicted in 1985 of spying for Israel; the canonical proven case of Israeli espionage against the United States; cited by John Kiriakou in his 2024 Piers Morgan debate with a former Mossad director who denied any Israeli spying on the U.S.

caspar-weinberger.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
caspar-weinberger.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

caspar-weinberger.title: MOSSAD
caspar-weinberger.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

caspar-weinberger.title: Sheldon Adelson
caspar-weinberger.summary: American casino magnate and Republican megadonor; in John Kiriakou's account of the Jonathan Pollard case, Adelson sent his private jet to fly Pollard from prison to Israel upon his release, and Kiriakou says his political influence continued after his death through his widow, Miriam Adelson.

caspar-weinberger.title: Asset acquisition cycle
caspar-weinberger.summary: The four-step process — spot, assess, develop, recruit — taught as the first lesson of CIA case officer training

caspar-weinberger.title: Barack Obama
caspar-weinberger.summary: 44th U.S. president; in John Kiriakou's account, Obama publicly recounted refusing Benjamin Netanyahu's demand to bomb Iran and calling Israel's threat to use nuclear weapons a bluff — a bluff Kiriakou says Donald Trump later believed.

central-american-task-force.title: Iran-Contra
central-american-task-force.summary: The mid-1980s scandal in which the Reagan administration secretly sold weapons to Iran and diverted the proceeds — laundered through Cyprus — to fund the Contra rebels in Nicaragua. Per John Kiriakou, Iran-Contra marks the precise end of what he calls the ''golden age'' of congressional intelligence oversight: the roughly 1975–1982 window opened by the Church and Pike Committees, when ''serious people, heavyweights'' actually held the CIA accountable. After Iran-Contra, he says, the oversight committees reverted to being ''cheerleaders'' for the agency — a posture that has held ever since.

central-american-task-force.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
central-american-task-force.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

central-american-task-force.title: George W. Bush
central-american-task-force.summary: 43rd President of the United States. In John Kiriakou's telling, Bush signed the August 1, 2002 executive order that authorized the CIA torture program, spent years telling the public "we don't torture," and — days after Kiriakou's 2007 ABC interview — blamed torture on "a rogue CIA officer" while walking from the White House South Portico to Marine One, a moment Kiriakou instantly read as the White House preparing to pin the program on him. Bush also ordered the FBI removed from Abu Zubaydah's black site, flew the bin Laden family out of the country after 9/11, and loosened the assassination ban of Executive Order 12333.

central-american-task-force.title: Consortium News
central-american-task-force.summary: Independent investigative news outlet John Kiriakou has written for, founded by Polk Award-winning journalist Robert Parry, who broke major stories on Iran-Contra; Kiriakou says PayPal permanently shuttered the outlet's account and briefly seized its funds before backing down under public pressure, while still refusing to reinstate it.

central-american-task-force.title: Contra rebels
central-american-task-force.summary: The right-wing Nicaraguan insurgency armed by the Reagan administration against the Sandinista government. In John Kiriakou's account they were conservatives, right-wingers, in some cases fascists, and disgruntled military officers; they were split into a northern group the United States armed and a southern group that financed itself by selling cocaine — a distinction that became the pivot of the Gary Webb affair.

central-american-task-force.title: 1953 Iran coup
central-american-task-force.summary: The U.S.- and UK-backed overthrow of Iran's democratically elected prime minister, Mohammad Mossadegh; per John Kiriakou, the coup served British national interests rather than American ones, and the subsequent outlawing of secular political opposition under the Shah forced dissent into the mosques — producing a religious rather than secular revolution in 1979.

chaos-computer-club-wikileaks.title: Daniel Domscheit-Berg
chaos-computer-club-wikileaks.summary: A WikiLeaks associate discussed on the same panel as John Kiriakou; the anecdote about meeting him via the Chaos Computer Club was told by fellow panelist John Goetz, a Der Spiegel journalist — not by Kiriakou himself.

chaos-computer-club-wikileaks.title: Ai Whistleblower Initiative
chaos-computer-club-wikileaks.summary: The AI Whistleblower Initiative, working on legal protections for the wave of whistleblowers now coming out of the artificial-intelligence industry.

chaos-computer-club-wikileaks.title: Andrew Feinstein
chaos-computer-club-wikileaks.summary: Referenced on the same WikiLeaks-conference panel as John Kiriakou; the description of Feinstein's talk on the multiple factors that ended apartheid was given by another panelist putting a question to Kiriakou, not by Kiriakou himself.

chaos-computer-club-wikileaks.title: Belmarsh Prison
chaos-computer-club-wikileaks.summary: The London prison where Julian Assange was held — one more stage, Kiriakou notes, in a life spent almost entirely in some form of confinement.

chaos-computer-club-wikileaks.title: Chelsea Manning
chaos-computer-club-wikileaks.summary: Former U.S. Army intelligence analyst who provided WikiLeaks its 2010 trove of military and diplomatic documents. Per John Kiriakou, Manning meets the legal definition of whistleblower for exposing war crimes, was a torture victim of prolonged solitary confinement with forced nudity, and was sentenced to 35 years in prison before Barack Obama commuted — not pardoned — her sentence. Kiriakou says Manning later refused a grand jury's offer of immunity and chose renewed jail time rather than testify against Julian Assange.

chaos-computer-club-wikileaks.title: Central Intelligence Agency
chaos-computer-club-wikileaks.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

charles-samuels.title: Administrative remedy process
charles-samuels.summary: The Bureau of Prisons' internal grievance system, which Kiriakou describes as a fig leaf designed to run out the clock on prisoners' complaints rather than resolve them.

charles-samuels.title: Letter from Loretto
charles-samuels.summary: Prison newsletter written by John Kiriakou from FCI Loretto, modeled on Martin Luther King's "Letter from Birmingham Jail," which exposed two crimes committed against him by guards and went viral after being relayed to the Huffington Post, drawing national press to the prison.

charles-samuels.title: Bureau of Prisons
charles-samuels.summary: The federal agency that ran John Kiriakou's incarceration — and one of his most persistent post-prison targets. The BOP overrode his judge's camp recommendation by deeming him "a threat to the public safety," threatened him with "diesel therapy" until 1,600 logged phone calls and letters from a dozen House members and two senators backed it off, and, per Kiriakou, functions as "an employment agency for unemployable semi-literate rural white men" and "a dumping ground for failed medical professionals" — an agency for which a prisoner's death is cheaper than his treatment.

charles-samuels.title: Diesel Therapy
charles-samuels.summary: Per John Kiriakou, a punitive practice within the U.S. Federal Bureau of Prisons in which an inmate is placed into indefinite transit — moved continuously from facility to facility — for up to six months, with no access to phone, email, or pen and paper, and listed on the BOP website only as 'in transit' with no destination. Kiriakou described it as the one threat at FCI Loretto that actually frightened him.

charles-samuels.title: Jim Moran
charles-samuels.summary: Democratic congressman from Virginia who wrote twice to the director of the Bureau of Prisons asking that his constituent John Kiriakou receive at least nine months of halfway-house time, and whom Kiriakou thanked in a postscript to a letter from Loretto.

charles-samuels.title: This desk kills fascism
charles-samuels.summary: The sign Kiriakou taped to the cell desk on which he wrote the letters from Loretto, borrowed from Woody Guthrie's guitar, torn down by a guard within hours and kept by Kiriakou ever since.

charlie-kirk-shooting.title: Jeffrey Epstein
charlie-kirk-shooting.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

charlie-kirk-shooting.title: Iranian sleeper cells
charlie-kirk-shooting.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of Iran's clandestine reach abroad — that the IRGC and the Ministry of Intelligence and Security do run sleeper cells worldwide, but probably not in the United States, Canada or the UK, and that the greater danger is the unaffiliated lone attacker. He also argues Iranian operatives are consistently poor, and identifies the Gulf's real vulnerability as its tourist landmarks rather than its military bases.

charlie-kirk-shooting.title: Washington political culture
charlie-kirk-shooting.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how Washington changed across the forty-four years he has lived in it — from a city where members of opposing parties shared houses, churches and Friday-night poker games to one he calls hideous, angry and backstabbing, in which the polarisation is itself the reason nothing gets done and political violence keeps being waved past.

charlie-kirk-shooting.title: Butler rally shooting
charlie-kirk-shooting.summary: The July 2024 attempt on Donald Trump's life at a rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, on which John Kiriakou takes no position as to who was responsible but argues the published facts cannot be reconciled with a competent Secret Service — and that the questions it leaves open are owed an answer for the historical record whether or not anyone alive gets one.

charlie-kirk-shooting.title: Israeli non-extradition of Jews
charlie-kirk-shooting.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of Israel as a refuge that does not extradite Jewish fugitives regardless of the offence, illustrated by the case of an American lawyer who fled there after a child-abuse suit and was recovered only by an Interpol sting in Cyprus. Kiriakou uses the rule to frame a question about Jeffrey Epstein: why a man with jets and hidden billions did not flee there himself.

charlie-kirk-shooting.title: Office of Special Plans Israeli leak
charlie-kirk-shooting.summary: A major Israeli spy operation John Kiriakou says was uncovered in the 2000s involving a leak from the Pentagon's Office of Special Plans, headed by Paul Wolfowitz and Douglas Feith — both authors, with Richard Perle, of the "Clean Break" report advocating a dual-containment strategy against Iraq and Iran on behalf of Benjamin Netanyahu. Per Kiriakou, Wolfowitz and Feith did not merely fail to take Israeli counterintelligence seriously; he believes they actively helped abet it.

chas-freeman-gaza-plan-1991.title: Bezalel Smotrich
chas-freeman-gaza-plan-1991.summary: Israeli far-right minister whom John Kiriakou, alongside Itamar Ben-Gvir, blames for leaving Israel unprepared on October 7 by insisting any attack would come from the West Bank rather than Gaza.

chas-freeman-gaza-plan-1991.title: Abraham Accords
chas-freeman-gaza-plan-1991.summary: The Trump-brokered normalization deals between Israel and Gulf Arab states — in John Kiriakou's judgment "a terrible idea in the first place," a great victory for Israel and the Gulf Arabs that was "a punch in the throat to the Palestinians." He argues the Accords are how Trump meant to "solve the Middle East in a day" — by screwing the Palestinians — that Hamas read the abandonment correctly, that October 7 shattered the project, and that reviving the Accords (Saudis in, victory declared, Nobel collected) remains the organizing goal of Trump's regional policy.

chas-freeman-gaza-plan-1991.title: Church of Saint Porphyrios
chas-freeman-gaza-plan-1991.summary: The Greek Orthodox church in Gaza that John Kiriakou describes as the oldest continuously operating church in the world; per Kiriakou, Israel bombed it while 24 women and children were sheltering inside.

chas-freeman-gaza-plan-1991.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
chas-freeman-gaza-plan-1991.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

chas-freeman-gaza-plan-1991.title: Itamar Ben-Gvir
chas-freeman-gaza-plan-1991.summary: Israel's far-right Minister of National Security; John Kiriakou cites him as a convicted hate-crime felon placed in charge of security in Gaza and the West Bank over his victims, blames his insistence that any attack would come from the West Bank for diverting forces before October 7, and cites the death-penalty law passed under his portfolio for Palestinian detainees as the first reinstatement of capital punishment in Israel since it was abolished in 1956, excepting only the execution of Adolf Eichmann.

chas-freeman-gaza-plan-1991.title: King Abdullah II of Jordan
chas-freeman-gaza-plan-1991.summary: The Jordanian monarch whom John Kiriakou rates as knowing more about the Middle East than anyone else who leads or studies it, and as almost never wrong across twenty-five years of foreign-policy predictions. Kiriakou recounts the deathbed succession that made him king against his own expectations, and his refusal after October 7 to accept Palestinian refugees on the grounds that doing so would deliver Israel the ethnic cleansing it wanted.

chelsea-manning.title: Julian Assange
chelsea-manning.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

chelsea-manning.title: Jack Teixeira
chelsea-manning.summary: Massachusetts Air National Guard reservist arrested in April 2023 for leaking classified Pentagon documents to a small Discord server. John Kiriakou, discussing the case the day after Teixeira's arrest, initially suspected a covert action program rather than a genuine leak, ultimately concluded Teixeira was not a whistleblower, and predicted — correctly — that he would be charged under the Espionage Act and take a plea bargain.

chelsea-manning.title: Collateral Murder Video
chelsea-manning.summary: The 2010 WikiLeaks release of gun-camera footage from a 2007 U.S. Apache helicopter attack in Baghdad; part of the trove of Iraq and Afghan war logs, Guantanamo files, and State Department cables leaked by Chelsea Manning, which John Kiriakou credits with corroborating major abuses and helping to touch off the Arab Spring.

chelsea-manning.title: Der Spiegel
chelsea-manning.summary: At a 2026 Berlin panel, a former Der Spiegel journalist said it took him years before he could call Julian Assange a publisher rather than an activist.

chelsea-manning.title: Kiriakou Introduction to WikiLeaks
chelsea-manning.summary: Kiriakou first heard of WikiLeaks as a warning inside the secret spaces it existed to expose: ''Don''t touch that. Don''t go near that.''

chelsea-manning.title: Trump
chelsea-manning.summary: Kiriakou applied for a pardon on the last day of Trump's first term — and says Trump had agreed to it, until the last-minute reversal.

china-djibouti-base.title: Guantanamo Bay
china-djibouti-base.summary: U.S. naval base in Cuba; site of CIA detention operations during the post-9/11 enhanced interrogation program; briefly served by John Kiriakou as interim Chief during the summer of 2002.

china-djibouti-base.title: Al-Qaeda training manual interrogation-resistance tactics
china-djibouti-base.summary: A captured al-Qaeda training manual instructing operatives on how to resist interrogation, including feigning illness — a technique John Kiriakou says he saw a detainee use, and recognized, during a capture and interrogation in Pakistan.

china-djibouti-base.title: Bab al-Mandab
china-djibouti-base.summary: The strait where the Horn of Africa nearly meets the south-western tip of the Arabian Peninsula, which John Kiriakou identifies as one of the few American national interests in Yemen and as a chokepoint whose closure would push the global economy into recession.

china-djibouti-base.title: Democratic Party 2025 Political Snapshot
china-djibouti-base.summary: John Kiriakou's 2025 assessment of Democratic Party weakness — a record-low 24% approval rating, seven Senate Democrats crossing over to hand Trump a spending-bill win with no concessions, and California governor Gavin Newsom's surprising denial of parole to a large group of long-incarcerated eligible inmates, which Kiriakou reads as Newsom "playing the long game."

china-djibouti-base.title: Strait of Hormuz transit fees
china-djibouti-base.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Iran's proposal to charge ships up to $2 million to transit the Strait of Hormuz, payable in yuan rather than dollars, and of the U.S. Navy's subsequent announcement that it had taken control of the strait and closed it — reversing decades of U.S. policy that the strait must remain open.

china-djibouti-base.title: Irish intelligence services
china-djibouti-base.summary: Ireland's intelligence and law-enforcement services, which John Kiriakou toured and met with during a speaking trip to Belfast, Cork, Dublin, and Waterford. Per Kiriakou, Irish intelligence and the Garda are especially strong at anti-money-laundering investigation and counterterrorism — the latter traced, he says, to the large number of Irish militants trained by Carlos the Jackal in Libya and Lebanon during the 1970s.

china-economic-threat.title: CIA spy tech from Amazon
china-economic-threat.summary: John Kiriakou's account that roughly 95% of the CIA's spy technology is purchased commercially from Amazon.com rather than custom-built, illustrated by a $10 leather briefcase he had rigged into a listening device in a Pakistani market.

china-economic-threat.title: The Kite Runner rescue mission
china-economic-threat.summary: 2007 covert operation in which John Kiriakou, newly departed from the CIA and working as a corporate-intelligence consultant, was hired by Paramount Studios to secretly evacuate the Afghan child actors of the film "The Kite Runner" and their extended families after real death threats over the film's content.

china-economic-threat.title: PricewaterhouseCoopers
china-economic-threat.summary: The Big Four accounting firm that keeps intersecting John Kiriakou's story — as a target of the corporate human-source intelligence he collected after leaving the CIA, as the audience of 140 partners he told his Pakistan recruitment story to ("what I did and what you do really isn't that different"), as the auditor that spent three years trying to find the Pentagon's money before giving up, and as the Greek government's book-cooking auditor in the debt crisis, never prosecuted.

china-economic-threat.title: Kiriakou's mother's 2008 trip to Israel
china-economic-threat.summary: John Kiriakou recounts his mother's 2008 church-group trip to Israel and the West Bank, during which she was struck by the contrast between first-world Tel Aviv and a walled, mined Palestinian town, and witnessed an IDF soldier tear apart a Palestinian bus driver's novel as suspected "PLO propaganda." Kiriakou made two trips of his own to Israel in 2022, including one to cover the elections, during which he personally witnessed a fatal stabbing at Jerusalem's Iron Gate.

china-economic-threat.title: Sergey Lavrov
china-economic-threat.summary: Russian foreign minister, and previously Russian ambassador to the United Nations during John Kiriakou's assignment there. Kiriakou describes him as the most admired diplomat at the UN — the most powerful, important and strategic ambassador in the building despite operating with far smaller resources than his American, British, French and Chinese counterparts.

china-economic-threat.title: UK secrecy laws
china-economic-threat.summary: John Kiriakou's view that Britain is even harsher on whistleblowers and dissent than the United States, using the Official Secrets Act and Terrorism Act to stop people at airports and threaten arrest merely for supporting Palestinian rights.

china-illegal-fishing.title: Russia-Ukraine war origins
china-illegal-fishing.summary: John Kiriakou's account that the war began in 2014, not 2022 — rooted in broken U.S. promises that NATO would not expand to Russia's borders, the 2014 removal of a pro-Russian Ukrainian leader, and the seizure of Crimea; he says Russia is now winning and has no reason to negotiate.

china-illegal-fishing.title: Bahrain fishing officer demarche
china-illegal-fishing.summary: Kiriakou's account of serving, while stationed in Bahrain, as the embassy's econ officer and by extension its fishing, banking, aviation, and environment officer — including delivering a formal U.S. demarche to Bahrain's deputy foreign minister over a U.S.-Canada dispute about whether clams legally count as fish.

china-illegal-fishing.title: Below World's End
china-illegal-fishing.summary: Film in which John Kiriakou made his acting debut, filmed entirely in Mexico during October 2025; Kiriakou's performance earned him a Screen Actors Guild membership card, and Sean Penn told him after a private screening that he had unknowingly been acting throughout his entire CIA career.

china-illegal-fishing.title: Big Assawoman Bay NASA launch
china-illegal-fishing.summary: John Kiriakou's account of being taken, as a junior CIA analyst, to watch a NASA rocket launch near the village of Big Assawoman on Virginia's Eastern Shore, where he was startled to find foreign space-agency officials present unsupervised.

china-illegal-fishing.title: Iran Nuclear Assessment
china-illegal-fishing.summary: Per John Kiriakou's assessment, the US–Israeli military campaign against Iran was a war of choice driven by Israeli political pressure rather than genuine intelligence indicating an Iranian nuclear weapons threat. The CIA produced two National Intelligence Estimates concluding Iran had no nuclear weapons program; Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei issued a fatwa in the 1980s forbidding such a program. The U.S. went to war anyway, in Kiriakou's view, after President Trump replaced the Joint Chiefs of Staff with officers willing to accept Israeli intelligence and proceed.

china-illegal-fishing.title: Joe Weisberg
china-illegal-fishing.summary: Former CIA Counterterrorism Center officer and colleague of John Kiriakou who resigned abruptly, saying he did not have it in him to convince people to commit treason, then moved to Hollywood and created the television series The Americans.

chinese-spy-balloon-incident.title: Agnes von Kurowsky grave story
