citizens-united.title: Alec Baldwin
citizens-united.summary: Actor with whom John Kiriakou recounts a bitter falling-out over a planned off-Broadway play about his case — Baldwin calling him a liar at their first lunch, briefly attaching to the project, then dropping out without a word.

citizens-united.title: CIA animal surveillance experiments
citizens-united.summary: Cold-War CIA efforts to turn animals into listening devices, which John Kiriakou describes as failures — including microphones and cameras mounted on pigeons trained to land on the Soviet embassy, which could reach the compound but never captured anything meaningful.

citizens-united.title: Havana Syndrome
citizens-united.summary: Cluster of neurological symptoms — including nausea, ringing in the ears, vertigo, and traumatic brain injury — reported by American diplomatic and intelligence personnel beginning in Havana, Cuba, and subsequently at posts around the world. Per John Kiriakou, his initial skepticism gave way when a friend developed Havana Syndrome with an MRI-confirmed traumatic brain injury after a meeting outside the Russian Foreign Ministry; Kiriakou attributes the syndrome to Russian or Chinese directed-energy weapons and acknowledges the United States used a similar weapon during the operation to capture Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro.

classification-compartments.title: Kiriakou's transfer to the Directorate of Operations
classification-compartments.summary: John Kiriakou's roughly two-month internal campaign to transfer from the CIA's analytic Directorate of Intelligence to the operational Directorate of Operations, overcoming what he calls a "natural bias in operations against the eggheads on the analytic side," followed by an Athens posting secured because he was the only person in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic. Covers his full CIA career arc from 1988/1990 recruitment through analyst years on Iraq, the switch to operations, 9/11, the enhanced-interrogation refusal, executive assistant to the deputy director for operations, and his eventual resignation and post-CIA career.

classification-compartments.title: Thomas Drake
classification-compartments.summary: NSA whistleblower; per John Kiriakou, the source for the statement that on the morning of September 11, 2001, NSA Director Mike Hayden told agency personnel NSA had been 'waiting for a 9/11' to implement the mass-electronic-surveillance program that NSA's founding charter forbids.

classification-compartments.title: Central Intelligence Agency
classification-compartments.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

classification-compartments.title: CIA record deniability
classification-compartments.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how senior CIA officers occasionally decide to keep an event out of the written record — illustrated by a recruited asset who committed a public murder, after which the Deputy Director for Operations told Kiriakou, on second thought, 'let's not put that in writing.'

classification-compartments.title: CIA National Resources Division
classification-compartments.summary: The Central Intelligence Agency's domestic intelligence-collection arm, created in the 1980s by Director William J. Casey

classification-compartments.title: Donald Trump
classification-compartments.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

clint-goswick.title: FCI Loretto
clint-goswick.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

clint-goswick.title: Doing Time Like a Spy
clint-goswick.summary: Prison memoir by John Kiriakou, full title Doing Time Like a Spy: How the CIA Taught Me to Survive and Thrive in Prison; winner of two literary awards and reissued in a second edition by Simon and Schuster.

clint-goswick.title: Larry Raviv
clint-goswick.summary: Fellow federal prisoner of John Kiriakou, convicted of murder-for-hire after taking out a life insurance policy on his business partner to pay off a $100,000 mob gambling debt and hiring a hitman to kill him. Raviv negotiated a 20-year sentence, down from what would normally be life without parole, by testifying against the hitman, who died of a heart attack while awaiting extradition trial. Kiriakou later engineered a violent beating against Raviv after Raviv called him a "rat" for being summoned to the lieutenant's office for a Jake Tapper interview.

clint-goswick.title: Private prison system
clint-goswick.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the U.S. private prison industry as an incentive to keep beds filled and cut costs on food and medicine — illustrated by the 'sewer trout,' dog-food, and dead-rat-in-the-Kool-Aid stories from his own incarceration.

clint-goswick.title: Donnie Reynolds Jr.
clint-goswick.summary: Tennessee businessman and antique-firearms collector serving a life-plus-75-year federal sentence at the Communications Management Unit in Terre Haute, Indiana; per John Kiriakou and Marty Gottesfeld, a scapegoat for the fallout of the ATF's Operation Fast and Furious after refusing to become an undercover cartel weapons source.

clint-goswick.title: Prison racial segregation
clint-goswick.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the rigid racial and ethnic division of American prisons — a cafeteria split like the 1950s South — and his argument that segregating and hardening inmates for years, then releasing them with no skills, makes society less safe.

code-pink.title: Bureau of Prisons
code-pink.summary: The federal agency that ran John Kiriakou's incarceration — and one of his most persistent post-prison targets. The BOP overrode his judge's camp recommendation by deeming him "a threat to the public safety," threatened him with "diesel therapy" until 1,600 logged phone calls and letters from a dozen House members and two senators backed it off, and, per Kiriakou, functions as "an employment agency for unemployable semi-literate rural white men" and "a dumping ground for failed medical professionals" — an agency for which a prisoner's death is cheaper than his treatment.

code-pink.title: Counterterrorism Center
code-pink.summary: The CIA's Counterterrorism Center (CTC) — the unit where John Kiriakou spent the defining years of his operational career. He joined in the late 1990s as the only officer in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic, served as chief of counterintelligence in the bin Laden unit, watched the Center swell from a few hundred employees to nearly 2,000 by September 12, 2001, and it was to CTC that he walked back down in May 2002 to refuse the torture program — the moment, he says, the CIA began to turn on him.

code-pink.title: Arianna Huffington
code-pink.summary: Founder of the Huffington Post and the accidental amplifier who turned John Kiriakou's prison writing into a phenomenon. His first Letter from Loretto went to his attorney, then to a friend running Firedoglake who — unknown to Kiriakou — was close to Huffington; she plastered it as a banner headline and it drew over a million hits, bringing CNN and 60 Minutes to the prison gates. She published his open letter to Snowden, ran the diesel-therapy exposé that triggered the "hands off John Kiriakou" campaign, and came to Loretto herself with two young journalists.

code-pink.title: Watergate
code-pink.summary: The scandal that ended Nixon''s presidency and the standing benchmark in John Kiriakou''s vocabulary — the CIA spying on the Senate committee investigating its torture program was, to him, "a Watergate-level kind of scandal," except that this time nothing came of it. Watergate touches his own story directly: his lead defense attorney had been John Mitchell''s lawyer during Watergate. He also relays, with fascination, Danny Sheehan''s far darker theory of what the burglars were really after.

code-pink.title: Oliver Stone
code-pink.summary: American film director with whom John Kiriakou struck up a friendship after his release from prison. Stone optioned the rights to one chapter of Kiriakou's first book, co-developed an unmade History Channel series with him, blurbed his book on Abu Zubaydah, and was among the public figures who campaigned against the Bureau of Prisons' attempt to shut down Kiriakou's prison blog. The two disagree sharply over whether the CIA killed John F. Kennedy.

code-pink.title: Kiriakou's transfer to the Directorate of Operations
code-pink.summary: John Kiriakou's roughly two-month internal campaign to transfer from the CIA's analytic Directorate of Intelligence to the operational Directorate of Operations, overcoming what he calls a "natural bias in operations against the eggheads on the analytic side," followed by an Athens posting secured because he was the only person in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic. Covers his full CIA career arc from 1988/1990 recruitment through analyst years on Iraq, the switch to operations, 9/11, the enhanced-interrogation refusal, executive assistant to the deputy director for operations, and his eventual resignation and post-CIA career.

cofer-black.title: Condoleezza Rice
cofer-black.summary: U.S. National Security Advisor on 9/11; John Kiriakou recounts that he and Cofer Black had a meeting scheduled with her that morning over a mundane request to pull a few cables from an obscure declassified report to protect elderly former assets.

cofer-black.title: Magic box
cofer-black.summary: An improvised cell-phone locator that two CIA Directorate of Science and Technology officers built from parts bought in a Pakistani bazaar during the hunt for Abu Zubaydah; it could point toward a phone when switched on, but too slowly to act on.

cofer-black.title: Mike Pompeo
cofer-black.summary: CIA director and later Secretary of State under Trump. John Kiriakou read Pompeo's 2017 speech branding WikiLeaks a "hostile non-state intelligence service" as the groundwork for an Espionage Act case against Julian Assange in the Eastern District of Virginia — the "Espionage Court" where Kiriakou himself was prosecuted. Friends who briefed Pompeo told Kiriakou he was extraordinarily bright but wrong on Iran; Kiriakou's own verdict soured permanently when Pompeo named Gina Haspel deputy director, flirted publicly with reinstating torture, and called Chelsea Manning a traitor — a crime she was never convicted of.

cofer-black.title: Ruby Ridge
cofer-black.summary: 1992 federal standoff in Idaho involving Randy Weaver, triggered by an allegation that Weaver had sold a shotgun with a barrel two inches shorter than the legal minimum; per John Kiriakou, FBI sniper Lon Horiuchi shot and killed Weaver's wife while she was holding her baby, and Horiuchi was never punished. Kiriakou describes Ruby Ridge as one of the events that, after his own imprisonment, caused him to fundamentally reassess his earlier acceptance of the official government account.

cofer-black.title: Trump
cofer-black.summary: Kiriakou applied for a pardon on the last day of Trump's first term — and says Trump had agreed to it, until the last-minute reversal.

cofer-black.title: Waco Siege
cofer-black.summary: 1993 federal operation against the Branch Davidian compound near Waco, Texas, led by David Koresh, resulting in the deaths of more than twenty-seven people — more than half of them children. Per John Kiriakou, a CIA colleague's reaction upon hearing the news was 'It's about time.' Kiriakou describes this as the kind of response he once might have shared, but which his later experiences with government abuse of power caused him to revisit.

cold-cell.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
cold-cell.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

cold-cell.title: Sleep deprivation
cold-cell.summary: A CIA interrogation technique used against high-value detainees post-9/11; the agency was authorized to deny prisoners sleep for up to 12 days continuously; people died; at least one detainee was rendered permanently clinically insane.

cold-cell.title: Learned Helplessness
cold-cell.summary: Psychological concept adapted by the CIA as the theoretical basis for its post-9/11 enhanced interrogation program; per John Kiriakou, the goal of techniques including waterboarding was not primarily to elicit specific information but to render the prisoner so terrified of his captors that he would volunteer confessions on demand — a state of complete psychological collapse in which the prisoner loses any sense of agency or resistance.

cold-cell.title: Waco Siege
cold-cell.summary: 1993 federal operation against the Branch Davidian compound near Waco, Texas, led by David Koresh, resulting in the deaths of more than twenty-seven people — more than half of them children. Per John Kiriakou, a CIA colleague's reaction upon hearing the news was 'It's about time.' Kiriakou describes this as the kind of response he once might have shared, but which his later experiences with government abuse of power caused him to revisit.

cold-cell.title: Walling
cold-cell.summary: A CIA interrogation technique in which a detainee is slammed against a wall; designed on paper to use a padded fiberboard surface and a rolled towel around the neck, but applied in practice against bare concrete-block walls without protective measures, producing in at least one case permanent brain damage.

cold-cell.title: Ron Wyden
cold-cell.summary: U.S. senator and the lone real challenger of the CIA on the intelligence committees; John Kiriakou faults Wyden for challenging the agency only 'by the agency's rules' — refusing to read the Senate torture report into the record, and admitting at a dinner that fighting harder would cost him his security clearance.

cold-war.title: Soviet Union
cold-war.summary: The superpower whose collapse framed the start of John Kiriakou's CIA career — it was "literally in the process of collapsing" when he joined in January 1990, ushering in a brief "peace dividend" era when the agency's new threats were environmental degradation and AIDS. Kiriakou cites Brzezinski's "Afghan trap" that lured the Soviets into Afghanistan, argues the U.S. abandoned the radicalized mujahideen the moment the Soviets were beaten, notes America then took "a vacation from history," and recalls that Jonathan Pollard's stolen documents were traded by Israel to the Soviets in exchange for Russian Jews.

cold-war.title: Bilderberg and weapon sales
cold-war.summary: John Kiriakou's claim, sourced to someone he knew who attended, that elite gatherings like Bilderberg and the Shangri-La Dialogue are — beneath the talk of global issues — fundamentally 'all about weapon sales' and defense-contractor deals.

cold-war.title: Carlos the Jackal
cold-war.summary: Venezuelan-born militant (Ilich Ramírez Sánchez) active in the 1970s and 1980s; per John Kiriakou, 'the Osama bin Laden of the 70s and 80s.' Kiriakou spent his Athens posting trying to identify the middleman linking Carlos to the Greek terrorist group 17 November, then six months working the lead with MI5 in London; Carlos was finally run down by CIA contractor Billy Waugh in a Khartoum vegetable market and captured in 1994.

cold-war.title: CIA and FBI ties to organized crime
cold-war.summary: John Kiriakou's survey of documented U.S. intelligence partnerships with organized crime — the FBI securing wartime ports with the Genovese family, the CIA's Castro plots with the Trafficantes, its work with the Escobar cartel against Colombian communists, and a mob hitman deployed against the Klan.

cold-war.title: CIA and the UFO question
cold-war.summary: John Kiriakou's consistent answer that UFOs and alien technology are a Pentagon matter, not a CIA one — though he says nearly every former fighter-pilot friend of his has seen something inexplicable, sometimes emerging from the ocean.

cold-war.title: Zbigniew Brzezinski
cold-war.summary: Kiriakou links Brzezinski to the Analysis Corporation, and notes he once voted for the communist presidential candidate Gus Hall.

colin-powell.title: Iraq WMD intelligence
colin-powell.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how the case for Iraqi weapons of mass destruction was fabricated: the intelligence community''s consensus was that Iraq had no WMD, but the White House had already decided to invade and sought analysis to fit the policy.

colin-powell.title: MOSSAD
colin-powell.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

colin-powell.title: Lawrence Wilkerson
colin-powell.summary: Colonel and chief of staff to Secretary of State Colin Powell; John Kiriakou says Wilkerson told him on his program that Powell's UN case for the Iraq war was knowingly 'sold' to the public.

colin-powell.title: Saddam Hussein
colin-powell.summary: President of Iraq from 1979 until the 2003 U.S. invasion; subject of John Kiriakou's CIA portfolio from January 1990 onward, in which capacity Kiriakou became, at age 25, "Saddam Hussein's intelligence community biographer" and the analyst who briefed President George H. W. Bush in the Oval Office on the morning of the 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

colin-powell.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
colin-powell.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

colin-powell.title: Publications Review Board
colin-powell.summary: The CIA office that must clear anything a former officer publishes. John Kiriakou says everything he writes goes to it — books, articles, "even a letter to the editor of Home and Garden magazine" — and describes how the turnaround tracked his standing at the agency: his first book took 22 months to clear while the leadership hated him; his most recent six cleared in days.

collateral-murder-video.title: Chelsea Manning
collateral-murder-video.summary: Former U.S. Army intelligence analyst who provided WikiLeaks its 2010 trove of military and diplomatic documents. Per John Kiriakou, Manning meets the legal definition of whistleblower for exposing war crimes, was a torture victim of prolonged solitary confinement with forced nudity, and was sentenced to 35 years in prison before Barack Obama commuted — not pardoned — her sentence. Kiriakou says Manning later refused a grand jury's offer of immunity and chose renewed jail time rather than testify against Julian Assange.

collateral-murder-video.title: Afghan War Logs
collateral-murder-video.summary: A 2010 WikiLeaks publication discussed on a panel Kiriakou joined; the specific lines about it in the corpus belong to other panelists, not Kiriakou.

collateral-murder-video.title: Julian Assange
collateral-murder-video.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

collateral-murder-video.title: Iraqi invasion of Kuwait
collateral-murder-video.summary: John Kiriakou''s most detailed account of the intelligence process around the 1990 Iraqi invasion of Kuwait and its 1991 liberation. As a first-year CIA analyst on a ''training account'' covering Iraq, Kiriakou produced the June 30, 1990 warning paper for the White House; suggested calling the US Defense Attaché in Baghdad to drive to the border and report what he saw (the answer: ''Literally the entire Iraqi military is heading south''); briefed the August 2 Oval Office meeting with Bush; and later took a single phone call from General Colin Powell that led, eight hours later, to 47 cruise missiles striking the Iraqi Intelligence Service headquarters in Baghdad.

collateral-murder-video.title: Pete Seeger
collateral-murder-video.summary: American folk singer; John Kiriakou's personal hero alongside his father and grandfather; pleaded the First Amendment (rather than the Fifth) before the House Un-American Activities Committee in 1958 and was sent to prison for it (later overturned on appeal); befriended by Kiriakou over decades of concert-going and correspondence; rallied to Kiriakou's defense after Kiriakou's 2012 arrest; the subject of Kiriakou's favorite book, How Can I Keep From Singing?

collateral-murder-video.title: Russiagate
collateral-murder-video.summary: John Kiriakou''s rebuttal of the claim that Russia swung the 2016 U.S. election: the Mueller report found no interference, the DNC emails were leaked in person rather than remotely hacked, and Russia''s roughly $50,000 in Facebook ads — half spent after the election — was trivial against billions in campaign spending.

commercial-off-the-shelf-tradecraft.title: Surveillance detection route
commercial-off-the-shelf-tradecraft.summary: Tradecraft technique used by intelligence officers and assets to determine whether they are being followed before, during, or after an operational meeting

commercial-off-the-shelf-tradecraft.title: Operational vehicles
commercial-off-the-shelf-tradecraft.summary: The cars John Kiriakou used in the field. In the Middle East they were whatever the rental company supplied — usually a Toyota — on the reasoning that anonymity was the point; in Athens, where the threat justified it, he was issued a factory-built, level-four armoured BMW 540 that broke down constantly.

commercial-off-the-shelf-tradecraft.title: The CIA Insider's Guide to Surveillance and Surveillance Detection
commercial-off-the-shelf-tradecraft.summary: Book by John Kiriakou drawing on his experience as a surveillance detection instructor at the CIA and as a private surveillance training consultant. The book covers the techniques used by intelligence professionals to identify whether they are being followed — including the four-phase surveillance detection route, concealment device placement and retrieval, and counter-surveillance strategy — adapted for use by corporate executives, journalists, and others who want to confirm whether they are being followed.

commercial-off-the-shelf-tradecraft.title: Cover position
commercial-off-the-shelf-tradecraft.summary: The occupational identity under which an intelligence officer operates abroad. John Kiriakou''s account collapses the popular idea that certain embassy jobs are tell-tale: because a diplomatic mission has to do its real work every day, every position in and out of an embassy is simultaneously a genuine job and a possible cover, which is precisely what makes cover work.

commercial-off-the-shelf-tradecraft.title: The Islamabad surveillance incident
commercial-off-the-shelf-tradecraft.summary: The episode in which John Kiriakou, then the CIA's chief of counterterrorism operations in Pakistan, detected a motorcyclist following him, resolved to kill the man, and discovered on a passing impulse that the surveillance was friendly.

commercial-off-the-shelf-tradecraft.title: Sleeper Agent
commercial-off-the-shelf-tradecraft.summary: Per John Kiriakou, a person taken in early childhood, raised in a simulated version of a target country, given a false identity built from the birth record of a deceased infant, inserted into the target country, and then left dormant — sometimes for decades — until activated. Kiriakou says only Russia is known to use sleeper agents; no other country's intelligence service employs the technique. A former East German sleeper agent he interviewed on his podcast defected to the FBI after his daughter was born and a kill threat was delivered to him on the New York subway.

communications-management-unit.title: Julian Assange
communications-management-unit.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

communications-management-unit.title: Solitary confinement
communications-management-unit.summary: The prison isolation practice the United Nations calls a form of torture; John Kiriakou, drawing on his own ten days in a six-by-sixteen-foot cell, argues that jailing depressed prisoners like Daniel Hale in solitary 'for their own safety' is precisely what drives them to suicide.

communications-management-unit.title: Daniel Ellsberg
communications-management-unit.summary: The Pentagon Papers whistleblower Kiriakou calls 'the Godfather of all national security whistleblowers' — and one of the great mentors of his life.

communications-management-unit.title: Death threats against Kiriakou
communications-management-unit.summary: The threats John Kiriakou received after going public about the CIA torture program. On FBI advice that at least two of them were credible, he took his wife and children out of the country to Mexico for a fortnight.

communications-management-unit.title: Prosecutorial careerism
communications-management-unit.summary: John Kiriakou''s explanation for why senior federal prosecutors pursue high-profile national-security cases regardless of their merits: the conviction of a famous defendant is the entry ticket to a partnership at a large firm, a congressional candidacy, or a run for governor.

communications-management-unit.title: Sigurdur Thordarson
communications-management-unit.summary: The FBI's key witness against Julian Assange, described by John Kiriakou as a convicted paedophile, a convicted embezzler and a self-admitted liar — one of three facts he lists, alongside the bugging of the Ecuadorian embassy and the reported plot to kidnap or kill Assange, in asking whether judges can keep such things out of their heads.

condoleezza-rice.title: Cofer Black
condoleezza-rice.summary: Former head of the CIA Counterterrorism Center during and immediately after the September 11 attacks; principal architect of the agency's paramilitary turn on September 12, 2001; later Vice President of Blackwater under Erik Prince.

condoleezza-rice.title: George Tenet
condoleezza-rice.summary: Director of Central Intelligence from 1997 to 2004, spanning the September 11 attacks and the early enhanced-interrogation program; identified by John Kiriakou as John Brennan's institutional patron at the agency; the figure who ordered the Five Eyes intelligence services to "open the files" to each other in the early 2000s.

condoleezza-rice.title: Abu Zubaydah
condoleezza-rice.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

condoleezza-rice.title: Carlos the Jackal
condoleezza-rice.summary: Venezuelan-born militant (Ilich Ramírez Sánchez) active in the 1970s and 1980s; per John Kiriakou, 'the Osama bin Laden of the 70s and 80s.' Kiriakou spent his Athens posting trying to identify the middleman linking Carlos to the Greek terrorist group 17 November, then six months working the lead with MI5 in London; Carlos was finally run down by CIA contractor Billy Waugh in a Khartoum vegetable market and captured in 1994.

condoleezza-rice.title: CIA disguise program
condoleezza-rice.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the CIA's disguise and forgery specialists — including a master disguise maker recruited from a beauty academy who built him a custom bald-head mask over six weeks, and a master forger recruited off his college newspaper cartoons.

condoleezza-rice.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
condoleezza-rice.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

congressional-intelligence-oversight.title: CIA culture of lying
congressional-intelligence-oversight.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of deception as an occupational condition at the CIA — the tradecraft of detecting it, the training that instils it, and the institutional rot he says follows when officers cannot switch it off: a deputy director who married five successive secretaries, promotion panels that traded advancement for sex, and staff psychiatrists overheard planning how to push a colleague toward resignation or suicide.

congressional-intelligence-oversight.title: Jeffrey Sterling
congressional-intelligence-oversight.summary: Former CIA officer convicted of nine felonies, including seven counts of espionage, after giving a New York Times interview about a racial discrimination lawsuit he had filed against the CIA. Per John Kiriakou, Sterling was not accused of spying for a foreign country; his underlying case was that the CIA had passed him over for promotion and told him explicitly it was because of his race. Daniel Ellsberg asked Sterling to go to trial specifically so the constitutionality of the Espionage Act could be challenged; Sterling did, was convicted, and was sentenced by Judge Leonie Brinkema to what she described as 'Kiriakou plus 12 months.'

congressional-intelligence-oversight.title: Senate Intelligence Committee
congressional-intelligence-oversight.summary: The Senate Select Committee on Intelligence — the CIA's designated overseer, which John Kiriakou credits with the torture report's unimpeachable method (6 million contemporaneous CIA field cables) and simultaneously dismisses, along with its House counterpart, as "little more than cheerleaders for the CIA" since the mid-1980s. It sits in the official whistleblower channel he calls a proven dead end, and its own investigation was famously spied on by the very agency it oversees.

congressional-intelligence-oversight.title: FBI manufactured terrorism cases
congressional-intelligence-oversight.summary: John Kiriakou's account of terrorism prosecutions in which the FBI supplies the plot, the target, the explosives and the transport, then arrests the person it recruited. His central case is the 2026 Miami trial of a mentally ill homeless man facing six counts each carrying life without parole, in which Kiriakou testified for the defence and told the court that the FBI was "clearly the criminal in this case." The defendant was acquitted on every count.

congressional-intelligence-oversight.title: Deep state
congressional-intelligence-oversight.summary: John Kiriakou''s position on the deep state — that it is not a right-wing trope but an accurate description of something he served inside for fifteen years at the CIA and two more on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee staff. He is indifferent to the label ("call it the state, call it the federal bureaucracy") and insists on the substance: "It''s there to stay. It''s not going anywhere."

congressional-intelligence-oversight.title: Intelligence switching in the Iran–Iraq war
congressional-intelligence-oversight.summary: John Kiriakou''s account that during the Iran–Iraq war the United States supplied top-secret overhead imagery to whichever side was losing ground, switching as the front moved — giving the Iraqis imagery when Iran advanced, and the Iranians imagery when Iraq advanced. His summary: ''So it was hideous.''

consortium-news.title: Ray McGovern
consortium-news.summary: Former senior CIA analyst turned antiwar dissident, and one of John Kiriakou's closest friends — "like a brother to me." Kiriakou began working at the CIA on the Monday after the Friday McGovern retired in January 1990, so the two never overlapped inside; they became comrades in the whistleblower world instead. McGovern coined the "MICIMATT" framing Kiriakou often borrows, went into Putin's office with Oliver Stone for a 40-minute meeting, and — per Kiriakou — believes 9/11 was a conspiracy, a view Kiriakou affectionately notes is far from his own.

consortium-news.title: John Kiriakou
consortium-news.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

consortium-news.title: Julian Assange
consortium-news.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

consortium-news.title: Tucker Carlson
consortium-news.summary: American broadcaster and former Fox News host; a personal friend of John Kiriakou's for years, appearing on Kiriakou's radio and podcast work and hosting him roughly a dozen times on his own Fox show. Kiriakou calls him possibly the most brilliant and best-informed person he has ever encountered, and relays Glenn Greenwald's belief that Carlson could win the presidency — an idea Carlson privately dismisses.

consortium-news.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
consortium-news.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

consortium-news.title: Jason Leopold
consortium-news.summary: Bloomberg investigative journalist; characterized by John Kiriakou as the leading practitioner of Freedom of Information Act litigation against U.S. [intelligence agencies](/wiki/intelligence-agencies); broke the Hillary Clinton private-email-server story; whose FOIA suit against the CIA Office of Public Affairs produced documentary evidence that NBC's chief national-security correspondent had been sending articles to the CIA for clearance before sending them to his own editor.

contra-rebels.title: CIA Drug Facilitation
contra-rebels.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the CIA''s reported involvement in facilitating the arrival of cocaine into the United States during the era that became the crack epidemic, and his own firsthand discovery — as a Senate Foreign Relations Committee investigator — that under American military control Afghanistan produced 93% of the world''s heroin. A DEA contact told him the report would never be published because ''we want Iran and Russia to be addicted to heroin. It weakens their societies.'' Kiriakou draws a direct parallel to the current fentanyl crisis: China is doing to the US what the US did to Iran and Russia.

contra-rebels.title: Kill the Messenger (Gary Webb)
contra-rebels.summary: The 2014 film about journalist Gary Webb, on which John Kiriakou served as script advisor; when Kiriakou was arrested in January 2012, the FBI seized his electronics, including a draft of the unclassified Hollywood script, and stamped every page "top secret" despite Kiriakou having no role in writing it.

contra-rebels.title: Dark Alliance
contra-rebels.summary: Gary Webb's seven-part San Jose Mercury News investigation reporting that cocaine reaching Los Angeles and fuelling the crack epidemic had travelled through Nicaragua with the CIA's knowledge. John Kiriakou's account stresses what Webb did and did not claim — that the agency turned a blind eye rather than ran the operation — and that three separate federal investigations later found his reporting correct.

contra-rebels.title: Domino theory
contra-rebels.summary: The Cold War doctrine, described by John Kiriakou as Ronald Reagan's organising obsession in Central America, holding that if one country there fell to communism the rest would fall in sequence up to the American border — the stated rationale for backing the Contra rebels against the Sandinistas.

contra-rebels.title: Iran-Contra
contra-rebels.summary: The mid-1980s scandal in which the Reagan administration secretly sold weapons to Iran and diverted the proceeds — laundered through Cyprus — to fund the Contra rebels in Nicaragua. Per John Kiriakou, Iran-Contra marks the precise end of what he calls the ''golden age'' of congressional intelligence oversight: the roughly 1975–1982 window opened by the Church and Pike Committees, when ''serious people, heavyweights'' actually held the CIA accountable. After Iran-Contra, he says, the oversight committees reverted to being ''cheerleaders'' for the agency — a posture that has held ever since.

contra-rebels.title: Fentanyl and China
contra-rebels.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that China declines to stop the flow of fentanyl into the United States for the same reason he says the United States tolerated Afghan heroin reaching Iran and Russia — because an addicted society is a weaker one. He distinguishes Chinese-made illicit fentanyl, largely produced in Mexico, from the medical fentanyl that created the addiction pathway.

cori-bush.title: AIPAC
cori-bush.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

cori-bush.title: Jamaal Bowman
cori-bush.summary: Former U.S. Representative from New York; cited by John Kiriakou alongside Cori Bush as the second documented case of AIPAC successfully primarying an incumbent House member for criticizing Israeli conduct in the Gaza war.

cori-bush.title: Josh Shapiro
cori-bush.summary: Governor of Pennsylvania; veteran of the Israel Defense Forces, in which he served during his late-teen kibbutz year before returning to U.S. citizenship; cited by John Kiriakou as an example of the loyalty question raised by Jewish-American elected officials who have served the Israeli state.

cori-bush.title: AIPAC and foreign-agent registration
cori-bush.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that AIPAC is the only organization of its kind exempt from registering under the Foreign Agents Registration Act — set against his own experience around 2008, when a contract worth five or six thousand dollars to write four op-eds praising the Abu Dhabi Chamber of Commerce obliged him to register as a foreign agent.

cori-bush.title: BDS movement
cori-bush.summary: The Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement against Israel; John Kiriakou notes that some 40 U.S. states now have anti-BDS laws that can require a speaker at a publicly funded university to sign a pledge of support for Israel — which he refuses to do.

cori-bush.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
cori-bush.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

cory-booker.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
cory-booker.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

cory-booker.title: Jonathan Pollard
cory-booker.summary: U.S. Navy civilian intelligence analyst convicted in 1985 of spying for Israel; the canonical proven case of Israeli espionage against the United States; cited by John Kiriakou in his 2024 Piers Morgan debate with a former Mossad director who denied any Israeli spying on the U.S.

cory-booker.title: MOSSAD
cory-booker.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

cory-booker.title: AIPAC
cory-booker.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

cory-booker.title: Anwar al-Awlaki
cory-booker.summary: American-born al-Qaeda propagandist; in 1993 the imam of the Falls Church, Virginia mosque visited by John Kiriakou's CIA Arabic-language class on a field trip; in 2001 the cleric at whose mosque the 9/11 hijackers prayed the night before the attacks; killed by U.S. drone strike in Yemen in approximately 2011.

cory-booker.title: Restraint Camp
cory-booker.summary: A term for foreign-policy conservatives who favor ending forever wars and regime-change interventions; not attributable to Kiriakou in the corpus.

counterterrorism-center.title: Geneva Conventions
counterterrorism-center.summary: The laws of war at the center of John Kiriakou''s most-told confrontation story: finding hooded prisoners in Pakistan, he demanded of the officer in charge — "Are you seriously telling me that you have never read the Geneva Convention? It is a war crime to put hoods on them. Take the hoods off." The two reported each other to headquarters; Kiriakou got in trouble — "they didn''t give two shits about the Geneva Convention." He indicts the Bush administration''s twin dodges: that al-Qaeda fighters, as non-state actors, fell outside the Conventions'' protections, and that the techniques weren''t torture at all.

counterterrorism-center.title: Mort Halperin
counterterrorism-center.summary: Former Assistant Secretary of State, Assistant Secretary of Defense, and senior director of the National Security Council; author of the law John Kiriakou was convicted of violating (the Intelligence Identities Protection Act); wrote to President Obama stating that this is not why he wrote the law and that Kiriakou should be pardoned.

counterterrorism-center.title: Joseph Wilson
counterterrorism-center.summary: Former U.S. Ambassador to Niger and former Deputy Chief of Mission in Baghdad; husband of covert CIA officer Valerie Plame; in 2003 traveled to Niger at CIA request to investigate the Bush administration's claim that Iraq had attempted to purchase yellowcake uranium for a nuclear weapon, found no such Iraqi approach had occurred, and published a New York Times op-ed debunking the claim — triggering the administration's retaliatory outing of his wife.

counterterrorism-center.title: Mohamedou Ould Slahi
counterterrorism-center.summary: Mauritanian citizen, medical student in Germany at the time of his 2001 detention; held at Guantánamo Bay for fourteen years on the basis of one phone call from his cousin asking him to relay news of a family death to a second cousin who was in al-Qaeda; identified by John Kiriakou as one of the most morally significant figures of the post-9/11 period; subject of the film The Mauritanian; became a personal friend of Kiriakou's after both men were released.

counterterrorism-center.title: National Intelligence Council
counterterrorism-center.summary: Body housed at the CIA comprising the most senior analysts drawn from across the entire intelligence community. Its officers — National Intelligence Officers (NIOs) — hold positions at the Senior Intelligence Service level and are responsible for long-range strategic analysis on specific portfolio areas, as well as the production of National Intelligence Estimates. Per John Kiriakou, learning that the NIO for Warning had held the same job for forty-two years and just received a waiver to stay until seventy was the moment he first believed in the existence of the deep state.

counterterrorism-center.title: Taliban embassy raid
counterterrorism-center.summary: John Kiriakou's account of raiding the last functioning Taliban embassy, in Peshawar, in the middle of the night after 9/11 — a raid that turned up phone bills showing dozens of calls to U.S. cities that stopped on September 10 and resumed on September 16, evidence of possible sleeper cells the FBI never translated.

cover-position.title: Amaryllis Fox Kennedy
cover-position.summary: Former CIA non-official-cover officer who worked under commercial cover as an international art consultant, later a Trump campaign manager and nominee for deputy CIA director. Per John Kiriakou, Senator Tom Cotton threatened to filibuster her appointment; the president responded by naming her deputy national security adviser instead — a job Kiriakou considers more powerful, since the CIA director reports to the national security adviser.

cover-position.title: Operational vehicles
cover-position.summary: The cars John Kiriakou used in the field. In the Middle East they were whatever the rental company supplied — usually a Toyota — on the reasoning that anonymity was the point; in Athens, where the threat justified it, he was issued a factory-built, level-four armoured BMW 540 that broke down constantly.

cover-position.title: Surveillance detection route
cover-position.summary: Tradecraft technique used by intelligence officers and assets to determine whether they are being followed before, during, or after an operational meeting

cover-position.title: The botched pitch
cover-position.summary: The one operation John Kiriakou describes as a failure of his career: a two-year development of a terrorist working under journalist cover, brought to the point of a recruitment pitch and destroyed at the table when his station chief seized the meeting and threatened the target instead of pitching him. The target fled screaming for police, the host government''s deputy prime minister complained to the American ambassador, and the man later described the encounter to a third intelligence service as an approach by "two caricatures of CIA men."

cover-position.title: Commercial off-the-shelf tradecraft
cover-position.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how much CIA field equipment is simply bought rather than built. He describes the pen recorder arriving while he was in Pakistan and early GPS units in Athens being repurposed to map surveillance detection routes, and states the underlying economics: buying existing technology is far cheaper than developing it from scratch.

cover-position.title: 2028 presidential field
cover-position.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of the wide-open 2028 presidential race — the first in his life, he says, where he has no idea who either party will nominate. Predictive markets were listing 44 Democrats and 26 Republicans as possible candidates. His own preferred candidate is Tucker Carlson, whom he says he has repeatedly begged to run; his working assumption about anyone who does want the job is that they are "a narcissist and probably a sociopath on top of it."

covertaction-magazine.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
covertaction-magazine.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

covertaction-magazine.title: Julian Assange
covertaction-magazine.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

covertaction-magazine.title: Federal plea coercion
covertaction-magazine.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the federal justice system coerces guilty pleas by stacking charges and winning 98.2% of its cases — so that even innocent defendants take deals, as he did, told by his own attorney that the system is 'not about justice; it's about mitigating damage.'

covertaction-magazine.title: Guantanamo Bay
covertaction-magazine.summary: U.S. naval base in Cuba; site of CIA detention operations during the post-9/11 enhanced interrogation program; briefly served by John Kiriakou as interim Chief during the summer of 2002.

covertaction-magazine.title: Hamilton 68
covertaction-magazine.summary: A company founded by former CIA, FBI, NSA and Director of National Intelligence officials that rates news sites as reliable or unreliable, contracting mainly with the Pentagon to flag articles on government computers with green or red check marks; John Kiriakou says it threatened Consortium News with a "Kremlin apologist" red-check designation, after which PayPal permanently suspended the outlet's account and confiscated its funds.

covertaction-magazine.title: Pan Quake
covertaction-magazine.summary: An open-source, nonprofit, carbon-neutral social media platform based in Iceland and powered by geothermal energy, incorporated with lawyers in Luxembourg; John Kiriakou was asked to serve as a brand ambassador before its Icelandic bank account was frozen at the FBI's request over the platform's association with Julian Assange supporters.

craig-murray.title: Russiagate
craig-murray.summary: John Kiriakou''s rebuttal of the claim that Russia swung the 2016 U.S. election: the Mueller report found no interference, the DNC emails were leaked in person rather than remotely hacked, and Russia''s roughly $50,000 in Facebook ads — half spent after the election — was trivial against billions in campaign spending.

craig-murray.title: Bill Binney
craig-murray.summary: Former NSA technical director whom John Kiriakou cites as having debunked the DNC hack: Binney analyzed the upload speed of the leaked emails and concluded they could only have been copied in person to a thumb drive, not taken remotely by Russia.

craig-murray.title: Iran-Contra
craig-murray.summary: The mid-1980s scandal in which the Reagan administration secretly sold weapons to Iran and diverted the proceeds — laundered through Cyprus — to fund the Contra rebels in Nicaragua. Per John Kiriakou, Iran-Contra marks the precise end of what he calls the ''golden age'' of congressional intelligence oversight: the roughly 1975–1982 window opened by the Church and Pike Committees, when ''serious people, heavyweights'' actually held the CIA accountable. After Iran-Contra, he says, the oversight committees reverted to being ''cheerleaders'' for the agency — a posture that has held ever since.

craig-murray.title: Julian Assange
craig-murray.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

craig-murray.title: McCain-Feinstein Amendment
craig-murray.summary: 2015 amendment, sponsored by Senator John McCain, that formally and permanently banned torture by U.S. government personnel, codifying the Army Field Manual as the single interrogation standard for all agencies. Per John Kiriakou, it restored the original language of the 1946 Federal Torture Act after U.S. policy had drifted from it through post-9/11 reinterpretation — and passed, he says, in part because of his own 2007 whistleblowing.

craig-murray.title: John Bolton
craig-murray.summary: Former U.S. National Security Advisor; John Kiriakou predicted his 2019 departure from the Trump administration based on White House chatter, citing Trump's premium on loyalty and Bolton's habit of publicly contradicting the president — including reportedly joking the U.S. would be in four different wars if he had his way.

critical-analytic-thinking.title: Lie Detection
critical-analytic-thinking.summary: Per John Kiriakou, both a subject he addresses in his book The CIA Insider's Guide to Lying and Lie Detection and a practical skill he describes using throughout his career. Physical tells include gaze direction (down to conceal, up to construct), fidgeting, and throat-clearing; structural tells — losing the thread mid-conversation and self-contradiction — are more reliable, because the truth is stable while a lie requires maintenance and eventually collapses under its own complexity.

critical-analytic-thinking.title: Doing Time Like a Spy
critical-analytic-thinking.summary: Prison memoir by John Kiriakou, full title Doing Time Like a Spy: How the CIA Taught Me to Survive and Thrive in Prison; winner of two literary awards and reissued in a second edition by Simon and Schuster.

critical-analytic-thinking.title: Asset acquisition cycle
critical-analytic-thinking.summary: The four-step process — spot, assess, develop, recruit — taught as the first lesson of CIA case officer training

critical-analytic-thinking.title: Diesel Therapy
critical-analytic-thinking.summary: Per John Kiriakou, a punitive practice within the U.S. Federal Bureau of Prisons in which an inmate is placed into indefinite transit — moved continuously from facility to facility — for up to six months, with no access to phone, email, or pen and paper, and listed on the BOP website only as 'in transit' with no destination. Kiriakou described it as the one threat at FCI Loretto that actually frightened him.

critical-analytic-thinking.title: Moral Injury
critical-analytic-thinking.summary: Psychological diagnosis John Kiriakou received from a friend — a CIA veteran, brigadier general, and psychiatrist — who identified it as the source of Kiriakou's post-divorce PTSD. The concept describes the psychological damage caused when a person you fully trust does something that violates the moral framework you were raised to believe in; the brain cannot process that such a violation has occurred, and the result is a form of PTSD. Kiriakou had no PTSD from Pakistan or his CIA career but was, in his own description, destroyed by his divorce.

critical-analytic-thinking.title: Safe Housekeeper
critical-analytic-thinking.summary: Per John Kiriakou, a person recruited by a CIA officer to rent and maintain an apartment or other premises as a safe house, using their own name and identity to conceal any CIA connection. The role itself is minimal — rent the apartment, keep it clean, keep it stocked with water — but the recruitment is itself a covert operation requiring the same persuasion and pressure techniques used to acquire any sensitive asset. Kiriakou recruited a safe housekeeper overseas and believes the pressure he applied may have caused her a nervous breakdown.

curveball.title: Ahmed Chalabi
curveball.summary: Iraqi exile and founder of the Iraqi National Congress; per John Kiriakou, a Shia-Kurdish con man who looted Petra Bank in Jordan of $36 million in the 1980s, was sentenced to death in absentia, was pardoned at CIA request, then pocketed $6 million in CIA seed funding for the INC and bought a Mayfair house in cash; later resurrected by Dick Cheney to feed the Pentagon fabricated WMD intelligence used to justify the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

curveball.title: Valerie Plame
curveball.summary: Covert CIA case officer whose identity was publicly outed by the Bush administration in retaliation for her husband, former U.S. ambassador to Niger Joseph Wilson, publishing a New York Times op-ed debunking the administration's claim that Iraq had attempted to purchase yellowcake uranium from Niger. Per John Kiriakou, Plame's CIA career ended on the day her cover was blown — she could never travel overseas under cover again; no one was prosecuted for the leak.

curveball.title: Saddam Hussein
curveball.summary: President of Iraq from 1979 until the 2003 U.S. invasion; subject of John Kiriakou's CIA portfolio from January 1990 onward, in which capacity Kiriakou became, at age 25, "Saddam Hussein's intelligence community biographer" and the analyst who briefed President George H. W. Bush in the Oval Office on the morning of the 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

curveball.title: Joseph Wilson
curveball.summary: Former U.S. Ambassador to Niger and former Deputy Chief of Mission in Baghdad; husband of covert CIA officer Valerie Plame; in 2003 traveled to Niger at CIA request to investigate the Bush administration's claim that Iraq had attempted to purchase yellowcake uranium for a nuclear weapon, found no such Iraqi approach had occurred, and published a New York Times op-ed debunking the claim — triggering the administration's retaliatory outing of his wife.

curveball.title: George W. Bush
curveball.summary: 43rd President of the United States. In John Kiriakou's telling, Bush signed the August 1, 2002 executive order that authorized the CIA torture program, spent years telling the public "we don't torture," and — days after Kiriakou's 2007 ABC interview — blamed torture on "a rogue CIA officer" while walking from the White House South Portico to Marine One, a moment Kiriakou instantly read as the White House preparing to pin the program on him. Bush also ordered the FBI removed from Abu Zubaydah's black site, flew the bin Laden family out of the country after 9/11, and loosened the assassination ban of Executive Order 12333.

curveball.title: Publications Review Board
curveball.summary: The CIA office that must clear anything a former officer publishes. John Kiriakou says everything he writes goes to it — books, articles, "even a letter to the editor of Home and Garden magazine" — and describes how the turnaround tracked his standing at the agency: his first book took 22 months to clear while the leadership hated him; his most recent six cleared in days.

cyprus-green-line.title: Kiriakou's Cypriot ancestry
cyprus-green-line.summary: The DNA result showing John Kiriakou to be 24 per cent Cypriot — his largest single ancestry — which corrected a family belief that the line came from Crete and coincided with an invitation to address a Cypriot diaspora conference.

cyprus-green-line.title: Origin of the Kiriakou name
cyprus-green-line.summary: The Kiriakou surname originates in a clerical error at a Rhodes courthouse, where John Kiriakou's great-great-grandfather, arrested for stealing a potato while starving, gave a patronymic that was written down as his family name and never corrected.

cyprus-green-line.title: Abu Zubaydah
cyprus-green-line.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

cyprus-green-line.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
cyprus-green-line.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

cyprus-green-line.title: Bureau of Prisons advisory board
cyprus-green-line.summary: The advisory board John Kiriakou joined at the personal invitation of the Director of the Bureau of Prisons, who told him the president had tasked him with tearing the Bureau down and rebuilding it.

cyprus-green-line.title: Spy films John Kiriakou considers accurate
cyprus-green-line.summary: Kiriakou's assessment of which espionage films get it right — Argo, The Recruit and Bridge of Spies — and his flat rejection of the action genre's premises, including the hidden weapons stash.

daniel-domscheit-berg.title: Chaos Computer Club Wikileaks
daniel-domscheit-berg.summary: The Berlin hacker collective that shaped WikiLeaks' early years — and where a journalist first met Daniel Domscheit-Berg under a pseudonym.

daniel-domscheit-berg.title: Der Spiegel
daniel-domscheit-berg.summary: At a 2026 Berlin panel, a former Der Spiegel journalist said it took him years before he could call Julian Assange a publisher rather than an activist.

daniel-domscheit-berg.title: Wikileaks as a System
daniel-domscheit-berg.summary: Per John Kiriakou, WikiLeaks functions less as a single leader than as a durable system — one that protected whistleblowers, helped popularize the term "whistleblower" itself, was credited with contributing to the Arab Spring, weathered pressure to become a defanged NGO, and outlasted the political fallout of its 2010 cable releases (including, in Kiriakou's account, an unintended assist to Donald Trump's election).

daniel-domscheit-berg.title: Julian Assange
daniel-domscheit-berg.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

daniel-domscheit-berg.title: Chelsea Manning
daniel-domscheit-berg.summary: Former U.S. Army intelligence analyst who provided WikiLeaks its 2010 trove of military and diplomatic documents. Per John Kiriakou, Manning meets the legal definition of whistleblower for exposing war crimes, was a torture victim of prolonged solitary confinement with forced nudity, and was sentenced to 35 years in prison before Barack Obama commuted — not pardoned — her sentence. Kiriakou says Manning later refused a grand jury's offer of immunity and chose renewed jail time rather than testify against Julian Assange.

daniel-domscheit-berg.title: Daniel Ellsberg
daniel-domscheit-berg.summary: The Pentagon Papers whistleblower Kiriakou calls 'the Godfather of all national security whistleblowers' — and one of the great mentors of his life.

daniel-ellsberg.title: Espionage Act
daniel-ellsberg.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

daniel-ellsberg.title: Julian Assange
daniel-ellsberg.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

daniel-ellsberg.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
daniel-ellsberg.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

daniel-ellsberg.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
daniel-ellsberg.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

daniel-ellsberg.title: Tucker Carlson 2026 FARA referral
daniel-ellsberg.summary: The March 2026 criminal referral against Tucker Carlson to the U.S. Department of Justice accusing him of treason, espionage and Foreign Agents Registration Act violations that John Kiriakou says was widely misattributed to the CIA before the pro-Israel political activist Laura Loomer publicly claimed authorship the following day; Kiriakou treats the episode as an escalation from Israeli-aligned political actors and warns Carlson to worry less about legal jeopardy than about physical safety.

daniel-ellsberg.title: Watergate
daniel-ellsberg.summary: The scandal that ended Nixon''s presidency and the standing benchmark in John Kiriakou''s vocabulary — the CIA spying on the Senate committee investigating its torture program was, to him, "a Watergate-level kind of scandal," except that this time nothing came of it. Watergate touches his own story directly: his lead defense attorney had been John Mitchell''s lawyer during Watergate. He also relays, with fascination, Danny Sheehan''s far darker theory of what the burglars were really after.

daniel-hale.title: RDAP program
daniel-hale.summary: The Bureau of Prisons' Residential Drug and Alcohol Program, which can shave 12 to 18 months off a federal sentence; John Kiriakou repeatedly advises fellow whistleblowers that, combined with good behavior and a halfway house, it can turn a five-year sentence into as little as two and a half years.

daniel-hale.title: John Kiriakou
daniel-hale.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

daniel-hale.title: Tuesday morning kill list
daniel-hale.summary: Weekly CIA targeting meeting instituted by John Brennan in 2009 during his service as Deputy National Security Advisor for Counterterrorism in the Obama administration; produced a written list of individuals to be killed in the following week; per John Kiriakou, the program was a source of pride within the Obama administration and was made operationally possible by the targeting-software sophistication of the period.

daniel-hale.title: Diary of a CEO — January 2026 Kiriakou interview
daniel-hale.summary: The January 2026 long-form appearance by John Kiriakou on Steven Bartlett's Diary of a CEO podcast that a University of Texas at Austin sophomore then cut into TikTok shorts — sped and slowed, with lasers added — kicking off the Gen Z discovery of Kiriakou that pushed his cameo requests past 1,900 and drew a 2:30 a.m. representation call in Dubai from the Creative Artists Agency; Kiriakou treats it as the pivot after which stories he had been telling for nineteen years finally landed.

daniel-hale.title: National Bird
daniel-hale.summary: Award-winning documentary on the U.S. drone program featuring whistleblower Daniel Hale; John Kiriakou calls it essential viewing, noting its footage of drone operators debating on audio whether the figures in their crosshairs are children before firing.

daniel-hale.title: Phil Ochs
daniel-hale.summary: 1960s–70s protest folk singer; John Kiriakou retells a story from Pete Seeger about the night Ochs — who had fallen into depression after being unable to sing following a mugging in Africa — called Seeger just before taking his own life.

dark-alliance.title: Contra rebels
dark-alliance.summary: The right-wing Nicaraguan insurgency armed by the Reagan administration against the Sandinista government. In John Kiriakou's account they were conservatives, right-wingers, in some cases fascists, and disgruntled military officers; they were split into a northern group the United States armed and a southern group that financed itself by selling cocaine — a distinction that became the pivot of the Gary Webb affair.

dark-alliance.title: Oscar Blandón
dark-alliance.summary: The senior Contra leader whom Gary Webb's reporting identified as running the cocaine operation that moved product from Nicaragua to Los Angeles, and one of two men named in the Dark Alliance series.

dark-alliance.title: Kill the Messenger (Gary Webb)
dark-alliance.summary: The 2014 film about journalist Gary Webb, on which John Kiriakou served as script advisor; when Kiriakou was arrested in January 2012, the FBI seized his electronics, including a draft of the unclassified Hollywood script, and stamped every page "top secret" despite Kiriakou having no role in writing it.

dark-alliance.title: CIA Drug Facilitation
dark-alliance.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the CIA''s reported involvement in facilitating the arrival of cocaine into the United States during the era that became the crack epidemic, and his own firsthand discovery — as a Senate Foreign Relations Committee investigator — that under American military control Afghanistan produced 93% of the world''s heroin. A DEA contact told him the report would never be published because ''we want Iran and Russia to be addicted to heroin. It weakens their societies.'' Kiriakou draws a direct parallel to the current fentanyl crisis: China is doing to the US what the US did to Iran and Russia.

dark-alliance.title: Domino theory
dark-alliance.summary: The Cold War doctrine, described by John Kiriakou as Ronald Reagan's organising obsession in Central America, holding that if one country there fell to communism the rest would fall in sequence up to the American border — the stated rationale for backing the Contra rebels against the Sandinistas.

dark-alliance.title: Walter Pincus
dark-alliance.summary: The Washington Post reporter who, in John Kiriakou's account of the Gary Webb affair, took the CIA's side of the cocaine story and put it on the paper's front page — wrong, and Kiriakou believes knowingly so.

darpa-lifelog.title: Abu Zubaydah

darpa-lifelog.title: The CIA Insider's Guide to Surveillance and Surveillance Detection
darpa-lifelog.summary: Book by John Kiriakou drawing on his experience as a surveillance detection instructor at the CIA and as a private surveillance training consultant. The book covers the techniques used by intelligence professionals to identify whether they are being followed — including the four-phase surveillance detection route, concealment device placement and retrieval, and counter-surveillance strategy — adapted for use by corporate executives, journalists, and others who want to confirm whether they are being followed.

darpa-lifelog.title: Walk-in
darpa-lifelog.summary: In John Kiriakou's telling, someone who walks into an embassy offering information; 95% are lunatics or liars, some are 'intelligence peddlers' or hostile 'probes,' and about 1% are 'the real McCoy' — a framework he used to see through a supposed 'walk-in' tip during the Abu Zubaydah hunt. A genuine walk-in — a witness to a terrorist assassination — was later hypnotized by CIA psychologists in a London hotel room and read back a stolen van's license plate, verifying his account.

darpa-lifelog.title: Palantir Technologies
darpa-lifelog.summary: U.S. data-analytics and intelligence-software company; received its first $1.5 million in seed funding from the CIA's In-Q-Tel venture-capital arm around 2002; characterized by John Kiriakou as functionally inseparable from the CIA in 2025, drawing the majority of its revenue from agency contracts and operating across DARPA, NSA, and the broader U.S. national-security apparatus.

darpa-lifelog.title: Thomas Drake

darpa-lifelog.title: CIA animal surveillance experiments
darpa-lifelog.summary: Cold-War CIA efforts to turn animals into listening devices, which John Kiriakou describes as failures — including microphones and cameras mounted on pigeons trained to land on the Soviet embassy, which could reach the compound but never captured anything meaningful.

david-rockefeller-bahrain.title: Iran Nuclear Assessment
david-rockefeller-bahrain.summary: Per John Kiriakou's assessment, the US–Israeli military campaign against Iran was a war of choice driven by Israeli political pressure rather than genuine intelligence indicating an Iranian nuclear weapons threat. dead-drop-podcast.title: John Kiriakou's Briefing Room
dead-drop-podcast.summary: A twice-weekly news and commentary programme launched by John Kiriakou in July 2026, presented as analysis rather than partisan opinion, and distinct from his storytelling podcast Dead Drop.

dead-drop-podcast.title: President's Daily Brief
dead-drop-podcast.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the President's Daily Brief (PDB) is a roughly 16-page, top-secret intelligence document produced daily for the president, written in a uniform CIA house style, briefed each morning, and — in his account — used partly to gauge and flatter incoming presidents.

dead-drop-podcast.title: John Kiriakou

dead-drop-podcast.title: Threats against John Kiriakou
dead-drop-podcast.summary: The stalkers and death threats John Kiriakou has received since going public in 2007 — including a woman who believed he had proposed to her in code on C-SPAN and arrived at his office armed, and a caller who recited his son's home address.

dead-drop-podcast.title: Dead drop
dead-drop-podcast.summary: The classic tradecraft technique of passing material through a hidden location rather than a meeting. Per John Kiriakou, the hard part is not the drop but everything around it — in a sophisticated counterintelligence environment, merely identifying a viable site is very difficult, and the drop itself is bracketed by surveillance detection routes of two to three hours, or eight in Russia or China. Concealments run to the ingenious: one colleague built a dead drop container inside a condom, "because who''s going to touch a condom?"

dead-drop-podcast.title: Greater and Lesser Tunb Islands
dead-drop-podcast.summary: Two small, largely uninhabited islands in the Persian Gulf, belonging to the emirate of Sharjah in the UAE, occupied by Iran in a 1990s incident John Kiriakou recounts as CIA analyst; Kiriakou correctly predicted the UAE would not go to war over them given Sharjah's heavy trade dependence on Iran.

dead-drop.title: Dead Drop (podcast)

Written by Kiriakou with Alan Katz, produced by Costard & Touchstone Productions, with Kiriakou, Katz, and Nick Mechanic as executive producers. Its stated goal: "the deepest possible perspective on the world of spying and what makes any spy tick."

dead-drop.title: Sleeper Agent
dead-drop.summary: Per John Kiriakou, a person taken in early childhood, raised in a simulated version of a target country, given a false identity built from the birth record of a deceased infant, inserted into the target country, and then left dormant — sometimes for decades — until activated. Kiriakou says only Russia is known to use sleeper agents; no other country's intelligence service employs the technique. A former East German sleeper agent he interviewed on his podcast defected to the FBI after his daughter was born and a kill threat was delivered to him on the New York subway.

dead-drop.title: Advanced Counterterrorism Operations
dead-drop.summary: The six-week specialist course at CIA headquarters that John Kiriakou attended roughly eighteen months before 9/11 as one of fourteen officers selected worldwide — weapons, explosives, counterterrorist and desert driving, bugs, cameras, satellites and drones — and which, by accident of timing, meant a cadre was trained and able to deploy the moment the attacks came.

death-threats-against-kiriakou.title: Whistleblower psychology
death-threats-against-kiriakou.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of what distinguishes people who come forward: psychological studies showing whistleblowers hold a much more sharply defined sense of right and wrong than the general population, weighed against his own claim that there is no whistleblower who has not contemplated suicide in the period after going public.

death-threats-against-kiriakou.title: Communications management unit
death-threats-against-kiriakou.summary: The restricted-contact units inside American medium- and maximum-security federal prisons, which John Kiriakou groups with solitary confinement as a practice that amounts to torture.

death-threats-against-kiriakou.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

death-threats-against-kiriakou.summary: The FBI's key witness against Julian Assange, described by John Kiriakou as a convicted paedophile, a convicted embezzler and a self-admitted liar — one of three facts he lists, alongside the bugging of the Ecuadorian embassy and the reported plot to kidnap or kill Assange, in asking whether judges can keep such things out of their heads.

death-threats-against-kiriakou.title: CIA media relations
death-threats-against-kiriakou.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how the CIA shapes press coverage in the 2020s without needing an Operation Mockingbird-style infiltration program — because corporate media now recites CIA messaging willingly, most journalists simply rewrite emailed statements from the agency's Office of Public Affairs, and the CIA allegedly manipulates algorithms and backs podcasts to spread its point of view.

decapitation-strikes.title: 2026 Iran war

His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

decapitation-strikes.title: 2026 Iran war economic shock
decapitation-strikes.summary: John Kiriakou''s running assessment of the economic damage from the 2026 Iran war — an oil shock he says already exceeds both 1970s shocks combined, a natural-gas shock worse than the Nord Stream destruction, and a chokepoint problem that runs through fertilizer as much as fuel, since 65% of the world''s supply must transit the Strait of Hormuz. Per John Kiriakou, the access agent is funded generously to maintain an environment in which the targets feel comfortable and return repeatedly; kompromat — compromising photographs or recordings — may be collected as a secondary tool. Per John Kiriakou, learning that the NIO for Warning had held the same job for forty-two years and just received a waiver to stay until seventy was the moment he first believed in the existence of the deep state.

deep-state.title: Intelligence switching in the Iran–Iraq war
deep-state.summary: John Kiriakou''s account that during the Iran–Iraq war the United States supplied top-secret overhead imagery to whichever side was losing ground, switching as the front moved — giving the Iraqis imagery when Iran advanced, and the Iranians imagery when Iraq advanced. democratic-party-2025-approval-decline.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

democratic-party-2025-approval-decline.title: Djibouti
democratic-party-2025-approval-decline.summary: John Kiriakou's observations on Djibouti — Camp Lemonnier, once split by a fence between an American and a French base, now divided between an American side and a Chinese side; and the country's tiny intelligence service, whose entire director's office, Kiriakou says, was smaller than his own rental townhouse living room.

democratic-redistricting-collapse.title: Aldrich Ames
democratic-redistricting-collapse.summary: Senior CIA officer — a GS-15 who rose to chief of counterintelligence for the Soviet branch — who spied for the KGB.
