henry-kissinger.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

henry-kissinger.title: George H.W. Bush
henry-kissinger.summary: The 41st president — and the one John Kiriakou briefed a number of times, finding him "far more worldly" than the others, as befits a former CIA director. Kiriakou credits him with throwing away his presidency by keeping his word and stopping short of Baghdad, faults the ceasefire's helicopter loophole that let Saddam slaughter the Shia, calls him the last president to give the Arabs a fair shake — cutting off loan guarantees until Israel stopped building settlements — and traces the second Iraq war's personal edge to Saddam's 1993 attempt to assassinate him.

henry-kissinger.title: Osama bin Laden
henry-kissinger.summary: Founder and leader of al-Qaeda and the central target of the manhunt that shaped John Kiriakou's counterterrorism career. Per Kiriakou, bin Laden came from a billionaire Saudi construction family, was never one of the CIA-funded Afghan mujahideen, overruled subordinates who wanted to attack Israel and insisted the 9/11 attacks hit the United States to crash its economy, escaped Tora Bora dressed as a woman, and spent his final years next to Pakistan's equivalent of West Point — where, Kiriakou says, you would have to be a "mental defective" not to know he was there. Kiriakou believes the United States never intended to capture him alive.

henry-kissinger.title: Daniel Ellsberg
henry-kissinger.summary: The Pentagon Papers whistleblower Kiriakou calls 'the Godfather of all national security whistleblowers' — and one of the great mentors of his life.

henry-kissinger.title: Freedom of Information Act
henry-kissinger.summary: The U.S. transparency law that runs through John Kiriakou's story from every direction — his plea agreement banned him from ever filing a FOIA request on himself, so he filed one with the Bureau of Prisons anyway and got back pages stamped "FOIA EXEMPT — DO NOT RELEASE TO INMATE"; a FOIA request exposed the prison commissary skim; Jason Leopold's requests revealed that a detainee's eye was removed under sedation without his knowledge and that NBC's Ken Dilanian sent his stories to the CIA before his own editor; and a FOIA request is how Kiriakou learned Gary Johnson had quietly lobbied for his early release.

henry-kissinger.title: John Bolton
henry-kissinger.summary: Former U.S. National Security Advisor; John Kiriakou predicted his 2019 departure from the Trump administration based on White House chatter, citing Trump's premium on loyalty and Bolton's habit of publicly contradicting the president — including reportedly joking the U.S. would be in four different wars if he had his way.

hezbollah.title: Iran Nuclear Assessment
hezbollah.summary: Per John Kiriakou's assessment, the US–Israeli military campaign against Iran was a war of choice driven by Israeli political pressure rather than genuine intelligence indicating an Iranian nuclear weapons threat. The CIA produced two National Intelligence Estimates concluding Iran had no nuclear weapons program; Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei issued a fatwa in the 1980s forbidding such a program. The U.S. went to war anyway, in Kiriakou's view, after President Trump replaced the Joint Chiefs of Staff with officers willing to accept Israeli intelligence and proceed.

hezbollah.title: Khobar Towers bombing
hezbollah.summary: June 25, 1996 truck bombing of a U.S. military housing complex in Khobar, Saudi Arabia, that killed 19 U.S. Air Force personnel. John Kiriakou, then a CIA officer living across the water in Bahrain, felt the blast shatter his own windows and drove to the scene the next morning. He says the U.S. government worked hard to blame Iran and a small Saudi Hezbollah cell with no evidence, when the attack was in fact carried out by a radical Saudi group — a predecessor of al-Qaeda, which took credit for it.

hezbollah.title: Israeli False Flags
hezbollah.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the Mossad has been carrying out false flag operations since the founding of the state of Israel and is "usually very good at it"; he says his first suspicion on hearing of attacks on Saudi oil fields, Azerbaijan, and Cyprus was that they were Israeli false flags, and he fears a false flag against the Al-Aqsa Mosque blamed on Iran or the Arabs.

hezbollah.title: Hassan Nasrallah
hezbollah.summary: Long-serving Secretary-General of Hezbollah, killed in an Israeli strike on a complex in southern Lebanon; the strike, which killed approximately 300 people in addition to Nasrallah, decapitated Hezbollah's leadership and is characterized by John Kiriakou as a war crime under international law.

hezbollah.title: Lebanon-Israeli Conflict
hezbollah.summary: Per John Kiriakou, no Israeli government will allow Lebanon to flourish as a nation; he expects continued Israeli attacks and forced displacement of civilians, citing a statistic of up to 700,000 Lebanese internally displaced, and links the war to the "Greater Israel" rhetoric of US ambassador Mike Huckabee.

hezbollah.title: Black Cube
hezbollah.summary: Israeli [private intelligence firm](/wiki/private-intelligence) staffed by former Mossad personnel; reportedly used by attorney David Boies in the Jeffrey Epstein litigation; named by John Kiriakou as a representative of the no-compunction operating posture characteristic of Israeli private and public intelligence.

hillary-clinton.title: Reza Pahlavi
hillary-clinton.summary: The exiled Iranian crown prince whom John Kiriakou dismisses as an Israeli-backed fantasy candidate to rule Iran — a man who has not lived there since his teens, supported mainly by Beverly Hills exiles, whom Kiriakou says 'wouldn't survive the walk from the plane to the terminal.'

hillary-clinton.title: 1953 Iran coup
hillary-clinton.summary: The U.S.- and UK-backed overthrow of Iran's democratically elected prime minister, Mohammad Mossadegh; per John Kiriakou, the coup served British national interests rather than American ones, and the subsequent outlawing of secular political opposition under the Shah forced dissent into the mosques — producing a religious rather than secular revolution in 1979.

hillary-clinton.title: Bill Clinton
hillary-clinton.summary: 42nd U.S. president whom John Kiriakou describes as wholly disinterested in intelligence — briefed by the CIA only twice in eight years, with Vice President Al Gore taking the daily briefing instead and relaying anything important.

hillary-clinton.title: SPLC 2025 indictment
hillary-clinton.summary: Federal criminal case unveiled by FBI director Kash Patel and Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche against the Southern Poverty Law Center on multiple felony counts, described by John Kiriakou as concerning alleged payments to the Ku Klux Klan and Nazi groups and alleged money laundering; Kiriakou judges the charges are of the documentary kind that either happened or did not and that they could bring an end to an organisation whose 2024 balance sheet showed assets of roughly $786 to $822 million.

hillary-clinton.title: CIA political neutrality tradition
hillary-clinton.summary: The informal midcentury norm at the Central Intelligence Agency, described by John Kiriakou from his own 1990-era experience, under which employees did not share their partisan affiliations at work, small displays such as a Bob Dole campaign bumper sticker in a cubicle triggered severe internal discipline, and career officers steered clear of political endorsement — a tradition Kiriakou argues collapsed by 2020, when 51 former intelligence officials signed the letter dismissing the Hunter Biden laptop story.

hillary-clinton.title: Greenland
hillary-clinton.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the U.S. is seriously pursuing acquisition of Greenland — not by force, a White House contact told him, but by leaning on a 1951/1953 treaty with Denmark to claim de facto basing and resource rights; every EU member has pledged support for Denmark, and Kiriakou warns that forcibly taking Greenland could end NATO.

houthis.title: Bab al-Mandab
houthis.summary: The strait where the Horn of Africa nearly meets the south-western tip of the Arabian Peninsula, which John Kiriakou identifies as one of the few American national interests in Yemen and as a chokepoint whose closure would push the global economy into recession.

houthis.title: Ali Abdullah Saleh
houthis.summary: President of Yemen for decades, close to both Saudi Arabia and the United States until Yemen's 1990 Security Council vote on Kuwait, after which his country collapsed into civil war; he fled to Saudi Arabia and was killed by a bomb planted in the palace where he had taken refuge.

houthis.title: Iran regional war (2026)
houthis.summary: The widening of the 2026 Iran conflict from a war between Iran on one side and the United States and Israel on the other into a regional war — Iranian missiles striking a US base in Jordan, Iranian strikes across the Gulf states, Houthi attacks on Saudi shipping and oil, and Saudi forces striking pro-Iranian militias in Iraq. John Kiriakou notes he had forecast the expansion a week earlier.

houthis.title: Yemen
houthis.summary: Country on the southern Arabian Peninsula; setting of five John Kiriakou trips between 1990 and approximately 2010, spanning the country's brief unification, its civil war, and its present condition as a high-threat operating environment for U.S. and allied diplomatic personnel.

houthis.title: John Kiriakou's Briefing Room
houthis.summary: A twice-weekly news and commentary programme launched by John Kiriakou in July 2026, presented as analysis rather than partisan opinion, and distinct from his storytelling podcast Dead Drop.

houthis.title: John Kerry
houthis.summary: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts; chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee during John Kiriakou's 2009 service as the committee's senior investigator; subsequently U.S. Secretary of State; characterized by Kiriakou as a coward who buckled under CIA pressure on the Dasht-i-Leili reopening and as personally fixated on his perceived theft of the Secretary of State position by Hillary Clinton; the famously thrown medals were duplicates purchased at the post exchange.

how-can-i-keep-from-singing.title: Pete Seeger
how-can-i-keep-from-singing.summary: American folk singer; John Kiriakou's personal hero alongside his father and grandfather; pleaded the First Amendment (rather than the Fifth) before the House Un-American Activities Committee in 1958 and was sent to prison for it (later overturned on appeal); befriended by Kiriakou over decades of concert-going and correspondence; rallied to Kiriakou's defense after Kiriakou's 2012 arrest; the subject of Kiriakou's favorite book, How Can I Keep From Singing?

how-can-i-keep-from-singing.title: John Kiriakou
how-can-i-keep-from-singing.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

how-can-i-keep-from-singing.title: Aldrich Ames
how-can-i-keep-from-singing.summary: Senior CIA officer — a GS-15 who rose to chief of counterintelligence for the Soviet branch — who spied for the KGB. Per John Kiriakou, Ames's first act of betrayal was selling the identities of two CIA agents to the Russians for $50,000 to pay off a credit-card debt; both agents were immediately executed. He ultimately caused the deaths of twelve people, accumulated $2 million, bought a house in Arlington for that amount, drove a Jaguar to work on a $70,000 salary, and built an in-ground pool with a gazebo — all while being known throughout the office as a daily drunk. A 27-year-old officer sat on the initial security file for eighteen months. Analyst Sandy Grimes ultimately caught him.

how-can-i-keep-from-singing.title: Central Intelligence Agency
how-can-i-keep-from-singing.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

how-can-i-keep-from-singing.title: Robert Hanssen
how-can-i-keep-from-singing.summary: FBI counterintelligence chief and Soviet/Russian mole; framed CIA counterintelligence chief Brian Kelley as the source of compromised assets — leading the FBI to surveil Kelly for a year and a half and threaten his family with the death penalty — before Hanssen himself was identified as the actual traitor.

how-can-i-keep-from-singing.title: Sandy Grimes
how-can-i-keep-from-singing.summary: CIA analyst who, per John Kiriakou, was the person who actually broke the Aldrich Ames case. After a 27-year-old security officer sat on an Ames file for eighteen months without action, Grimes independently noticed that Ames made $100,000–$150,000 bank deposits within days of every trip to Mexico City — the pattern that identified him as a spy. After Ames's arrest, she submitted a hot-wash paper recommending 27 reprimands across the chain of command that had promoted a known alcoholic into the most sensitive counterintelligence position in the CIA. Director John Deutch responded with strongly worded letters for seven. Grimes resigned in 1993.

human-rights-watch.title: Amnesty International
human-rights-watch.summary: The human rights organization whose 2006 torture report forms part of John Kiriakou's core defense — the CIA's crimes were already public knowledge before he confirmed them on ABC — and the organization whose silence during his own prosecution he cannot forgive. He begged Amnesty for even a one-sentence statement about his case; the director of Amnesty International USA sent him a New Yorker subscription and a letter saying they wanted nothing to do with it. "After about a year I got tired of begging."

human-rights-watch.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
human-rights-watch.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

human-rights-watch.title: Kiriakou's transfer to the Directorate of Operations
human-rights-watch.summary: John Kiriakou's roughly two-month internal campaign to transfer from the CIA's analytic Directorate of Intelligence to the operational Directorate of Operations, overcoming what he calls a "natural bias in operations against the eggheads on the analytic side," followed by an Athens posting secured because he was the only person in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic. Covers his full CIA career arc from 1988/1990 recruitment through analyst years on Iraq, the switch to operations, 9/11, the enhanced-interrogation refusal, executive assistant to the deputy director for operations, and his eventual resignation and post-CIA career.

human-rights-watch.title: Osama bin Laden
human-rights-watch.summary: Founder and leader of al-Qaeda and the central target of the manhunt that shaped John Kiriakou's counterterrorism career. Per Kiriakou, bin Laden came from a billionaire Saudi construction family, was never one of the CIA-funded Afghan mujahideen, overruled subordinates who wanted to attack Israel and insisted the 9/11 attacks hit the United States to crash its economy, escaped Tora Bora dressed as a woman, and spent his final years next to Pakistan's equivalent of West Point — where, Kiriakou says, you would have to be a "mental defective" not to know he was there. Kiriakou believes the United States never intended to capture him alive.

human-rights-watch.title: Senate Intelligence Committee
human-rights-watch.summary: The Senate Select Committee on Intelligence — the CIA's designated overseer, which John Kiriakou credits with the torture report's unimpeachable method (6 million contemporaneous CIA field cables) and simultaneously dismisses, along with its House counterpart, as "little more than cheerleaders for the CIA" since the mid-1980s. It sits in the official whistleblower channel he calls a proven dead end, and its own investigation was famously spied on by the very agency it oversees.

human-rights-watch.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
human-rights-watch.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

hummus.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
hummus.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

hummus.title: Senate Torture Report
hummus.summary: The December 2014 executive summary of the U.S. Senate Select Committee on Intelligence's study of the CIA's post-9/11 detention and interrogation program; the first public disclosure of techniques including rectal feeding with hummus, sexual assault with broomsticks, and prolonged sleep deprivation.

hummus.title: Guantanamo Bay
hummus.summary: U.S. naval base in Cuba; site of CIA detention operations during the post-9/11 enhanced interrogation program; briefly served by John Kiriakou as interim Chief during the summer of 2002.

hummus.title: Strawberry Fields
hummus.summary: The CIA's nickname for a secret black-site annex at the Guantanamo Bay Naval Base used for the post-9/11 detention and interrogation program.

hummus.title: Jeff Fahey
hummus.summary: American actor; star of the Tyrell Vanto film in which John Kiriakou made his acting debut in late 2025; characterized by Kiriakou as generous with his time and on-set advice.

hummus.title: Tyrell Vanto
hummus.summary: Hollywood screenwriter and director; son of Jesse Vanto; friend of John Kiriakou; wrote and directed the late-2025 film in which Kiriakou made his acting debut.

hunter-biden-laptop.title: National Security vs Civil Liberties
hunter-biden-laptop.summary: Kiriakou's recurring argument that invoking "national security" is used to excuse the erosion of civil liberties and that the secrecy regime cannot coexist with constitutional democracy.

hunter-biden-laptop.title: Kamala Harris
hunter-biden-laptop.summary: Vice President under Joe Biden and 2024 Democratic presidential nominee; per John Kiriakou, installed as the party's nominee without a competitive primary despite having failed to reach the 2020 Iowa caucus, and closed out her 2024 campaign courting the Cheney family as a symbol of American values.

hunter-biden-laptop.title: Abolish the CIA
hunter-biden-laptop.summary: John Kiriakou's position that the CIA should be abolished because its functions are already duplicated by the other 17 U.S. intelligence agencies — analysis by the State Department, human spying by the Pentagon, technology by DARPA, NSA and the private sector.

hunter-biden-laptop.title: Abu Omar rendition
hunter-biden-laptop.summary: The CIA's kidnapping of a Milan cleric, Abu Omar, who was sent to Egypt to be tortured; the case is what ultimately sent John Kiriakou to prison, after he confirmed a former colleague's surname to a journalist writing a book about it.

hunter-biden-laptop.title: Afghanistan 2011 Kerry Trip
hunter-biden-laptop.summary: John Kiriakou's 2011 trip to Afghanistan as senior investigator for the Senate Foreign Relations Committee under Chairman John Kerry, where the pair sat through a briefing with 11 one-to-four-star generals presenting an optimistic account of the war — after which Kerry mused the U.S. might win, only for Kiriakou to tell him the U.S. controlled only Kabul, and that the same rosy briefing had been given every year since 2002.

hunter-biden-laptop.title: CIA/FBI Budget Fearmongering
hunter-biden-laptop.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how the FBI, under J. Edgar Hoover, pioneered the tactic of citing a shifting parade of enemies before Congress to justify annual budget increases — communists, anarchists, gangsters, beatniks, anti-war protesters — a tactic the CIA later adopted wholesale, citing "communism" until 2001 and "terrorism" since, without needing further explanation to win budget increases.

hussein-kamel.title: Saddam Hussein
hussein-kamel.summary: President of Iraq from 1979 until the 2003 U.S. invasion; subject of John Kiriakou's CIA portfolio from January 1990 onward, in which capacity Kiriakou became, at age 25, "Saddam Hussein's intelligence community biographer" and the analyst who briefed President George H. W. Bush in the Oval Office on the morning of the 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

hussein-kamel.title: Uday Hussein
hussein-kamel.summary: Eldest son of Saddam Hussein; described by John Kiriakou as so dangerous a successor-in-waiting that Saddam's two sons-in-law — Hussein Kamel and Saddam Kamel — defected to Jordan in January 1993 specifically out of fear of him.

hussein-kamel.title: Ali Hassan al-Majid
hussein-kamel.summary: Saddam Hussein cousin known as "Chemical Ali" and "the Butcher of Kurdistan"; per John Kiriakou, also briefly served as the Iraqi-installed governor of occupied Kuwait — "the Butcher of Kuwait" — and was engaged in the wholesale slaughter of Kurds in the north, Shia in the south, and Kuwaitis under occupation.

hussein-kamel.title: April Glaspie
hussein-kamel.summary: U.S. Ambassador to Iraq in the run-up to the 1990 invasion of Kuwait; per John Kiriakou, delivered to Saddam Hussein — on a State Department cable from Secretary James Baker — the line that the United States had "no position on inter-Arab disputes," which Saddam read as a green light to invade.

hussein-kamel.title: Iraq WMD intelligence
hussein-kamel.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how the case for Iraqi weapons of mass destruction was fabricated: the intelligence community''s consensus was that Iraq had no WMD, but the White House had already decided to invade and sought analysis to fit the policy.

hussein-kamel.title: Norman Schwarzkopf
hussein-kamel.summary: U.S. Army general and commander of CENTCOM during the 1991 Gulf War; per John Kiriakou, the architect of the "visionary" flanking maneuver that bypassed Iraq's fortified Kuwait–Saudi border, struck from the north, and produced the Highway of Death.

ilhan-omar.title: Espionage Act
ilhan-omar.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

ilhan-omar.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
ilhan-omar.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

ilhan-omar.title: Intelligence Identities Protection Act
ilhan-omar.summary: U.S. law enacted in 1982 that makes it a crime to knowingly disclose the identity of a covert intelligence officer; per John Kiriakou, his 2012 prosecution under the act arose from confirming a single surname of a former CIA colleague to a journalist — a confirmation that was never published. The name passed through a chain from journalist to Human Rights Watch to Guantanamo defense attorneys before reaching a judge and ultimately the FBI, which traced it back to Kiriakou.

ilhan-omar.title: Leonie Brinkema
ilhan-omar.summary: U.S. federal judge in the Eastern District of Virginia — informally the 'Espionage Court' — a Reagan appointee John Kiriakou calls "a hanging judge." Per Kiriakou, Brinkema systematically reserved all major national security cases for herself rather than allowing them to be distributed randomly among judges, and ruled in Kiriakou's case that his reason for blowing the whistle was legally irrelevant and that classified documents could not be used in his defense — effectively making it impossible to mount one.

ilhan-omar.title: Plato Cacheris
ilhan-omar.summary: Legendary Washington, D.C. defense attorney who served as John Kiriakou''s lead counsel in his 2012–2013 Espionage Act prosecution. Per Kiriakou, when discovery revealed the FBI had run a fake-diplomat sting against him, Cacheris explained the government''s posture bluntly: ''Because they have a shit case and they know it''s shit, and that''s why we''re going to trial.'' He spent most of the case urging trial, then drove to Kiriakou''s house on decision day and said ''You stupid son of a bitch — take the deal.'' Cacheris also represented FBI spy Robert Hanssen.

ilhan-omar.title: Mark Zuckerberg–Angela Merkel Meeting
ilhan-omar.summary: Kiriakou on Zuckerberg flying to Berlin to help Chancellor Merkel define hate speech — and why he objects to that call being Zuckerberg's.

imran-khan.title: Abolish the CIA
imran-khan.summary: John Kiriakou's position that the CIA should be abolished because its functions are already duplicated by the other 17 U.S. intelligence agencies — analysis by the State Department, human spying by the Pentagon, technology by DARPA, NSA and the private sector.

imran-khan.title: Alex Karp
imran-khan.summary: Co-founder and CEO of Palantir Technologies; subject of a biographical assessment commissioned from John Kiriakou by an unnamed interest group; characterized as militarily-industrially conservative despite a Democratic Party registration, religious, extremely patriotic, and "driven by profit."

imran-khan.title: Arrais Corporation
imran-khan.summary: Private intelligence firm; companion entity to The Analysis Corporation; originally an LLC pass-through for retired Senior Intelligence Service personnel from the CIA's operations side; subsequently acquired by IBM for over $1 billion.

imran-khan.title: Asset acquisition cycle
imran-khan.summary: The four-step process — spot, assess, develop, recruit — taught as the first lesson of CIA case officer training

imran-khan.title: Bluffdale NSA Data Center
imran-khan.summary: The NSA's purpose-built facility in the Utah desert, characterized by John Kiriakou as having storage capacity for every phone call, text message, and email of every American for the next 500 years.

imran-khan.title: Kashmir
imran-khan.summary: The disputed territory John Kiriakou says is front and centre for every Pakistani and largely absent from Indian minds, and on which his own sympathies lie with Pakistan — a promised 1940s referendum that never happened. He also describes the appearance that ended his participation in South Asian media: an Indian programme cut his pro-Pakistani answer, aired only his prediction that India would win a conventional war, and the death threats resumed.

in-q-tel.title: Palantir Technologies
in-q-tel.summary: U.S. data-analytics and intelligence-software company; received its first $1.5 million in seed funding from the CIA's In-Q-Tel venture-capital arm around 2002; characterized by John Kiriakou as functionally inseparable from the CIA in 2025, drawing the majority of its revenue from agency contracts and operating across DARPA, NSA, and the broader U.S. national-security apparatus.

in-q-tel.title: Will Hurd
in-q-tel.summary: Former CIA case officer, congressman and OpenAI board member whom John Kiriakou says he mentored at the agency; Kiriakou cites him as an example of the intelligence and tech worlds merging.

in-q-tel.title: Alex Karp
in-q-tel.summary: Co-founder and CEO of Palantir Technologies; subject of a biographical assessment commissioned from John Kiriakou by an unnamed interest group; characterized as militarily-industrially conservative despite a Democratic Party registration, religious, extremely patriotic, and "driven by profit."

in-q-tel.title: Peter Thiel
in-q-tel.summary: U.S. venture capitalist; co-founder of Palantir Technologies; subject of a biographical assessment commissioned from John Kiriakou by an unnamed interest group alongside Palantir CEO Alex Karp.

in-q-tel.title: James Bond
in-q-tel.summary: The fictional spy who got John Kiriakou — and, he says, half the Directorate of Operations — into the business. Kiriakou wanted to be Bond as a kid (walkie-talkies at nine, logs on the neighbor kids), concedes "literally none of it is true to life" (he carried a gun only in Athens and Pakistan), but vouches for one scene: Bond always runs into the CIA officer at the party, "and that happens every day in real life." Even the CIA''s venture fund In-Q-Tel, he notes, put the Q in its name as a wink to Bond''s gadget master.

in-q-tel.title: US Military Venture Capital
in-q-tel.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the U.S. military now purchases technology using a venture-capital investment model, a shift he cites as a warning sign about how national-security institutions acquire emerging tech.

india.title: Kashmir
india.summary: The disputed territory John Kiriakou says is front and centre for every Pakistani and largely absent from Indian minds, and on which his own sympathies lie with Pakistan — a promised 1940s referendum that never happened. He also describes the appearance that ended his participation in South Asian media: an Indian programme cut his pro-Pakistani answer, aired only his prediction that India would win a conventional war, and the death threats resumed.

india.title: The Intercept
india.summary: The investigative news outlet that published Daniel Hale's drone leak; John Kiriakou notes that the same Intercept reporter, Matthew Cole, was involved in cases that led to the exposure of both Kiriakou himself and NSA leaker Reality Winner — though he insists Hale outed himself rather than being burned by the outlet.

india.title: Sanctions Effectiveness
india.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment that U.S. sanctions have been so overused against disfavored countries that nations like China now route around them entirely, and that sanctions work only when reserved for the worst actors and imposed in concert with other countries — citing apartheid South Africa as a success and Cuba/Venezuela as failures that instead entrench nationalist narratives.

india.title: Spies of Arlington National Cemetery
india.summary: On the Walk With History podcast, John Kiriakou — author of Remains of the Day: A Definitive Guide to Washington D.C.''s Historic Cemeteries — toured Arlington National Cemetery and told personal and historical stories about the intelligence figures buried there, including OSS founder William Donovan, deputy CIA director Vernon Walters, codebreakers William and Elizabeth Friedman, slain station chiefs Richard Welch and William Buckley, U-2 pilot Francis Gary Powers, and Mike Spann, the first CIA officer killed after 9/11.

india.title: Bab al-Mandab
india.summary: The strait where the Horn of Africa nearly meets the south-western tip of the Arabian Peninsula, which John Kiriakou identifies as one of the few American national interests in Yemen and as a chokepoint whose closure would push the global economy into recession.

india.title: Beirut
india.summary: The Lebanese capital John Kiriakou confirms was a genuine espionage playground — though he dates the peak to the 1950s through the mid-1970s, when Beirut was the Paris and the banking centre of the Middle East, and when, beneath the CIA, KGB and Israeli presence, "more secretly the French ran the place." He also explains why the enormous new American embassy there is about fortification rather than a regional CIA headquarters.

intelligence-agencies.title: FBI
intelligence-agencies.summary: Kiriakou says FBI agents were sticklers for the law in a way the CIA never was — and that the bureau 'leaks like a sieve.'

intelligence-agencies.title: NSA
intelligence-agencies.summary: Kiriakou on the agency whose Utah facility boasts room to store every American's calls, texts and emails for the next 500 years.

intelligence-agencies.title: President's Daily Brief
intelligence-agencies.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the President's Daily Brief (PDB) is a roughly 16-page, top-secret intelligence document produced daily for the president, written in a uniform CIA house style, briefed each morning, and — in his account — used partly to gauge and flatter incoming presidents.

intelligence-agencies.title: CIA Democrats (2016)
intelligence-agencies.summary: John Kiriakou's term for a wave of 2016-era congressional candidates with intelligence or military backgrounds who ran for office opposing Trump from the right on Russia — including former CIA officer Abigail Spanberger, who won a one-term-limited Virginia governorship, and former DIA official Elissa Slotkin, who moved from intelligence into Congress and the Senate — both of whom Kiriakou suggests are positioning for future presidential runs.

intelligence-agencies.title: Abu Zubaydah
intelligence-agencies.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

intelligence-agencies.title: FBI Arrest Strategies
intelligence-agencies.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the FBI deliberately times arrests for Thursdays or Friday evenings because no federal arraignments happen on Fridays, forcing detainees to spend the weekend in jail before facing a judge on Monday — a tactic he says he saw applied to January 6 defendants as well as to himself.

intelligence-identities-protection-act.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
intelligence-identities-protection-act.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

intelligence-identities-protection-act.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
intelligence-identities-protection-act.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

intelligence-identities-protection-act.title: John Kiriakou
intelligence-identities-protection-act.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

intelligence-identities-protection-act.title: Haroon Yenor trial
intelligence-identities-protection-act.summary: Federal terrorism prosecution in which John Kiriakou testified as a defense expert witness; Yenor, arrested in November 2024 on charges tied to an alleged plot to bomb the New York Stock Exchange and a synagogue, was acquitted on all six charges on June 30; Kiriakou's expert testimony argued the FBI supplied the idea, the bomb, the explosives, the timer, the detonation cord, and the getaway car.

intelligence-identities-protection-act.title: John McCain
intelligence-identities-protection-act.summary: Late U.S. Senator from Arizona who gave the most consequential Senate-floor defense of John Kiriakou — declaring that 'if it weren't for John Kiriakou, the American people would never have had any idea what the CIA was doing in their name' — and sponsored the McCain–Feinstein amendment banning torture.

intelligence-identities-protection-act.title: Jesselyn Radack
intelligence-identities-protection-act.summary: American national-security attorney and former Justice Department ethics official who directs the whistleblower-defense practice at the Government Accountability Project. Per John Kiriakou, Radack was herself driven out of the Justice Department, had her law license threatened, and was placed on the no-fly list after blowing the whistle in the John Walker Lindh case; she went on to represent Kiriakou after his 2012 arrest and, separately, helped connect him to a path to reach Edward Snowden in 2013.

international-criminal-court.title: Hague Invasion Act
international-criminal-court.summary: The American statute, described by John Kiriakou as having been passed during the Obama administration, that authorises the president to use the United States military to invade the Netherlands and free an American or allied national held by the International Criminal Court — the standing legal answer to the possibility that Benjamin Netanyahu might be arrested abroad.

international-criminal-court.title: Graham–Netanyahu ICC tapes
international-criminal-court.summary: Recordings of Lindsey Graham coordinating with Benjamin Netanyahu on how to discredit the International Criminal Court over its arrest warrant. On the tapes Graham lines up Senate signatories for a protest letter, jokes that he should be paid "tons of shekels," and asks Netanyahu to telephone two Democratic senators to thank them. John Kiriakou argues the conduct meets the definition of espionage his own judge applied to him.

international-criminal-court.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
international-criminal-court.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

international-criminal-court.title: Netanyahu arrest poll
international-criminal-court.summary: The 2026 survey finding that a majority of Americans — not a plurality — support the arrest of Benjamin Netanyahu, a figure John Kiriakou notes is higher than the share who supported arresting Nicolás Maduro and which, per CNN, represents a fifty-point move in American opinion over five years.

international-criminal-court.title: Lindsey Graham
international-criminal-court.summary: Republican senator from South Carolina who died in July 2026, and John Kiriakou's standing shorthand for the permanent war caucus — a "show horse" rather than a workhorse, a "chameleon" who "never saw a war that he didn't want to jump into with both feet," and, on posthumously released documentary footage, a man offering the US Air Force to bomb a country America was not at war with.

international-criminal-court.title: Donald Trump
international-criminal-court.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

international-spy-museum.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
international-spy-museum.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

international-spy-museum.title: John Kiriakou
international-spy-museum.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

international-spy-museum.title: 2028 presidential field
international-spy-museum.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of the wide-open 2028 presidential race — the first in his life, he says, where he has no idea who either party will nominate. Predictive markets were listing 44 Democrats and 26 Republicans as possible candidates. His own preferred candidate is Tucker Carlson, whom he says he has repeatedly begged to run; his working assumption about anyone who does want the job is that they are "a narcissist and probably a sociopath on top of it."

international-spy-museum.title: Amaryllis Fox Kennedy
international-spy-museum.summary: Former CIA non-official-cover officer who worked under commercial cover as an international art consultant, later a Trump campaign manager and nominee for deputy CIA director. Per John Kiriakou, Senator Tom Cotton threatened to filibuster her appointment; the president responded by naming her deputy national security adviser instead — a job Kiriakou considers more powerful, since the CIA director reports to the national security adviser.

international-spy-museum.title: Andrew Bustamante
international-spy-museum.summary: Former CIA officer who sells CIA-style training online; John Kiriakou identifies him as the lone critic of his work hosting a show on a Russian network, and argues Bustamante's training business — open to anyone who pays — is the more problematic of the two.

international-spy-museum.title: Angry Birds
international-spy-museum.summary: The mobile game John Kiriakou describes as his only vice besides buying art, played every morning for nine consecutive years and cited by his ex-wife as a grievance in their marriage.

iran-12-day-war.title: Mohsen Rafighdoost
iran-12-day-war.summary: Iranian journalist and political figure whom John Kiriakou identifies as a co-founder of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and the propaganda voice behind the audio tapes distributed in Iran before the 1979 revolution; interviewed on the PBD Podcast, he conceded that the Shah's regime held only 3,000–3,500 political prisoners rather than the 100,000 opposition figures claimed at the time and that the Shah was, in his own judgment, a better man than Ayatollah Khomeini.

iran-12-day-war.title: Trita Parsi
iran-12-day-war.summary: Iran scholar; in a Foreign Affairs piece published August 10, 2025, predicted a renewed Israeli–Iranian war by the end of August 2025; described by John Kiriakou as "one of the greatest Iran scholars on the planet."

iran-12-day-war.title: Hassan Nasrallah
iran-12-day-war.summary: Long-serving Secretary-General of Hezbollah, killed in an Israeli strike on a complex in southern Lebanon; the strike, which killed approximately 300 people in addition to Nasrallah, decapitated Hezbollah's leadership and is characterized by John Kiriakou as a war crime under international law.

iran-12-day-war.title: Lebanon-Israeli Conflict
iran-12-day-war.summary: Per John Kiriakou, no Israeli government will allow Lebanon to flourish as a nation; he expects continued Israeli attacks and forced displacement of civilians, citing a statistic of up to 700,000 Lebanese internally displaced, and links the war to the "Greater Israel" rhetoric of US ambassador Mike Huckabee.

iran-12-day-war.title: Mexican 9 Month Work Visas
iran-12-day-war.summary: A George W. Bush-administration proposal, negotiated with Mexico in the six to eight months before 9/11, to give undocumented Mexican workers renewable nine-month U.S. work visas requiring federal income tax payment — killed by the September 11 attacks before it could be ratified.

iran-12-day-war.title: Trump Iran Ceasefire Efforts
iran-12-day-war.summary: Per John Kiriakou, Donald Trump reached out behind the scenes twice in ten days seeking a ceasefire with Iran and was rebuffed; Kiriakou also says Benjamin Netanyahu called the White House to check reports of the outreach, and that on foreign policy Netanyahu "has just as much authority as whoever happens to be president of the United States."

iran-2024-drone-retaliation.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
iran-2024-drone-retaliation.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

iran-2024-drone-retaliation.title: Israel's cell-phone assassinations in Iran
iran-2024-drone-retaliation.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how Israel wiped out Iran's military leadership by tracking cell phones — recruiting destitute Afghan refugees as $100-a-month spotters, and, when the generals stopped carrying phones, targeting their bodyguards' phones instead.

iran-2024-drone-retaliation.title: Itamar Ben-Gvir
iran-2024-drone-retaliation.summary: Israel's far-right Minister of National Security; John Kiriakou cites him as a convicted hate-crime felon placed in charge of security in Gaza and the West Bank over his victims, blames his insistence that any attack would come from the West Bank for diverting forces before October 7, and cites the death-penalty law passed under his portfolio for Palestinian detainees as the first reinstatement of capital punishment in Israel since it was abolished in 1956, excepting only the execution of Adolf Eichmann.

iran-2024-drone-retaliation.title: Israeli intelligence presence in the United States
iran-2024-drone-retaliation.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Israeli intelligence activity inside the United States — dozens of undeclared Mossad and Shin Bet officers identified by the FBI, a critical-threat counterintelligence classification alongside Russia, North Korea and Cuba, and a pattern of harassment and intimidation directed at declared CIA officers posted to Israel.

iran-2024-drone-retaliation.title: Kiriakou and third parties
iran-2024-drone-retaliation.summary: John Kiriakou's advocacy for viable third parties, and his 2016 experience touring the West with Libertarian candidate Gary Johnson — including the disorganization that convinced him the party would never break through, epitomized by a colleague who ignored an airport page thinking it was 'NSA tracking my movements.'

iran-2024-drone-retaliation.title: Bezalel Smotrich
iran-2024-drone-retaliation.summary: Israeli far-right minister whom John Kiriakou, alongside Itamar Ben-Gvir, blames for leaving Israel unprepared on October 7 by insisting any attack would come from the West Bank rather than Gaza.

iran-contra.title: Adnan Khashoggi
iran-contra.summary: Saudi arms dealer and Iran-Contra middleman whom John Kiriakou says was mentioned 'all the time' at the CIA — in pointed contrast to Jeffrey Epstein, whose name he never once heard there.

iran-contra.title: CIA Drug Facilitation
iran-contra.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the CIA''s reported involvement in facilitating the arrival of cocaine into the United States during the era that became the crack epidemic, and his own firsthand discovery — as a Senate Foreign Relations Committee investigator — that under American military control Afghanistan produced 93% of the world''s heroin. A DEA contact told him the report would never be published because ''we want Iran and Russia to be addicted to heroin. It weakens their societies.'' Kiriakou draws a direct parallel to the current fentanyl crisis: China is doing to the US what the US did to Iran and Russia.

iran-contra.title: MOSSAD
iran-contra.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

iran-contra.title: John Kiriakou
iran-contra.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

iran-contra.title: Contra rebels
iran-contra.summary: The right-wing Nicaraguan insurgency armed by the Reagan administration against the Sandinista government. In John Kiriakou's account they were conservatives, right-wingers, in some cases fascists, and disgruntled military officers; they were split into a northern group the United States armed and a southern group that financed itself by selling cocaine — a distinction that became the pivot of the Gary Webb affair.

iran-contra.title: Central American Task Force
iran-contra.summary: CIA unit that led the agency's early-to-mid-1980s effort to overthrow the Sandinista government and support the Contras in Nicaragua. John Kiriakou describes serving as assistant to the unit's head as one of his first, and most controversial, CIA jobs; he denies the accusation that the CIA trained Contra and Salvadoran insurgents to garrote nuns, saying the agency instead worked to stop such atrocities, while acknowledging it was associated with people who did terrible things.

iran-iraq-war-intelligence-switching.title: Saddam Hussein
iran-iraq-war-intelligence-switching.summary: President of Iraq from 1979 until the 2003 U.S. invasion; subject of John Kiriakou's CIA portfolio from January 1990 onward, in which capacity Kiriakou became, at age 25, "Saddam Hussein's intelligence community biographer" and the analyst who briefed President George H. W. Bush in the Oval Office on the morning of the 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

iran-iraq-war-intelligence-switching.title: Bahrain Posting (1994–1996)
iran-iraq-war-intelligence-switching.summary: John Kiriakou's 1994–1996 assignment to Bahrain under U.S. State Department cover as second secretary for economic affairs — arriving with his wife Joanne and infant son Chris on August 1, 1994, into a tiny Gulf monarchy whose sectarian tensions erupted, two months later, into the first Intifada.

iran-iraq-war-intelligence-switching.title: Deep state
iran-iraq-war-intelligence-switching.summary: John Kiriakou''s position on the deep state — that it is not a right-wing trope but an accurate description of something he served inside for fifteen years at the CIA and two more on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee staff. He is indifferent to the label ("call it the state, call it the federal bureaucracy") and insists on the substance: "It''s there to stay. It''s not going anywhere."

iran-iraq-war-intelligence-switching.title: Iraq WMD intelligence
iran-iraq-war-intelligence-switching.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how the case for Iraqi weapons of mass destruction was fabricated: the intelligence community''s consensus was that Iraq had no WMD, but the White House had already decided to invade and sought analysis to fit the policy.

iran-iraq-war-intelligence-switching.title: Israeli espionage in the United States
iran-iraq-war-intelligence-switching.summary: The long-running Israeli intelligence effort against American targets, which John Kiriakou describes from inside the CIA: Israelis barred from the headquarters building, 187 spies identified by the FBI in 1990, a critical-threat counterintelligence ranking alongside Russia and China, and a 2026 warning that activity had intensified.

iran-iraq-war-intelligence-switching.title: MOSSAD
iran-iraq-war-intelligence-switching.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

iran-nuclear-assessment.title: Israeli False Flags
iran-nuclear-assessment.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the Mossad has been carrying out false flag operations since the founding of the state of Israel and is "usually very good at it"; he says his first suspicion on hearing of attacks on Saudi oil fields, Azerbaijan, and Cyprus was that they were Israeli false flags, and he fears a false flag against the Al-Aqsa Mosque blamed on Iran or the Arabs.

iran-nuclear-assessment.title: Glenn-Symington Act
iran-nuclear-assessment.summary: U.S. federal statute, co-authored by Senators John Glenn and Stuart Symington, that prohibits the U.S. government from providing foreign aid of any kind to any country possessing a nuclear weapons program that has not signed the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty; per John Kiriakou, Israel is the only country in the world meeting both criteria, making the law the principal reason the U.S. government officially declines to acknowledge the Israeli nuclear program.

iran-nuclear-assessment.title: Truman's regret over Israel
iran-nuclear-assessment.summary: John Kiriakou's account that Harry Truman called his role in the creation of the state of Israel the act of 'a damn fool' and the biggest regret of his presidency, because the situation spun out of control almost immediately.

iran-nuclear-assessment.title: Mexican 9 Month Work Visas
iran-nuclear-assessment.summary: A George W. Bush-administration proposal, negotiated with Mexico in the six to eight months before 9/11, to give undocumented Mexican workers renewable nine-month U.S. work visas requiring federal income tax payment — killed by the September 11 attacks before it could be ratified.

iran-nuclear-assessment.title: Nixon's guarantee of Israeli national security
iran-nuclear-assessment.summary: John Kiriakou's account that AIPAC, having begun to focus on election fundraising in the late 1960s, succeeded in getting President Nixon to guarantee Israeli national security in 1969 — a commitment he says no American president had made before.

iran-nuclear-assessment.title: Trump Iran Ceasefire Efforts
iran-nuclear-assessment.summary: Per John Kiriakou, Donald Trump reached out behind the scenes twice in ten days seeking a ceasefire with Iran and was rebuffed; Kiriakou also says Benjamin Netanyahu called the White House to check reports of the outreach, and that on foreign policy Netanyahu "has just as much authority as whoever happens to be president of the United States."

iran-regional-war-2026.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
iran-regional-war-2026.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

iran-regional-war-2026.title: Houthis
iran-regional-war-2026.summary: The Iran-aligned movement that controls the most important parts of Yemen, described by John Kiriakou as fierce fighters who beat the Saudi military over a decade of war and who in July 2026 declared a naval blockade of Saudi shipping.

iran-regional-war-2026.title: Reza Pahlavi
iran-regional-war-2026.summary: The exiled Iranian crown prince whom John Kiriakou dismisses as an Israeli-backed fantasy candidate to rule Iran — a man who has not lived there since his teens, supported mainly by Beverly Hills exiles, whom Kiriakou says 'wouldn't survive the walk from the plane to the terminal.'

iran-regional-war-2026.title: South Caucasus realignment
iran-regional-war-2026.summary: John Kiriakou''s reading of the post-election South Caucasus: Russia has lost Armenia, Georgia has split from Armenia and moved closer to Moscow, and Iran — contrary to the assumption that two Muslim neighbours would be natural partners — keeps far closer relations with Christian Armenia than with Azerbaijan.

iran-regional-war-2026.title: Pickaxe Mountain
iran-regional-war-2026.summary: The Iranian site whose ongoing excavation Benjamin Netanyahu publicised in July 2026 and which Donald Trump, in response, said he already knew about — using the exchange to tell an ally publicly not to brief the press ahead of him. John Kiriakou reads the episode as Netanyahu attempting to move American public opinion and Trump refusing to be moved.

iran-regional-war-2026.title: Donald Trump
iran-regional-war-2026.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

iran-strike-factions-2026.title: Iran 12-Day War
iran-strike-factions-2026.summary: 2025 Israeli air campaign against Iran during which Israel killed at least fourteen Iranian nuclear scientists by destroying the apartment buildings they lived in; preceded for each scientist by Farsi-language telephone calls from Iranian-Jewish Mossad and Shin Bet officers offering defection in lieu of certain death; characterized by John Kiriakou as a categorical departure from CIA targeting doctrine in its acceptable-civilian-casualty calculus.

iran-strike-factions-2026.title: Reza Pahlavi
iran-strike-factions-2026.summary: The exiled Iranian crown prince whom John Kiriakou dismisses as an Israeli-backed fantasy candidate to rule Iran — a man who has not lived there since his teens, supported mainly by Beverly Hills exiles, whom Kiriakou says 'wouldn't survive the walk from the plane to the terminal.'

iran-strike-factions-2026.title: MOSSAD
iran-strike-factions-2026.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

iran-strike-factions-2026.title: Mark Levin Iran Policy
iran-strike-factions-2026.summary: Per Sean Davis, speaking on the same Megyn Kelly panel as Kiriakou, radio host Mark Levin was among the "outside voices" — alongside Senator Lindsey Graham — who effectively made the real policy call to invade Iran. Separately, per John Kiriakou, Levin is one of the very few prominent commentators who consistently defends Israel publicly online.

iran-strike-factions-2026.title: Trita Parsi
iran-strike-factions-2026.summary: Iran scholar; in a Foreign Affairs piece published August 10, 2025, predicted a renewed Israeli–Iranian war by the end of August 2025; described by John Kiriakou as "one of the greatest Iran scholars on the planet."

iran-strike-factions-2026.title: U.S. diplomatic vacancies
iran-strike-factions-2026.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how the mass dismissal of career U.S. ambassadors — never replaced — left the Gulf without American envoys as war with Iran loomed, so allied royals had to ask him personally whether the U.S. would attack.

iranian-sleeper-cells.title: Charlie Kirk shooting
iranian-sleeper-cells.summary: Kiriakou questions the official account: a court filing says the ATF could not match the autopsy bullet to the rifle tied to the suspect.

iranian-sleeper-cells.title: Israel-United States relations
iranian-sleeper-cells.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the U.S.-Israel relationship, including his own first visit to Israel as a tourist in 2022 and his characterization of Israel's willingness to destroy an entire city block to kill a single target, confident that the United States will not object.

iranian-sleeper-cells.title: Israeli espionage in the United States
iranian-sleeper-cells.summary: The long-running Israeli intelligence effort against American targets, which John Kiriakou describes from inside the CIA: Israelis barred from the headquarters building, 187 spies identified by the FBI in 1990, a critical-threat counterintelligence ranking alongside Russia and China, and a 2026 warning that activity had intensified.

iranian-sleeper-cells.title: Maduro Capture
iranian-sleeper-cells.summary: CIA-driven nighttime operation in which a team of Delta Force commandos entered Venezuela and removed Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife from their beds. Per John Kiriakou, the key enabling intelligence — per a New York Times account he cited — came from a CIA asset inside Maduro''s presidential palace who called when Maduro went to sleep: ''He''s sound asleep. If you''re going to do it, do it now.'' At least eighty people were killed in the operation, including approximately thirty-five Cubans. Kiriakou compares it to the 1989 capture of Manuel Noriega, in which US forces blasted death metal at the Vatican Embassy until Noriega was asked to leave.

iranian-sleeper-cells.title: Principals Committee Meeting (February 2003)
iranian-sleeper-cells.summary: Senior-most interagency forum of the U.S. national security apparatus, normally chaired by the president. Per John Kiriakou — who served as notetaker for CIA Director George Tenet at the eve-of-Iraq-invasion meeting on February 19–20, 2003 — Vice President Dick Cheney chaired in place of Bush, General Tommy Franks ended his order-of-battle briefing with 'If all goes as planned, we can be in Tehran by August,' and an NSC senior director said 'When we cross that border tomorrow morning, they're going to throw flowers at us.'

iranian-sleeper-cells.title: 2026 Iran war
iranian-sleeper-cells.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

iraq-war-israeli-tower-sabotage.title: Guantánamo Bay detention camp
iraq-war-israeli-tower-sabotage.summary: Per John Kiriakou — as chief of counterterrorism operations in Pakistan after September 11, 2001 — the Guantanamo detention facility began as a temporary holding measure intended to last two to three weeks while the CIA and Justice Department determined which federal district court should try each prisoner, not as a long-term detention infrastructure. The Rawalpindi jail had reached capacity, Pakistani intelligence demanded the prisoners be removed, and CIA headquarters directed Kiriakou to load them onto a C-12 cargo plane and fly them to Cuba.

iraq-war-israeli-tower-sabotage.title: Pakistan Station (2002)
iraq-war-israeli-tower-sabotage.summary: John Kiriakou's January 2002 arrival in Islamabad to become CIA chief of counterterrorism operations — a journey via London and Kuwait with lost luggage, a warning that steered him away from the soon-to-be-bombed Marriott, a skeleton counterterrorism branch of seven CIA retirees, and the raids that followed.

iraq-war-israeli-tower-sabotage.title: 9/11 Commission
iraq-war-israeli-tower-sabotage.summary: The federal commission of inquiry into the September 11 attacks, which John Kiriakou describes as structurally incapable of reaching the truth because it was barred from interviewing serving CIA officers or any Guantanamo detainee, and was blocked by the CIA from pursuing the Saudi thread.

iraq-war-israeli-tower-sabotage.title: 9/11 plea agreements
iraq-war-israeli-tower-sabotage.summary: The Biden-era plea deals under which Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and co-defendants agreed to plead guilty to murdering 2,976 people in exchange for life without parole and a guarantee against transfer to the Colorado supermax — vacated by the Secretary of Defense after public backlash. Per John Kiriakou, the deals existed because torture had rendered every confession inadmissible, leaving no usable evidence.

iraq-war-israeli-tower-sabotage.title: Abu Zubaydah
iraq-war-israeli-tower-sabotage.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

iraq-war-israeli-tower-sabotage.title: Agnes von Kurowsky grave story
iraq-war-israeli-tower-sabotage.summary: John Kiriakou's account of discovering the Washington, D.C. grave of Agnes von Kurowsky, the World War I Red Cross nurse whose four-month wartime romance with a young ambulance driver, Ernest Hemingway, made her the model for the lead female character in six of his books, including A Farewell to Arms.

iraq-wmd-intelligence.title: Principals Committee Meeting (February 2003)
iraq-wmd-intelligence.summary: Senior-most interagency forum of the U.S. national security apparatus, normally chaired by the president. Per John Kiriakou — who served as notetaker for CIA Director George Tenet at the eve-of-Iraq-invasion meeting on February 19–20, 2003 — Vice President Dick Cheney chaired in place of Bush, General Tommy Franks ended his order-of-battle briefing with 'If all goes as planned, we can be in Tehran by August,' and an NSC senior director said 'When we cross that border tomorrow morning, they're going to throw flowers at us.'

iraq-wmd-intelligence.title: Wesley Clark
iraq-wmd-intelligence.summary: Retired U.S. Army four-star general and former Clinton administration adviser; per John Kiriakou, "a very good guy" and the public source of the now-famous account that, in the week of 9/11, the Pentagon was ordered to draw up a plan to overthrow seven governments — Iraq, Iran, Libya, Syria, Somalia, Sudan, and one other — on the theory that they would fall like dominoes.

iraq-wmd-intelligence.title: Lawrence Wilkerson
iraq-wmd-intelligence.summary: Colonel and chief of staff to Secretary of State Colin Powell; John Kiriakou says Wilkerson told him on his program that Powell's UN case for the Iraq war was knowingly 'sold' to the public.

iraq-wmd-intelligence.title: Richard Perle
iraq-wmd-intelligence.summary: Prominent neoconservative adviser to the George W. Bush White House whom John Kiriakou credits with planting the idea of invading Iraq in Dick Cheney's mind the day after 9/11.

iraq-wmd-intelligence.title: Colin Powell
iraq-wmd-intelligence.summary: U.S. Secretary of State whose 2003 UN testimony made the case for the Iraq war; John Kiriakou says the white powder in Powell's prop tube was nothing, and that Powell's own chief of staff later told him the presentation was knowingly 'sold.'

iraq-wmd-intelligence.title: Omar al-Bayoumi
iraq-wmd-intelligence.summary: The Saudi national who housed and funded two of the 9/11 hijackers in California; John Kiriakou describes him as a Saudi intelligence officer working under a ghost job, places him at President Bush's Crawford ranch before the attacks, and says the CIA blocked the 9/11 Commission from investigating him.

irish-intelligence-services.title: John Kiriakou
irish-intelligence-services.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

irish-intelligence-services.title: Al-Qaeda training manual interrogation-resistance tactics
irish-intelligence-services.summary: A captured al-Qaeda training manual instructing operatives on how to resist interrogation, including feigning illness — a technique John Kiriakou says he saw a detainee use, and recognized, during a capture and interrogation in Pakistan.

irish-intelligence-services.title: Djibouti
irish-intelligence-services.summary: John Kiriakou's observations on Djibouti — Camp Lemonnier, once split by a fence between an American and a French base, now divided between an American side and a Chinese side; and the country's tiny intelligence service, whose entire director's office, Kiriakou says, was smaller than his own rental townhouse living room.

irish-intelligence-services.title: CIA and the UFO question
irish-intelligence-services.summary: John Kiriakou's consistent answer that UFOs and alien technology are a Pentagon matter, not a CIA one — though he says nearly every former fighter-pilot friend of his has seen something inexplicable, sometimes emerging from the ocean.

irish-intelligence-services.title: Guantanamo Bay
irish-intelligence-services.summary: U.S. naval base in Cuba; site of CIA detention operations during the post-9/11 enhanced interrogation program; briefly served by John Kiriakou as interim Chief during the summer of 2002.

irish-intelligence-services.title: Iran 12-Day War
irish-intelligence-services.summary: 2025 Israeli air campaign against Iran during which Israel killed at least fourteen Iranian nuclear scientists by destroying the apartment buildings they lived in; preceded for each scientist by Farsi-language telephone calls from Iranian-Jewish Mossad and Shin Bet officers offering defection in lieu of certain death; characterized by John Kiriakou as a categorical departure from CIA targeting doctrine in its acceptable-civilian-casualty calculus.

isa-bin-salman-al-khalifa.title: Bahrain Posting (1994–1996)
isa-bin-salman-al-khalifa.summary: John Kiriakou's 1994–1996 assignment to Bahrain under U.S. State Department cover as second secretary for economic affairs — arriving with his wife Joanne and infant son Chris on August 1, 1994, into a tiny Gulf monarchy whose sectarian tensions erupted, two months later, into the first Intifada.

isa-bin-salman-al-khalifa.title: Bahrain Intifada (1994)
isa-bin-salman-al-khalifa.summary: The first Bahraini Intifada, a Shia uprising against the Sunni Al Khalifa monarchy that began roughly two months into John Kiriakou's 1994 Bahrain posting with a bombing at the Ministry of Labor, led by Abdul Amir Al-Jamri, and met by the government first with police, then armored personnel carriers and tanks, and executions.

isa-bin-salman-al-khalifa.title: Bahrain Prime Minister "Mr. 10 Percent"
isa-bin-salman-al-khalifa.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Bahrain's long-serving prime minister, the Amir's uncle, universally nicknamed "Mr. 10 Percent" for allegedly requiring a 10 percent cash cut on business deals — a cold, calculating figure Kiriakou calls "the definition of corruption," pointedly excluded from the national motto, yet credited with turning Bahrain into the Gulf's banking hub.

isa-bin-salman-al-khalifa.title: Admiral William Crowe
isa-bin-salman-al-khalifa.summary: Former Chairman of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff; visited Bahrain during John Kiriakou's posting there, with Kiriakou assigned as his control officer; present during Kiriakou's "I have my eye on you" handshake confrontation with the Bahraini Prime Minister, Prince Khalifa bin Salman Al Khalifa.

isa-bin-salman-al-khalifa.title: John Kiriakou
isa-bin-salman-al-khalifa.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

isa-bin-salman-al-khalifa.title: Office of Leadership Analysis
isa-bin-salman-al-khalifa.summary: CIA analytic office — internally called LDA, for Leadership Development Analysis — founded by CIA psychiatrist Jerome Post, where John Kiriakou was hired at the start of his CIA career and spent his first seven and a half years as Saddam Hussein's classified psychological profiler. His first assignment, given on his first day, was covering Iraq and Kuwait, a portfolio his boss described as so quiet the office sometimes went days without a single incoming cable.

isi.title: A.Q. Khan
isi.summary: Pakistani nuclear scientist and the architect of Pakistan's bomb, who ran a black-market proliferation network that, per John Kiriakou, smuggled nuclear material and technology to North Korea and Libya. Kiriakou says the U.S. could easily have killed him — 'we knew where he lived, we knew how he spent his day' — but the Saudi government insisted the U.S. leave him alone, which Kiriakou calls a grave mistake and speculates was because the Saudis were pursuing their own nuclear capability. Khan was eventually pardoned by Pervez Musharraf, ending all investigations.

isi.title: Pervez Musharraf
isi.summary: Pakistani general and military dictator who ruled during John Kiriakou's 2002 posting as CIA chief of counterterrorism operations in Pakistan. Per Kiriakou, the United States 'essentially just purchased Musharraf,' paying tens of millions in cash to the ISI and meeting him several times a week — and in return 'he would let us do whatever we wanted.' Kiriakou says Musharraf, fearing the nuclear arsenal could fall into terrorist hands, unofficially turned control of Pakistan's nuclear weapons over to the Pentagon. Musharraf later pardoned proliferator A.Q. Khan.

isi.title: Tora Bora
isi.summary: Mountainous cave complex in eastern Afghanistan that served as an al-Qaeda redoubt after the September 11 attacks. Per John Kiriakou — chief of counterterrorism operations in Pakistan at the time — the CIA killed al-Qaeda military-affairs chief Mohammed Atef there in October 2001, and Tora Bora was the backdrop to the hunt for the senior al-Qaeda leadership that culminated in the capture of Abu Zubaydah. Kiriakou also recounts an Egyptian al-Qaeda fighter he later recruited who survived a cruise-missile strike on a Tora Bora cave — one of only two who came out alive, his ears bleeding, describing the explosion as the most hideous sound he had ever heard.

isi.title: Abu Zubaydah
isi.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

isi.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
isi.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

isi.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
isi.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

isis.title: Kurds
isis.summary: The stateless people John Kiriakou calls generationally pro-American — he escorted visiting Kurdish delegations around Washington as a young analyst and bristled at officials who talked down to them. In his telling the Kurds were the only genuine opposition inside Saddam's Iraq, the only faction of the exile circus that ever amounted to anything (Jalal Talabani ended up president of Iraq), the victims of Saddam's chemical weapons and of a no-fly zone that forgot to ban helicopters — and the common enemy that actually united Turkey and ISIS.

isis.title: Bashar al-Assad
isis.summary: President of Syria; John Kiriakou recounts warning Senator John Kerry to stop publicly calling Assad 'my dear friend' after a speech enraged Washington's Lebanese community, with Kerry citing motorcycle rides they had taken together to the Golan Heights.

isis.title: Muammar Gaddafi
isis.summary: Libya's ruler and, in John Kiriakou's telling, the cautionary tale that teaches every proliferator never to disarm. In February 2003 the CIA's Steve Kappes secretly visited Gaddafi with an ultimatum — the U.S. was about to overthrow Saddam, and Libya would meet the same fate unless it surrendered its weapons of mass destruction. Gaddafi complied — and was later overthrown and lynched anyway, "at the insistence of the United States." A bad guy, Kiriakou stresses, but one Washington had a healthy working relationship with, who hated al-Qaeda as much as America did; flipping sides to destroy him was "a terrible policy error" that left anarchy.

isis.title: George W. Bush
isis.summary: 43rd President of the United States. In John Kiriakou's telling, Bush signed the August 1, 2002 executive order that authorized the CIA torture program, spent years telling the public "we don't torture," and — days after Kiriakou's 2007 ABC interview — blamed torture on "a rogue CIA officer" while walking from the White House South Portico to Marine One, a moment Kiriakou instantly read as the White House preparing to pin the program on him. Bush also ordered the FBI removed from Abu Zubaydah's black site, flew the bin Laden family out of the country after 9/11, and loosened the assassination ban of Executive Order 12333.

isis.title: Iraq WMD intelligence
isis.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how the case for Iraqi weapons of mass destruction was fabricated: the intelligence community''s consensus was that Iraq had no WMD, but the White House had already decided to invade and sought analysis to fit the policy.

isis.title: Liberty University
isis.summary: Evangelical university in Lynchburg, Virginia — the largest in the world — where John Kiriakou taught for several years as an adjunct professor of intelligence studies in the Jesse Helms School of Government. He says he warned the school he disagreed with it on 95% of the issues and was hired anyway, on the dean's reasoning that "torture's not Christian"; he enjoyed the post while clashing constantly with the institution over the treatment of Middle Eastern Christians.

islamofascism-term.title: Muslim Brotherhood terrorist designation
islamofascism-term.summary: John Kiriakou''s objection to the designation of the Muslim Brotherhood, or elements of it, as a terrorist organisation: that the group is more than a century old, has never carried out an anti-American terrorist operation, and had never been so designated by any previous administration. He distinguishes fundamentalism and hostility from terrorism.

islamofascism-term.title: Permanent wartime economy
islamofascism-term.summary: John Kiriakou's thesis that since 9/11 the United States has run a permanent wartime economy so large that cutting the defense budget would trigger a depression — likening the dependency to crack addiction and warning it makes war almost inevitable.

islamofascism-term.title: Abu Zubaydah
islamofascism-term.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

islamofascism-term.title: Antisemitism and anti-Zionism
