project-stargate.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the United States criminalizes too much — locking up 25% of the world's prisoners with 5% of its population, and adding roughly 50 new felonies a year — illustrated by a NOAA employee prosecuted for whistling at a whale.

project-stargate.title: Private prison system
project-stargate.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the U.S. private prison industry as an incentive to keep beds filled and cut costs on food and medicine — illustrated by the 'sewer trout,' dog-food, and dead-rat-in-the-Kool-Aid stories from his own incarceration.

project-stargate.title: Thomas Drake
project-stargate.summary: NSA whistleblower; per John Kiriakou, the source for the statement that on the morning of September 11, 2001, NSA Director Mike Hayden told agency personnel NSA had been 'waiting for a 9/11' to implement the mass-electronic-surveillance program that NSA's founding charter forbids.

prosecutorial-careerism.title: Julian Assange
prosecutorial-careerism.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

prosecutorial-careerism.title: Sigurdur Thordarson
prosecutorial-careerism.summary: The FBI's key witness against Julian Assange, described by John Kiriakou as a convicted paedophile, a convicted embezzler and a self-admitted liar — one of three facts he lists, alongside the bugging of the Ecuadorian embassy and the reported plot to kidnap or kill Assange, in asking whether judges can keep such things out of their heads.

prosecutorial-careerism.title: Daniel Ellsberg
prosecutorial-careerism.summary: The Pentagon Papers whistleblower Kiriakou calls 'the Godfather of all national security whistleblowers' — and one of the great mentors of his life.

prosecutorial-careerism.title: Communications management unit
prosecutorial-careerism.summary: The restricted-contact units inside American medium- and maximum-security federal prisons, which John Kiriakou groups with solitary confinement as a practice that amounts to torture.

prosecutorial-careerism.title: Solitary confinement
prosecutorial-careerism.summary: The prison isolation practice the United Nations calls a form of torture; John Kiriakou, drawing on his own ten days in a six-by-sixteen-foot cell, argues that jailing depressed prisoners like Daniel Hale in solitary 'for their own safety' is precisely what drives them to suicide.

prosecutorial-careerism.title: Whistleblower psychology
prosecutorial-careerism.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of what distinguishes people who come forward: psychological studies showing whistleblowers hold a much more sharply defined sense of right and wrong than the general population, weighed against his own claim that there is no whistleblower who has not contemplated suicide in the period after going public.

ptsd.title: Espionage Act
ptsd.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

ptsd.title: John Kiriakou
ptsd.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

ptsd.title: Recruitment attempts on Kiriakou
ptsd.summary: A series of episodes in which foreign intelligence officers tried to recruit John Kiriakou himself — an over-eager Hungarian during his CIA application, a French counterterrorism officer who staged a car pickup in Islamabad, and a Shin Bet officer at his first liaison briefing.

ptsd.title: Vietnam War
ptsd.summary: The war John Kiriakou grew up in the shadow of — his parents marched against it — and the deep precedent for everything he fights: entered on the Gulf of Tonkin lie, prosecuted by generals who knew for a decade they were losing (per the Pentagon Papers), studded with torture whose victims recited the Green Bay Packers'' starting lineup as "intelligence," and ended in part by Daniel Ellsberg, "the godfather of all modern national security whistleblowers." Even Robert McNamara, he notes, understood waterboarding was a bridge too far.

ptsd.title: Aryan Brotherhood
ptsd.summary: The white prison gang that adopted John Kiriakou on his first day at FCI Loretto. Two hours in, two Aryans with swastika neck tattoos walked into his cell to check his paperwork — not a rat, not a "chomo" — and invited him to the Aryan table, which ran from hardcore Nazis at one end to merely white guys at the other. A rumor that he had been a CIA assassin earned him the nickname "the Muslim killer," which he never corrected; asked directly, he answered "we all did stuff we weren't proud of — it was wartime," and the Aryans loved it. He sat with them a year before the Italians took him in.

ptsd.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
ptsd.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

public-interest-defense.title: Edward Snowden
public-interest-defense.summary: Former NSA contractor who in 2013 disclosed the scope of U.S. [mass surveillance](/wiki/mass-surveillance), including the Section 702 collection program. Per John Kiriakou — who counts Snowden among the small group of national-security whistleblowers prosecuted under the Espionage Act — Snowden was ''stuck between two awful slippery slopes'': breaking his oath and chain of command on one side, and on the other catching something ''cut and dry against the Constitution'' that no one would act on. Kiriakou notes Snowden could not use his chain of command (as Kiriakou could not, his own chain being Jose Rodriguez), and that Judge Leonie Brinkema had reserved the Snowden case for herself before he fled the country.

public-interest-defense.title: Espionage Act
public-interest-defense.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

public-interest-defense.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
public-interest-defense.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

public-interest-defense.title: Leonie Brinkema
public-interest-defense.summary: U.S. federal judge in the Eastern District of Virginia — informally the 'Espionage Court' — a Reagan appointee John Kiriakou calls "a hanging judge." Per Kiriakou, Brinkema systematically reserved all major national security cases for herself rather than allowing them to be distributed randomly among judges, and ruled in Kiriakou's case that his reason for blowing the whistle was legally irrelevant and that classified documents could not be used in his defense — effectively making it impossible to mount one.

public-interest-defense.title: Jose Rodriguez
public-interest-defense.summary: Senior CIA officer of the post-9/11 era; identified by John Kiriakou as among those responsible for crimes committed in the name of national security; described as believing himself to be a good guy.

public-interest-defense.title: Jack Teixeira
public-interest-defense.summary: Massachusetts Air National Guard reservist arrested in April 2023 for leaking classified Pentagon documents to a small Discord server. John Kiriakou, discussing the case the day after Teixeira's arrest, initially suspected a covert action program rather than a genuine leak, ultimately concluded Teixeira was not a whistleblower, and predicted — correctly — that he would be charged under the Espionage Act and take a plea bargain.

public-safety-factor.title: David Petraeus
public-safety-factor.summary: Retired U.S. Army general and director of the CIA who, per John Kiriakou, confirmed the names of ten covert CIA operatives to his biographer and girlfriend and was never criminally charged — a contrast Kiriakou cites repeatedly as proof that his own prosecution under the Intelligence Identities Protection Act was selective. Kiriakou''s explanation for the disparity: Petraeus had not blown the whistle on the torture program and embarrassed the agency.

public-safety-factor.title: Intelligence Identities Protection Act
public-safety-factor.summary: U.S. law enacted in 1982 that makes it a crime to knowingly disclose the identity of a covert intelligence officer; per John Kiriakou, his 2012 prosecution under the act arose from confirming a single surname of a former CIA colleague to a journalist — a confirmation that was never published. The name passed through a chain from journalist to Human Rights Watch to Guantanamo defense attorneys before reaching a judge and ultimately the FBI, which traced it back to Kiriakou.

public-safety-factor.title: Bureau of Prisons
public-safety-factor.summary: The federal agency that ran John Kiriakou's incarceration — and one of his most persistent post-prison targets. The BOP overrode his judge's camp recommendation by deeming him "a threat to the public safety," threatened him with "diesel therapy" until 1,600 logged phone calls and letters from a dozen House members and two senators backed it off, and, per Kiriakou, functions as "an employment agency for unemployable semi-literate rural white men" and "a dumping ground for failed medical professionals" — an agency for which a prisoner's death is cheaper than his treatment.

public-safety-factor.title: Administrative remedy process
public-safety-factor.summary: The Bureau of Prisons' internal grievance system, which Kiriakou describes as a fig leaf designed to run out the clock on prisoners' complaints rather than resolve them.

public-safety-factor.title: Kiriakou on mass incarceration
public-safety-factor.summary: The argument Kiriakou developed in the letters from Loretto and has repeated since: that the United States holds a quarter of the world''s prisoners with five per cent of its people, that the cause is the drug war and election-year legislating, and that reform died in the Senate without a vote.

public-safety-factor.title: Prison Legal News
public-safety-factor.summary: The longest-running publication produced by and for current and former prisoners in American history, co-founded by former prisoner Paul Wright, and a recurring source in Kiriakou's account of Bureau of Prisons practice.

publications-review-board.title: AIPAC
publications-review-board.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

publications-review-board.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
publications-review-board.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

publications-review-board.title: MOSSAD
publications-review-board.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

publications-review-board.title: Beirut
publications-review-board.summary: The Lebanese capital John Kiriakou confirms was a genuine espionage playground — though he dates the peak to the 1950s through the mid-1970s, when Beirut was the Paris and the banking centre of the Middle East, and when, beneath the CIA, KGB and Israeli presence, "more secretly the French ran the place." He also explains why the enormous new American embassy there is about fortification rather than a regional CIA headquarters.

publications-review-board.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
publications-review-board.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

publications-review-board.title: Colin Powell
publications-review-board.summary: U.S. Secretary of State whose 2003 UN testimony made the case for the Iraq war; John Kiriakou says the white powder in Powell's prop tube was nothing, and that Powell's own chief of staff later told him the presentation was knowingly 'sold.'

qala-i-jangi-uprising.title: John Walker Lindh
qala-i-jangi-uprising.summary: American citizen captured while fighting alongside the Taliban in late 2001; present at the Qala-i-Jangi fortress in northern Afghanistan at the start of the prisoner uprising that killed CIA officer Mike Spann.

qala-i-jangi-uprising.title: Mike Spann
qala-i-jangi-uprising.summary: CIA officer; first American killed in combat in Afghanistan after the September 11 attacks; killed during the November 2001 Qala-i-Jangi prison uprising; worked in the Counterterrorism Center bullpen alongside John Kiriakou.

qala-i-jangi-uprising.title: Dasht-i-Leili massacre
qala-i-jangi-uprising.summary: Late-November 2001 mass suffocation of approximately 2,000 surrendered Taliban prisoners in unventilated shipping containers in the Afghan desert; the prisoners' surrender was negotiated by the CIA via the Northern Alliance, the transport order was issued by the CIA, and the operation was overseen by Northern Alliance warlord Abdul Rashid Dostum; John Kiriakou in 2009 as Senate Foreign Relations Committee investigator attempted to reopen the case under a 2008 Obama campaign promise; the CIA's classified response was, per Kiriakou, "go fuck yourself."

qala-i-jangi-uprising.title: Spies of Arlington National Cemetery
qala-i-jangi-uprising.summary: On the Walk With History podcast, John Kiriakou — author of Remains of the Day: A Definitive Guide to Washington D.C.''s Historic Cemeteries — toured Arlington National Cemetery and told personal and historical stories about the intelligence figures buried there, including OSS founder William Donovan, deputy CIA director Vernon Walters, codebreakers William and Elizabeth Friedman, slain station chiefs Richard Welch and William Buckley, U-2 pilot Francis Gary Powers, and Mike Spann, the first CIA officer killed after 9/11.

qala-i-jangi-uprising.title: Bill Buckley
qala-i-jangi-uprising.summary: CIA station chief in Beirut kidnapped by Palestinian Islamic Jihad in March 1984; tortured at length over fifteen months; killed in captivity; the case from which the agency derived a generation of operational-security lessons including the abandonment of single-point tracking devices in CIA officers' personal kit.

qala-i-jangi-uprising.title: General Abdul Rashid Dostum
qala-i-jangi-uprising.summary: Northern Alliance Afghan warlord; overseer of the November–December 2001 Dasht-i-Leili massacre; characterized by John Kiriakou as a serial defector between the Taliban and the Northern Alliance and as a psychopath.

radio-and-tv-marti.title: Italian election covert action
radio-and-tv-marti.summary: What John Kiriakou calls the CIA''s very first covert action: bribing Italian journalists in the 1949 election to write in favor of the Christian Democrats, who narrowly beat the Communists — a operation he says amounted to stealing the election.

radio-and-tv-marti.title: Operation Mockingbird
radio-and-tv-marti.summary: The CIA's mid-twentieth-century program of recruiting and managing American journalists as influence assets; in John Kiriakou's account, no longer operationally necessary in the contemporary period because the U.S. media voluntarily reprints CIA-supplied material, and in at least one documented case sends articles to the agency for clearance before sending them to its own editor.

radio-and-tv-marti.title: Thomas Massie
radio-and-tv-marti.summary: Republican U.S. Representative from Kentucky known for a constitutionalist voting record and consistent opposition to foreign military intervention; per John Kiriakou, a principled America-First congressman who votes with the president on the vast majority of issues, and whose opposition to U.S. funding of Israel and foreign wars is the only plausible explanation for the roughly $30 million spent by the Israel lobby to unseat him in a primary.

radio-and-tv-marti.title: Tulsi Gabbard
radio-and-tv-marti.summary: U.S. Director of National Intelligence; a longtime family friend of John Kiriakou's, who has known her since she was 12; Kiriakou calls her appointment "an inspired choice" despite disagreeing with her decision to join the Republican Party, and says she appears to have given up her opposition to Section 702 surveillance to secure Senate confirmation.

radio-and-tv-marti.title: CIA animal surveillance experiments
radio-and-tv-marti.summary: Cold-War CIA efforts to turn animals into listening devices, which John Kiriakou describes as failures — including microphones and cameras mounted on pigeons trained to land on the Soviet embassy, which could reach the compound but never captured anything meaningful.

radio-and-tv-marti.title: Jason Leopold
radio-and-tv-marti.summary: Bloomberg investigative journalist; characterized by John Kiriakou as the leading practitioner of Freedom of Information Act litigation against U.S. [intelligence agencies](/wiki/intelligence-agencies); broke the Hillary Clinton private-email-server story; whose FOIA suit against the CIA Office of Public Affairs produced documentary evidence that NBC's chief national-security correspondent had been sending articles to the CIA for clearance before sending them to his own editor.

ramzi-bin-al-shibh.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
ramzi-bin-al-shibh.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

ramzi-bin-al-shibh.title: Sleep deprivation
ramzi-bin-al-shibh.summary: A CIA interrogation technique used against high-value detainees post-9/11; the agency was authorized to deny prisoners sleep for up to 12 days continuously; people died; at least one detainee was rendered permanently clinically insane.

ramzi-bin-al-shibh.title: Muhammad Atar
ramzi-bin-al-shibh.summary: Nephew of Khalid Sheikh Mohammed; subjected by the CIA to the walling interrogation technique against a concrete-block wall without protective equipment, producing permanent brain damage that has prevented him from participating in his own defense.

ramzi-bin-al-shibh.title: Abu Zubaydah
ramzi-bin-al-shibh.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

ramzi-bin-al-shibh.title: Mitchell and Jessen
ramzi-bin-al-shibh.summary: The two American psychologists who pitched the CIA's enhanced interrogation program to Director George Tenet at a cocktail party in late October 2001; designers of the program and its theoretical underpinning, "learned helplessness."

ramzi-bin-al-shibh.title: Senate Torture Report
ramzi-bin-al-shibh.summary: The December 2014 executive summary of the U.S. Senate Select Committee on Intelligence's study of the CIA's post-9/11 detention and interrogation program; the first public disclosure of techniques including rectal feeding with hummus, sexual assault with broomsticks, and prolonged sleep deprivation.

rand-paul-eric-holder.title: Anwar al-Awlaki
rand-paul-eric-holder.summary: American-born al-Qaeda propagandist; in 1993 the imam of the Falls Church, Virginia mosque visited by John Kiriakou's CIA Arabic-language class on a field trip; in 2001 the cleric at whose mosque the 9/11 hijackers prayed the night before the attacks; killed by U.S. drone strike in Yemen in approximately 2011.

rand-paul-eric-holder.title: MOSSAD
rand-paul-eric-holder.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

rand-paul-eric-holder.title: Ron Wyden
rand-paul-eric-holder.summary: U.S. senator and the lone real challenger of the CIA on the intelligence committees; John Kiriakou faults Wyden for challenging the agency only 'by the agency's rules' — refusing to read the Senate torture report into the record, and admitting at a dinner that fighting harder would cost him his security clearance.

rand-paul-eric-holder.title: CIA cash room
rand-paul-eric-holder.summary: John Kiriakou's description of the rooms at large CIA stations stacked floor-to-ceiling with cash — tens or hundreds of millions of dollars — from which an officer can sign out whatever an operation needs, as when he took $2 million to buy safe houses for the Abu Zubaydah capture.

rand-paul-eric-holder.title: Executive Order 12333
rand-paul-eric-holder.summary: The U.S. presidential directive — in its post-9/11 amended form — that grants the CIA the legal authority to kill any individual anywhere in the world deemed by the agency to pose a "clear and present danger" to the United States; the legal foundation underlying both CIA paramilitary operations and the agency's contractor relationships including with Blackwater.

rand-paul-eric-holder.title: Trump Dni Replacement
rand-paul-eric-holder.summary: Trump privately asked cabinet members about replacing his Director of National Intelligence, frustrated that the DNI had protected Joe Kent.

ray-davis-lahore-shooting.title: FCI Loretto
ray-davis-lahore-shooting.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

ray-davis-lahore-shooting.title: Private prison system
ray-davis-lahore-shooting.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the U.S. private prison industry as an incentive to keep beds filled and cut costs on food and medicine — illustrated by the 'sewer trout,' dog-food, and dead-rat-in-the-Kool-Aid stories from his own incarceration.

ray-davis-lahore-shooting.title: Zero Dark Thirty
ray-davis-lahore-shooting.summary: 2012 film dramatizing the CIA hunt for Osama bin Laden, criticized on release for suggesting torture produced the intelligence that led to his capture. John Kiriakou surveys the mixed critical reception — praise from Time and the New Yorker for its craft, condemnation from journalist Michael Wolff and director Kathryn Bigelow's critics for what they called pro-torture propaganda — and notes his friend Senator John McCain said the film left him "sick... because it is wrong."

ray-davis-lahore-shooting.title: Abu Nidal Organization
ray-davis-lahore-shooting.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the CIA destroyed the Abu Nidal Organization from within by exploiting Abu Nidal''s pathological paranoia: rather than recruiting members (impossible given the group''s extreme anti-American orientation), the agency planted false signals that various members were already cooperating with US intelligence. Members began killing each other one by one. Kiriakou: ''Next thing you know, they''ve all killed each other and the only one left is Abu Nidal.'' He also disbelieves the official heart-attack cause of Abu Nidal''s death, attributing it to a Saddam Hussein ''control'' decision.

ray-davis-lahore-shooting.title: The 1991 Saudi plan for Gaza
ray-davis-lahore-shooting.summary: A proposal John Kiriakou says he watched Ambassador Chas Freeman float to the Saudis during his first overseas tour in 1991 — that Saudi Arabia fund a port, an airport, a desalination plant and an electrical grid in Gaza. The Saudis agreed; Israel refused outright. Kiriakou raises it because the identical arrangement resurfaced in the Israeli press more than three decades later.

ray-davis-lahore-shooting.title: CIA animal surveillance experiments
ray-davis-lahore-shooting.summary: Cold-War CIA efforts to turn animals into listening devices, which John Kiriakou describes as failures — including microphones and cameras mounted on pigeons trained to land on the Soviet embassy, which could reach the compound but never captured anything meaningful.

ray-mcgovern.title: Vladimir Putin
ray-mcgovern.summary: President of Russia. Per John Kiriakou, Putin twice raised joining NATO — floating it to Bill Clinton and later telling Barack Obama Russia would like to explore membership — and was refused both times; Kiriakou has never believed Putin wants to conquer Ukraine or Eastern Europe, argues U.S. hostility toward Russia is driven by defense contractors and a permanent wartime economy, and notes the irony that Putin was the anti-communist the U.S. itself backed in the Yeltsin era.

ray-mcgovern.title: John Kiriakou
ray-mcgovern.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

ray-mcgovern.title: Kiriakou's transfer to the Directorate of Operations
ray-mcgovern.summary: John Kiriakou's roughly two-month internal campaign to transfer from the CIA's analytic Directorate of Intelligence to the operational Directorate of Operations, overcoming what he calls a "natural bias in operations against the eggheads on the analytic side," followed by an Athens posting secured because he was the only person in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic. Covers his full CIA career arc from 1988/1990 recruitment through analyst years on Iraq, the switch to operations, 9/11, the enhanced-interrogation refusal, executive assistant to the deputy director for operations, and his eventual resignation and post-CIA career.

ray-mcgovern.title: Consortium News
ray-mcgovern.summary: Independent investigative news outlet John Kiriakou has written for, founded by Polk Award-winning journalist Robert Parry, who broke major stories on Iran-Contra; Kiriakou says PayPal permanently shuttered the outlet's account and briefly seized its funds before backing down under public pressure, while still refusing to reinstate it.

ray-mcgovern.title: Sam Adams Award
ray-mcgovern.summary: The integrity-in-intelligence award John Kiriakou received in 2016 at American University, joining a laureate list that includes Edward Snowden, Julian Assange, and Sy Hersh. Named not for the founding father but for the CIA analyst who insisted the true enemy strength in Vietnam was double what General Westmoreland allowed to be reported, it is given by Veteran Intelligence Professionals for Sanity — a community Kiriakou describes as doubling as a support group for whistleblowers.

ray-mcgovern.title: Bob Woodward's CIA headquarters access
ray-mcgovern.summary: John Kiriakou's account of watching Washington Post journalist Bob Woodward walk the halls of CIA headquarters unescorted while researching a book, after the CIA director ordered staff to cooperate with him — an episode Kiriakou cites as evidence of how close the relationship between senior CIA officials and favored journalists really is.

rdap-program.title: Daniel Hale
rdap-program.summary: Per John Kiriakou, drone whistleblower Daniel Hale — an NSA contractor and drone targeting analyst who exposed an 80% civilian death rate in the U.S. drone program, was ordered to fire on two young girls his superior called "goats," and was sentenced to 45 months (of which Kiriakou says he actually served about 18) despite prosecutors seeking nine to eleven years.

rdap-program.title: Solitary confinement
rdap-program.summary: The prison isolation practice the United Nations calls a form of torture; John Kiriakou, drawing on his own ten days in a six-by-sixteen-foot cell, argues that jailing depressed prisoners like Daniel Hale in solitary 'for their own safety' is precisely what drives them to suicide.

rdap-program.title: The Drone Papers
rdap-program.summary: The trove of classified documents leaked by Daniel Hale and published by The Intercept — later collected in book form as 'The Assassination Complex' — exposing how the U.S. drone program selected and killed targets; John Kiriakou relied on it in his own writing on the war in Afghanistan.

rdap-program.title: Espionage Act
rdap-program.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

rdap-program.title: Jeffrey Sterling
rdap-program.summary: Former CIA officer convicted of nine felonies, including seven counts of espionage, after giving a New York Times interview about a racial discrimination lawsuit he had filed against the CIA. Per John Kiriakou, Sterling was not accused of spying for a foreign country; his underlying case was that the CIA had passed him over for promotion and told him explicitly it was because of his race. Daniel Ellsberg asked Sterling to go to trial specifically so the constitutionality of the Espionage Act could be challenged; Sterling did, was convicted, and was sentenced by Judge Leonie Brinkema to what she described as 'Kiriakou plus 12 months.'

rdap-program.title: Julian Assange
rdap-program.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

recruitment-attempts-on-kiriakou.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
recruitment-attempts-on-kiriakou.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

recruitment-attempts-on-kiriakou.title: Espionage Act
recruitment-attempts-on-kiriakou.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

recruitment-attempts-on-kiriakou.title: PTSD
recruitment-attempts-on-kiriakou.summary: Post-traumatic stress disorder runs through John Kiriakou''s life and worldview — he had it coming out of Greece after an assassination attempt, brought it home from Pakistan alongside his shock at colleagues'' willingness to kill, and was blindsided by a delayed post-prison version that helped end his marriage. For six months after release he dreamed the same dream nightly: that he was out by mistake and had to get back inside before midnight count. He still takes a repurposed blood-pressure drug that stops the dreams, and he extends the diagnosis outward — to secret-site interrogators who came back crying, to drone pilots, and to prisoners released angry and untreated.

recruitment-attempts-on-kiriakou.title: The Reluctant Spy
recruitment-attempts-on-kiriakou.summary: John Kiriakou''s 2009 memoir, The Reluctant Spy: My Secret Life in the CIA''s War on Terror, begun in secret months before he blew the whistle and reaching number five on the New York Times bestseller list.

recruitment-attempts-on-kiriakou.title: Shin Bet
recruitment-attempts-on-kiriakou.summary: Israel's internal security service; per John Kiriakou, one of the two declared Israeli intelligence officers at the Washington embassy, and the service whose officer, alongside a Mossad officer, he says tried to recruit him at his first CIA liaison briefing.

recruitment-attempts-on-kiriakou.title: Japanese diplomat FBI sting
recruitment-attempts-on-kiriakou.summary: John Kiriakou's account of an FBI entrapment operation in which an agent posing as a Japanese diplomat cold-pitched him for classified information over five lunches, hoping he would commit actual espionage they could charge — a scheme he discovered only in his own case discovery.

remains-of-day-treasury-clerk-story.title: Agnes von Kurowsky grave story
remains-of-day-treasury-clerk-story.summary: John Kiriakou's account of discovering the Washington, D.C. grave of Agnes von Kurowsky, the World War I Red Cross nurse whose four-month wartime romance with a young ambulance driver, Ernest Hemingway, made her the model for the lead female character in six of his books, including A Farewell to Arms.

remains-of-day-treasury-clerk-story.title: Kiriakou's personal anecdotes
remains-of-day-treasury-clerk-story.summary: Three personal stories John Kiriakou has told in interviews — tracking down and meeting Andy Warhol as a college senior, a Congolese vice president's remark that Americans promise democracy while the Chinese provide food, and Kiriakou's own Zelle account being suspended over Cuba-sanctions compliance after a paid article about his Cuba trip.

remains-of-day-treasury-clerk-story.title: Bashar al-Assad
remains-of-day-treasury-clerk-story.summary: President of Syria; John Kiriakou recounts warning Senator John Kerry to stop publicly calling Assad 'my dear friend' after a speech enraged Washington's Lebanese community, with Kerry citing motorcycle rides they had taken together to the Golan Heights.

remains-of-day-treasury-clerk-story.title: Chinese spy balloon incident
remains-of-day-treasury-clerk-story.summary: 2023 controversy over a high-altitude balloon that crossed U.S. airspace, widely labeled in media coverage as a "Chinese spy balloon"; John Kiriakou notes no U.S. government official ever officially confirmed it was conducting espionage, and says he personally believes it was likely a weather balloon, since satellite surveillance already renders such balloons unnecessary for spying.

remains-of-day-treasury-clerk-story.title: CIA adultery culture
remains-of-day-treasury-clerk-story.summary: John Kiriakou's recurring characterization of the CIA officer corps as riddled with adultery and casual sex — which he frames not as gossip but as a systemic counterintelligence vulnerability that makes officers easy to recruit.

remains-of-day-treasury-clerk-story.title: The CIA Insider's Guide to Surveillance and Surveillance Detection
remains-of-day-treasury-clerk-story.summary: Book by John Kiriakou drawing on his experience as a surveillance detection instructor at the CIA and as a private surveillance training consultant. The book covers the techniques used by intelligence professionals to identify whether they are being followed — including the four-phase surveillance detection route, concealment device placement and retrieval, and counter-surveillance strategy — adapted for use by corporate executives, journalists, and others who want to confirm whether they are being followed.

remains-of-the-day-book.title: Kiriakou's writing process
remains-of-the-day-book.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how he actually writes — books in waves over roughly nine months, op-eds in forty-five minutes to an hour once an idea has sat for a few days, and a habit of getting up at two in the morning to write one because he cannot sleep. He wrote *Remains of the Day* in six weeks during COVID, losing whole evenings to it: "I look at the clock again, it''s 2:00 in the morning. I''m like, oh my god, what happened?"

remains-of-the-day-book.title: Israel Boyd and the Wonder Bread story
remains-of-the-day-book.summary: John Kiriakou's account of finding the grave of Israel Boyd, one of two brothers forced by their parents into the family bakery business, who went on to invent the first industrial dough mixer and dough-cutting machine, pioneer adding milk to bread dough, and build the largest bakery in America before World War I — before selling the business, whose flagship "Mrs. McGill's Delicious Bread" was renamed Wonder Bread by its buyer.

remains-of-the-day-book.title: John Kiriakou
remains-of-the-day-book.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

remains-of-the-day-book.title: Gore Vidal
remains-of-the-day-book.summary: American novelist and essayist; per John Kiriakou, a Sidwell Friends/St. Albans/Phillips Exeter alumnus who enlisted after Pearl Harbor rather than attend college, wrote the controversial 1948 novel The City and the Pillar, won a National Book Award in 1993, and was buried near his one lasting partner, Howard Austen, and his boyhood best friend, James Trimble, who was killed at Iwo Jima.

remains-of-the-day-book.title: Arkady Shevchenko
remains-of-the-day-book.summary: Soviet diplomat and Undersecretary General of the United Nations who secretly spied for the CIA before defecting to the United States in 1978 — described by John Kiriakou as the single most important spy the CIA ever had inside the Soviet power structure.

remains-of-the-day-book.title: Joseph B. Chambers
remains-of-the-day-book.summary: Civil War Medal of Honor recipient buried at Oak Park Cemetery in New Castle, Pennsylvania, whose grave John Kiriakou discovered as a child while looking for salamanders — sparking a lifelong interest in history.

restraint-camp.title: Cory Booker
restraint-camp.summary: Per John Kiriakou, he was "especially furious" with Democratic senator Cory Booker for running through the halls of Congress to get to a photo op standing behind Benjamin Netanyahu, which Kiriakou cites as an example of Democratic silence in the face of AIPAC pressure.

revolutionary-organization-17-november.title: John Kiriakou
revolutionary-organization-17-november.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

revolutionary-organization-17-november.title: Richard Welch
revolutionary-organization-17-november.summary: CIA Athens station chief assassinated December 23, 1975; the first victim of [Revolutionary Organization 17 November](/wiki/revolutionary-organization-17-november)

revolutionary-organization-17-november.title: Carlos the Jackal
revolutionary-organization-17-november.summary: Venezuelan-born militant (Ilich Ramírez Sánchez) active in the 1970s and 1980s; per John Kiriakou, 'the Osama bin Laden of the 70s and 80s.' Kiriakou spent his Athens posting trying to identify the middleman linking Carlos to the Greek terrorist group 17 November, then six months working the lead with MI5 in London; Carlos was finally run down by CIA contractor Billy Waugh in a Khartoum vegetable market and captured in 1994.

revolutionary-organization-17-november.title: Stephen Saunders
revolutionary-organization-17-november.summary: British defense attaché in Athens assassinated by Revolutionary Organization 17 November in March 2000

revolutionary-organization-17-november.title: Heather Saunders
revolutionary-organization-17-november.summary: Widow of British Brigadier General Stephen Saunders, the British defense attaché in Athens assassinated by Revolutionary Organization 17 November on April 22, 2000; per John Kiriakou, the person whose post-assassination Greek-television statement — "this organization is not a political organization nor is it a phantom group; it's a gang of criminals" — for the first time since 17 November's 1975 founding turned Greek public opinion against the group.

revolutionary-organization-17-november.title: Mike Baker
revolutionary-organization-17-november.summary: Former CIA case officer; John Kiriakou's predecessor as the CIA's lead officer working the Revolutionary Organization 17 November problem in Athens; characterized by Kiriakou as "the real deal" and as having laid the groundwork for the operations Kiriakou subsequently inherited.

reza-pahlavi.title: Iran 12-Day War
reza-pahlavi.summary: 2025 Israeli air campaign against Iran during which Israel killed at least fourteen Iranian nuclear scientists by destroying the apartment buildings they lived in; preceded for each scientist by Farsi-language telephone calls from Iranian-Jewish Mossad and Shin Bet officers offering defection in lieu of certain death; characterized by John Kiriakou as a categorical departure from CIA targeting doctrine in its acceptable-civilian-casualty calculus.

reza-pahlavi.title: Donald Trump
reza-pahlavi.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

reza-pahlavi.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
reza-pahlavi.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

reza-pahlavi.title: Israel's cell-phone assassinations in Iran
reza-pahlavi.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how Israel wiped out Iran's military leadership by tracking cell phones — recruiting destitute Afghan refugees as $100-a-month spotters, and, when the generals stopped carrying phones, targeting their bodyguards' phones instead.

reza-pahlavi.title: Mohsen Rafighdoost
reza-pahlavi.summary: Iranian journalist and political figure whom John Kiriakou identifies as a co-founder of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and the propaganda voice behind the audio tapes distributed in Iran before the 1979 revolution; interviewed on the PBD Podcast, he conceded that the Shah's regime held only 3,000–3,500 political prisoners rather than the 100,000 opposition figures claimed at the time and that the Shah was, in his own judgment, a better man than Ayatollah Khomeini.

reza-pahlavi.title: Leadership profiling
reza-pahlavi.summary: The CIA practice of producing classified psychological profiles of foreign leaders for the president, vice president, national security advisor and the secretaries of state and defense before any meeting. It was John Kiriakou's first job at the agency, where he served as Saddam Hussein's classified psychological biographer working alongside psychiatrists, psychologists and anthropologists.

rfk-assassination.title: JFK assassination
rfk-assassination.summary: November 22, 1963 killing of President John F. Kennedy in Dallas, Texas. John Kiriakou's position, drawn from a Pakistan-station encounter with Bay of Pigs commander Jean Gately, an RFK Jr. account of CIA Director John McCone's same-day exchange with Bobby Kennedy Sr., and a White House contact's confirmation that the remaining classified Kennedy documents all contain the word "Israel," is that elements of the CIA were probably involved and that Israeli intelligence was involved as well.

rfk-assassination.title: Kent State shooting
rfk-assassination.summary: The 1970 shooting of unarmed student protesters by the Ohio National Guard; John Kiriakou says a family friend's daughter was among those killed — an event that, alongside the King and Kennedy assassinations, helped form his political conscience.

rfk-assassination.title: MK-Ultra
rfk-assassination.summary: The CIA's mid-twentieth-century umbrella program of mind-control, behavioral-modification, and biological-warfare experimentation, encompassing subprojects such as MK-Chickwit and MK-Seesaw; active 1952–1975; documented practices included LSD dosing of unwitting American citizens in CIA-rented brothels and the aerosolized release of pathogens into the San Francisco fog; 80% of the program's documentation was destroyed by the CIA in defiance of a 1975 preservation order from Senator Frank Church.

rfk-assassination.title: John Kiriakou
rfk-assassination.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

rfk-assassination.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
rfk-assassination.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

rfk-assassination.title: MLK assassination
rfk-assassination.summary: The April 1968 killing of Martin Luther King Jr. John Kiriakou, having set out to read everything he could find on it, concluded that if James Earl Ray fired the shot he was a patsy — citing the implausibility of a lifelong alcoholic making a perfect shot from a flophouse bathroom a block away, and the FBI's documented attempt two years earlier to push King into suicide.

rhodes-jewish-deportation-family-story.title: Greek death rituals
rhodes-jewish-deportation-family-story.summary: The five-year grave rental, exhumation and ossuary practice of rural Greece as John Kiriakou describes it — bones washed in red wine, blessed, boxed, and eventually laid beneath the foundations of a new church, with cremation strictly forbidden. He visits the ossuary in his ancestral Rhodes village, where the records stop in the nineteenth century because the Ottomans burned everything earlier.

rhodes-jewish-deportation-family-story.title: Zakynthos Holocaust rescue
rhodes-jewish-deportation-family-story.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the Greek Ionian island of Zakynthos, where the mayor and Orthodox bishop responded to a Nazi demand for a list of the island's Jews by submitting only their own two names, while residents hid every Jewish islander — making Zakynthos, per Kiriakou, the only place in Greece where no Jew died in the Holocaust.

rhodes-jewish-deportation-family-story.title: Abraham Accords
rhodes-jewish-deportation-family-story.summary: The Trump-brokered normalization deals between Israel and Gulf Arab states — in John Kiriakou's judgment "a terrible idea in the first place," a great victory for Israel and the Gulf Arabs that was "a punch in the throat to the Palestinians." He argues the Accords are how Trump meant to "solve the Middle East in a day" — by screwing the Palestinians — that Hamas read the abandonment correctly, that October 7 shattered the project, and that reviving the Accords (Saudis in, victory declared, Nobel collected) remains the organizing goal of Trump's regional policy.

rhodes-jewish-deportation-family-story.title: Alan Dershowitz
rhodes-jewish-deportation-family-story.summary: American attorney and Harvard Law professor; John Kiriakou describes debating him on Piers Morgan's show over Jeffrey Epstein, telling Dershowitz he would have wanted to see him "hanging from a tree" had he sought leniency for Epstein as an Israeli spy — and cites attorney David Boies's on-air statement that Dershowitz was far more than Epstein's lawyer, also serving as his publicist, friend, and a guest on Epstein's island.

rhodes-jewish-deportation-family-story.title: Arrais Corporation
rhodes-jewish-deportation-family-story.summary: Private intelligence firm; companion entity to The Analysis Corporation; originally an LLC pass-through for retired Senior Intelligence Service personnel from the CIA's operations side; subsequently acquired by IBM for over $1 billion.

rhodes-jewish-deportation-family-story.title: BDS movement
rhodes-jewish-deportation-family-story.summary: The Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement against Israel; John Kiriakou notes that some 40 U.S. states now have anti-BDS laws that can require a speaker at a publicly funded university to sign a pledge of support for Israel — which he refuses to do.

rhodes-jewish-deportation.title: Israeli property acquisition in Greece and Cyprus
rhodes-jewish-deportation.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Israelis buying land in Greece and Cyprus at a scale he considers destabilising — entire villages rather than holiday homes, a Jewish-only village outside Paphos with a casino attached, a rejected bid for an island in the Ionian Sea, and a request to open the first Zionist high school in Cyprus.

rhodes-jewish-deportation.title: Zakynthos Holocaust rescue
rhodes-jewish-deportation.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the Greek Ionian island of Zakynthos, where the mayor and Orthodox bishop responded to a Nazi demand for a list of the island's Jews by submitting only their own two names, while residents hid every Jewish islander — making Zakynthos, per Kiriakou, the only place in Greece where no Jew died in the Holocaust.

rhodes-jewish-deportation.title: Israel, Turkey, and NATO Article 5
rhodes-jewish-deportation.summary: John Kiriakou's scenario in which an Israeli attack on Turkey would oblige every NATO member, the United States included, to come to Turkey's defence — and in which the alliance would sooner dissolve than honour that obligation against Israel.

rhodes-jewish-deportation.title: Israeli drone factories in Serbia
rhodes-jewish-deportation.summary: Five drone factories John Kiriakou was told the Israelis are building in Serbia — a fact relayed to him by members of a Serbian delegation who welcomed it on the grounds that Israel is effective against Islamists, and which Kiriakou treats as the same emotional play he sees used on Greeks and Cypriots.

rhodes-jewish-deportation.title: Antisemitism and anti-Zionism
rhodes-jewish-deportation.summary: The conflation of criticism of the Israeli state with hatred of Jews, which John Kiriakou describes as a worldwide confusion and, according to a young Israeli he spoke to, an explicit lesson of the Israeli school system; a subject Kiriakou says he personally struggles with.

rhodes-jewish-deportation.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
rhodes-jewish-deportation.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

richard-helms.title: MK-Ultra
richard-helms.summary: The CIA's mid-twentieth-century umbrella program of mind-control, behavioral-modification, and biological-warfare experimentation, encompassing subprojects such as MK-Chickwit and MK-Seesaw; active 1952–1975; documented practices included LSD dosing of unwitting American citizens in CIA-rented brothels and the aerosolized release of pathogens into the San Francisco fog; 80% of the program's documentation was destroyed by the CIA in defiance of a 1975 preservation order from Senator Frank Church.

richard-helms.title: CIA National Resources Division
richard-helms.summary: The Central Intelligence Agency's domestic intelligence-collection arm, created in the 1980s by Director William J. Casey

richard-helms.title: Family Jewels
richard-helms.summary: The CIA's internal catalogue of its own abuses, demanded by the Church and Pike Committees in the mid-1970s; per John Kiriakou, MK-Ultra and associated assassination programs were the first things to surface.

richard-helms.title: Jason Leopold
richard-helms.summary: Bloomberg investigative journalist; characterized by John Kiriakou as the leading practitioner of Freedom of Information Act litigation against U.S. [intelligence agencies](/wiki/intelligence-agencies); broke the Hillary Clinton private-email-server story; whose FOIA suit against the CIA Office of Public Affairs produced documentary evidence that NBC's chief national-security correspondent had been sending articles to the CIA for clearance before sending them to his own editor.

richard-helms.title: Operation Midnight Climax
richard-helms.summary: Sub-project of the CIA's MK-Ultra program, conducted in San Francisco. Per John Kiriakou, the CIA rented a safe house and paid sex workers to bring men back to it, where agents dosed the men with LSD without their knowledge or consent, then observed their behavior through one-way mirrors. The operation followed an earlier phase in which the CIA had dosed its own employees; when that produced suicides, it moved to using unconsenting members of the public.

richard-helms.title: Vault 7
richard-helms.summary: The 2017 WikiLeaks disclosure of thousands of pages of CIA Directorate of Science and Technology documents — leaked by agency engineer Joshua Schulte — revealing CIA technical capabilities including remote takeover of internet-connected cars, conversion of smart-TV speakers into covert microphones, and the planting of Russian or Persian language fragments in foreign systems to mislead attribution.

richard-perle.title: Dick Cheney
richard-perle.summary: U.S. Vice President under George W. Bush. Per John Kiriakou — recounting CIA Director George Tenet's memoir — Cheney intercepted the presidential finding authorizing the CIA's enhanced interrogation program in the Oval Office anteroom and took it from Tenet before Bush could sign it. Tenet later concluded the president probably never actually signed the finding and probably told the truth when he said he had no idea the program was taking place. Kiriakou characterizes Cheney as the one who actually ran foreign policy, intelligence policy, and defense policy during the Bush years.

richard-perle.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
richard-perle.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

richard-perle.title: Iraq WMD intelligence
richard-perle.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how the case for Iraqi weapons of mass destruction was fabricated: the intelligence community''s consensus was that Iraq had no WMD, but the White House had already decided to invade and sought analysis to fit the policy.

richard-perle.title: Israeli intelligence presence in the United States
richard-perle.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Israeli intelligence activity inside the United States — dozens of undeclared Mossad and Shin Bet officers identified by the FBI, a critical-threat counterintelligence classification alongside Russia, North Korea and Cuba, and a pattern of harassment and intimidation directed at declared CIA officers posted to Israel.

richard-perle.title: Donald Trump
richard-perle.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

richard-perle.title: Principals Committee Meeting (February 2003)
richard-perle.summary: Senior-most interagency forum of the U.S. national security apparatus, normally chaired by the president. Per John Kiriakou — who served as notetaker for CIA Director George Tenet at the eve-of-Iraq-invasion meeting on February 19–20, 2003 — Vice President Dick Cheney chaired in place of Bush, General Tommy Franks ended his order-of-battle briefing with 'If all goes as planned, we can be in Tehran by August,' and an NSC senior director said 'When we cross that border tomorrow morning, they're going to throw flowers at us.'

richard-welch.title: Revolutionary Organization 17 November
richard-welch.summary: Greek far-left urban guerrilla group active 1975–2002; the deadliest terrorist organization in Greek history

richard-welch.title: Carlos the Jackal
richard-welch.summary: Venezuelan-born militant (Ilich Ramírez Sánchez) active in the 1970s and 1980s; per John Kiriakou, 'the Osama bin Laden of the 70s and 80s.' Kiriakou spent his Athens posting trying to identify the middleman linking Carlos to the Greek terrorist group 17 November, then six months working the lead with MI5 in London; Carlos was finally run down by CIA contractor Billy Waugh in a Khartoum vegetable market and captured in 1994.

richard-welch.title: The Welch .45
richard-welch.summary: The single .45 caliber pistol used by Revolutionary Organization 17 November in every confirmed assassination over the group's twenty-seven-year operational life

richard-welch.title: Gust Avrakotos
richard-welch.summary: CIA case officer, John Kiriakou's operations mentor, and a central figure in Charlie Wilson's War — the prolific, divisive covert-war veteran Kiriakou credits as the greatest teacher of his adult life.

richard-welch.title: Stephen Saunders
richard-welch.summary: British defense attaché in Athens assassinated by Revolutionary Organization 17 November in March 2000

richard-welch.title: Kissinger and the petrodollar
richard-welch.summary: John Kiriakou's endorsement of the theory that Henry Kissinger deliberately structured the 1970s petrodollar to tie the U.S. to Middle Eastern oil — creating a standing rationale for policing the region, even as America exports its own fracked oil.

richard-wolff.title: Trump tariffs
richard-wolff.summary: The across-the-board tariffs imposed by Donald Trump on United States trading partners, which John Kiriakou describes as having shaken up the economy faster than any president in generations — causing chaos in global stock markets, laying the groundwork for inflation and economic contraction, and producing political upheaval at home.

richard-wolff.title: Donald Trump
richard-wolff.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

richard-wolff.title: Elon Musk
richard-wolff.summary: Kiriakou met Musk by chance at a Washington hotel bar in 2009, when he was worth $1 billion and talking about Tesla, SpaceX and colonizing Mars.

richard-wolff.title: China as economic threat
richard-wolff.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that China is the real threat to the West not militarily — it has one aircraft carrier to America's two dozen and rarely invades — but economically, buying friends worldwide while the U.S. spends a trillion dollars a year on weapons.

richard-wolff.title: John Kiriakou
richard-wolff.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

richard-wolff.title: Youngstown Sheet and Tube
richard-wolff.summary: The Ohio steel producer whose closure John Kiriakou treats as the moment the economy of his hometown region ended; he remembers the day it shut and classmates weeping in the school hallways because their fathers had lost their jobs, and dates the collapse of New Castle, Pennsylvania to it.

robert-f-kennedy-jr.title: JFK assassination
robert-f-kennedy-jr.summary: November 22, 1963 killing of President John F. Kennedy in Dallas, Texas. John Kiriakou's position, drawn from a Pakistan-station encounter with Bay of Pigs commander Jean Gately, an RFK Jr. account of CIA Director John McCone's same-day exchange with Bobby Kennedy Sr., and a White House contact's confirmation that the remaining classified Kennedy documents all contain the word "Israel," is that elements of the CIA were probably involved and that Israeli intelligence was involved as well.

robert-f-kennedy-jr.title: John McCone
robert-f-kennedy-jr.summary: Director of the Central Intelligence Agency on November 22, 1963; per John Kiriakou's retelling of an account from Robert F. Kennedy Jr., responded to Bobby Kennedy Sr.'s same-day question "Tell me your people didn't do this" not with denial but with "I don't know who did it."

robert-f-kennedy-jr.title: Donald Trump
robert-f-kennedy-jr.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

robert-f-kennedy-jr.title: Executive Order 12333
robert-f-kennedy-jr.summary: The U.S. presidential directive — in its post-9/11 amended form — that grants the CIA the legal authority to kill any individual anywhere in the world deemed by the agency to pose a "clear and present danger" to the United States; the legal foundation underlying both CIA paramilitary operations and the agency's contractor relationships including with Blackwater.

robert-f-kennedy-jr.title: Central Intelligence Agency
robert-f-kennedy-jr.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

robert-f-kennedy-jr.title: Maria Butina
robert-f-kennedy-jr.summary: Russian gun-rights activist convicted in the United States of failing to register as a foreign agent; John Kiriakou cites her case as an example of the "process crime" of FARA violations, contrasting the severity of her 18-month solitary-confinement sentence with federal guidelines calling for 0-6 months.

robert-hanssen.title: Aldrich Ames
robert-hanssen.summary: Senior CIA officer — a GS-15 who rose to chief of counterintelligence for the Soviet branch — who spied for the KGB. Per John Kiriakou, Ames's first act of betrayal was selling the identities of two CIA agents to the Russians for $50,000 to pay off a credit-card debt; both agents were immediately executed. He ultimately caused the deaths of twelve people, accumulated $2 million, bought a house in Arlington for that amount, drove a Jaguar to work on a $70,000 salary, and built an in-ground pool with a gazebo — all while being known throughout the office as a daily drunk. A 27-year-old officer sat on the initial security file for eighteen months. Analyst Sandy Grimes ultimately caught him.

robert-hanssen.title: John Kiriakou
robert-hanssen.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

robert-hanssen.title: Brian Kelley
robert-hanssen.summary: Chief of counterintelligence at the CIA; framed by FBI counterintelligence chief Robert Hanssen — the actual Soviet/Russian mole — as the source of executed agents; spent a year and a half on leave without pay, surrounded around the clock by FBI agents, while his daughter was approached and told her father would face the death penalty if he did not confess.

robert-hanssen.title: Central Intelligence Agency
robert-hanssen.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

robert-hanssen.title: Sandy Grimes
robert-hanssen.summary: CIA analyst who, per John Kiriakou, was the person who actually broke the Aldrich Ames case. After a 27-year-old security officer sat on an Ames file for eighteen months without action, Grimes independently noticed that Ames made $100,000–$150,000 bank deposits within days of every trip to Mexico City — the pattern that identified him as a spy. After Ames's arrest, she submitted a hot-wash paper recommending 27 reprimands across the chain of command that had promoted a known alcoholic into the most sensitive counterintelligence position in the CIA. Director John Deutch responded with strongly worded letters for seven. Grimes resigned in 1993.

robert-hanssen.title: Harold James Nicholson
robert-hanssen.summary: Former CIA Station Chief, Singapore; the third major modern CIA mole for the Russians after Aldrich Ames and Robert Hanssen. Per John Kiriakou, Nicholson was a senior officer at the CIA Counterterrorism Center during Kiriakou's tenure there. Sentenced to 31 years and seven months in 1997. While in prison, attempted to recruit his own son to act as a courier between him and the Russian intelligence service so his espionage payments could continue to compound for his eventual release — and was caught when his son walked up to the Russian embassy in Washington under FBI surveillance.

robert-maclean.summary: Former U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York and Mayor of New York City; in 2018 attempted to extort $2 million from John Kiriakou in exchange for arranging a presidential pardon from President Trump; the attempt was reported to the New York Times by Kiriakou himself and corroborated by Giuliani's then-aide Noelle Dunphy after Giuliani sexually harassed her.

robert-maxwell.summary: British socialite and convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, her father Robert Maxwell was a prolific Mossad spy, and she is the likely conduit through whom Jeffrey Epstein was introduced to and recruited by Mossad.

robert-maxwell.title: Peter Mandelson
robert-maxwell.summary: British politician; described by John Kiriakou as the former British ambassador to Washington and as someone likely to be charged with serious crimes in connection with Jeffrey Epstein.

robert-maxwell.title: Eli Cohen

robert-mueller.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
robert-mueller.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

robert-mueller.title: Ali Soufan
robert-mueller.summary: FBI special agent who handled Abu Zubaydah immediately after his March 2002 capture; through patient, respectful interrogation produced the only actionable intelligence ever obtained from the detainee, including the first identification of "Mukhtar" as Khalid Sheikh Mohammed.

robert-mueller.title: John Brennan
robert-mueller.summary: Former Director of the CIA; characterized in KiriPedia's source corpus as the principal architect of the agency's enhanced interrogation program and as having plotted against an elected President

robert-mueller.title: John Kiriakou
robert-mueller.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

robert-mueller.title: Plato Cacheris
robert-mueller.summary: Legendary Washington, D.C. defense attorney who served as John Kiriakou''s lead counsel in his 2012–2013 Espionage Act prosecution. Per Kiriakou, when discovery revealed the FBI had run a fake-diplomat sting against him, Cacheris explained the government''s posture bluntly: ''Because they have a shit case and they know it''s shit, and that''s why we''re going to trial.'' He spent most of the case urging trial, then drove to Kiriakou''s house on decision day and said ''You stupid son of a bitch — take the deal.'' Cacheris also represented FBI spy Robert Hanssen.

roger-waters.title: Shireen Abu Akleh
roger-waters.summary: Al Jazeera journalist, U.S. citizen and Greek Orthodox Christian; John Kiriakou recounts that she was shot in the face by an Israeli sniper while wearing clearly marked press gear, and that the IDF then beat pallbearers at her funeral.

roger-waters.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
roger-waters.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

roger-waters.title: Antisemitism and anti-Zionism
roger-waters.summary: The conflation of criticism of the Israeli state with hatred of Jews, which John Kiriakou describes as a worldwide confusion and, according to a young Israeli he spoke to, an explicit lesson of the Israeli school system; a subject Kiriakou says he personally struggles with.

roger-waters.title: Famine in Gaza
roger-waters.summary: The starvation of the civilian population of the Gaza Strip, which John Kiriakou describes as a United Nations-declared famine caused not by an absence of food but by an Israeli refusal to let food reach the people who need it; Kiriakou characterises it as a war crime, a crime against humanity and a form of genocide, attributing that characterisation to the United Nations and the International Court of Justice rather than to himself.

roger-waters.title: Germany and Israel
roger-waters.summary: John Kiriakou's account of German support for Israeli policy as an overcorrection driven by shame over the Nazi past, and of the resulting cultural blacklisting of critics of Israel in Germany — a pattern he put to Roger Waters, who described being effectively unpublishable in the German press.

roger-waters.title: October 7 attack
roger-waters.summary: John Kiriakou's analysis of the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack as a policy failure, not an intelligence one — Israel was warned repeatedly, but Itamar Ben-Gvir diverted response forces to the West Bank, and Kiriakou believes Israel welcomed a pretext for overwhelming retaliation.

ron-wyden.title: Rand Paul Eric Holder
ron-wyden.summary: Rand Paul asked whether the president may kill an American on US soil without trial. Kiriakou recounts Holder''s eventual answer: yes.

ron-wyden.title: James Clapper
ron-wyden.summary: Director of National Intelligence under Obama; John Kiriakou recounts Clapper being pressed by Senator Rand Paul on whether the president could legally use a drone to kill an American on U.S. soil who had never been charged — the eventual answer being yes.

ron-wyden.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
ron-wyden.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

ron-wyden.title: FCI Loretto
ron-wyden.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

ron-wyden.title: Julian Assange
ron-wyden.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

ron-wyden.title: Kiriakou's transfer to the Directorate of Operations
ron-wyden.summary: John Kiriakou's roughly two-month internal campaign to transfer from the CIA's analytic Directorate of Intelligence to the operational Directorate of Operations, overcoming what he calls a "natural bias in operations against the eggheads on the analytic side," followed by an Athens posting secured because he was the only person in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic. Covers his full CIA career arc from 1988/1990 recruitment through analyst years on Iraq, the switch to operations, 9/11, the enhanced-interrogation refusal, executive assistant to the deputy director for operations, and his eventual resignation and post-CIA career.

ross-ulbricht.title: Abraham Bolden
ross-ulbricht.summary: The first African-American Secret Service agent assigned to a presidential detail; per John Kiriakou, he quite literally saved John F. Kennedy's life in Chicago in October 1963 and was subjected to overt racism by fellow agents, who told him to his face they would not protect Kennedy from assassination because of his civil-rights sympathies.

ross-ulbricht.title: Alan Dershowitz
ross-ulbricht.summary: American attorney and Harvard Law professor; John Kiriakou describes debating him on Piers Morgan's show over Jeffrey Epstein, telling Dershowitz he would have wanted to see him "hanging from a tree" had he sought leniency for Epstein as an Israeli spy — and cites attorney David Boies's on-air statement that Dershowitz was far more than Epstein's lawyer, also serving as his publicist, friend, and a guest on Epstein's island.

ross-ulbricht.title: Dick Cheney
ross-ulbricht.summary: U.S. Vice President under George W. Bush. Per John Kiriakou — recounting CIA Director George Tenet's memoir — Cheney intercepted the presidential finding authorizing the CIA's enhanced interrogation program in the Oval Office anteroom and took it from Tenet before Bush could sign it. Tenet later concluded the president probably never actually signed the finding and probably told the truth when he said he had no idea the program was taking place. Kiriakou characterizes Cheney as the one who actually ran foreign policy, intelligence policy, and defense policy during the Bush years.

ross-ulbricht.title: Donald Trump
ross-ulbricht.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

ross-ulbricht.title: Kill the Messenger (Gary Webb)
ross-ulbricht.summary: The 2014 film about journalist Gary Webb, on which John Kiriakou served as script advisor; when Kiriakou was arrested in January 2012, the FBI seized his electronics, including a draft of the unclassified Hollywood script, and stamped every page "top secret" despite Kiriakou having no role in writing it.
