uk-secrecy-laws.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

uk-secrecy-laws.title: BDS movement
uk-secrecy-laws.summary: The Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement against Israel; John Kiriakou notes that some 40 U.S. states now have anti-BDS laws that can require a speaker at a publicly funded university to sign a pledge of support for Israel — which he refuses to do.

uk-secrecy-laws.title: Andrew Bustamante
uk-secrecy-laws.summary: Former CIA officer who sells CIA-style training online; John Kiriakou identifies him as the lone critic of his work hosting a show on a Russian network, and argues Bustamante's training business — open to anyone who pays — is the more problematic of the two.

uk-secrecy-laws.title: China as economic threat
uk-secrecy-laws.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that China is the real threat to the West not militarily — it has one aircraft carrier to America's two dozen and rarely invades — but economically, buying friends worldwide while the U.S. spends a trillion dollars a year on weapons.

uk-secrecy-laws.title: Donald Trump
uk-secrecy-laws.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

uk-secrecy-laws.title: John Kiriakou
uk-secrecy-laws.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

united-food-and-commercial-workers.title: Jerrold Post
united-food-and-commercial-workers.summary: American political psychiatrist and CIA officer who recruited John Kiriakou into the agency in 1988 through the CIA's covert campus recruiting program, working undercover as a George Washington University professor; founder of the CIA's Political Psychology Division (also called the Office of Leadership Analysis). Held a bachelor's, master's, and PhD in psychology and a PhD in political science, all from Yale, plus an MD from Harvard, and authored a dozen books on the psychology of world leaders and terrorists. Per Kiriakou, Post identified in him not just writing talent but "sociopathic tendencies" — and, when Kiriakou later blew the whistle, called to congratulate him, telling him that reaction proved he was not a true sociopath. Died of COVID-19, approximately 2022.

united-food-and-commercial-workers.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
united-food-and-commercial-workers.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

united-food-and-commercial-workers.title: CIA Political Psychology Division
united-food-and-commercial-workers.summary: The Central Intelligence Agency unit founded by Dr. Gerald Post in the 1970s to produce long-distance psychiatric evaluations of foreign leaders

united-food-and-commercial-workers.title: John Kiriakou
united-food-and-commercial-workers.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

united-food-and-commercial-workers.title: Kiriakou's transfer to the Directorate of Operations
united-food-and-commercial-workers.summary: John Kiriakou's roughly two-month internal campaign to transfer from the CIA's analytic Directorate of Intelligence to the operational Directorate of Operations, overcoming what he calls a "natural bias in operations against the eggheads on the analytic side," followed by an Athens posting secured because he was the only person in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic. Covers his full CIA career arc from 1988/1990 recruitment through analyst years on Iraq, the switch to operations, 9/11, the enhanced-interrogation refusal, executive assistant to the deputy director for operations, and his eventual resignation and post-CIA career.

united-food-and-commercial-workers.title: Yalta conference
united-food-and-commercial-workers.summary: The February 1945 Allied conference, which John Kiriakou uses as his teaching example of what a well-placed spy is worth: Stalin, told by a source inside the White House that Roosevelt was ill, insisted on a venue requiring a punishing multi-leg journey, then refused to delay the talks — and an exhausted Roosevelt, Kiriakou says, conceded Poland in order to go to bed.

united-fruit-arbenz-coup.title: Maduro Capture
united-fruit-arbenz-coup.summary: CIA-driven nighttime operation in which a team of Delta Force commandos entered Venezuela and removed Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife from their beds. Per John Kiriakou, the key enabling intelligence — per a New York Times account he cited — came from a CIA asset inside Maduro''s presidential palace who called when Maduro went to sleep: ''He''s sound asleep. If you''re going to do it, do it now.'' At least eighty people were killed in the operation, including approximately thirty-five Cubans. Kiriakou compares it to the 1989 capture of Manuel Noriega, in which US forces blasted death metal at the Vatican Embassy until Noriega was asked to leave.

united-fruit-arbenz-coup.title: Allen Dulles
united-fruit-arbenz-coup.summary: Long-serving CIA director whom John Kiriakou calls a 'monster' — a United Fruit board member who helped overthrow Guatemala's Arbenz, whose bust greeted visitors at CIA headquarters, and who was, unlike James Angleton, aware of his own guilt.

united-fruit-arbenz-coup.title: Monroe Doctrine
united-fruit-arbenz-coup.summary: John Kiriakou's history of the Monroe Doctrine — ignored for decades after 1823, humiliated in the Falklands and Venezuela, and only made real by Teddy Roosevelt in 1905 — which he sees revived today in the seizure of Maduro as a message that the hemisphere is America's.

united-fruit-arbenz-coup.title: CIA cable priority levels
united-fruit-arbenz-coup.summary: The five levels of immediacy assigned to U.S. government cable traffic, as described by John Kiriakou. From lowest to highest: Routine, Priority, Immediate, Flash, CRITIC. Most career officers will never see a CRITIC; during the Gulf War, Kiriakou''s desk was receiving multiple CRITICs a day, each one announcing a hostile missile launch.

united-fruit-arbenz-coup.title: 1953 Iran coup
united-fruit-arbenz-coup.summary: The U.S.- and UK-backed overthrow of Iran's democratically elected prime minister, Mohammad Mossadegh; per John Kiriakou, the coup served British national interests rather than American ones, and the subsequent outlawing of secular political opposition under the Shah forced dissent into the mosques — producing a religious rather than secular revolution in 1979.

united-fruit-arbenz-coup.title: Operation Paperclip
united-fruit-arbenz-coup.summary: The program by which the CIA's predecessor brought Nazi scientists to the United States after World War II; John Kiriakou notes the FBI opposed it, that the Nazis surrendered to the U.S. fearing the Soviets, and that V-2 rocket father Wernher von Braun is buried near his home in Virginia.

us-diplomatic-vacancies.title: Gulf security bargain
us-diplomatic-vacancies.summary: The decades-old arrangement — traced by John Kiriakou to FDR and the Saudi king, and originally British — under which Gulf Arab monarchies host U.S. bases and sell oil in dollars in exchange for American protection; a bargain Kiriakou says collapsed when those bases failed to shield them during the war on Iran.

us-diplomatic-vacancies.title: Iran strike factions (2026)
us-diplomatic-vacancies.summary: John Kiriakou's reporting, sourced to a former colleague at the White House, that a 2026 decision to strike Iran pitted an anti-war camp of JD Vance and Tulsi Gabbard against a pro-war camp led by Marco Rubio — with the Joint Chiefs newly compliant because Trump had replaced them all.

us-diplomatic-vacancies.title: Marco Rubio
us-diplomatic-vacancies.summary: U.S. official whom John Kiriakou identifies as the real motivator behind pressure on Venezuela; Kiriakou argues Venezuela is not a meaningful drug threat to the U.S. and that Rubio simply wants Maduro gone.

us-diplomatic-vacancies.title: Tony Blinken
us-diplomatic-vacancies.summary: American secretary of state under Joe Biden, and a former colleague of John Kiriakou's on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee. Kiriakou calls him a very nice man but holds that he owed the office to three decades of proximity to Biden rather than to being the most capable strategist the United States could have identified — an example of what he calls poor leadership.

us-diplomatic-vacancies.title: Gulf consultations before the Iran war
us-diplomatic-vacancies.summary: John Kiriakou's account of travelling in Kuwait, Abu Dhabi, Dubai and Doha in the weeks before the 2026 strikes on Iran, and finding that the United States had made no diplomatic case to its Gulf partners at all — in sharp contrast to the worldwide campaign that preceded the Iraq war. He told a senior Emirati royal that two carrier strike groups meant an attack was coming.

us-diplomatic-vacancies.title: Iran 12-Day War
us-diplomatic-vacancies.summary: 2025 Israeli air campaign against Iran during which Israel killed at least fourteen Iranian nuclear scientists by destroying the apartment buildings they lived in; preceded for each scientist by Farsi-language telephone calls from Iranian-Jewish Mossad and Shin Bet officers offering defection in lieu of certain death; characterized by John Kiriakou as a categorical departure from CIA targeting doctrine in its acceptable-civilian-casualty calculus.

us-forces-in-syria-legality.title: Agnes von Kurowsky grave story
us-forces-in-syria-legality.summary: John Kiriakou's account of discovering the Washington, D.C. grave of Agnes von Kurowsky, the World War I Red Cross nurse whose four-month wartime romance with a young ambulance driver, Ernest Hemingway, made her the model for the lead female character in six of his books, including A Farewell to Arms.

us-forces-in-syria-legality.title: Kiriakou's personal anecdotes
us-forces-in-syria-legality.summary: Three personal stories John Kiriakou has told in interviews — tracking down and meeting Andy Warhol as a college senior, a Congolese vice president's remark that Americans promise democracy while the Chinese provide food, and Kiriakou's own Zelle account being suspended over Cuba-sanctions compliance after a paid article about his Cuba trip.

us-forces-in-syria-legality.title: Bashar al-Assad
us-forces-in-syria-legality.summary: President of Syria; John Kiriakou recounts warning Senator John Kerry to stop publicly calling Assad 'my dear friend' after a speech enraged Washington's Lebanese community, with Kerry citing motorcycle rides they had taken together to the Golan Heights.

us-forces-in-syria-legality.title: Chinese spy balloon incident
us-forces-in-syria-legality.summary: 2023 controversy over a high-altitude balloon that crossed U.S. airspace, widely labeled in media coverage as a "Chinese spy balloon"; John Kiriakou notes no U.S. government official ever officially confirmed it was conducting espionage, and says he personally believes it was likely a weather balloon, since satellite surveillance already renders such balloons unnecessary for spying.

us-forces-in-syria-legality.title: CIA adultery culture
us-forces-in-syria-legality.summary: John Kiriakou's recurring characterization of the CIA officer corps as riddled with adultery and casual sex — which he frames not as gossip but as a systemic counterintelligence vulnerability that makes officers easy to recruit.

us-forces-in-syria-legality.title: The CIA Insider's Guide to Surveillance and Surveillance Detection
us-forces-in-syria-legality.summary: Book by John Kiriakou drawing on his experience as a surveillance detection instructor at the CIA and as a private surveillance training consultant. The book covers the techniques used by intelligence professionals to identify whether they are being followed — including the four-phase surveillance detection route, concealment device placement and retrieval, and counter-surveillance strategy — adapted for use by corporate executives, journalists, and others who want to confirm whether they are being followed.

us-military-venture-capital.title: John Kiriakou
us-military-venture-capital.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

us-military-venture-capital.title: In-Q-Tel
us-military-venture-capital.summary: The CIA's openly acknowledged venture capital arm; provided Palantir Technologies its first $1.5 million in seed funding; in John Kiriakou's account the principal vehicle by which the agency finances private-sector development of technologies it intends to use.

us-military-venture-capital.title: Central Intelligence Agency
us-military-venture-capital.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

us-military-venture-capital.title: Ai Whistleblower Initiative
us-military-venture-capital.summary: The AI Whistleblower Initiative, working on legal protections for the wave of whistleblowers now coming out of the artificial-intelligence industry.

us-military-venture-capital.title: Akrotiri Village Evacuation
us-military-venture-capital.summary: Kiriakou says the drone that hit Britain's Akrotiri base in Cyprus was likely an Israeli operation, staged and then falsely blamed on Iran.

us-military-venture-capital.title: Aldrich Ames
us-military-venture-capital.summary: Senior CIA officer — a GS-15 who rose to chief of counterintelligence for the Soviet branch — who spied for the KGB. Per John Kiriakou, Ames's first act of betrayal was selling the identities of two CIA agents to the Russians for $50,000 to pay off a credit-card debt; both agents were immediately executed. He ultimately caused the deaths of twelve people, accumulated $2 million, bought a house in Arlington for that amount, drove a Jaguar to work on a $70,000 salary, and built an in-ground pool with a gazebo — all while being known throughout the office as a daily drunk. A 27-year-old officer sat on the initial security file for eighteen months. Analyst Sandy Grimes ultimately caught him.

usaid-cia-front-operations.title: Afghan heroin policy
usaid-cia-front-operations.summary: The post-2001 U.S. policy in Afghanistan of protecting, and per John Kiriakou actively encouraging, the cultivation of heroin poppy. Under the Taliban in 2000 Afghanistan produced 0% of the world's heroin; by 2009 under American occupation it produced 93%. Per a DEA officer Kiriakou consulted with on the policy paper he was preparing for Senator Kerry, the strategic rationale was that nearly all of the heroin flowed to Iran and Russia, addiction in those countries was considered desirable as a long-run societal weakener, and the same logic now operates in reverse with Chinese fentanyl flowing into the United States.

usaid-cia-front-operations.title: William J. Casey
usaid-cia-front-operations.summary: Director of Central Intelligence under the Reagan administration; creator of the CIA's domestic intelligence-collection arm

usaid-cia-front-operations.title: Carlos the Jackal
usaid-cia-front-operations.summary: Venezuelan-born militant (Ilich Ramírez Sánchez) active in the 1970s and 1980s; per John Kiriakou, 'the Osama bin Laden of the 70s and 80s.' Kiriakou spent his Athens posting trying to identify the middleman linking Carlos to the Greek terrorist group 17 November, then six months working the lead with MI5 in London; Carlos was finally run down by CIA contractor Billy Waugh in a Khartoum vegetable market and captured in 1994.

usaid-cia-front-operations.title: Christopher Steele dossier
usaid-cia-front-operations.summary: The 2016 opposition-research dossier alleging Trump-Russia ties, compiled by former MI6 officer Christopher Steele. Per John Kiriakou, who worked directly with Steele on an MI6 operation in London in the 1990s, Steele was so respected at MI6 that other officers wanted to be like him — a reputation Kiriakou says the dossier episode reduced to caricature, because in private practice there was no team of analysts to vet the raw intelligence before it reached the Clinton campaign.

usaid-cia-front-operations.title: Church Committee
usaid-cia-front-operations.summary: U.S. Senate investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 that examined domestic intelligence abuses by the CIA, FBI, and NSA; per John Kiriakou, the Church Committee — alongside the concurrent Pike Committee in the House — was the last genuine moment of legislative oversight over the intelligence community, born of a national consensus that government had gone dangerously off course. Its work led to the creation of the permanent Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, which Kiriakou says ceased to function as real oversight roughly seven years after its founding.

usaid-cia-front-operations.title: Dasht-i-Leili massacre
usaid-cia-front-operations.summary: Late-November 2001 mass suffocation of approximately 2,000 surrendered Taliban prisoners in unventilated shipping containers in the Afghan desert; the prisoners' surrender was negotiated by the CIA via the Northern Alliance, the transport order was issued by the CIA, and the operation was overseen by Northern Alliance warlord Abdul Rashid Dostum; John Kiriakou in 2009 as Senate Foreign Relations Committee investigator attempted to reopen the case under a 2008 Obama campaign promise; the CIA's classified response was, per Kiriakou, "go fuck yourself."

va-benefits-for-idf-service.title: Israel's counterintelligence threat ranking
va-benefits-for-idf-service.summary: John Kiriakou's repeated point that the American intelligence community formally ranks Israel a critical counterintelligence threat — the same tier as North Korea, China, Russia, Iran and Cuba — specifically for spying on and infiltrating the US government, and that policy has responded by giving Israel more access rather than less.

va-benefits-for-idf-service.title: MOSSAD
va-benefits-for-idf-service.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

va-benefits-for-idf-service.title: NDAA 2027 US–Israel fusion provisions
va-benefits-for-idf-service.summary: Provisions in the proposed National Defense Authorization Act for 2027 and the companion intelligence authorization bill that would create a permanent Pentagon executive agent for US–Israeli military fusion and lock in permanent intelligence sharing tied to Israel's qualitative military edge. John Kiriakou describes the effect as handing over voluntarily the technology Israel previously ran spies to steal.

va-benefits-for-idf-service.title: Jonathan Pollard
va-benefits-for-idf-service.summary: U.S. Navy civilian intelligence analyst convicted in 1985 of spying for Israel; the canonical proven case of Israeli espionage against the United States; cited by John Kiriakou in his 2024 Piers Morgan debate with a former Mossad director who denied any Israeli spying on the U.S.

va-benefits-for-idf-service.title: F-35 avionics dispute with Israel
va-benefits-for-idf-service.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how Israel demanded F-35 fighters without the deliberately degraded avionics the U.S. installs on export models — and, refused, allegedly worked through American defense contractors to steal the technology instead.

va-benefits-for-idf-service.title: Iran Nuclear Assessment
va-benefits-for-idf-service.summary: Per John Kiriakou's assessment, the US–Israeli military campaign against Iran was a war of choice driven by Israeli political pressure rather than genuine intelligence indicating an Iranian nuclear weapons threat. The CIA produced two National Intelligence Estimates concluding Iran had no nuclear weapons program; Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei issued a fatwa in the 1980s forbidding such a program. The U.S. went to war anyway, in Kiriakou's view, after President Trump replaced the Joint Chiefs of Staff with officers willing to accept Israeli intelligence and proceed.

valerie-plame.title: Joseph Wilson
valerie-plame.summary: Former U.S. Ambassador to Niger and former Deputy Chief of Mission in Baghdad; husband of covert CIA officer Valerie Plame; in 2003 traveled to Niger at CIA request to investigate the Bush administration's claim that Iraq had attempted to purchase yellowcake uranium for a nuclear weapon, found no such Iraqi approach had occurred, and published a New York Times op-ed debunking the claim — triggering the administration's retaliatory outing of his wife.

valerie-plame.title: Curveball
valerie-plame.summary: Cryptonym for the German-handled Iraqi defector whose fabricated WMD intelligence the German BND laundered to the CIA in the run-up to the 2003 Iraq War; per John Kiriakou, in fact a dishwasher at a Shish Kebab restaurant who scraped fake reports from newspaper articles and told the Germans he was an Iraqi scientist with access to weapons of mass destruction; the Germans refused to let the CIA meet or polygraph him, and his fabricated intelligence — biological, chemical, nuclear, and long-range delivery — became one of the central pillars of the Bush administration's WMD case.

valerie-plame.title: Matthew Cole
valerie-plame.summary: American national-security journalist whose reporting tradecraft, per John Kiriakou, has led to the federal incarceration of five whistleblowers — including Kiriakou himself. In Kiriakou's account, Cole emailed him in 2010 ostensibly researching a book on the rendition of Abu Omar, asked Kiriakou to confirm the surname of a CIA officer who appeared in Kiriakou's own first book under the alias 'John', and Kiriakou's confirmation was the act of confirming a covert officer's identity for which he was eventually prosecuted under the Intelligence Identities Protection Act.

valerie-plame.title: Leon Panetta
valerie-plame.summary: CIA Director under President Obama (2009–2011) and subsequent Secretary of Defense; per John Kiriakou, the official who on arrival as Director shut down the Blackwater-operated CIA worldwide assassination program — and in the course of explaining the decision to the House Intelligence Committee publicly outed Erik Prince. Also one of Kiriakou's two go-to examples (with David Petraeus) of senior intelligence figures who disclosed the identities of covert CIA officers without consequence while Kiriakou himself was prosecuted for the same statute.

valerie-plame.title: Cofer Black
valerie-plame.summary: Former head of the CIA Counterterrorism Center during and immediately after the September 11 attacks; principal architect of the agency's paramilitary turn on September 12, 2001; later Vice President of Blackwater under Erik Prince.

valerie-plame.title: John Kiriakou
valerie-plame.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

vault-7.title: Julian Assange
vault-7.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

vault-7.title: Espionage Act
vault-7.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

vault-7.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
vault-7.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

vault-7.title: Michael Hastings
vault-7.summary: American investigative journalist whose 2013 death in a single-vehicle Los Angeles car crash is invoked by John Kiriakou as the canonical real-world referent for the CIA car-remote-takeover capability disclosed in the 2017 Vault 7 documents.

vault-7.title: Three Felonies a Day
vault-7.summary: Book by Harvard Law professor Harvey Silverglate, cited by John Kiriakou, arguing that the United States is so overcriminalized and so overregulated that the average American going about normal daily life inadvertently commits three felonies every day. Kiriakou cites the book in the context of warrantless government surveillance: if authorities decide they want a particular person, they can obtain that person''s metadata, sift it for technical violations, and destroy their life — without any genuine predicate offense.

vault-7.title: Walk-in
vault-7.summary: In John Kiriakou's telling, someone who walks into an embassy offering information; 95% are lunatics or liars, some are 'intelligence peddlers' or hostile 'probes,' and about 1% are 'the real McCoy' — a framework he used to see through a supposed 'walk-in' tip during the Abu Zubaydah hunt. A genuine walk-in — a witness to a terrorist assassination — was later hypnotized by CIA psychologists in a London hotel room and read back a stolen van's license plate, verifying his account.

venezuela-boat-strikes.title: Sanctions Effectiveness
venezuela-boat-strikes.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment that U.S. sanctions have been so overused against disfavored countries that nations like China now route around them entirely, and that sanctions work only when reserved for the worst actors and imposed in concert with other countries — citing apartheid South Africa as a success and Cuba/Venezuela as failures that instead entrench nationalist narratives.

venezuela-boat-strikes.title: Maduro Capture
venezuela-boat-strikes.summary: CIA-driven nighttime operation in which a team of Delta Force commandos entered Venezuela and removed Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife from their beds. Per John Kiriakou, the key enabling intelligence — per a New York Times account he cited — came from a CIA asset inside Maduro''s presidential palace who called when Maduro went to sleep: ''He''s sound asleep. If you''re going to do it, do it now.'' At least eighty people were killed in the operation, including approximately thirty-five Cubans. Kiriakou compares it to the 1989 capture of Manuel Noriega, in which US forces blasted death metal at the Vatican Embassy until Noriega was asked to leave.

venezuela-boat-strikes.title: Kissinger and the petrodollar
venezuela-boat-strikes.summary: John Kiriakou's endorsement of the theory that Henry Kissinger deliberately structured the 1970s petrodollar to tie the U.S. to Middle Eastern oil — creating a standing rationale for policing the region, even as America exports its own fracked oil.

venezuela-boat-strikes.title: 9/11 Commission
venezuela-boat-strikes.summary: The federal commission of inquiry into the September 11 attacks, which John Kiriakou describes as structurally incapable of reaching the truth because it was barred from interviewing serving CIA officers or any Guantanamo detainee, and was blocked by the CIA from pursuing the Saudi thread.

venezuela-boat-strikes.title: Aafia Siddiqui
venezuela-boat-strikes.summary: Pakistani-American scientist arrested in Afghanistan in 2008 and convicted in the U.S. of attempting to shoot two FBI agents; per John Kiriakou, who covered the arrest as a terrorism consultant for ABC News, newer evidence indicates she never had a gun and never fired at anyone, and her claim that the CIA seized her three children at arrest has never been resolved for the youngest, who would now be 18.

venezuela-boat-strikes.title: Venezuela regime change (2026)
venezuela-boat-strikes.summary: John Kiriakou''s assessment of the American operation that removed Venezuela''s president — a clear violation of international law, since none of the three recognised grounds for one state attacking another applied, but not a violation of US law, which since 1985 has expressly permitted special forces to cross borders and seize people for trial. His reluctant conclusion at the time: "as much as I hate admitting it, this regime change seems to be working right now."

venezuela-regime-change-2026.title: Venezuela Boat Strikes
venezuela-regime-change-2026.summary: September 2025 U.S. military strike on a boat in the Caribbean that killed 11 people the White House called drug traffickers; John Kiriakou calls it piracy on the high seas followed by mass murder, arguing the victims were never charged with a crime and that the boat's unusual passenger count undercuts the drug-trafficking story.

venezuela-regime-change-2026.title: Islamofascism
venezuela-regime-change-2026.summary: A term John Kiriakou says was introduced into American media around 2004 and 2005, was created by a public relations firm working for the Republican National Committee, was pushed hard into everyday usage, failed to catch on, and was quietly abandoned. He offers it as his clearest example of manufactured vocabulary intended as domestic propaganda.

venezuela-regime-change-2026.title: Sanctions Effectiveness
venezuela-regime-change-2026.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment that U.S. sanctions have been so overused against disfavored countries that nations like China now route around them entirely, and that sanctions work only when reserved for the worst actors and imposed in concert with other countries — citing apartheid South Africa as a success and Cuba/Venezuela as failures that instead entrench nationalist narratives.

venezuela-regime-change-2026.title: Strait of Hormuz transit fees
venezuela-regime-change-2026.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Iran's proposal to charge ships up to $2 million to transit the Strait of Hormuz, payable in yuan rather than dollars, and of the U.S. Navy's subsequent announcement that it had taken control of the strait and closed it — reversing decades of U.S. policy that the strait must remain open.

venezuelan-embassy-2019.title: Aafia Siddiqui
venezuelan-embassy-2019.summary: Pakistani-American scientist arrested in Afghanistan in 2008 and convicted in the U.S. of attempting to shoot two FBI agents; per John Kiriakou, who covered the arrest as a terrorism consultant for ABC News, newer evidence indicates she never had a gun and never fired at anyone, and her claim that the CIA seized her three children at arrest has never been resolved for the youngest, who would now be 18.

venezuelan-embassy-2019.title: Juan Guaidó
venezuelan-embassy-2019.summary: Venezuelan opposition figure whom the United States recognized as interim president starting in 2019; John Kiriakou dismisses him as having been, in substance, nothing more than a George Washington University grad student, and says the U.S. attempt to install him — followed later by María Corina Machado — failed because Venezuelan support for Nicolás Maduro rests on loyalty to Chavista revolutionary ideology rather than to Maduro personally.

venezuelan-embassy-2019.title: Kiriakou's Cuba trip
venezuelan-embassy-2019.summary: John Kiriakou's account of his first visit to Cuba, where his books sit in the national library and officials treated him warmly — and a Cuban vice president told him every U.S. president is 'the same,' blaming Cuba while it cannot keep the lights on. He was invited as a guest of the Havana international book fair after his first two books were translated into Spanish, and later wrote about how the U.S. embargo shapes daily life there, from a dengue-fever hospital bill he had to pay in euros to a diet dominated by squash.

venezuelan-embassy-2019.title: Kiriakou's Iran trips
venezuelan-embassy-2019.summary: John Kiriakou's account of his own visits to Iran and his Iranian-American partner's regular travel there — noting Tehran's status as the cosmetic-surgery capital of the Middle East, a warning to Iranian state TV viewers about American fast food rather than American generals, and his own repeated but unfulfilled invitations to visit.

venezuelan-embassy-2019.title: Kuwait Liberation Day
venezuelan-embassy-2019.summary: February 1991 expulsion of Iraqi forces from Kuwait by the U.S.-led coalition; John Kiriakou entered the country with U.S. Marines on the day of liberation; the small American flags waved by the crowds — and the post-liberation arrival of Democratic and Republican National Committee personnel ostensibly to assist the country's transition to democracy — were, per Kiriakou, the work of professional propagandist John Rendon.

venezuelan-embassy-2019.title: Sanctions Effectiveness
venezuelan-embassy-2019.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment that U.S. sanctions have been so overused against disfavored countries that nations like China now route around them entirely, and that sanctions work only when reserved for the worst actors and imposed in concert with other countries — citing apartheid South Africa as a success and Cuba/Venezuela as failures that instead entrench nationalist narratives.

vernon-walters.title: Spies of Arlington National Cemetery
vernon-walters.summary: On the Walk With History podcast, John Kiriakou — author of Remains of the Day: A Definitive Guide to Washington D.C.''s Historic Cemeteries — toured Arlington National Cemetery and told personal and historical stories about the intelligence figures buried there, including OSS founder William Donovan, deputy CIA director Vernon Walters, codebreakers William and Elizabeth Friedman, slain station chiefs Richard Welch and William Buckley, U-2 pilot Francis Gary Powers, and Mike Spann, the first CIA officer killed after 9/11.

vernon-walters.title: Francis Gary Powers
vernon-walters.summary: U-2 pilot whose 1960 shoot-down over the Soviet Union and subsequent capture the CIA initially denied any knowledge of, denying not only that he was CIA but that he was U.S. government at all, until trading him in a bridge-of-spies prisoner exchange. Buried at Arlington National Cemetery. Per John Kiriakou, after his U-2 career Powers ended up piloting a Los Angeles traffic helicopter, and was killed when it crashed.

vernon-walters.title: William Donovan
vernon-walters.summary: General William "Wild Bill" Donovan — Medal of Honor recipient, decorated World War I veteran, Wall Street figure, and founder of the wartime Office of Strategic Services (OSS). Per John Kiriakou, Donovan became the natural first leader of American centralized intelligence after President Truman cleared the path by lying to FBI Director J. Edgar Hoover — telling him the new CIA would be a division of the FBI to get him to drop his opposition.

vernon-walters.title: William and Elizabeth Friedman
vernon-walters.summary: American cryptologists who, per John Kiriakou, broke the Nazi Enigma encryption largely by exploiting a single known fact: every German communication ended with ''Heil Hitler'' — sometimes spelled out, sometimes abbreviated ''HH.'' Working outward from the letters H, E, I, L, T, R, they cracked the code one letter at a time. Their work led directly to the founding of the National Security Agency. Both are buried at Arlington National Cemetery.

vernon-walters.title: Bill Buckley
vernon-walters.summary: CIA station chief in Beirut kidnapped by Palestinian Islamic Jihad in March 1984; tortured at length over fifteen months; killed in captivity; the case from which the agency derived a generation of operational-security lessons including the abandonment of single-point tracking devices in CIA officers' personal kit.

vernon-walters.title: Mike Spann
vernon-walters.summary: CIA officer; first American killed in combat in Afghanistan after the September 11 attacks; killed during the November 2001 Qala-i-Jangi prison uprising; worked in the Counterterrorism Center bullpen alongside John Kiriakou.

veteran-intelligence-professionals-for-s.title: Joe Kent
veteran-intelligence-professionals-for-s.summary: Kiriakou on the former counterterrorism director he gave an award to, publicly opposed for a nomination, and has never actually spoken to.

veteran-intelligence-professionals-for-s.title: Bill Clinton
veteran-intelligence-professionals-for-s.summary: 42nd U.S. president whom John Kiriakou describes as wholly disinterested in intelligence — briefed by the CIA only twice in eight years, with Vice President Al Gore taking the daily briefing instead and relaying anything important.

veteran-intelligence-professionals-for-s.title: Watching naval movements
veteran-intelligence-professionals-for-s.summary: One of the first lessons John Kiriakou says he learned at the CIA: to read American military intentions, watch naval movements — one carrier strike group means business, two means war. He used it to correctly predict the 2026 strike on Iran days in advance.

veteran-intelligence-professionals-for-s.title: Barack Obama
veteran-intelligence-professionals-for-s.summary: 44th U.S. president; in John Kiriakou's account, Obama publicly recounted refusing Benjamin Netanyahu's demand to bomb Iran and calling Israel's threat to use nuclear weapons a bluff — a bluff Kiriakou says Donald Trump later believed.

veteran-intelligence-professionals-for-s.title: Donald Trump
veteran-intelligence-professionals-for-s.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

veteran-intelligence-professionals-for-s.title: John Kerry
veteran-intelligence-professionals-for-s.summary: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts; chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee during John Kiriakou's 2009 service as the committee's senior investigator; subsequently U.S. Secretary of State; characterized by Kiriakou as a coward who buckled under CIA pressure on the Dasht-i-Leili reopening and as personally fixated on his perceived theft of the Secretary of State position by Hillary Clinton; the famously thrown medals were duplicates purchased at the post exchange.

vietnam-war.title: PTSD
vietnam-war.summary: Post-traumatic stress disorder runs through John Kiriakou''s life and worldview — he had it coming out of Greece after an assassination attempt, brought it home from Pakistan alongside his shock at colleagues'' willingness to kill, and was blindsided by a delayed post-prison version that helped end his marriage. For six months after release he dreamed the same dream nightly: that he was out by mistake and had to get back inside before midnight count. He still takes a repurposed blood-pressure drug that stops the dreams, and he extends the diagnosis outward — to secret-site interrogators who came back crying, to drone pilots, and to prisoners released angry and untreated.

vietnam-war.title: Espionage Act
vietnam-war.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

vietnam-war.title: Jeffrey Sterling
vietnam-war.summary: Former CIA officer convicted of nine felonies, including seven counts of espionage, after giving a New York Times interview about a racial discrimination lawsuit he had filed against the CIA. Per John Kiriakou, Sterling was not accused of spying for a foreign country; his underlying case was that the CIA had passed him over for promotion and told him explicitly it was because of his race. Daniel Ellsberg asked Sterling to go to trial specifically so the constitutionality of the Espionage Act could be challenged; Sterling did, was convicted, and was sentenced by Judge Leonie Brinkema to what she described as 'Kiriakou plus 12 months.'

vietnam-war.title: Prison racial segregation
vietnam-war.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the rigid racial and ethnic division of American prisons — a cafeteria split like the 1950s South — and his argument that segregating and hardening inmates for years, then releasing them with no skills, makes society less safe.

vietnam-war.title: Daniel Ellsberg
vietnam-war.summary: The Pentagon Papers whistleblower Kiriakou calls 'the Godfather of all national security whistleblowers' — and one of the great mentors of his life.

vietnam-war.title: Sam Adams Award
vietnam-war.summary: The integrity-in-intelligence award John Kiriakou received in 2016 at American University, joining a laureate list that includes Edward Snowden, Julian Assange, and Sy Hersh. Named not for the founding father but for the CIA analyst who insisted the true enemy strength in Vietnam was double what General Westmoreland allowed to be reported, it is given by Veteran Intelligence Professionals for Sanity — a community Kiriakou describes as doubling as a support group for whistleblowers.

virginia-redistricting-supreme-court-rul.title: Bahrain Posting (1994–1996)
virginia-redistricting-supreme-court-rul.summary: John Kiriakou's 1994–1996 assignment to Bahrain under U.S. State Department cover as second secretary for economic affairs — arriving with his wife Joanne and infant son Chris on August 1, 1994, into a tiny Gulf monarchy whose sectarian tensions erupted, two months later, into the first Intifada.

virginia-redistricting-supreme-court-rul.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
virginia-redistricting-supreme-court-rul.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

virginia-redistricting-supreme-court-rul.title: Deloitte Consulting Career
virginia-redistricting-supreme-court-rul.summary: John Kiriakou's post-CIA career at Deloitte Consulting (2004–2008), covering two corporate acquisitions he says he drove — India Tiger Analysis and, in effect, Bering Point — and ending in his effective firing weeks before his ABC News whistleblower interview aired.

virginia-redistricting-supreme-court-rul.title: Donald Trump
virginia-redistricting-supreme-court-rul.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

virginia-redistricting-supreme-court-rul.title: Guantánamo Bay detention camp
virginia-redistricting-supreme-court-rul.summary: Per John Kiriakou — as chief of counterterrorism operations in Pakistan after September 11, 2001 — the Guantanamo detention facility began as a temporary holding measure intended to last two to three weeks while the CIA and Justice Department determined which federal district court should try each prisoner, not as a long-term detention infrastructure. The Rawalpindi jail had reached capacity, Pakistani intelligence demanded the prisoners be removed, and CIA headquarters directed Kiriakou to load them onto a C-12 cargo plane and fly them to Cuba.

virginia-redistricting-supreme-court-rul.title: Ilhan Omar
virginia-redistricting-supreme-court-rul.summary: U.S. Representative whom John Kiriakou credits with sponsoring a rewrite of the Espionage Act in two consecutive Congresses — legislation he says is dead on arrival with a Republican House because of who she is.

vladimir-putin.title: Russia-Ukraine war origins
vladimir-putin.summary: John Kiriakou's account that the war began in 2014, not 2022 — rooted in broken U.S. promises that NATO would not expand to Russia's borders, the 2014 removal of a pro-Russian Ukrainian leader, and the seizure of Crimea; he says Russia is now winning and has no reason to negotiate.

vladimir-putin.title: Ray McGovern
vladimir-putin.summary: Former senior CIA analyst turned antiwar dissident, and one of John Kiriakou's closest friends — "like a brother to me." Kiriakou began working at the CIA on the Monday after the Friday McGovern retired in January 1990, so the two never overlapped inside; they became comrades in the whistleblower world instead. McGovern coined the "MICIMATT" framing Kiriakou often borrows, went into Putin's office with Oliver Stone for a 40-minute meeting, and — per Kiriakou — believes 9/11 was a conspiracy, a view Kiriakou affectionately notes is far from his own.

vladimir-putin.title: Donald Trump
vladimir-putin.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

vladimir-putin.title: Bill Clinton
vladimir-putin.summary: 42nd U.S. president whom John Kiriakou describes as wholly disinterested in intelligence — briefed by the CIA only twice in eight years, with Vice President Al Gore taking the daily briefing instead and relaying anything important.

vladimir-putin.title: Nord Stream pipeline sabotage
vladimir-putin.summary: The 2022 destruction of the Nord Stream gas pipelines, whose responsibility John Kiriakou treats as genuinely unresolved — citing Seymour Hersh's reporting that the CIA did it, a later Ukrainian special-forces claim of a sailboat-based operation carried out without Zelensky's knowledge, and a retired CIA colleague's private theory that Putin blew up his own pipeline to blame the Americans.

vladimir-putin.title: Kiriakou's father and grandfather
vladimir-putin.summary: The two men John Kiriakou names as the greatest influences on his life: a grandfather with a third-grade education who pushed his children through doctorates and handed his grandson an 11th-century gold coin dug from a Greek garden, and a father, an elementary school principal, who was twice passed over for promotion because he refused to pay the bribe the school board demanded. Kiriakou says that refusal is what made him a whistleblower.

volodymyr-zelensky.title: Donald Trump
volodymyr-zelensky.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

volodymyr-zelensky.title: Russia-Ukraine war origins
volodymyr-zelensky.summary: John Kiriakou's account that the war began in 2014, not 2022 — rooted in broken U.S. promises that NATO would not expand to Russia's borders, the 2014 removal of a pro-Russian Ukrainian leader, and the seizure of Crimea; he says Russia is now winning and has no reason to negotiate.

volodymyr-zelensky.title: Lindsey Graham
volodymyr-zelensky.summary: Republican senator from South Carolina who died in July 2026, and John Kiriakou's standing shorthand for the permanent war caucus — a "show horse" rather than a workhorse, a "chameleon" who "never saw a war that he didn't want to jump into with both feet," and, on posthumously released documentary footage, a man offering the US Air Force to bomb a country America was not at war with.

volodymyr-zelensky.title: Marco Rubio
volodymyr-zelensky.summary: U.S. official whom John Kiriakou identifies as the real motivator behind pressure on Venezuela; Kiriakou argues Venezuela is not a meaningful drug threat to the U.S. and that Rubio simply wants Maduro gone.

volodymyr-zelensky.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
volodymyr-zelensky.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

volodymyr-zelensky.title: China as economic threat
volodymyr-zelensky.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that China is the real threat to the West not militarily — it has one aircraft carrier to America's two dozen and rarely invades — but economically, buying friends worldwide while the U.S. spends a trillion dollars a year on weapons.

waco-siege.title: Ruby Ridge
waco-siege.summary: 1992 federal standoff in Idaho involving Randy Weaver, triggered by an allegation that Weaver had sold a shotgun with a barrel two inches shorter than the legal minimum; per John Kiriakou, FBI sniper Lon Horiuchi shot and killed Weaver's wife while she was holding her baby, and Horiuchi was never punished. Kiriakou describes Ruby Ridge as one of the events that, after his own imprisonment, caused him to fundamentally reassess his earlier acceptance of the official government account.

waco-siege.title: Edward Snowden
waco-siege.summary: Former NSA contractor who in 2013 disclosed the scope of U.S. [mass surveillance](/wiki/mass-surveillance), including the Section 702 collection program. Per John Kiriakou — who counts Snowden among the small group of national-security whistleblowers prosecuted under the Espionage Act — Snowden was ''stuck between two awful slippery slopes'': breaking his oath and chain of command on one side, and on the other catching something ''cut and dry against the Constitution'' that no one would act on. Kiriakou notes Snowden could not use his chain of command (as Kiriakou could not, his own chain being Jose Rodriguez), and that Judge Leonie Brinkema had reserved the Snowden case for herself before he fled the country.

waco-siege.title: John Kiriakou
waco-siege.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

waco-siege.title: Abu Zubaydah
waco-siege.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

waco-siege.title: Central Intelligence Agency
waco-siege.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

waco-siege.title: Cofer Black
waco-siege.summary: Former head of the CIA Counterterrorism Center during and immediately after the September 11 attacks; principal architect of the agency's paramilitary turn on September 12, 2001; later Vice President of Blackwater under Erik Prince.

walk-in.title: Abu Zubaydah
walk-in.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

walk-in.title: John Kiriakou
walk-in.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

walk-in.title: Julian Assange
walk-in.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

walk-in.title: Vault 7
walk-in.summary: The 2017 WikiLeaks disclosure of thousands of pages of CIA Directorate of Science and Technology documents — leaked by agency engineer Joshua Schulte — revealing CIA technical capabilities including remote takeover of internet-connected cars, conversion of smart-TV speakers into covert microphones, and the planting of Russian or Persian language fragments in foreign systems to mislead attribution.

walk-in.title: CIA–FBI interagency rivalry and 9/11
walk-in.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the historical CIA–FBI rivalry, dating to J. Edgar Hoover's opposition to the 1947 National Security Act, and how it manifested before September 11 when Cofer Black's Counterterrorism Center withheld from the FBI that hijackers Nawaf al-Hazmi and Khalid al-Mihdhar had been granted U.S. visas.

walk-in.title: DARPA LifeLog
walk-in.summary: A Pentagon research program meant to track every email, photo, location and purchase of a person; John Kiriakou notes it was killed on February 4, 2004 — one day before Mark Zuckerberg filed the Facebook LLC.

walling.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
walling.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

walling.title: Cold cell
walling.summary: A CIA interrogation technique in which a stripped detainee is chained to a ceiling eyebolt in a cell chilled to 50°F, then doused with a bucket of ice water at hourly intervals; never authorized; documented to have killed at least two prisoners.

walling.title: Sleep deprivation
walling.summary: A CIA interrogation technique used against high-value detainees post-9/11; the agency was authorized to deny prisoners sleep for up to 12 days continuously; people died; at least one detainee was rendered permanently clinically insane.

walling.title: Mitchell and Jessen
walling.summary: The two American psychologists who pitched the CIA's enhanced interrogation program to Director George Tenet at a cocktail party in late October 2001; designers of the program and its theoretical underpinning, "learned helplessness."

walling.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
walling.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

walling.title: Muhammad Atar
walling.summary: Nephew of Khalid Sheikh Mohammed; subjected by the CIA to the walling interrogation technique against a concrete-block wall without protective equipment, producing permanent brain damage that has prevented him from participating in his own defense.

walter-pincus.title: Kill the Messenger (Gary Webb)
walter-pincus.summary: The 2014 film about journalist Gary Webb, on which John Kiriakou served as script advisor; when Kiriakou was arrested in January 2012, the FBI seized his electronics, including a draft of the unclassified Hollywood script, and stamped every page "top secret" despite Kiriakou having no role in writing it.

walter-pincus.title: Dark Alliance
walter-pincus.summary: Gary Webb's seven-part San Jose Mercury News investigation reporting that cocaine reaching Los Angeles and fuelling the crack epidemic had travelled through Nicaragua with the CIA's knowledge. John Kiriakou's account stresses what Webb did and did not claim — that the agency turned a blind eye rather than ran the operation — and that three separate federal investigations later found his reporting correct.

walter-pincus.title: CIA Drug Facilitation
walter-pincus.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the CIA''s reported involvement in facilitating the arrival of cocaine into the United States during the era that became the crack epidemic, and his own firsthand discovery — as a Senate Foreign Relations Committee investigator — that under American military control Afghanistan produced 93% of the world''s heroin. A DEA contact told him the report would never be published because ''we want Iran and Russia to be addicted to heroin. It weakens their societies.'' Kiriakou draws a direct parallel to the current fentanyl crisis: China is doing to the US what the US did to Iran and Russia.

walter-pincus.title: Contra rebels
walter-pincus.summary: The right-wing Nicaraguan insurgency armed by the Reagan administration against the Sandinista government. In John Kiriakou's account they were conservatives, right-wingers, in some cases fascists, and disgruntled military officers; they were split into a northern group the United States armed and a southern group that financed itself by selling cocaine — a distinction that became the pivot of the Gary Webb affair.

walter-pincus.title: Oscar Blandón
walter-pincus.summary: The senior Contra leader whom Gary Webb's reporting identified as running the cocaine operation that moved product from Nicaragua to Los Angeles, and one of two men named in the Dark Alliance series.

walter-pincus.title: Domino theory
walter-pincus.summary: The Cold War doctrine, described by John Kiriakou as Ronald Reagan's organising obsession in Central America, holding that if one country there fell to communism the rest would fall in sequence up to the American border — the stated rationale for backing the Contra rebels against the Sandinistas.

washington-political-culture.title: Butler rally shooting
washington-political-culture.summary: The July 2024 attempt on Donald Trump's life at a rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, on which John Kiriakou takes no position as to who was responsible but argues the published facts cannot be reconciled with a competent Secret Service — and that the questions it leaves open are owed an answer for the historical record whether or not anyone alive gets one.

washington-political-culture.title: Charlie Kirk shooting
washington-political-culture.summary: Kiriakou questions the official account: a court filing says the ATF could not match the autopsy bullet to the rifle tied to the suspect.

washington-political-culture.title: Advanced Counterterrorism Operations
washington-political-culture.summary: The six-week specialist course at CIA headquarters that John Kiriakou attended roughly eighteen months before 9/11 as one of fourteen officers selected worldwide — weapons, explosives, counterterrorist and desert driving, bugs, cameras, satellites and drones — and which, by accident of timing, meant a cadre was trained and able to deploy the moment the attacks came.

washington-political-culture.title: Anwar al-Awlaki
washington-political-culture.summary: American-born al-Qaeda propagandist; in 1993 the imam of the Falls Church, Virginia mosque visited by John Kiriakou's CIA Arabic-language class on a field trip; in 2001 the cleric at whose mosque the 9/11 hijackers prayed the night before the attacks; killed by U.S. drone strike in Yemen in approximately 2011.

washington-political-culture.title: CIA directorates
washington-political-culture.summary: The four-part internal division of the CIA as John Kiriakou describes it to lay audiences — the Directorate of Intelligence that analyses, the Directorate of Operations that recruits spies and steals secrets, the administrative arm that makes the trains run on time, and the Directorate of Science and Technology that supplies the scientists, forgers and disguise makers — the structure that determines which training a new officer receives.

washington-political-culture.title: CIA liaison relationships
washington-political-culture.summary: John Kiriakou's critique of CIA intelligence-liaison relationships with foreign governments — sharply expanded after 9/11 — arguing that officers do not consider the long-term risk that disclosing sensitive operations to foreign services hands those governments leverage, including potential blackmail material, over the United States, and that no one left in Congress has the will to provide real oversight of the practice.

watching-naval-movements.title: Veteran Intelligence Professionals for Sanity
watching-naval-movements.summary: A group of former U.S. intelligence officials, of which John Kiriakou is a member, that issues the Sam Adams Award for Integrity in Intelligence — which Kiriakou arranged to give to whistleblower-adjacent figure Joe Kent.

watching-naval-movements.title: Joe Kent
watching-naval-movements.summary: Kiriakou on the former counterterrorism director he gave an award to, publicly opposed for a nomination, and has never actually spoken to.

watching-naval-movements.title: Bill Clinton
watching-naval-movements.summary: 42nd U.S. president whom John Kiriakou describes as wholly disinterested in intelligence — briefed by the CIA only twice in eight years, with Vice President Al Gore taking the daily briefing instead and relaying anything important.

watching-naval-movements.title: Bill Richardson
watching-naval-movements.summary: U.S. Congressman, Ambassador to the United Nations, Secretary of Energy, and Governor of New Mexico; became friends with John Kiriakou at McClarty Associates; promised Secretary of State in exchange for endorsing Barack Obama in the 2008 Democratic primary; ultimately offered Commerce instead, then CIA director informally, before withdrawing his Commerce nomination.

watching-naval-movements.title: FISA court
watching-naval-movements.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the secret Foreign Intelligence Surveillance court — created under Carter, sitting atop the Justice Department, issuing warrants that are never public — which he says was abused against Carter Page as part of what he believes was John Brennan's plan to deny Trump the presidency.

watching-naval-movements.title: John Kerry
watching-naval-movements.summary: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts; chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee during John Kiriakou's 2009 service as the committee's senior investigator; subsequently U.S. Secretary of State; characterized by Kiriakou as a coward who buckled under CIA pressure on the Dasht-i-Leili reopening and as personally fixated on his perceived theft of the Secretary of State position by Hillary Clinton; the famously thrown medals were duplicates purchased at the post exchange.

waterboarding.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
waterboarding.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

waterboarding.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
waterboarding.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

waterboarding.title: Cold cell
waterboarding.summary: A CIA interrogation technique in which a stripped detainee is chained to a ceiling eyebolt in a cell chilled to 50°F, then doused with a bucket of ice water at hourly intervals; never authorized; documented to have killed at least two prisoners.

waterboarding.title: Christopher Hitchens
waterboarding.summary: British-American journalist and author who, at John Kiriakou's telling, famously argued in the mid-2000s that CIA waterboarding was 'nothing … not a big deal,' agreed in 2008 to undergo a filmed waterboarding demonstration, tapped out after roughly seventeen seconds, and thereafter suffered panic attacks for the rest of his life whenever he could not breathe for a moment.

waterboarding.title: Learned Helplessness
waterboarding.summary: Psychological concept adapted by the CIA as the theoretical basis for its post-9/11 enhanced interrogation program; per John Kiriakou, the goal of techniques including waterboarding was not primarily to elicit specific information but to render the prisoner so terrified of his captors that he would volunteer confessions on demand — a state of complete psychological collapse in which the prisoner loses any sense of agency or resistance.

waterboarding.title: Federal Torture Act
waterboarding.summary: United States statute criminalizing torture; per John Kiriakou, on the books since at least 1946, with concrete enforcement history — after World War II the United States executed Japanese soldiers convicted of waterboarding American prisoners of war, meaning waterboarding was at that time a capital offense under U.S. law. The act was effectively set aside for the CIA's enhanced interrogation program after 2002.

watergate.title: Code Pink
watergate.summary: The women-led peace group co-founded by Medea Benjamin. John Kiriakou first saw them as a Senate staffer — a room full of pink t-shirts at a hearing he'd organized for Senator Kerry, where he was caught smiling at their chants and told to keep his opinions to himself. When he was arrested, Code Pink "was right there next to me," threw his going-away party before prison, ran the sustained call campaign that helped stop his diesel-therapy transfer, stood with him through the 2019 Venezuelan embassy siege — and after prison he volunteered as coordinator of Code Pink Congress.

watergate.title: Kiriakou's transfer to the Directorate of Operations
watergate.summary: John Kiriakou's roughly two-month internal campaign to transfer from the CIA's analytic Directorate of Intelligence to the operational Directorate of Operations, overcoming what he calls a "natural bias in operations against the eggheads on the analytic side," followed by an Athens posting secured because he was the only person in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic. Covers his full CIA career arc from 1988/1990 recruitment through analyst years on Iraq, the switch to operations, 9/11, the enhanced-interrogation refusal, executive assistant to the deputy director for operations, and his eventual resignation and post-CIA career.

watergate.title: Daniel Ellsberg
watergate.summary: The Pentagon Papers whistleblower Kiriakou calls 'the Godfather of all national security whistleblowers' — and one of the great mentors of his life.

watergate.title: Espionage Act
watergate.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

watergate.title: Bureau of Prisons
watergate.summary: The federal agency that ran John Kiriakou's incarceration — and one of his most persistent post-prison targets. The BOP overrode his judge's camp recommendation by deeming him "a threat to the public safety," threatened him with "diesel therapy" until 1,600 logged phone calls and letters from a dozen House members and two senators backed it off, and, per Kiriakou, functions as "an employment agency for unemployable semi-literate rural white men" and "a dumping ground for failed medical professionals" — an agency for which a prisoner's death is cheaper than his treatment.

watergate.title: Dianne Feinstein
watergate.summary: Longtime Democratic U.S. senator from California and Senate Intelligence Committee chair; per John Kiriakou, one of the greatest disappointments on Capitol Hill — fully bought into the intelligence community even after CIA director John Brennan called her a liar over the committee's finding that the CIA had monitored Senate investigators, a finding that proved true.

watermark.title: Fort Gordon
watermark.summary: The U.S. Army installation in Georgia where NSA whistleblower Reality Winner, interviewed on Kiriakou's show, worked as a contractor linguist before her arrest.

watermark.title: Miranda Rights
watermark.summary: Reality Winner, interviewed on Kiriakou's show, says she was never read her Miranda rights during her 2017 arrest by the FBI.

watermark.title: Terry Aubry
watermark.summary: Named by Kiriakou both as an FBI whistleblower who exposed racism at the bureau and as one of two Intercept journalists who sent him to prison.

watermark.title: Afghan Languages
watermark.summary: The three major languages of Afghanistan — Pashto, Dari (a form of Persian), and Arabic — as discussed on John Kiriakou's show with NSA whistleblower and former military linguist Reality Winner.

watermark.title: Edward Snowden
watermark.summary: Former NSA contractor who in 2013 disclosed the scope of U.S. [mass surveillance](/wiki/mass-surveillance), including the Section 702 collection program. Per John Kiriakou — who counts Snowden among the small group of national-security whistleblowers prosecuted under the Espionage Act — Snowden was ''stuck between two awful slippery slopes'': breaking his oath and chain of command on one side, and on the other catching something ''cut and dry against the Constitution'' that no one would act on. Kiriakou notes Snowden could not use his chain of command (as Kiriakou could not, his own chain being Jose Rodriguez), and that Judge Leonie Brinkema had reserved the Snowden case for herself before he fled the country.

watermark.title: FBI Arrest Strategies
watermark.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the FBI deliberately times arrests for Thursdays or Friday evenings because no federal arraignments happen on Fridays, forcing detainees to spend the weekend in jail before facing a judge on Monday — a tactic he says he saw applied to January 6 defendants as well as to himself.

wealth-concentration.title: CIA intelligence failures
wealth-concentration.summary: John Kiriakou's standing position that the CIA has missed every major world event since its founding in 1947 — the building and the fall of the Berlin Wall, the collapse of the Soviet Union, the Iran hostage crisis, 9/11 — and that the remedy is therefore not more money but fewer overseas bases and actual accountability, of which he says there has been none.

wealth-concentration.title: 2028 presidential field
wealth-concentration.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of the wide-open 2028 presidential race — the first in his life, he says, where he has no idea who either party will nominate. Predictive markets were listing 44 Democrats and 26 Republicans as possible candidates. His own preferred candidate is Tucker Carlson, whom he says he has repeatedly begged to run; his working assumption about anyone who does want the job is that they are "a narcissist and probably a sociopath on top of it."

wealth-concentration.title: Amaryllis Fox Kennedy
wealth-concentration.summary: Former CIA non-official-cover officer who worked under commercial cover as an international art consultant, later a Trump campaign manager and nominee for deputy CIA director. Per John Kiriakou, Senator Tom Cotton threatened to filibuster her appointment; the president responded by naming her deputy national security adviser instead — a job Kiriakou considers more powerful, since the CIA director reports to the national security adviser.

wealth-concentration.title: Andrew Bustamante
wealth-concentration.summary: Former CIA officer who sells CIA-style training online; John Kiriakou identifies him as the lone critic of his work hosting a show on a Russian network, and argues Bustamante's training business — open to anyone who pays — is the more problematic of the two.

wealth-concentration.title: Angry Birds
wealth-concentration.summary: The mobile game John Kiriakou describes as his only vice besides buying art, played every morning for nine consecutive years and cited by his ex-wife as a grievance in their marriage.

wealth-concentration.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
wealth-concentration.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

welch-45.title: Revolutionary Organization 17 November
welch-45.summary: Greek far-left urban guerrilla group active 1975–2002; the deadliest terrorist organization in Greek history

welch-45.title: Stephen Saunders
welch-45.summary: British defense attaché in Athens assassinated by Revolutionary Organization 17 November in March 2000

welch-45.title: Richard Welch
welch-45.summary: CIA Athens station chief assassinated December 23, 1975; the first victim of [Revolutionary Organization 17 November](/wiki/revolutionary-organization-17-november)

welch-45.title: Carlos the Jackal
welch-45.summary: Venezuelan-born militant (Ilich Ramírez Sánchez) active in the 1970s and 1980s; per John Kiriakou, 'the Osama bin Laden of the 70s and 80s.' Kiriakou spent his Athens posting trying to identify the middleman linking Carlos to the Greek terrorist group 17 November, then six months working the lead with MI5 in London; Carlos was finally run down by CIA contractor Billy Waugh in a Khartoum vegetable market and captured in 1994.

welch-45.title: Gust Avrakotos
welch-45.summary: CIA case officer, John Kiriakou's operations mentor, and a central figure in Charlie Wilson's War — the prolific, divisive covert-war veteran Kiriakou credits as the greatest teacher of his adult life.

welch-45.title: Heather Saunders
welch-45.summary: Widow of British Brigadier General Stephen Saunders, the British defense attaché in Athens assassinated by Revolutionary Organization 17 November on April 22, 2000; per John Kiriakou, the person whose post-assassination Greek-television statement — "this organization is not a political organization nor is it a phantom group; it's a gang of criminals" — for the first time since 17 November's 1975 founding turned Greek public opinion against the group.

wesley-clark.title: Donald Trump
wesley-clark.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

wesley-clark.title: George Tenet
wesley-clark.summary: Director of Central Intelligence from 1997 to 2004, spanning the September 11 attacks and the early enhanced-interrogation program; identified by John Kiriakou as John Brennan's institutional patron at the agency; the figure who ordered the Five Eyes intelligence services to "open the files" to each other in the early 2000s.

wesley-clark.title: Iraq WMD intelligence
wesley-clark.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how the case for Iraqi weapons of mass destruction was fabricated: the intelligence community''s consensus was that Iraq had no WMD, but the White House had already decided to invade and sought analysis to fit the policy.

wesley-clark.title: Israeli Nuclear Program
wesley-clark.summary: Israel's widely assumed but officially unacknowledged nuclear arsenal; per John Kiriakou, the conventional wisdom within the CIA is that Israel possesses between 120 and 220 nuclear weapons, and the U.S. government's refusal to formally acknowledge this is driven by a specific legal obligation under the Glenn-Symington Act, which would require cutting off all foreign aid to any nuclear-armed country not party to the Non-Proliferation Treaty.

wesley-clark.title: John Kiriakou
wesley-clark.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

wesley-clark.title: Mary Margaret Graham
wesley-clark.summary: CIA Senior Intelligence Service officer and later Deputy Director of National Intelligence for Collection under John Negroponte — described by John Kiriakou as a career "reports officer" who had never personally recruited a source, and as his difficult chief of station in a later domestic assignment.

whispers-in-the-dirt-book.title: Kiriakou's writing process
whispers-in-the-dirt-book.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how he actually writes — books in waves over roughly nine months, op-eds in forty-five minutes to an hour once an idea has sat for a few days, and a habit of getting up at two in the morning to write one because he cannot sleep. He wrote *Remains of the Day* in six weeks during COVID, losing whole evenings to it: "I look at the clock again, it''s 2:00 in the morning. I''m like, oh my god, what happened?"
